# Multi-Product Engineering and Delivery Operating System

## Master Specification v4.0

**Status:** Canonical. This document supersedes the prior research documents (versions 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5) and incorporates the Lumiverse Engineering KRA/KPI workbook as current configuration. It is the single specification from which the operating system is built and operated. Changes to this specification follow its own platform-change process (Part VII).

**Identity:** This is the internal operating system for the founder's own company. It is not productised for third parties.

**Date:** 2026-08-26. **Amended 2026-08-27**, version unchanged: the pre-implementation self-consistency check (D81–D86) and the readiness audit (D87–D105) closed gaps in this document without reversing an invariant, invalidating an acceptance test or undoing an architectural decision. Appendix A records every amendment.

---

## How to Read This Document

The specification is organised into eleven parts:

| Part | Sections | Covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I — Foundations | 1–6 | Purpose, goals, the dynamic operating model, source of truth, unified terminology |
| II — Organisation and People Operations | 7–14 | Registries, capabilities, assignments, access, person lifecycles, succession, founder continuity |
| III — Products and Portfolio | 15–22 | Product contracts, ownership, lifecycle, shared services, customer commitments, support |
| IV — Change and Delivery | 23–34 | Review routing, gates, verification, evidence chain, CI/CD, deployment, migrations |
| V — AI Governance | 35–39 | AI runtimes, untrusted input, background machine layer, AI in the product, seat lifecycle |
| VI — Operations, Reliability and Security | 40–51 | Secrets, observability, incidents, security, backup/DR, degraded modes, cost, control plane |
| VII — Operating System Governance | 52–66 | OS health, reconciliation, exceptions, policies, debt, patterns, platform evolution, topology |
| VIII — Economics, Capacity and Forecasting | 67–73 | Attention economics, load model, capacity, utilisation, forecasting, staffing diagnosis |
| IX — People, Performance and Management Intelligence | 74–91 | Decision authority, performance framework, evidence, capability, access control, fairness |
| X — Views and Operating Rhythm | 92–94 | Dashboard architecture, the founder view, the daily operating picture |
| XI — Implementation | 95–104 | Bootstrap mode, brownfield transition, data conventions, phases, tests, invariants, edge cases |

Three reading paths:

* **The founder** reads Sections 1, 4, 14, 93 and 104, then Part IX when people questions arise.
* **The team lead** reads Parts I–IV in full, then Sections 52–66 and 92–94.
* **The implementer** (engineer or AI coding agent) reads everything, in order, and treats Section 99 (Build Surface) plus Section 98 (Phases) as the work plan.

Throughout the document, **real names and product names appear only in clearly labelled current-configuration snapshots**. The team can grow or shrink, people can come or go, products can launch, pause or be discontinued, and the KRA/KPI framework can be replaced entirely — none of that changes this architecture. Only configuration changes.

# Part I - Foundations

## Section 1. Purpose, Scope and North Star

### 1.1 Purpose

A software company of roughly nine people operates approximately eight products today and approximately twenty within roughly a year. It must do so without the founder becoming a coordinator, without the team lead becoming a review bottleneck, and without adopting metered tooling whose cost scales with usage. This document specifies the complete operating system for that company: how work is planned, built with AI assistance, verified, deployed to production, observed, recovered when it fails, governed as it evolves, and how the people who run it are understood, developed and supported — using only fixed-cost, self-hosted tooling for the engineering estate itself.

This is an internal operating system for the company's own use. It is not productised for third parties, and nothing in it is designed for external sale, multi-tenancy or external administration.

*Lineage note: this is Master Specification v4.0, consolidating prior research versions 3.3–3.5 and the engineering KRA/KPI workbook into a single specification. This note is the only place in the specification body that lineage appears; the front-matter status line and Appendix A record the same consolidation. Everywhere else, there is one specification, and changes to it follow its own platform-change process (Part VII).*

### 1.2 The two load-bearing ideas

**The first load-bearing idea is the verification contract.** A product that can prove its own health does not need a human watching it. A product that cannot needs a human watching it forever. Everything else in this specification — cross-review networks, planning horizons, immutable artifacts, the background machine layer, the evidence chain — exists to make that first condition achievable product by product.

**The second load-bearing idea is that the operating system is configuration-driven, versioned, reconciled and extensible.** When the company changes — people, roles, products, ownership, technology, AI provider, even the performance philosophy — configuration and contracts change, not the architecture. When the operating system itself changes, that change is versioned, impact-analysed, canaried, verified, rolled out gradually and reversible. Adding products, people, roles, capabilities, shared services, customers and technology stacks must increase configuration complexity, not architectural complexity.

### 1.3 The three questions the operating system answers

The specification answers three questions in sequence, and each depends on the one before it:

1. **How does this company build and ship software safely with a small team?** Registries, contracts, gates, the verification contract, immutable artifacts, and a background machine layer that produces volume without holding authority (Parts II–VI).
2. **How does the company operate, observe, evolve, govern and pay for the operating system over time without turning it into bureaucracy?** Observability of the operating system itself, a drift budget so that not all deviation screams equally, an exception registry where exceptions expire, a policy lifecycle so that rules can be retired, failure-pattern learning, human-attention economics, product load modelling, capacity forecasting, deterministic scenario planning, platform SLOs, and a change budget that protects the team from process churn (Parts VII–VIII). The test of success is not more automation; it is less human coordination per unit of verified output, measured rather than asserted.
3. **How does the company understand people capacity, bandwidth, workload, team health, capability, role performance and staffing needs — using evidence the operating system already produces — without turning that evidence into surveillance or into a single productivity score?** The people layer separates capacity, utilisation, bandwidth, workload, performance, capability, potential, team health and organisational constraint into distinct measurable concepts that are never collapsed. It maps the performance framework in force onto operating-system evidence, marking honestly where evidence exists, where instrumentation is required and where human judgment is irreplaceable. It produces management decision support — rebalance, coach, recognise, promote, develop, hire, formal review — with mandatory systemic-versus-individual diagnosis before any individual attribution. It refuses to make people decisions: every formal people decision in this system is made by the Founder (Part IX).

### 1.4 North Star

A small technical team operates a large and changing software portfolio with low coordination overhead, high verified output, strong production safety, distributed product knowledge, predictable cost, evidence-driven hiring, minimal founder intervention and continuous machine assistance — and the operating system becomes more capable over time without becoming more bureaucratic: able to see its own health, budget its own change, expire its own exceptions, retire its own policies, learn from its own failures, and prove — in attention hours rather than assertion — that it is worth what it costs.

The company changes. People join and leave. Roles appear and disappear. Products multiply. The performance framework is rewritten. Technology changes. Leadership structure evolves. The operating system does not need to be redesigned; only configuration, assignments, capability profiles, framework versions, product state and effective dates change.

The operating system must eventually answer all of the following without a status meeting:

* **Products** — which product needs attention, why, and whether the issue is engineering, reliability, business, or people and capacity.
* **Team** — how much capacity exists, how much bandwidth remains, whether utilisation is sustainable, who is overloaded, who is under-utilised, and where work and knowledge are concentrated.
* **People** — whether a person is succeeding in their role, what evidence supports that, what context explains the result, what capability they are developing, whether they need support, and whether they are ready for more responsibility.
* **Management** — whether to rebalance, coach, recognise, promote, change role, hire, engage a specialist, or begin a formal process.
* **Business** — whether people are allocated to the right products, whether human attention is going to the right places, which products deserve more engineering capacity, and which should enter maintenance or sunset.

The system never says "fire this person". It says "persistent performance concern requiring Founder review", and shows the evidence, the context and the confidence. The system never says "promote this person". It says "promotion candidate based on these sustained next-level indicators". The system never says "hire another QA because there are twenty products". It says "verification demand exceeds sustainable QA capacity for the calibrated sustained window after these alternatives were evaluated". The system provides the evidence and the context. The Team Lead operates engineering. The Founder decides.

The Monday-morning test: the Founder opens one private view and can answer, with evidence, context and confidence — do I need to change the team, change the allocation, change the roadmap, change the process, coach someone, recognise someone, promote someone, hire someone, or do nothing?

### 1.5 Audience and reading conventions

The intended audience is an implementation engineer or AI coding agent who will execute this specification, plus the team lead who will operate it daily and the founder who governs it. Where a capability depends on a platform tier or an unverified tool behaviour, it is labelled as an implementation dependency rather than asserted.

Every person name, product number and headcount figure in this document is an example or a clearly labelled current-configuration snapshot. The system enumerates people, roles, capabilities, assignments and products dynamically. Nothing in the architecture depends on there being three developers, one QA, one team lead, eight products or twenty.

## Section 2. Goals and Non-Goals

### 2.1 Business goals

| Goal | Metric |
| --- | --- |
| Operate approximately 20 products with 7–9 people | Products in portfolio ÷ headcount ≥ 2.2, subject to measured capacity |
| Remove the founder from daily coordination | Founder daily coordination time under 30 minutes; zero status meetings |
| Keep total tooling spend fixed and predictable | Zero metered tooling line items; monthly spend variance under 5% |
| Make product carrying cost fall as the portfolio grows | Median engineering hours per product per month declining quarter over quarter |
| Make hiring decisions evidence-driven | Every hire traced to a diagnosed constraint, not a symptom |
| Absorb organisational change without architectural change | Adding a product, a person, a role or a technology stack requires configuration and onboarding only, with zero changes to workflow or platform design |
| Make the operating system itself observable and self-governing | Operating-system health, drift, exception count and ritual cost measured; less human coordination per unit of verified output over time |
| Make people decisions rest on evidence in context | Every formal people decision supported by an evidence bundle with systemic-context adjustment; no decision made from a single score |

### 2.2 User goals

| Role | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Founder | Opens one dashboard and knows where to spend attention; opens one private view and knows what people decisions, if any, are needed |
| Team Lead | Plans across the three planning horizons instead of reacting to notifications |
| Developer | Always has a prepared next task; never asks "what now?" |
| Cross-Reviewer | Holds genuine working knowledge of the products they review, not shallow exposure to all of them |
| QA | Defines what proves a feature works before it is built, rather than testing after |
| New joiner | Becomes productive through cross-review before taking ownership, on a defined path |
| Temporary specialist | Receives exactly the access their scope requires, which expires without anyone remembering to remove it |

### 2.3 Non-goals

* **Not a product for third parties.** This operating system is internal to the company. It is not productised, licensed, or designed for external tenants; no requirement in this specification may be justified by a hypothetical external customer of the operating system itself.
* **Not building a custom internal developer portal.** Backstage-class platforms need roughly 2 FTE platform engineers and are not justified below roughly 300 engineers.
* **Not replacing human engineers with agents.** Agents amplify judgment; they do not hold it.
* **Not adopting any metered or usage-billed service for tooling.** Fixed cost is a hard constraint for the engineering tool estate, not a preference. This constraint applies to TOOLING — the systems the team uses to build and operate software. Metered inference inside a product, as product cost of goods sold, is a distinct category: permitted, budgeted and monitored under Section 38 (AI in the Product).
* **Not dependent on any named third-party system.** The designated work-management system and execution truth are the operating system's own boards and control-plane records. No workflow, gate, metric or KPI depends on Bitrix24 or on any other named external tool; any integration with such a system is an optional, registered external integration with a declared exit condition, and removing it changes nothing in the operating system. Tool independence is a tested property (Section 100, Acceptance Tests). It governs integrations; the one declared platform substrate — the git host, which is the enforcement plane itself — is exempt by the stated carve-out of Section 62.5, where the exit and loss disciplines that replace the independence test are defined.
* **Not building a second workflow overlay alongside GSD Core.** Two systems owning hooks, skills and state produce silent gate failures.
* **Not introducing Kubernetes, service meshes, or any infrastructure requiring a dedicated operator.**
* **Not creating a meeting-driven management model.** The system carries operational state; meetings carry judgment only.
* **Not building an HR system.** The People Registry is an operational identity and capability registry. The people layer holds operational people evidence; it does not hold payroll, attendance systems, medical information, psychological profiling or automated disciplinary machinery.
* **Not building a graph database for dependency analysis.** The relationships are declared; impact calculation starts as a query over declarations and grows only if it must.
* **Not a management reporting layer.** Every metric has a named owner and a defined action when it breaches; metrics with no action are removed at review.
* **Not surveillance, not a leaderboard, not an automated decision engine.** The people layer produces no ranking of people by output, has no authority to promote, demote, warn or terminate, and does not infer wellbeing or internal states. Formal people decisions are the Founder's alone (Section 74, People Decision Authority).
* **Not an AI decision-maker for the operating system itself.** Forecasting and scenario modelling begin as deterministic arithmetic over existing metrics. A model may later improve a projection; no gate, decision or alert may depend on one.
* **Not an enterprise operating model.** Domains, second Team Leads and specialist groups are defined as dormant capabilities with explicit activation triggers, not as structures to adopt now (Section 66).

## Section 3. User Stories

### 3.1 Founder — portfolio and operations

* As the founder, I want to open one dashboard on Monday and see which products need attention, so that I do not have to ask anyone for status.
* As the founder, I want to know what is currently limiting throughput — review, verification, planning, architecture, capacity, priority, or my own decision latency — so that I hire against a diagnosed cause rather than a symptom.
* As the founder, I want to change portfolio priority without rearranging individual developer tasks, so that the team lead translates strategy into sequencing.
* As the founder, I want production reliability and business health visible in the same place as delivery metrics, so that I do not build an excellent engineering machine for products nobody uses.
* As the founder, I want to be informed of SEV-1 incidents without becoming the incident dispatcher.
* As the founder, I want engineering to continue while I am unreachable, so that my absence is not a company outage.
* As the founder, I want to know which responsibilities became orphaned when someone left, before a customer discovers it.

### 3.2 Founder — people and capacity

* As the founder, I want to know how much capacity the team actually has, how much is committed and to what kind of work, and how much safe bandwidth remains, so that commitments are made against evidence rather than optimism.
* As the founder, I want to see who is overloaded, who is under-utilised, and why — with the systemic context that explains it — so that I never attribute a system problem to a person.
* As the founder, I want to see where work, review, incident load and knowledge are concentrated, so that I can remediate dependency risk before a departure exposes it.
* As the founder, I want to know whether a person is succeeding in their role, on the evidence, in context, so that reviews are grounded in what actually happened rather than recollection.
* As the founder, I want to see what capability is developing and where the gaps are, so that growth and succession are planned rather than improvised.
* As the founder, I want the system to tell me when someone may need support, recognition, more responsibility or a different role — as a decision prompt with evidence, never as a score or a ranking.
* As the founder, I want to know whether to rebalance, automate, reprioritise, delegate or hire — in that order — so that hiring is the last resort, not the first reflex.
* As the founder, I want to know which products are consuming human attention and whether that consumption is justified by the product's business position, so that portfolio decisions and people decisions inform each other.

### 3.3 Team Lead

* As the team lead, I want to plan across the three planning horizons — from today's committed work to next quarter's candidates — so that the team always has prepared work.
* As the team lead, I want routine pull requests to route away from me automatically, so that I am not interrupted by work that does not need my authority.
* As the team lead, I want plans rejected automatically when they cannot be verified, so that I approve intent rather than hunting for missing test coverage.
* As the team lead, I want my own capacity measured, so that the founder can see when the operating model needs adjusting rather than assuming I should work harder.
* As the team lead, I want to see which products depend on a single person's knowledge, so that I can remediate before someone leaves.
* As the team lead, I want to surge capacity onto a product temporarily without permanently restructuring ownership.
* As the team lead, I want a shared workflow change to show me which products it will affect before I roll it out.
* As the team lead, I want to hand over cleanly when I am away, so that plan approvals do not become a two-week queue.

### 3.4 Developer

* As a developer, I want a prepared next task waiting when I finish, so that I never lose half a day to planning.
* As a developer, I want to review products beyond the ones I own, so that I build real portfolio knowledge and can cover absence.
* As a developer, I want every product to have the same local setup commands, so that switching between products costs minutes rather than a day.
* As a developer, I want the plan checked for hallucinated functions and fake package names before I execute it, so that I am not debugging invented code.
* As a developer, I want to say "I do not understand this change well enough to approve it" without penalty, so that review remains honest.
* As a developer, I want to stop at the end of my working day with no evening obligation.
* As a developer, I want to change role without a week of manual permission edits across twenty repositories.

### 3.5 QA

* As QA, I want to define the verification contract before implementation starts, so that unprovable work is rejected at plan time.
* As QA, I want manual UAT steps versioned in git alongside the code, so that verification is reviewable and diffable rather than living in a spreadsheet.
* As QA, I want the background machine layer to draft test suites overnight, so that my role shifts from authoring to reviewing.
* As QA, I want production smoke tests separate from staging UAT, so that "it worked in staging" is never mistaken for "it works in production."
* As QA, I want to block a release on verification grounds without being asked to review code line by line.
* As QA, I want a new product to arrive with a verification skeleton already scaffolded, so that I author content rather than structure.

### 3.6 Machine

* As the background machine layer, I want a whitelist of safe task types and draft-PR-only authority, so that I can produce volume without holding any power to merge, approve or deploy.
* As the reconciliation job, I want to compare declared state against actual platform state continuously, so that drift is detected rather than discovered during an incident.

## Section 4. The Dynamic Operating Model

This section is foundational. Every later section depends on it. (Priority: P0)

### 4.1 The concept ladder

Seven concepts are kept strictly separate. Collapsing any two of them is what makes an operating system brittle when the company changes.

```
PERSON      — a human identity, independent of what they do
   ↓
ROLE        — the shape of their job
   ↓
CAPABILITY  — what they are authorised and competent to do
   ↓
ASSIGNMENT  — their relationship to a specific product, scoped and dated
   ↓
PRODUCT     — a business and operational unit
   ↓
REPOSITORY  — a technical implementation unit; a product may have several
   ↓
DEPENDENCY  — relationships between products, shared services and externals

PLATFORM VERSION — the version of the operating system itself,
                   independent of all the above
```

The people layer extends the same ladder without collapsing it. A person resolves to expectations through their role and the performance framework version in force, and to workload through assignments and a capacity profile:

```
Person → Role → Expectation Profile (from the framework in force) → Evidence → Performance Period
Person → Capability Profile → Assignments → Capacity Profile → Allocation
```

Performance expectations are never embedded in the person record. This is what makes a framework replacement a configuration change rather than a migration project.

### 4.2 The rule that follows

> When the company changes, configuration and contracts change. When the operating system itself changes, the change is versioned, impact-analysed, canaried, verified, rolled out and reversible.

A person may change role without any product needing to be restructured. A product may change owner without any person needing new tooling. A person may join, leave, change role, change products, gain capabilities, shed responsibilities, take a temporary assignment, become acting Team Lead, become Team Lead, move into QA, move into engineering, or become a specialist — none of these requires architectural change. All of them are registry operations with effective dates. That independence is the point.

### 4.3 Prohibited hard-coding

No architectural logic in this system may depend on: a specific person, a specific number of people, a specific product, a specific number of products, a specific technology stack, or a specific AI provider. Those appear only in examples and in current-state configuration.

Concretely, the implementation must contain no logic of the form:

* `if person == "<name>"`
* `if role_count == 1`
* `developers = [A, B, C]`
* any assumption of exactly one Team Lead, exactly one QA engineer, exactly one mobile engineer or exactly one specialist
* any assumption of a fixed number of people, products, KRAs or KPIs
* any dependency on a named third-party system such that removing that system would require changing the operating system (Section 62, Tool Register and Platform Exit)

Names appear in this specification only in clearly labelled current-configuration snapshots and illustrative worked examples. They are never schema entities and never branch conditions. Roles may have zero, one or many holders; a Role Profile must never contain a hard-coded person, a hard-coded product, or an assumption that exactly one person holds it.

### 4.4 Architecture versus configuration versus history

This distinction is binding on every implementation decision.

| Layer | Status | Changes how |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Operating-system architecture: concepts, separations, invariants, diagnosis rules, access model | Stable | Only through the platform-change process (Section 61), versioned, impact-analysed, canaried and reversible |
| Person records | Configuration | Registry entry, effective-dated |
| Role definitions and role profiles | Configuration | Registry entry, effective-dated |
| Capability definitions and maturity assessments | Configuration | Registry entry, effective-dated |
| Assignments and allocations | Configuration | Registry entry, effective-dated |
| Product contracts and dependency declarations | Configuration | Contract change, reviewed and reconciled |
| Performance framework: KRAs, KPIs, weights, targets, rating scale, review cadence | Configuration | New framework version with an effective date (Section 77) |
| Thresholds, sustainable-utilisation bands, confidence windows, drift budgets | Configuration | Calibration (Section 84) |
| Historical evidence, decisions, approvals and framework versions | Immutable | Never; append-only (Section 63) |

The operating consequence: the company changes — people join and leave, roles appear and disappear, products multiply, the performance philosophy is rewritten — and the architecture does not need redesign. Only configuration, assignments, capability profiles, framework versions, product state and effective dates change. Changing current configuration never overwrites history: a person who leaves has their record made inactive, not deleted; a retired KPI does not erase the periods it governed; who was assigned, when, to what, under which framework version, remains an immutable, access-controlled record.

### 4.5 Scaling requirements

The model must remain valid without architectural change at 7, 10, 15, 20, 30 and more people; at 8, 20, 30 and 50 or more products; and across topology changes:

```
Founder → Team Lead → Developers

then, when justified:

Founder → Team Lead A, Team Lead B → product domains
```

Domains are activated only when the delegation and second-Lead conditions in Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution) are met. Activating a domain is a configuration change: new role instance, new assignments, new capacity aggregation grouping. Nothing is rewritten.

### 4.6 Worked example

An example, not a specification:

```yaml
person: dev-a
role: developer
capabilities: [backend, frontend, code-review, production-approval]
assignments:
  - product: product-3
    type: primary_owner
  - product: product-7
    type: cross_reviewer

person: qa-1
role: qa
capabilities: [verification, uat, release-signoff]
assignments:
  - scope: portfolio
    type: verification_authority

person: lead-1
role: team_lead
capabilities: [architecture, plan-approval, escalation, production-approval]
assignments:
  - scope: portfolio
    type: portfolio_lead
```

## Section 5. Source of Truth Hierarchy

Made explicit so that no future implementer or agent invents ownership of information.

### 5.1 The hierarchy

```
GitHub
    code · pull requests · workflows · permissions · boards
    environments · deployment definitions

people.yaml + roles.yaml
    authoritative people, employment, capability and availability state

Leave records (control plane)
    authoritative working-calendar and approved-leave state —
    a load-bearing capacity input (Section 69)

product.yaml (assignments block) + service.yaml
    authoritative product relationship state — who owns, reviews,
    backs up and responds for what

product.yaml (remainder)
    the Product Operating Contract — lifecycle, environments,
    support model, recovery expectations, dependencies,
    business criticality, reliability criticality, commitments,
    data properties

topology.yaml
    authoritative organisational topology — domains, domain leads,
    escalation resolution (Section 66)

.planning/
    engineering reasoning · decisions · roadmap · current state

verification/
    verification truth — contract, automated tests, UAT, smoke,
    evaluation suites for AI-dependent products

CI/CD
    build and deployment truth — artifact digests, SBOMs,
    deploy records, approval records

platform.yaml
    authoritative operating-system version, supported contract
    versions, workflow versions, canary set

changes/*.yaml
    authoritative state of cross-product and platform changes

Records stores (records repository, append-only)
    canonical operational records — incidents, postmortems,
    UAT results, estimates-vs-actuals, deployment records,
    decisions, demo records (Section 97). Held in their own
    repository, not the control-plane repository, so that the
    machine credential which writes them reaches no registry
    (Section 40.1, D89)

Layer B people-intelligence stores (separately credentialed)
    capability maturity, capacity profiles, performance framework
    registry, performance periods, evidence bundles, management
    decisions (Sections 89 and 90) — never present in the general
    engineering datasource

Grafana / Prometheus / DevLake
    derived engineering and operational metrics

Business and customer systems
    business truth — customers, revenue, support load, usage
```

### 5.2 Rules

* No single artifact becomes a dumping ground. A registry-of-files table (Section 52) lists every control-plane artifact with its owner and purpose; any proposed new artifact must state which existing file cannot hold it.
* Derived metrics are never edited by hand. If a value can be computed from GitHub, CI, DevLake, Grafana or the registries, it is computed. Human input is reserved for genuine judgment — a policy's purpose, an exception's reason, a debt item's business impact.
* Metrics derive from the records stores and platform telemetry, never from hand-maintained numbers (Section 97).
* Business truth does not live in the product contract beyond the small set of fields needed for prioritisation.
* Sensitive people data never enters the general engineering datasource. Layer B stores are separately credentialed and access-controlled (Section 90).
* **Where two sources appear to disagree, this hierarchy resolves it, and reconciliation repairs the loser** (Section 53).

## Section 6. Unified Terminology and Glossary

One specification, one vocabulary. This section fixes the meaning of every term that could otherwise drift, and every later section uses these meanings without redefining them.

### 6.1 The two criticality fields

Every product contract carries two independent criticality fields. Every rule elsewhere in this specification that depends on "criticality" names which of the two it reads; an unqualified "criticality" is a specification defect.

| Field | Meaning | Read by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `business.criticality` | Business importance of the product | Portfolio economics and product load justification (Section 68); lifecycle and exit decisions (Section 18); investment and prioritisation decisions (Section 59); founder attention ranking (Section 93) |
| `classification.reliability_criticality` | Operational stringency the product must be run at | Canary set selection (Section 61); verification depth and required performance verification (Section 31); migration patterns (Section 34); manual-rollback requirement during platform outages (Section 46); restore-test cadence tightening (Section 44); monitoring depth (Section 41); incident severity inheritance (Section 42) and incident reserve (Section 69) |

The two are independent by design: a revenue-critical product may be operationally simple, and an internal service may be operationally critical. `reliability_criticality` may only tighten operational requirements relative to the portfolio floor, never loosen them. The two-field rule governs product criticality only; `tools.yaml.criticality` is a separate tool-register field with its own enumeration, defined in Section 62.1.

### 6.2 The three senses of "attention"

Three distinct concepts, named distinctly and never interchanged:

| Term | Meaning | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Attention Ranking** | *Where to look*: the ordered ranking of products (and of operating-system signals) by need for human attention — Healthy / Watch / Action Required at product level | A triage ordering on dashboards (Sections 92–93). Never a measure of effort spent |
| **Attention Hours** | *Measured effort*: the human attention hour, the unit of the attention ledger and of capacity, utilisation and product-load accounting | A measured quantity, derived per the category derivation rules (Section 67), using the single eight-category taxonomy in 6.6 |
| **Management Attention** | *Intervention burden*: how much management intervention a person currently requires — unblock requests, clarification, follow-up, review escalations, rework, ownership reminders | A diagnostic-only signal (Section 86). It is never a performance score, never displayed as one, and feeds exactly one decision use: diagnosis of autonomy, role readiness, onboarding need, requirement clarity, management burden or role mismatch. Founder-only when concerning an identified individual |

A sentence such as "attention allocation" is prohibited without qualification; write "attention ranking" or "attention hours".

### 6.3 The enumerated health surfaces

"Health" is not one number anywhere in this specification. The complete set of health surfaces is enumerated here; no other health surface exists, and composite scores are prohibited on all of them.

| Surface | Structure | Defined in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product health | Four independently reported dimensions: Engineering, Reliability, Business, People/Capacity. Never combined into a composite | Section 92 |
| Product operational health | The product's own `/health` and verification evidence — the product proving itself | Sections 31–32 |
| Operating-system health | One signal table, single ID space SIG-01 onwards, each signal with exactly one owner and one drift class per declared state (6.7); headline state Healthy / Degrading / Impaired as a triage entry point, not a score, always naming its top contributing signals | Section 52 |
| Knowledge health | Distribution and depth of product knowledge across people; feeds succession and dependency risk | Sections 82 and 87 |
| Team health | Team-level capacity, utilisation, reserve and quality signals — always aggregate, never a person ranking | Sections 70–71 |
| Individual workload health | Per-person workload classification across the six states of Section 83.2 (Healthy / Busy / Overloaded / Unsustainable / Underutilised / Blocked), visible only inside Layer B | Section 83 |
| People operating health | The people layer's own instrument health — signal confidence, instrumentation coverage, calibration state | Sections 79 and 84 |

Composite scores are prohibited everywhere: for products, for people, and for the operating-system drill-down. A surface that cannot name which dimension or signal is driving its state is defective.

### 6.4 Person availability versus calendar and leave

Two formerly colliding uses of "availability" are separated:

* **`availability` on the person record** is a lifecycle state: `active | on_leave | departing | departed`. It answers "is this person operationally present?" and drives access reconciliation (Section 7).
* **Working calendar and approved leave** live in the leave records in the control plane — the declared source of truth for time-based capacity (Section 69), with approval authority held by the Founder or a named delegate per the decision matrices (Section 85). The same records carry the **company working calendar**: the operating timezone, the standard working days, the core-hours window, and the public-holiday list per location — the holiday input 6.5 already treats as mandatory. Every business-day, working-hour and wall-clock rule in this specification — the Friday freeze (Section 34.2), the background-layer hard stop (Section 37), support response targets (22.4), drift response times (53.4) and the worst-case undetected window (42.2) — resolves against that calendar in the declared operating timezone, never against whatever timezone a runner happens to hold. Leave records are a load-bearing capacity input; they are never inferred from activity.

A person record never stores calendar detail, and leave records never store lifecycle state. `availability` names the lifecycle state and nothing else: the Team Lead's three-state allocation field is `allocation_state` (Section 90.5), which reads the lifecycle state as an input rather than being it.

### 6.5 Capacity, utilisation, bandwidth, workload

Four concepts, never collapsed (Part VIII defines each fully):

* **Capacity** — the realistically available productive attention a person or team can provide in a defined period, after working schedule, approved leave, public holidays and standing obligations. An input, measured in attention hours.
* **Utilisation** — how much of that capacity is currently consumed, and by what category of work (the taxonomy in 6.6). A composition, not a score.
* **Remaining safe bandwidth** — the capacity a person or team can accept without breaching sustainable utilisation or exhausting operational reserve. The number commitments are made against.
* **Workload** — what a specific person is actually carrying: its volume, composition, concentration and trajectory. Classified for health (Section 83), never ranked.

**Sustainable utilisation** is the calibrated band within which the team can absorb incidents, review, verification and learning indefinitely; continuous maximum utilisation is a fragility signal, not an achievement. Every "sustained" threshold in this specification (overload, staffing, under-utilisation) is calibrated configuration with an initial value of 6 consecutive weeks.

### 6.6 The attention and utilisation taxonomy

One taxonomy, eight categories, used identically by the attention ledger, the utilisation composition and the product load model:

Engineering · Review · Verification · Planning · Architecture · Incident · Operational · Coordination

Any entry may additionally carry an **unplanned** flag: work that entered the current horizon (H1) without preparation in the weekly horizon (H2). "Founder coordination time" is defined as Coordination-category hours attributed to the Founder. No second taxonomy may be introduced; a new category is a calibrated configuration change to this one.

### 6.7 The drift severity scale

One scale for all drift, everywhere:

* **Drift classes:** Green, Amber, Red, Blocking.
* **Reconciliation response levels:** Level 1 Detect, Level 2 Warn, Level 3 Auto-repair, Level 4 Block, Level 5 Escalate.

Every operating-system health signal (Section 52) declares exactly one drift class per declared state, and every declared state names a class from this scale: a graded signal (6.8) declares a warn state and a breach state, and the class on breach is what the drift budget counts. A signal row in `os-health.yaml` whose class cell names anything other than Green, Amber, Red or Blocking fails control-plane CI validation. The drift budget (Section 53) is expressed in these classes. The older vocabulary — "dangerous", "correctable", "informational" — is retired; its one-time retirement mapping is stated in Section 53. Auto-repair may only move actual state toward declared state, never loosen declared state to match actuality.

### 6.8 Bottleneck and overload signals

Where a person-shaped constraint appears in operating-system health, it is one graded signal, not several: Team Lead bottleneck/overload is a single signal with graded Amber and Red states, and QA bottleneck/overload likewise (Section 52). "Reviewer imbalance" and "review concentration" are one signal: review concentration. The bottleneck taxonomy used for throughput diagnosis has seven categories: review, verification, planning, architecture, engineering capacity, product priority, and Founder-decision latency (Section 73).

### 6.9 "Shipped"

Merge is not release. A change is **shipped** only when all of the following are true:

* Pull request merged
* Artifact built and digest recorded
* Deployed to the target environment
* Deployment reported success
* Smoke tests passed
* Production version recorded and matching the intended digest
* Health checks green
* `STATE.md` updated

Merged and deployed are tracked as separate metrics. Without this split, delivery data measures merge activity rather than delivery. Every use of "shipped" and "verified output" in this specification means this definition (Sections 27, 32, 34). "Delivered" carries this definition wherever it qualifies a change, a release or engineering output — including the framework KPI targets of Section 78, whose evidence sources are bound separately in Section 79.2. Where its object is not engineering output — a customer data export (Section 18), a push event routed to a messaging channel (Section 92.11), a generated self-view document (Section 90.6) — it carries its ordinary sense. The strict sense exists because delivery data otherwise measures merge activity; it is not a claim about the word.

### 6.10 The designated work-management system

The **designated work-management system** is the operating system's own execution-truth boards and control-plane records — the GitHub boards and records stores defined in Sections 29 and 97. Every performance-framework KPI and every operational rule that references a work-management system references this designated system. No named third-party tool is the designated system; any integration with one is optional, registered, and carries a declared exit condition (Section 62).

### 6.11 Layers A and B

* **Layer A** — the general engineering surfaces: dashboards, boards, records and datasources visible to the team. Layer A aggregates at product, team and portfolio level; it contains no per-person raw-activity drill-downs and no sensitive people data.
* **Layer B** — the access-controlled people-intelligence stores and the two distinct surfaces drawn from them (D110). **Layer B-M, the management surface**: a second, Founder-only Grafana instance carrying the separately credentialed people datasource (D75), holding every person's evidence and every comparative view. It is gated by the `people-intelligence` capability, which the Founder holds and which is **not delegable** (D109); its continuity path is the sealed contingency credential of Section 14.4, not a delegate. **Layer B-S, the self-view**: a generated, encrypted per-person document containing one person's own evidence and nothing else, delivered to the person it describes. A person reading their own self-view is not accessing Layer B-M and holds no capability; the two surfaces share a source and share nothing else — different audience, different access rule, different retention. Where this specification says "Layer B" without qualification it means Layer B-M (Sections 89–90).

### 6.12 Glossary of standing terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Control plane | The version-controlled repositories holding the declarations by which the company operates. The **control-plane repository** holds the registries, contracts, policies, exceptions and platform configuration, and admits no machine bypass actor. The **records repository** holds the append-only records and event stores, written by a scoped machine credential that reaches no registry (Section 40.1, D89). The Layer B people-data store and the sealed conduct store are separately credentialed stores outside both (Section 90) |
| Product Operating Contract | The `product.yaml` declaration of a product's lifecycle state, environments, support model, recovery expectations, dependencies, criticalities, commitments and data properties (Section 15) |
| Verification contract | The per-product declaration of what proves the product works — automated tests, UAT, smoke tests, evaluation suites — enforced at plan time and release time (Section 31) |
| Evidence chain | The unbroken record from approved plan to verified production state for every change (Section 32) |
| Change manifest | The declared scope, impact and rollout state of a cross-product or platform change (Section 25) |
| Exception registry | The single registry of expiring, owned exceptions to any policy or gate; an exception re-opened for the same scope after closure is a renewal, never a fresh entry (Section 54) |
| Break-glass | The audited emergency path that bypasses a gate under declared conditions, always leaving a record (Section 54) |
| Background machine layer | Scheduled AI agents with a whitelist of safe task types and draft-PR-only authority — volume without authority (Section 37) |
| GSD | The engineering workflow (plan, check, execute, verify) through which all planned work flows (Section 30) |
| Planning horizons | H1 current and committed / H2 ready-next and prepared / H3 future candidate (Section 29) |
| PLU | Product Load Unit — the weighted measure of how much human attention a product consumes; context for portfolio economics, never individual performance evidence (Section 68) |
| Performance framework | The versioned KRA/KPI configuration in force for people reviews; currently Framework v1, with the v1.1 edits approved and effective at people-tier registry activation (Sections 77–78) |
| Evidence bundle | The access-controlled, append-only package of role-specific evidence, context adjustment and confidence assembled for a Founder-owned review (Section 89) |
| Systemic context adjustment | The mandatory step that classifies variance as systemic or individual before any individual attribution (Section 80) |
| Drift budget | The tolerated volume of Green/Amber drift before escalation; Blocking drift has no budget (Section 53) |
| Reconciliation | The continuous comparison of declared state against actual platform state, with graded responses per 6.7 (Section 53) |
| Bootstrap Mode | The declared operating mode in which gates whose independence requirements exceed current headcount run under expiring, registered bootstrap exceptions (Section 95) |
| Pre-onboarding mode | The governed transitional mode for a brownfield product not yet fully onboarded: minimal ruleset, accepted risks, named deadline (Section 96) |
| Individual-metrics invariant | (a) Attention hours, utilisation, PLU and output volume are never individual performance evidence; (b) role-specific outcome and quality evidence may inform a Founder-owned review only with mandatory systemic context adjustment (Sections 80 and 91) |
