# Part II - Organisation and People Operations

The operating system treats people, roles, capabilities and assignments as four separate registries, because they change at four different speeds. A person's identity is stable for years; their role changes occasionally; their capabilities change deliberately; their assignments change routinely. Collapsing these into one structure is what makes small companies brittle - every personnel change becomes a restructuring. Keeping them separate is what allows a nine-person company to run twenty products: temporary capacity, delegation, succession and departure all become registry edits plus reconciliation, never hand-surgery across repositories. Every authority decision anywhere in this specification is evaluated against these registries, and against nothing else.

## Section 7. People Registry

**Priority: P0.**

A single declarative file in the control-plane repository, version-controlled and CI-validated. Not an HR system - an operational identity and capability registry.

```yaml
# people.yaml — control-plane repository
registry_version: 1

people:
  - id: dev-a                       # stable identifier, never reused
    display_name: "Example Developer A"
    github_login: exampledev-a
    role: developer
    employment_type: employee       # employee | contractor | intern
                                    # | temporary_specialist | consultant
    capabilities:
      - backend
      - frontend
      - code-review
      - production-approval
    ai_runtime: claude-code         # from the approved runtime list
    availability: active            # active | on_leave | departing | departed
    access_status: provisioned      # pending | provisioned | suspended | revoked
    work_arrangement:               # the declared working calendar — see 7.3
      timezone: Asia/Kolkata        # IANA identifier, never a UTC offset
      arrangement: hybrid           # onsite | hybrid | remote
      schedule:                     # per weekday; omit a day to declare it non-working
        mon: { start: "09:30", end: "18:30" }
        tue: { start: "09:30", end: "18:30" }
        wed: { start: "09:30", end: "18:30" }
        thu: { start: "09:30", end: "18:30" }
        fri: { start: "09:30", end: "18:30" }
      fte: 1.0                      # 0 < fte <= 1; part-time is configuration
      public_holiday_set: IN        # the calendar its non-working days come from
      accepted_coverage_window: null # only where this person is on a declared
                                    # rota (Section 15.6); null means they are not
    start_date: 2025-03-01
    end_date: null                  # required for non-employees

  - id: sec-1
    display_name: "Example Security Specialist"
    github_login: examplesec-1
    role: specialist
    employment_type: temporary_specialist
    capabilities:
      - security-review
    ai_runtime: null
    availability: active
    access_status: provisioned
    start_date: 2026-04-01
    end_date: 2026-06-30            # access expires automatically
    scope:
      products: [product-4, product-9]
      repositories_only: true       # no ownership, no production authority
```

### 7.1 Registry rules

* **Employment types are open-ended.** New types may be added without redesigning anything, because authority derives from capability, not from employment type.
* `end_date` **is mandatory for every non-employee.** A CI check fails if a contractor, intern, temporary specialist or consultant has a null end date. Expired access is revoked by the reconciliation job, not by someone remembering.
* **Departure is a state, not a deletion.** A departed person's record is retained with `availability: departed` and `access_status: revoked` so that historical evidence - who approved what, who reviewed what - remains interpretable. Their identifier is never reused.
* **`availability` and `access_status` are two enums on one record, and not every pairing is legal.** CI validates the combination and rejects the rest: `departed` implies `revoked`; `revoked` implies `departed` or a non-employee past `end_date`; `suspended` is valid only with `active` or `on_leave`. Both fields are eligibility inputs to review routing (Section 23.2) and recomputation triggers for the capacity profile (Section 69.3). Left unconstrained, a person suspended mid-incident keeps `availability: active`, stays an eligible Gate 2 reviewer and keeps contributing full net planning capacity to forecasts the Team Lead allocates against — planned around for hours that cannot be worked and routed reviews that cannot be approved, with nothing raised, because the one existing guard fires only for recorded leave.
* `ai_runtime` **is a declaration, not a coupling.** It records which approved runtime this person uses (Section 35, AI Runtime Contract) so that a provider outage can be scoped. Changing it changes nothing else.
* **New people enter at minimum authority.** A new entry defaults to no production access, no environment access, no `production-approval` and no dangerous capabilities. Capabilities are granted individually and explicitly, never inherited silently from a role default. Where a value is missing or malformed, the resolution is denial, not a default that permits (Section 64, Safe Defaults and Fail-Closed Classification).
* `access_status: suspended` exists as a first-class state so that access can be halted without deleting anything - used during a security incident (Section 43) and during a conduct investigation (Section 88).
* **Suspension has a defined way out.** `suspended → provisioned` requires a recorded reinstatement decision citing the evidence that closed the matter, decided by the escalation role on the security path (Section 43.2, containment authority) and by the Founder on the conduct path (Section 88.4); re-provisioning runs through the normal reconciliation path. `suspended → revoked` is the termination outcome and follows the exit lifecycle of Section 12.2. Every suspension carries a mandatory **review-by date** - **calibrated configuration**; initial value 10 working days from suspension, recalibrated from measured investigation durations - and an unreviewed suspension past that date is Red drift. Every other held state in this system is dated; suspension is the one the system reaches for under time pressure, and the failure mode it invites is becoming permanent by inaction.

### 7.2 Leave and calendar

Planned absence is operational data, not private calendar trivia - it is a load-bearing input to capacity (Sections 69-72) and to review-routing feasibility (Section 23).

* **Leave records in the control-plane repository are the declared source of truth for planned absence.** Each record names the person, the period, the type (leave, travel, reduced availability) and the approver.
* **Approval authority for leave is the Founder or a named delegate**, recorded in the decision matrices (Section 85, Decision Matrices and the Performance Concern Protocol).
* `availability` in `people.yaml` reflects the current operational state; reconciliation (Section 53) transitions it against the leave records - `on_leave` when a leave period starts, back to `active` when it ends - so that dashboards, capacity forecasts and reviewer availability never depend on someone remembering to flip a flag.
* Leave records feed the capacity profile (Section 69) and the weekly operating picture (Section 94). A review or approval routed to a person on recorded leave is a drift finding, not a surprise.

### 7.3 Work arrangement — the declared working calendar

Several rules across this specification read "the person's declared working calendar" as though it existed: capacity is computed after "working schedule for the period" (Section 69.1), the Capacity Profile lists scheduled availability as a declared field sourced from a working calendar (Section 69.2), and the day plan applies core hours "per each person's declared working calendar, with one to two hours of personal flex; part-time schedules are configuration, not exceptions" (Section 94.2). No section defined it, and no control-plane file held it. The `work_arrangement` block above is that calendar (D111).

Rules, binding:

* **Leave and schedule are different declarations and neither substitutes for the other.** The working calendar says which hours a person works in an ordinary week; leave records (7.2) say which of those hours they are absent for. Capacity is the first net of the second. A system holding only leave cannot tell a part-time week from a week of absence, and would price them identically.
* **Timezone is an IANA identifier, never a UTC offset**, because offsets move twice a year in some jurisdictions and the response targets that read them do not. Every time-bounded obligation resolves against the *person's* timezone where it concerns a person, and against the *product's* declared window where it concerns a product (Section 15.6).
* **`fte` is a capacity multiplier, not a status.** A part-time person is a full member of the team at a declared fraction of hours. No signal, threshold or evidence model reads `fte` as anything other than an input to capacity, and none may be introduced that does — a person at 0.6 who meets their role's expectations at 0.6 is meeting them.
* **The coverage check resolves against this block.** The `extended` and `24x7` staffing validator (Section 15.6) resolves each named rota member's `accepted_coverage_window` against the product's declared coverage window, and fails closed where a member has no work arrangement, no accepted window, or an accepted window that does not cover the segment assigned to them. Without this block that validator has nothing to read, which was the defect it corrects.
* **`arrangement` is operational context, never people evidence.** It exists so that onsite-dependent obligations — hardware handover, the in-person self-view key exchange of Section 12.1, physical access — resolve to the right person, and so that the day plan's overlap assumption (Section 94.2) is checkable rather than assumed. It is not a performance dimension, does not appear in any evidence bundle, and no signal reads it. The no-surveillance rules of Section 91.2 apply to it in full: a declared arrangement is a scheduling fact, and presence within it is never measured.
* **Changes are effective-dated registry edits** like any other configuration, and recalculate capacity automatically (Section 69.3). A schedule change is never applied retroactively across a closed performance period (Section 84.2).

## Section 8. Role Registry

**Priority: P0.**

Roles are configuration. New roles are added without workflow redesign because every authority decision is made against capability, never against role name.

```yaml
# roles.yaml — control-plane repository
registry_version: 1

roles:
  - id: founder
    default_capabilities: [strategy, budget, hiring, lifecycle-decision,
                           customer-commitment, exceptional-approval,
                           people-intelligence]
  - id: team_lead
    default_capabilities: [architecture, plan-approval, escalation,
                           reviewer-matrix-change]
                                    # production-approval and
                                    # platform-change-approval are granted
                                    # explicitly, never by default — see 8.1
  - id: acting_team_lead
    default_capabilities: [architecture, plan-approval, escalation,
                           reviewer-matrix-change]
                                    # dormant until activation (Section 13.1);
                                    # production-approval granted explicitly
                                    # for the recorded activation period
  - id: developer
    default_capabilities: [code-review]
  - id: mobile_developer
    default_capabilities: [code-review, mobile-release]
  - id: senior_developer
    default_capabilities: [code-review, architecture]
  - id: qa
    default_capabilities: [verification, uat, release-signoff]
  - id: devops
    default_capabilities: [devops, code-review]
  - id: foundational_developer
    default_capabilities: [code-review]
  - id: specialist
    default_capabilities: []        # granted explicitly, never by default
  - id: contractor
    default_capabilities: []        # granted explicitly, never by default
```

Roles that may be added later without architectural change - illustrative only: security engineer, platform engineer, product engineer, data engineer, release engineer, second team lead, support engineer.

* `default_capabilities` **are a starting point, not an entitlement.** A person's effective capabilities are what `people.yaml` declares. The role default exists to make onboarding fast, not to grant silently.
* **No role default carries a dangerous capability (D106).** Section 7.1 and Section 64.1 both state that a new person enters with no `production-approval` and no dangerous capabilities, and that capabilities are granted individually and explicitly, never inherited silently from a role default; invariant 79 makes minimum privilege binding. A role default that grants one of them contradicts all three, and the contradiction resolves in favour of the safe default. The dangerous set is therefore **granted only by explicit entry in `people.yaml`, never by role**: `production-approval`, `platform-change-approval`, `platform-admin`, `security-review`, `migration-review`, `exceptional-approval`, `lifecycle-decision` and `people-intelligence`. Control-plane CI rejects a `roles.yaml` default containing any of them. What remains in a role default is the set that describes the shape of the job — competence declarations, `code-review`, `architecture`, the verification set — none of which reaches production or widens authority on its own.
* **A developer does not automatically hold every capability.** Architecture, security review and platform change approval are granted explicitly to individuals who hold them.
* The `acting_team_lead` role holds its capabilities dormant until activation (Section 13, Team Lead Succession and Delegation); `platform-change-approval` is added for the recorded activation period, not held permanently.
* The `founder` role's `people-intelligence` capability gates Layer B access (Section 9; Section 90, Access Control Architecture).

## Section 9. Capability Model

**Priority: P0.**

Capability is the unit of authority. Every gate, approval and escalation in this specification is evaluated against capability.

| Capability | Grants the ability to |
| --- | --- |
| `backend`, `frontend`, `mobile`, `data` | Technical competence declaration; used for assignment matching and canary selection, not for authority |
| `code-review` | Act as Primary-Owner reviewer or Cross-Reviewer at Gate 2 |
| `architecture` | Review architecture-class changes; make cross-product technical decisions |
| `security-review` | Review security-sensitive changes |
| `migration-review` | Review destructive or high-risk database migrations |
| `verification` | Author and own verification contracts |
| `uat` | Execute and sign off manual UAT |
| `release-signoff` | Block or release on verification grounds |
| `production-approval` | Approve a verified artifact for production deployment |
| `incident-response` | Act as Primary or Backup Responder; execute rollback during SEV-1 |
| `plan-approval` | Approve at Gate 1 |
| `reviewer-matrix-change` | Modify ownership and cross-review assignments |
| `platform-change-approval` | Approve operating-system and shared-workflow changes |
| `platform-admin` | Administer the control plane and organisation settings |
| `devops` | Execute infrastructure, pipeline, environment and credential operations: provision and decommission product infrastructure, run `create product` scaffolding, retire domains and DNS, revoke third-party integrations and rotate control-plane machine credentials (Sections 19.2, 19.3, 40.1, 49.2) |
| `lifecycle-decision` | Change a product's lifecycle status |
| `escalation` | Act as the resolved escalation target for a product or domain: architecture-class review, security-sensitive escalation, cross-product decisions, disputed classification, and the case where both Primary Owner and Cross-Reviewer are unavailable (Section 17.1). Resolved through `topology.yaml`, never named on a product contract (Section 66) |
| `mobile-release` | Execute store submission and release management for products declaring `conformance_profile: client-app` — signing, store account operations, staged-rollout advancement and halt (Sections 15.7, 28.2) |
| `exceptional-approval` | Authorise an action outside the normal flow, per the exceptional-authorisation list of Section 26.3 and the exception-authority mapping of Section 54.3 — **except SEV-1 response initiation, which requires no prior authorisation (Section 47.2)**. Founder-class; delegable only through a dated `founder_decision_delegate` assignment (Section 10) |
| `people-intelligence` | Access Layer B people data and views (Section 90); receive evidence bundles containing individual-level evidence (Section 89) |
| `strategy`, `budget`, `hiring`, `customer-commitment` | Founder-class business authority |

### 9.1 Capability rules

* **Authority checks read capability, never role name.** This is what allows an Acting Team Lead, a senior developer with delegated architecture authority, or a future security engineer to slot in without any workflow change.
* **Every capability is defined before it is granted.** The table above is the complete capability vocabulary. A capability appearing in a `roles.yaml` default, in a `people.yaml` grant, or in any assignment type without a row in this table fails control-plane CI validation. This closes the fail-open path the safe-defaults rule of Section 64.1 exists to remove: an undefined capability is a grant with no defined authority, and the resolution for an undefined value is denial, never permission.
* **Capability is validated against assignment.** Holding `production-approval` does not permit approving production on a product where you hold no assignment. Both must be true.
* **`people-intelligence` is held by the Founder and is not delegable** (D109). Continuity under incapacity runs through the sealed contingency credential of Section 14.4, which is a break-glass event with its own record, never a standing grant. No role default other than `founder` includes it; no reconciliation, scaffolding or onboarding path grants it implicitly. It is the single gate on Layer B access: sensitive people data never enters the general engineering datasource, and general dashboards carry no per-person drill-downs (Section 90; Section 91).
* Founder-class capabilities (`strategy`, `budget`, `hiring`, `lifecycle-decision`, `customer-commitment`, `exceptional-approval`) may be delegated only through dated founder-delegation assignments (Section 10; Section 14) - never through role defaults.

## Section 10. Assignment Registry and Delegation

**Priority: P0.**

A person's identity is separate from their relationship to a product. Assignments are scoped and dated, which is what makes temporary capacity, partial delegation and succession possible without permanent restructuring.

```yaml
# in each product's product.yaml
assignments:
  - person: dev-a
    type: primary_owner
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null

  - person: dev-b
    type: cross_reviewer
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null

  - person: dev-b
    type: backup_owner
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null

  - person: dev-c
    type: temporary_contributor      # surge capacity, expires cleanly
    start_date: 2026-05-01
    end_date: 2026-06-15
    reason: "Q2 billing rework — Team Lead decision 2026-04-22"

  - person: sec-1
    type: security_reviewer
    start_date: 2026-04-01
    end_date: 2026-06-30

escalation: team_lead                # resolved via topology.yaml, not a person
```

### 10.1 Assignment types

All assignment types in the operating system, in one table (17 types):

| Type | Grants | Expires cleanly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `primary_owner` | Continuity, context, normal decisions, review of others' changes | Only by reassignment |
| `cross_reviewer` | Independent review of owner-authored changes | Only by reassignment |
| `backup_owner` | Operational takeover during absence | Only by reassignment |
| `temporary_contributor` | Write and review on this product for a bounded period | Yes, on `end_date` |
| `incident_responder` | Named primary or backup responder | Only by reassignment |
| `verification_responsibility` | Owns this product's verification contract | Only by reassignment |
| `architecture_responsibility` | Delegated architecture authority for this product | Yes, if dated |
| `production_approval_delegate` | Delegated production approval for a bounded period | Yes, on `end_date` |
| `security_reviewer` | Security review scope on this product | Yes, if dated |
| `plan_approval_delegate` | Gate 1 approval for a named scope | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `incident_coordination_delegate` | The full `escalation` capability for a named window — containment authority, hotfix authorisation, Blocking-drift response and break-glass post-use review, not coordination alone | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `domain_lead` | Team Lead authority within one domain (Section 66) | Optional; reviewed quarterly |
| `founder_decision_delegate` | A named founder-class decision scope, delegated for a bounded period (Section 14). **The delegable scope excludes every formal people decision** (Section 74.5) — recognition, promotion, role change affecting employment responsibility or status, hiring, formal warning, improvement plan, exit consideration, compensation and permanent headcount. A delegation naming one of them fails schema validation (D108) | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `registry_owner_delegate` | Owner-review authority (Section 26.4) over a named list of Founder-owned control-plane files, so that the registry edits an absence itself creates — a capability grant, an explicit availability edit, an unplanned Acting Team Lead activation — can merge while the Founder is away. Delegable only to the Team Lead or a holder of `platform-admin`; conveys review of the named files and nothing else | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `verification_delegate` | Dated, scoped verification authority. Conveys `verification` for named low-risk change classes during QA absence; conveys `uat` and `release-signoff` where the delegate's capability matrix (Section 82) records the relevant maturity at Working independently or above and the assignment names the products and manual-UAT scripts in scope — a delegate covering one of three capabilities does not govern QA leave, it governs a slice of it. May also be issued in steady state, scoped to restore-test integrity verification (Section 44.2) and background-layer draft-PR adjudication (Section 37.5), so that the two duties which scale with product count rotate to Primary Owners rather than binding the single verification authority | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `cross_review_shadow` | Observation of reviews only - no approval authority; visible on the review-network view (Section 17) | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |
| `mentor` | Dated guidance assignment for a person in a foundational role; the mentoring load is counted as Coordination attention (Section 67) | Yes, mandatory `end_date` |

**Delegation expiry is warned, never silent.** Every delegation-type assignment receives a 14-day advance expiry warning in the daily expiry check, exactly as expiring assets do (Section 49). When an expired delegation bounces an approval, the error surface is a named exception prompt - identifying the expired assignment, its holder and its expiry date - never a silent failure.

### 10.2 Assignment rules

* **Escalation is declared as a role, not a person.** `escalation: team_lead` in a product contract resolves through `topology.yaml` - to the domain lead where domains are active and the product belongs to a led domain, otherwise to the single portfolio Team Lead (Section 66, Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution). When the Team Lead changes, no product file changes. Product contracts never name a person.
* **Escalation resolution has a fallback of its own.** Section 54.4 routes reviewer unavailability *to* the escalation role, so it cannot be the one role with nowhere to go. Where the resolved holder is the author or the subject of the act, or is unreachable within the act's response time, escalation resolves in order: first to the Acting Team Lead designate, whose `escalation` capability becomes non-dormant for that single act and is recorded as a routing event; then to the Founder; then, where neither is reachable inside the response time, the act proceeds under a recorded exception naming its compensating control (Section 54). Resolution is recorded either way — a conflicted escalation that resolves silently is the same defect as an unowned one. Section 88.2 already builds this bypass for conduct; the engineering escalation chain gets the same one.
* **Temporary assignments never transfer ownership.** They expire and are removed by reconciliation. A temporary contributor never becomes an accidental owner through inaction.
* **Every assignment is visible on the portfolio dashboard**, including its expiry date, so that surge capacity and delegation are never invisible.
* **Ownership and reviewer-matrix changes are Team Lead decisions.** The Team Lead executes reviewer-matrix and product-ownership changes - temporary and permanent - under the `reviewer-matrix-change` capability, and each change is recorded as a decision (Section 97, Records, Events and Data Conventions). Every permanent ownership change generates a Founder-view notification: visibility, not approval. Only role changes affecting employment responsibility or status are Founder decisions (Section 74, People Decision Authority). The same rule is stated with the cross-review network in Section 17 (Ownership and the Cross-Review Network).

### 10.3 Delegation rules

Delegation is partial and routine, not only a full handover during absence. Every delegation records: the capability delegated, the scope (products, domain or portfolio), the duration, and the reason.

* **Delegation never widens authority.** A delegate cannot hold a capability the delegator does not hold.
* `reviewer-matrix-change` and `platform-change-approval` may be delegated only to a person holding `architecture`, and only within a named scope.
* **Delegation does not transfer accountability.** The Team Lead remains accountable for the portfolio; the Founder remains accountable for founder-class decisions.
* `founder_decision_delegate` carries the same registry rigour as every other delegation: dated, scoped, reasoned, visible, and expired by reconciliation - the Founder's own delegations are not exempt from the mechanics that govern everyone else's (Section 14; Section 74). Its scope excludes every formal people decision (D108), and Layer B access is not delegable by any assignment type (D109).
* Sustained delegation of the same capability for more than two consecutive quarters is a topology signal, not a delegation: it prompts the one-time formalise-or-confirm-standing decision of Section 10.3 (Section 13; Section 66).
* **Standing delegations are a distinct class (D79).** A delegation the Founder explicitly records as *standing* is reviewed annually rather than carrying an end date, and is exempt from the two-quarter formalisation signal. When the two-quarter signal fires for any sustained delegation, it produces a one-time decision - formalise the role, or confirm the delegation as standing with a recorded rationale - after which the signal does not re-fire for that delegation. Ordinary delegations keep their mandatory end dates; only the standing class renews annually. The standing leave-approval delegate of Section 14.2 is the class's first member.

## Section 11. Organisation and Access

**Priority: P0.**

* **Single organisation.** All products live in one company-owned GitHub organisation. Personal accounts are prohibited as product homes - company IP must not depend on an individual's login.
* **Repositories are enumerated dynamically** from the product registry. No workflow, dashboard or script contains a hard-coded list of repository names.
* **Shared code extraction.** Where products genuinely share logic, extract it to its own versioned repository governed as a Shared Service (Section 20, Shared Services and the Dependency Graph) rather than merging the products. Renovate propagates updates.
* **Access removal.** Removing a person from the organisation removes all access in one action. This is the security argument against split accounts.

### 11.1 GitHub permission semantics — verified, not assumed

Verified against GitHub documentation on protected branches, pull request reviews, and organisation repository roles:

| Capability | Read | Triage | Write | Maintain | Admin |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| View and clone code | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Comment on a pull request | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Submit a review (comment, approve, request changes) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Approval counts toward required approving reviews** | **No** | **No** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Request reviewers on a pull request | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Push branches to the repository | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Mark a draft pull request ready for review | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Merge into a protected branch | No | No | Only when all protection rules are satisfied | Same | May bypass only if explicitly permitted |
| Deploy to a protected environment | Governed by Environment protection rules, not by repository role | | | | |

**The consequence for this system.** A Cross-Reviewer holding only Read permission can open a pull request, read it, comment on it, and submit a review that visually reads as an approval - but that approval does **not** satisfy branch protection. The merge stays blocked. Any design assuming "Read is sufficient for cross-review" fails silently and produces exactly the outcome this operating system exists to prevent: a gate that appears to be working and is not.

**Therefore Cross-Reviewers require Write on the repositories they review.**

**Least privilege is preserved by branch protection, not by withholding Write.** Write permits pushing a branch. It does not permit merging into a protected branch unless every protection rule is satisfied, and it does not permit deploying to a protected environment. The security boundary lives in branch protection and, for deployment, the Section 27.2 workflow-identity gate — with environment protection rules as an added layer where the plan tier provides them.

### 11.2 The permission model

**Organisation base permission: Read.** Every member can read every repository. This is a deliberate choice - a small team benefits far more from being able to help each other than it loses to an internal threat that is largely theoretical. Client contractual isolation, if it ever arises, is handled by a separate organisation under company control, not by restricting reads inside this one. Temporary specialists and contractors are the exception: their access is scoped explicitly and they are not granted organisation-wide Read unless their scope requires it.

**Organisation-enforced two-factor authentication is mandatory.** The organisation setting requiring 2FA is enabled and stays enabled; an account without 2FA cannot be a member. The Founder, organisation Owners and holders of the platform-admin capability authenticate with hardware security keys or passkeys, not weaker second factors.

**Write is granted through Teams, derived from the registries.**

| Person class | Organisation role | Write on | Read on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder | Owner | All (implicit) | All |
| Team Lead / Acting Team Lead | Member | All product repositories | All |
| QA | Member | All product repositories | All |
| Developer | Member | Repositories of products where they hold `primary_owner`, `cross_reviewer`, `backup_owner` or `temporary_contributor` | All others |
| Contractor / temporary specialist | Outside collaborator or scoped member | Only repositories named in their `scope` | Only repositories named in their `scope` |
| Background machine layer | Machine account | Branch push only on whitelisted repositories; no merge, no environment access | Repositories in its queue |

A second organisation Owner - or an escrowed break-glass owner credential - exists as part of founder continuity (Section 14); organisation ownership is never a population of one with no recovery path.

**Team structure.** One Team per product, named for the product, containing everyone holding a current assignment on it. Two organisation-wide Teams grant Write to the Team Lead role and the QA role. **Team membership is derived from the registries and reconciled continuously** - a mismatch between `people.yaml`, `product.yaml` and actual GitHub Team membership fails CI and raises a drift finding (Section 53).

### 11.3 Branch protection configuration, per repository

* Require a pull request before merging.
* Require at least 1 approving review.
* **Require review from Code Owners.** CODEOWNERS is generated to contain human identities only - no machine account ever appears in it - so a machine-account approval can never satisfy branch protection: the required Code Owner review must come from a human. The Phase 1 completion check verifies this negatively.
* **Require approval of the most recent reviewable push.** This mechanically prevents an author's own approval from satisfying the requirement, and is the enforcement behind the no-self-approval invariant (Section 101).
* Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed.
* Require status checks to pass: tests, build, security scan, contract validation, reviewer matrix validation, parity check, verification contract, and `control-plane/blocking-drift` — the check the reconciler holds at failure while Blocking-class drift is open against the product (Section 53.2).
* Require branches to be up to date before merging.
* Block force pushes and deletions on the default branch.
* Apply rules to administrators. An exception exists only for a documented break-glass procedure with an audit record (Section 54, Exception Registry and Break-Glass).
* **Every environment carries a deployment branch and tag policy** restricting `staging` and `production` to the default branch and protected release tags (Section 33.4). Branch protection governs what merges; the deployment branch policy governs what may reach an environment's secrets. Neither substitutes for the other, and a repository with the first and not the second holds production credentials behind nothing.
* **CODEOWNERS** routes review requests automatically and is generated from the registries rather than hand-maintained; the generator emits human identities only. `verification/` is owned by whoever holds `verification_responsibility`. `product.yaml`, migration directories and CI workflow files are owned by the Team Lead role. Product source paths are owned by the product Team.

New repositories are created private, with branch protection applied from the template at creation, no environment access and no third-party app access - safe defaults, activation explicit (Section 64).

### 11.4 Implementation dependencies — plan-tier facts

| Capability | Plan-tier fact | Mechanism of record on the Team plan |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch protection or rulesets on private repositories | Available on the Team plan | Configured as specified in Section 11.3. Non-negotiable; the one item that forces a paid plan |
| Environment deployment protection rules (required reviewers, wait timers) on private repositories | A GitHub Enterprise feature; **not available on the Team plan** | The Section 27.2 workflow-identity gate: the deploy workflow verifies that the approving identity differs from the deploying identity and fails closed. This is the production-approval mechanism of record - the design, not a fallback. Buying Enterprise is a recorded Founder budget decision that would add environment required reviewers as a strengthening (D73) |
| Custom repository roles (approval authority without branch push) | GitHub Enterprise Cloud only | Write via Teams as specified. This is the assumed configuration throughout |
| Self-review prevention on production deployment | Environment required reviewers are Enterprise-only on private repositories (above) | The same Section 27.2 workflow-identity gate; branch protection's most-recent-push approval rule covers the review side (Section 11.3) |
| Outside collaborator scoping for contractors | Available on all tiers | — |

If custom repository roles were available, a role inheriting Read plus approval permission would be strictly better for Cross-Reviewers than Write. The specification assumes the Write configuration because it works on the Team plan.

## Section 12. Person Lifecycles

**Priority: P0** (lifecycles), **P1** (scaffolding automation).

### 12.1 New person lifecycle

```
CANDIDATE
  ↓
ADDED — people.yaml entry, availability: active,
        access_status: pending
  ↓
ACCESS PROVISIONED — organisation invitation, base Read
  ↓
ROLE ASSIGNED — from roles.yaml
  ↓
CAPABILITIES ASSIGNED — explicit, not inherited wholesale
  ↓
AI RUNTIME ASSIGNED — from the approved list, their choice
  ↓
SELF-VIEW KEY EXCHANGED — the encryption key for their
  self-view document, handed once, in person (Section 90.6)
  ↓
ONBOARDING
  read the constitution · read AGENTS.md on the first product
  run make setup · run make test · verify no API keys present
  ↓
CROSS-REVIEW SHADOW
  observes reviews on 2–3 products without approval authority
  Write not yet granted
  ↓
CROSS-REVIEW ACTIVE
  cross_reviewer assignment on 1–2 products
  Write granted on exactly those repositories
  code-review capability granted
  ↓
READY WORK
  takes prepared H2 items on products they cross-review
  ↓
PRODUCT OWNERSHIP
  primary_owner assignment on a product where they have
  demonstrated cross-review competence
  ↓
ACTIVE
```

**A new person does not become Primary Owner immediately.** Cross-review first, ownership later. Reviewing three products builds portfolio knowledge faster than owning one, and it preserves knowledge redundancy rather than creating a new single point of dependency on day one.

Typical progression is measured in weeks, not days, and the Team Lead decides readiness. There is no fixed duration - the signal is demonstrated review competence, not elapsed time. Onboarding effectiveness is measured by time to milestone, not checklist completion (Section 103, Success Metrics and Baselines).

**Who runs add-person.** The `add person` scaffolding operation (Section 12.6) is executed by the Founder or by a holder of the `platform-admin` capability; the organisation invitation itself requires organisation Owner rights. At one week before the start date (T-minus-one-week) the operator works a pre-provisioning checklist: GitHub account confirmed, hardware ready, email account created, AI-runtime choice asked of the joiner, the runtime seat purchased, and an asset-inventory entry recorded for issued hardware (Section 49).

**The joiner is told who protects them.** The external conduct-adviser contact and the fairness rules of Section 81.8 are named items on the onboarding checklist issue - every joiner learns, in writing and on day one, who the conduct adviser is and which fairness rules apply.

**The shadow phase is recorded, not informal.** Cross-review shadowing is recorded as `cross_review_shadow` assignments (Section 10.1) on the observed products, so the review-network view (Section 17) shows shadowing explicitly instead of inferring it.

**Targets are visible to the joiner.** The Section 12.7 milestone bands render automatically onto the onboarding checklist issue, so the joiner sees target-versus-actual for every milestone without asking.

Onboarding on each product honours that product's declared `ai_restrictions` (Section 36, Untrusted Input and Agent Toolchain Supply Chain): the person's runtime configuration on that product is constrained at onboarding, not discovered later.

### 12.2 Person exit lifecycle

```
DEPARTURE KNOWN
  ↓
people.yaml: availability: departing, end_date set
  ↓
KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER WINDOW
  update STATE.md on every owned product
  record any undocumented context in .planning/
  Backup Owner pairs on in-flight work
  ↓
LAST WORKING DAY
  ↓
availability: departed, access_status: revoked
  ↓
RECONCILIATION EXECUTES:
  ├── remove from organisation
  ├── remove from every GitHub Team
  ├── revoke every environment access
  ├── revoke production capability
  ├── deactivate AI runtime
  ├── stop self-view generation and retire the
  │   registered self-view key material (Section 90.6)
  ├── remove from reviewer matrix
  ├── recalculate ownership
  └── recalculate incident responder assignments
  ↓
ORPHAN DETECTION RUNS
  ↓
ORPHANS RESOLVED (Team Lead)
  ↓
EXIT RECORD COMPLETED
  ↓
Person record RETAINED — never deleted, identifier never reused
```

* **Orphan detection runs immediately when `availability` becomes `departing`**, in prospective mode against the declared `end_date`: it emits the transfer worklist - every responsibility that would orphan on that date - so the knowledge-transfer window works from a generated list for the notice period, not from memory.
* **Exit recalculations include `topology.yaml` succession-block membership.** A departing person who is a succession designate is flagged immediately and a new designate is named at once (Founder decision) - succession is never left vacant by a departure.
* **Final-period closure.** The departing person's review-period segment closes at `end_date`; the Founder decides whether a closing review is held.
* **Temporary-person expiry is an exit.** Expiry of a temporary specialist or contractor triggers the same exit record and orphan scan as `remove person`. Expiry with open gate-relevant work - an unfinished security review, an open review or verification item that a gate is waiting on - is the fourteenth orphan type below.

**Orphan detection — what the system surfaces** (16 orphan types):

| Orphan type | Detection | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product with no Primary Owner | Assignment registry | **Blocking** |
| Product with no Cross-Reviewer | Assignment registry | **Blocking** |
| Product with no Backup Owner | Assignment registry | High |
| Product with no Primary Responder | Contract operations block | **Blocking** |
| Shared service with no owner | Service registry | **Blocking** |
| Certificate with no owner | Asset inventory | High |
| Domain with no owner | Asset inventory | **Blocking** |
| Vendor relationship with no owner | Asset inventory | Medium |
| Operational asset with no owner | Asset inventory | Medium |
| Customer commitment with no owner | Contract operations block | **Blocking** |
| Platform migration with no owner | Compatibility state | High |
| Verification responsibility unassigned | Assignment registry | High |
| In-flight H1 work with no assignee | Board | High |
| Temporary person expired with open gate-relevant work | Assignment registry + open reviews and gate items at expiry | High |
| Policy with no owner | Policy register | **Blocking** |
| Open exception whose requester or authority has departed | Exception registry | High |

**No departure silently creates an orphaned responsibility.** Blocking orphans appear on the Founder View's product attention dimension as Action Required and cannot be dismissed without resolution (Section 93, The Founder View).

### 12.3 Role transition

```
ROLE CHANGE DECIDED (Founder for role, Team Lead for assignments)
  ↓
people.yaml: role updated
  ↓
CAPABILITY RECALCULATION
  new role defaults reviewed; explicit grants confirmed;
  capabilities no longer appropriate are removed
  ↓
PERMISSION RECALCULATION
  Team membership adjusted by reconciliation
  ↓
REVIEWER MATRIX REASSESSMENT
  does the change alter review load or knowledge distribution?
  ↓
OWNERSHIP REASSESSMENT
  moving to Team Lead or QA usually means shedding ownership
  ↓
INCIDENT RESPONDER REASSESSMENT
  ↓
PERFORMANCE-FRAMEWORK MAPPING CONFIRMED
  a framework mapping for the new role instance exists,
  effective-dated to the change (Section 86.3)
  ↓
DASHBOARD UPDATE — automatic
```

Illustrative transitions, all handled by the same mechanism: developer to senior developer; developer to team lead; developer to QA; QA to developer; mobile to generalist; contractor to employee; developer to specialist.

**No manual editing across repositories.** A role change is a registry edit plus reconciliation. A role change affecting employment responsibility or status is a Founder decision; assignment changes within a role are Team Lead decisions (Section 74).

### 12.4 Contractor and temporary specialist model

```yaml
- id: sec-1
  role: specialist
  employment_type: temporary_specialist
  capabilities: [security-review]
  start_date: 2026-04-01
  end_date: 2026-06-30
  scope:
    products: [product-4, product-9]
    repositories_only: true
  sponsor: dev-a                    # mandatory named internal contact
```

| Property | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | Named products or repositories only. Not organisation-wide Read unless required |
| Capability | Explicitly granted. Never inherited from a role default |
| Ownership | **Never.** A temporary person is never Primary Owner, Cross-Reviewer or Backup Owner |
| Production | **Never.** No `production-approval`, no environment access |
| Duration | `end_date` mandatory. CI fails if null |
| Expiry | Reconciliation revokes access on the date. No human action required |
| Extension | Deliberate edit to `end_date`, with a reason. The Team Lead may extend within the original scope by up to 30 days; any longer extension, or any scope change, is a Founder decision |
| Sponsor | Mandatory `sponsor:` field naming the internal contact who answers the person's scope questions and requests any extension |

Reconciliation emits a T-minus-7-day expiry warning to the sponsor, listing the person's open pull requests and open reviews, so expiry never strands in-flight work.

**No permanent permissions for temporary people.** The most common real-world failure - a contractor whose access persists for years - is prevented by making the end date mandatory and the revocation automatic.

A contractor's review may satisfy Gate 2 only if they hold `code-review` and the change is on a product in their scope. Their approval never satisfies architecture-class, security-sensitive or destructive-migration requirements unless they explicitly hold the corresponding capability, which is the normal reason a security specialist is engaged.

### 12.5 Temporary capacity loans

A product needing more capacity does not require permanent restructuring.

```yaml
- person: dev-c
  type: temporary_contributor
  start_date: 2026-05-01
  end_date: 2026-06-15
  reason: "Q2 billing rework — Team Lead decision 2026-04-22"
```

* Grants Write on that product's repositories for the period.
* Does **not** transfer ownership, review responsibility or incident responsibility.
* Their changes route to the Primary Owner for Gate 2 as any non-owner change would.
* Expires cleanly. Reconciliation removes Team membership on the end date.
* Visible on the portfolio dashboard with its expiry, so surge capacity is never invisible.

This lets the Team Lead surge without the organisational cost of a permanent change, and without the risk that a temporary arrangement quietly becomes permanent. Temporary rebalances carry a mandatory end date; a temporary rebalance never becomes permanent ownership through inaction, and every rebalance decision records the human who made it (Section 73, Workforce Staffing Diagnosis and Rebalancing).

### 12.6 Scaffolding operations

Conceptual operations, implemented as scripts in the control-plane repository. Not an application.

* `create product` produces: repository or set from template; `product.yaml` at current version; GitHub Team; generated CODEOWNERS; branch protection from template; environments; CI workflows at pinned tag; verification skeleton; local environment contract; required endpoints; and registration in the portfolio board, Grafana, Scorecard, DevLake and the dependency graph.
* `add person` produces: `people.yaml` entry; organisation invitation; Team membership per assignments; capability grants; AI runtime assignment honouring per-product `ai_restrictions`; onboarding checklist issue; and registration in the review network view.
* `change role` triggers: role update; capability recalculation; permission recalculation; reviewer matrix reassessment; ownership reassessment prompt; incident responder reassessment; and dashboard update.
* `remove person` triggers: access revocation; Team removal; environment access revocation; AI runtime deactivation; reviewer matrix recalculation; **orphan detection**; and an exit record.

**No ordinary personnel or product change should require hand-editing files across twenty repositories.** If it does, the scaffolding is incomplete and that is a platform defect.

### 12.7 Onboarding effectiveness

Onboarding is not measured by checklist completion. It is measured by time to milestone, per joiner. Milestones derived from pull requests, reviews and the board are recorded automatically. The two workstation-local milestones - local setup working and first test executed - leave no machine trace, and are recorded as a one-line human confirmation on the onboarding checklist issue instead. All milestone records are stored in the onboarding records store per Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions):

| Milestone | Target band (indicative — calibrate locally) |
| --- | --- |
| Local setup working on first product (`make setup`, `make dev`, `make test`) | Day 1 |
| First test executed against a real product | Day 1–2 |
| First cross-review submitted | Week 1 |
| First accepted PR merged | Week 1–2 |
| First Ready item taken independently | Week 2–3 |
| First independent product work as owner or co-owner | Week 4–8 |
| First incident participation | First quarter |

The portfolio-level question this answers is whether the operating system actually reduces context-switching cost. **If the second product a person touches takes materially longer than the first, the Local Environment Contract (Section 33) is not being honoured somewhere, and the specific product is identifiable.**

Offboarding and ownership transfer are measured the same way: time from departure notice to zero orphaned responsibilities, and time from transfer decision to the new owner shipping a verified change (Section 103, Success Metrics and Baselines). These milestones also feed the ramp factor in each person's Capacity Profile (Section 69).

## Section 13. Team Lead Succession and Delegation

**Priority: P0** (succession), **P1** (routine partial delegation).

The Team Lead cannot be a single permanent point of failure.

### 13.1 Acting Team Lead

```yaml
# topology.yaml — succession block
succession:
  team_lead:
    acting: dev-a        # pre-designated, not chosen during a crisis
```

**The Acting Team Lead is designated in advance, not chosen during a crisis.** The designation lives in the succession block of `topology.yaml`, alongside the other resolution rules that map roles to people (Section 66) - `roles.yaml` maps roles to capabilities and never names a person (Section 8), and the current Team Lead is already resolvable from the registries. They hold `plan-approval` and `architecture` capability continuously, dormant until activation, so that activation is a configuration change rather than a competence question. On activation, the full `team_lead` capability set - including `platform-change-approval` - is granted for the recorded activation period and expires with it.

**Acting Team Lead authority:**

| Can | Cannot without founder delegation |
| --- | --- |
| Approve plans (Gate 1) | Change company strategy |
| Handle architecture escalation | Hire |
| Coordinate incidents | Sign major contracts |
| Modify reviewer assignments | Change budget |
| Approve high-risk engineering decisions | Change portfolio priority |
| Approve production for architecture-class changes | Make lifecycle decisions |
| Approve platform changes (during activation) | Accept new support commitments |

### 13.2 Absence tiers

```
SHORT ABSENCE (up to ~2 days)
  Gate 1 approvals pause. Visible and acceptable.
  Escalation never pauses: it resolves to the Acting
  designate for the window (Section 10.2).
  No activation needed.

MEDIUM ABSENCE (2 days to ~2 weeks)
  Acting Team Lead activates.
  Recorded with a start and expected end date.
  Capabilities granted for the period; expire automatically.

EXTENDED ABSENCE (beyond ~2 weeks)
  Acting Team Lead continues.
  Founder assesses whether ownership rebalancing is needed.

DEPARTURE
  Acting Team Lead provides continuity immediately.
  Founder decides the permanent replacement.
  If the Acting Team Lead becomes permanent, a new
  Acting Team Lead is designated at once.
```

**Activation mechanics.** For planned medium absence, the Acting Team Lead activates on day one of leave - activation is never deferred until something breaks. The `topology.yaml` activation PR is authored by the departing Team Lead before leaving and reviewed by the Founder as the file's owner. Activation explicitly swaps alert-channel membership and the documented phone-escalation position to the acting holder; both revert at expiry, and reconciliation (Section 53) checks the swap and the reversion. Activation also auto-records a reciprocal `plan_approval_delegate` so that plans authored by the Acting Team Lead have a named approver; where no second architecture-capable senior exists, acting-authored plans run under a pre-recorded leave-scoped exception (Section 54) with Gate 2 as the compensating control.

**Dormancy is not paralysis.** The dormant Acting designate may approve Team-Lead-authored plans without activation - that is precisely what the continuously-held dormant `plan-approval` and `architecture` capabilities are for. Activation is required only to assume the wider Team Lead authority set.

**Handover and return are generated, not remembered.** A pre-leave handover report - open manifests, exception renewals falling due in the window, pending reviewer-matrix changes, and recurring duties in the window - is generated at leave approval, and it covers every role, not only the Team Lead: for QA it lists every open verification-block record, each of which is closed or handed to another `release-signoff` holder before the leave begins (Section 27). A return digest - decisions, exceptions, matrix changes, platform transitions and drift closures since the leave start date - is generated at return. Both digests are machine-generated artifacts produced by the platform's own generator workflows (Section 99.2); the Hermes Agent background worker may at most trigger a generation early through a `workflow_dispatch` — Hermes proposes; the platform disposes (D71) — and delivery follows the notification contract of Section 92.11. The digest is a wait-surface convenience, never replacement state: the boards remain the source of truth, and every digest entry carries a link back to them (D72).

### 13.3 Routine partial delegation

Succession covers absence; delegation covers load. The Team Lead may delegate partially and routinely, without a full handover, using the delegation assignment types of Section 10 (`plan_approval_delegate`, `incident_coordination_delegate`, `production_approval_delegate`, `architecture_responsibility`, and `domain_lead` where topology warrants it).

* Every delegation records the capability delegated, the scope, the duration and the reason, and is visible on the portfolio dashboard exactly as temporary assignments are.
* Delegation never widens authority, and accountability stays with the Team Lead (Section 10.3).
* **First-time delegate calibration.** A first-time `plan_approval_delegate`'s first five delegated approvals are same-day co-reviewed by the Team Lead and recorded as calibration - a convention that builds shared judgement, not a re-approval gate.
* **The two-quarter formalisation signal.** Sustained delegation of the same capability for more than two consecutive quarters is a topology signal, not a delegation: it prompts a one-time decision — formalise the role (a domain lead, a second Team Lead, or a standing specialist role, Section 66) or confirm the delegation as standing under Section 10.3, after which the signal does not re-fire. The operating system surfaces this; the Founder decides the structure.
* Routine partial delegation is the direct structural remedy to the most likely portfolio-scale failure mode: the Team Lead becoming the bottleneck. Team Lead overload is a graded health signal with its own remediation ladder (Section 52; Section 73).

The Team Lead's operational authority - task assignment, sequencing, within-team rebalancing, cross-review routing within matrix rules, horizon preparation, coaching and normal work feedback - is defined in Section 74 (People Decision Authority) and is exercised without Founder involvement. What the Team Lead must never do independently - formal warnings, employment decisions, compensation, permanent headcount - is defined there too.

## Section 14. Founder Continuity and Absence

**Priority: P0.**

The Founder is the final authority for strategy, budget, hiring, lifecycle, customer commitments and formal people decisions - and is therefore the operating system's most concentrated dependency. This section governs that dependency the way Section 13 governs the Team Lead's: absence is planned for, delegation is dated and recorded, incapacity has a pre-built path, and the Founder's own decision latency is measured like any other constraint.

### 14.1 Founder absence

```
FOUNDER UNAVAILABLE (sick, travelling, unreachable, on leave)

CONTINUES — no founder involvement required:
  ✓ H1 execution
  ✓ H2 preparation and assignment
  ✓ H3 sequencing within existing strategic priority
  ✓ Architecture decisions
  ✓ Review routing and Gate 1 and Gate 2
  ✓ Normal production deployment
  ✓ Incident response including SEV-1
  ✓ Rollback and hotfix
  ✓ Weekend exception authorisation (Team Lead may authorise)
  ✓ Platform changes and canary rollouts

PAUSES — founder-only, waits unless pre-delegated:
  ✗ Major strategy change
  ✗ Hiring
  ✗ Major budget commitment
  ✗ Lifecycle decisions (sunset, archive, pause)
  ✗ Major customer commitments
  ✗ New support model commitments
  ✗ Major portfolio reallocation
  ✗ Customer notification in a security incident

PRE-DELEGATION for planned absence:
  Founder may delegate named decisions to the Team Lead
  with a scope and an end date, recorded in the control-plane
  repository.
```

**Founder absence does not halt engineering.** If it does, the operating model has failed. The founder-only list is deliberately short and strategic; everything operational continues.

For a SEV-1 during founder absence: the incident proceeds fully, including rollback, hotfix and weekend activation. Only customer notification and legal decisions wait, and if they cannot wait, the Team Lead escalates through the emergency contact path declared in the continuity plan below.

**Founder-wake criteria.** Three incident conditions wake the Founder through the emergency contact path regardless of absence: customer data loss in progress, a breach-notification clock at risk of expiring, and a security incident with legal exposure. Everything else waits for normal availability.

### 14.2 Founder delegation as registry mechanics

Founder pre-delegation is not an email - it is a `founder_decision_delegate` assignment (Section 10): a named decision scope, a named delegate, a start date, a mandatory end date and a reason, recorded in the control-plane repository and visible on the portfolio dashboard. Founder delegation carries the same registry rigour as Team Lead delegation: it never widens authority, it expires by reconciliation, and accountability remains with the Founder.

**Two founder-class scopes are not delegable at all.** The first is every formal people decision of Section 74.5 (D108): the Founder is the final authority for each of them by invariant 36, the system emits decision support and never a decision by invariant 38, and a delegation mechanism that could carry them would contradict both. A `founder_decision_delegate` naming one fails schema validation. The second is **Layer B access** (D109). Individual people-performance intelligence is Founder-only, and the routine delegate that previously widened it is removed: at the scale this operating system is built for there is no holder for it — the Team Lead is barred from that data by Section 90.2 and Section 90.5, and the design test of Section 90.5 is precisely that the Team Lead can allocate engineering work without being able to answer who is being considered for promotion or exit. A standing delegate would have widened the most sensitive boundary in the system for no operational gain. Continuity is served instead by the incapacity path that already exists: the sealed Layer B contingency credential held in the Section 14.4 escrow, usable only under the incapacity trigger, logged and disclosed like any break-glass event. Absence pauses Layer B generation; it does not delegate it.

**Routine founder items do not queue behind absence.** A standing leave-approval delegate is named (initially the Team Lead) so that leave approval never waits on the Founder. Any planned Founder absence prompts a pre-delegation checklist, and launch sign-off and leave approval are standing items on that checklist.

### 14.3 The standing delegation trigger

One pre-delegation is permanent and dormant: **if the Founder is unreachable beyond a declared number of consecutive days** (calibrated configuration; initial value 5 working days), a standing delegation activates automatically. It grants the Team Lead the minimum founder-class scope needed to keep the company operating - customer communication in incidents, urgent vendor and billing actions, and acceptance of time-critical commitments - and it notifies the successor arrangement of Section 14.4. Activation requires the Team Lead's declaration of unreachability countersigned by the successor-arrangement custodian - no single person activates founder-class authority alone. The activation is filed as its own exception type with its own authority row in the exception registry (Section 54), and it fires an automatic alert mirroring the escrow alerting of Section 14.4. Deactivation is a recorded event, executed the moment the Founder is reachable again.

### 14.4 Incapacity and death plan

Temporary absence pauses decisions; permanent loss must not halt the company legally and administratively while engineering coasts. The continuity plan has five standing components, maintained with the same rigour the specification applies to Team Lead succession:

1. **Organisation ownership recovery.** A second GitHub organisation Owner exists, or an escrowed break-glass Owner credential is held under sealed, audited escrow. Organisation ownership is never recoverable only through one person's login. Use of the escrowed credential is a break-glass event (Section 54) and appears in the DR failure-scenario table (Section 45, Disaster Recovery and GitHub Organisation Loss).
2. **Founder-account inventory.** Every founder-only account - billing, domain registrar, banking, app-store accounts, AI vendor administration, cloud root accounts - is enumerated in the operational asset inventory (Section 49) as an operational asset with a named owner and a continuity note stating how it is reached if the Founder cannot be. The inventory is reviewed on the asset-inventory cadence; an unlisted founder-only account discovered later is a drift finding.
3. **Successor arrangement.** A pre-designated successor or legal arrangement (attorney, family member with authority, or equivalent) exists outside the operating system, and the control plane records that it exists and where it is held - not its contents. The Team Lead's emergency escalation path during founder absence terminates here.
4. **Layer B and conduct-store contingency access.** A sealed contingency credential for the Layer B people-data store (Section 90) is held in the same escrow, usable only under the incapacity trigger, so that employment records and performance history - which the company legally needs to keep operating - do not become unreachable. Conduct records live in a separate sealed conduct store (Section 88.4), with primary custody held by the external adviser plus a minimal Founder-held encrypted copy; that store carries its **own** sealed contingency credential in this escrow, distinct from the Layer B credential, so that neither credential ever opens the other store. Use of either credential is logged and disclosed like any break-glass event.
5. **Standing delegation trigger** - Section 14.3 - which bridges the gap between "unreachable" and "successor arrangement engaged".

**Escrow mechanics.** An inventory match is not a functional test, and the failure this escrow exists to prevent is silent: a credential named in the manifest that authenticates to nothing passes every inventory audit until the incapacity that needed it. The escrow has a named custodian, recorded in the operational asset inventory. The seal is audited quarterly: the audit confirms the escrow is intact, its contents match the declared inventory of escrowed credentials, and no access has occurred outside a recorded break-glass event. The audit also verifies that each escrowed item still **works**: the escrowed Owner credential authenticates - the dormant-account authentication alert logs exactly this - and each escrowed store credential and encryption key decrypts a canary blob. That verification is recorded as a drill record, distinct from a break-glass record. Any credential **or encryption-key** rotation on a covered account, store or archive - the dormant Owner account, the Layer B store, the conduct store, the organisation-export archive - triggers mandatory re-escrow of the replacement before the rotation is considered complete, and re-escrow is a blocking step in the rotation runbook (Section 40.1): a rotation is not recordable as done until the replacement is escrowed. Automatic alerting fires on any authentication of the dormant Owner account and on any use of an escrowed credential; the alert routes to the Founder and, under the incapacity trigger, to the successor arrangement.

### 14.5 The Founder as a diagnosable constraint

The operating system treats founder capacity as a measurable bottleneck, not a fact of nature:

* **Founder-decision latency is a bottleneck category** in the bottleneck taxonomy (Section 73), alongside review, verification, planning and the others.
* **Every decision prompt issued to the Founder opens an entry in `records/decisions/pending/`** (Section 97), closed by the decision record that resolves it - the pending register is the Founder's queue, not a reconstruction from inboxes.
* **Median time from decision prompt to Founder decision is a measured metric**: the clock starts when the pending entry is opened - the moment a decision prompt or evidence bundle (Section 89) reaches the Founder's queue - and stops when the closing decision is recorded. The metric is visible in the Founder View (Section 93) and feeds operating-system health (Section 52).
* A sustained latency breach is remedied the same way Team Lead overload is: first by delegation (Section 14.2), then - if delegation of the same scope persists beyond two quarters - by the Section 10.3 one-time decision: formalise the structure (Section 66), including the dormant governance-evolution rule for a second founder-class principal, or confirm the delegation as standing with recorded rationale.
* Founder coordination time is Coordination-category hours attributed to the Founder in the attention ledger (Section 67, Human Attention Economics) - measured with the same taxonomy as everyone else's attention, and never used as individual performance evidence (Section 91).

---

# Part III - Products and Portfolio

Every product in the portfolio is governed by one machine-readable contract, one ownership model, one lifecycle and one dependency graph. This part defines what a product is, what it must declare, who owns it, how it enters and leaves the portfolio, how it relates to shared services and other products, and what the company has promised its customers about it. The rules here are written so that adding the twentieth product is configuration plus onboarding, never redesign.

## Section 15. Product Operating Contract

*Priority: P0*

Every product carries `product.yaml`, machine-readable and CI-validated. A product without a valid contract cannot be onboarded.

`product.yaml` is the Product Operating Contract, not a dumping ground. Where information belongs elsewhere, it is referenced rather than duplicated. Business truth lives in business systems; the `business:` block holds only what the portfolio dashboard needs to prioritise, reviewed quarterly rather than maintained continuously.

### 15.1 The contract

```yaml
contract_version: 2                  # schema version — see Section 60
platform_compatibility: supported    # supported | transitional | unsupported
conformance_profile: service         # service | client-app | library | batch
                                     # | customer-hosted | white-label
                                     # | static-site — see 15.7

identity:
  id: product-name                   # stable, never reused
  display_name: "Example Product"
  lifecycle: active                  # active | maintenance | paused
                                     # | sunset | archived
  launch_status: launched            # pre-launch | launched
  created: 2025-01-15

classification:
  class: commercial                  # internal | experimental | commercial
                                     # | strategic | regulated | legacy —
                                     # extensible list, configuration not code
  reliability_criticality: high      # low | medium | high | critical
  domain: commerce                   # optional; resolves via topology.yaml
                                     # — see Section 66

assignments:                         # see Section 10
  - person: dev-a
    type: primary_owner
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null
  - person: dev-b
    type: cross_reviewer
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null
  - person: dev-b
    type: backup_owner
    start_date: 2025-06-01
    end_date: null
escalation: team_lead                # role; resolves through topology.yaml to
                                     # the domain lead where domains are active,
                                     # otherwise to the portfolio Team Lead

code:
  repositories:                      # a product may have several — see Section 16
    - name: org/product-name-api
      role: primary
      deploys: true
    - name: org/product-name-web
      role: frontend
      deploys: true
    - name: org/product-name-mobile
      role: mobile
      deploys: true
  default_branch: main
  gsd_version: v1.11.0               # pinned tag, never latest or next
  accepts_external_contributions: false
                                     # flipping to true — or flipping any
                                     # repository public — re-triggers the
                                     # workflow-trigger privilege review and
                                     # the Section 36 controls, and additionally
                                     # triggers a self-hosted-runner-group
                                     # detachment review: the runner group
                                     # holding the estate's runners is
                                     # restricted to named private repositories
                                     # (Section 36), and a repository leaving
                                     # that posture must leave the group before
                                     # the change lands (D80)

verification:
  automated: required
  manual_uat: required               # required | not-applicable
  smoke_tests: required
  performance: required              # required | optional | not-applicable
                                     # required when reliability_criticality
                                     # is high or critical — see Section 31
  contract_path: verification/contract.yaml

environments:
  local: docker-compose.dev.yml
  staging: https://staging.example
  production: https://example

  build: github-actions

reversibility_default: fully-reversible
                                     # fully-reversible | partially-reversible

infrastructure:

  database: postgres-16
  cache: redis-7
  provider: example-cloud
  region: eu-west-1
  provider_outage_behaviour: degraded-read-only
  monthly_budget_band:               # see Section 50
    currency: EUR
    expected: 180                    # per month
    ceiling: 300                     # spend above this is a cost anomaly

dependencies:

    - auth-service
    - event-service

    - stripe
    - sendgrid

    - postgres-provider

ai_runtime_dependency:               # only where the product's RUNTIME consumes
  providers: [example-llm-provider]  # pinned model snapshots — full schema Section 38.1
  evaluation:

security:
  secrets_location: github-environments

  production_db_access: ci-only

ai_restrictions:                     # full schema Section 36.4
  ai_processing_permitted: true

  classification: customer-pii      # public | internal | customer-data
                                     # | customer-pii | regulated

  isolation: shared-tenant           # shared-tenant | dedicated-tenant
                                     # | dedicated-infrastructure
  deletion_supported: true

  health_endpoint: /health
  version_endpoint: /version

  integrity_check: docs/restore.md#integrity   # the agreed check the restore must pass

  rpo_minutes: 1440                  # daily backups imply a 24-hour RPO unless
                                     # point-in-time recovery is declared
  rto_minutes: 240

operations:
  support_model: business-hours      # business-hours | extended | 24x7
  coverage_window: null              # REQUIRED where support_model is extended

                                     # business-hours — see Section 47.9
  detection_expectation: next-business-morning

                                     # per the Section 42.2 mapping:
                                     # next-business-morning | rostered-window
                                     # | continuous. A declared value differing
                                     # from the derived value fails CI
  intake_channel: support@example    # per-product customer intake — Section 22
  triager: primary_owner             # role or assignment type that triages
  weekend_exception_eligible: true
  primary_responder: dev-a           # DERIVED — generated from the
  backup_responder: dev-b            # incident_responder assignments, which
                                     # are authoritative; validated by
                                     # reconciliation — see Section 10
  critical_incident_response: next-business-day

commitments:                         # per-customer commitments — see Section 21
  - customer: customer-ref-017       # reference, not the customer's legal name
    sla_uptime_pct: 99.5
    measurement_window: monthly
    support_commitment: business-hours
    breach_notification_hours: 48
    service_credit: per-msa
    contract_end: 2027-03-31
    termination_notice_period_days: 90  # notice owed on termination — feeds
                                     # sunset planning (Section 18)
    conflict_check: waived-with-decision  # NOT passed, deliberately — see 21.4.
                                     # 99.5% monthly allows ~219 minutes of
                                     # downtime; this product's worst-case
                                     # undetected window (business-hours
                                     # support, next-business-morning
                                     # detection, across a weekend) plus its
                                     # 240-minute RTO exceeds that budget.
                                     # The uptime-SLA feasibility row of 21.4
                                     # therefore returns a blocking conflict,
                                     # and the entry carries a recorded Founder
                                     # waiver rather than a false pass. A
                                     # combination like this one is the normal
                                     # case for a business-hours product, and
                                     # the honest resolutions are: fund an
                                     # extended rota, lower the promised SLA,
                                     # or record the waiver as shown here.

business:
  criticality: high                  # high | medium | low — business importance
  active_customers: 42
  revenue_importance: high
```

### 15.2 Two criticality fields, deliberately distinct

The contract carries two criticality declarations, and every rule in this specification that depends on criticality names which one it reads.

* `business.criticality` expresses **business importance**. It drives portfolio economics (Section 68), lifecycle decisions (Section 18), and platform investment decisions (Section 59). A high-revenue product has high business criticality even if its users tolerate occasional degradation.
* `classification.reliability_criticality` expresses **operational stringency**. It drives canary-set selection (Section 61), verification depth and mandatory performance verification (Section 31), migration patterns (Section 34), the manual-rollback requirement during platform outages (Section 46), restore-test cadence (Section 44), monitoring depth (Section 41), incident severity inheritance (Section 20), and the incident capacity reserve (Section 69).

They are different questions. A low-revenue internal product can carry critical reliability requirements; a high-revenue product may tolerate degradation. Collapsing them into one field forces one of the two decisions to be wrong.

### 15.3 What classification influences

| Attribute | Low reliability_criticality / experimental class | High or critical reliability_criticality / regulated class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verification depth | Automated only; UAT where user-facing | Full automated, UAT, smoke, performance verification, plus verification review by QA at plan time |
| Production approval (informative — the Section 27.1 routing table is authoritative) | Per the Section 27.1 routing table | Per the Section 27.1 routing table; for security-sensitive, high-risk or non-reversible changes on high or critical reliability products the QA sign-off and recovery-plan requirements of that table apply |
| Progressive delivery | Optional | Required for `partially-reversible` and `non-reversible` changes |
| Monitoring | Health endpoint plus error rate | Full signal set plus business-critical synthetic checks |
