The background layer must never: merge any change; approve any change; deploy to any environment; hold production credentials or deploy keys; access production databases; execute destructive changes; approve UAT; declare an incident resolved; or modify `people.yaml`, `product.yaml`, workflows or branch protection.

These are prohibited because the machine account does not hold the permissions required. Documentation-only restrictions fail. The machine account does hold Write on whitelisted repositories, so one further mechanism closes the approval path: branch protection requires Code Owner review and CODEOWNERS is generated to contain human identities only (Section 11.3), which mechanically prevents a machine-account approval from ever satisfying a gate.

**Dispatch authority is Write-derived, and the task whitelist does not bound it.** On GitHub, pushing a branch and triggering a `workflow_dispatch` are the same permission, and D71 positively authorises the machine layer to dispatch — so Write alone would let the machine account run `migrate.yml`, `deploy-production.yml` and the rollback workflow, three of the prohibitions above. The closing mechanism is an **actor gate as the first step of every privileged workflow**: `deploy-staging.yml`, `deploy-production.yml`, `migrate.yml`, the rollback workflow and the production-restore workflow fail closed unless `github.actor` resolves to a human identity in `people.yaml` holding the capability the action requires — `production-approval`, `incident-response` or `devops`. The machine account's permitted dispatch set is a **positive allowlist checked inside each workflow**, not a sentence in this document: the digest generators of Section 94.7 and nothing else. Removing an actor gate is a workflow-file change and is therefore already Blocking drift (Section 53.1).

### 37.4 Isolation requirements

* Dedicated host — the background layer runs on its own machine, never on the operations VM; the two hosts share no credentials
* Network egress restricted by the Section 37.8 allowlist: only GitHub, the package registries and the LAN inference endpoint
* No production credentials, no deploy keys, no environment access — enforced by the machine account's permissions, not by the task whitelist
* Branch push only, on whitelisted repositories only (a repository with `ai_processing_permitted: false` is never whitelisted — Section 36.4)
* Draft pull requests only
* Hard stop at 07:00 on weekdays
* Whitelist enforced at the queue level
* Subject to the untrusted-input constitutional rule (Section 36.1)

### 37.5 Output lifecycle

```
Generated → CI runs → Pass or Fail
                          ↓
                  Human review (verification authority or product reviewer)
                          ↓
                  Accept or Reject, with a task-class reason
                          ↓
                  Task-class statistics updated
                          ↓
          Acceptance below threshold → class auto-suspends
                          ↓
          Team Lead investigates and may restore the class
```

**Failed and rejected pull requests are not deleted.** The failure signal is the input to task-class analysis. Closing a PR is fine; destroying the record of why it failed removes the system's ability to learn which task types produce value.

When output quality degrades for a task class, acceptance falls below threshold and the class auto-suspends; rejected PRs and their reasons are retained; the Team Lead investigates prompt, model or task selection and may restore the class.

**Task-class metrics.** Owner for all five: the **Team Lead** — the role that investigates a suspended class and may restore it. Each is measured over a trailing window of background nights, calibrated configuration with an initial value of 20 nights, so that one bad night never moves a class.

| Metric | Definition | Source | Response when poor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Queue depth | Whitelisted tasks waiting at the start of the background window | Event log (Section 97.3) | A capacity signal only: refill or narrow the whitelist, never throttle the layer (Section 37.7 interpretation rule) |
| Per-class acceptance rate | Draft PRs accepted ÷ draft PRs raised in the class, over the trailing window | Event log (Section 97.3) | Below the auto-suspend threshold the class suspends automatically; the Team Lead investigates prompt, model or task selection and may restore it |
| CI pass rate | Draft PRs in the class passing CI on first run | GitHub Actions | Fix the task template before touching the whitelist — a class failing CI is a template defect, not a bad task type |
| Rejection reason distribution | Rejection reasons recorded for the class over the trailing window | Event log (Section 97.3) | The dominant reason names the defect: prompt, context, or task selection |
| Reviewer load contributed | Human review minutes spent on this class's draft PRs, by class and by reviewer | Attention ledger, Review category (Section 67.2) | Feeds review concentration (SIG-04); the response is to narrow the class, never to cap volume |

**The auto-suspend threshold.** Calibrated configuration, declared per class in `os-health.yaml` beside the class definition. Initial value: **acceptance below 0.3 over the trailing window, with a floor of 10 draft PRs raised in the class** — the floor exists so that a class does not suspend on a night of three PRs. It is refitted against the observed distribution of per-class acceptance at the first calibration review after the layer has run a full quarter, and every six or twelve months after that (Section 84.6). No first threshold is assumed correct, and a threshold with no first value cannot be refitted at all.

Downstream production usefulness is not a sixth metric here: it is measured as accepted-PR yield, rework rate and net attention effect in Section 37.7, against these same task classes. A metric whose name carries its own opt-out — "where measurable" — is the kind of row Section 84.6 exists to delete.

### 37.6 Benchmark gate

Before any of this is built: run a small quantised coding model via llama.cpp, single-shot generation, on one real source file. Measure time per file and show the output to QA. Single-shot is mandatory — agentic loops re-process a growing context every turn, and on CPU the prompt-processing cost dominates. **Throughput per night is the metric, not peak model capability.**

* Under 10 minutes per file with usable output → build the queue.
* 30–60 minutes with usable output → marginal; evaluate hardware.
* Slower or unusable → park the layer. Nothing in the critical path depends on it.

**The harness.** The queue and generation harness is **Hermes Agent** (the open-source agent harness at github.com/nousresearch/hermes-agent, MIT licence), pinned at commit `8e9459c97f707047be5915a5c8b4c503756daa9b` (D69). Its scheduler is the whitelist queue, its per-class skills encode the task templates, and its no-agent script jobs and single-turn runs against the local inference endpoint implement the single-shot default. Committing to a harness changes nothing about the governing rules: the benchmark gate decides whether the layer is built at all; single-shot generation remains the default on CPU (an agentic loop is permitted only if the benchmark's agentic variant passes on a measured accepted-drafts-per-night threshold sustained over at least five consecutive nights — realistically only on GPU hardware, and GPU or other hardware spend for this purpose is a Founder budget decision recorded in the asset inventory (Section 49) and the automation ledger (Section 57)); the machine account's permissions, the task whitelist, the draft-PR-only rule, the 07:00 hard stop and the untrusted-input rule all bind identically whatever the harness is. The harness's own conveniences that exceed the layer's authority are disabled under the cage configuration contract (Section 37.8): authority is limited by the machine account and the host, never by trusting the harness. The background worker harness gets a `tools.yaml` entry with an owner, the pinned commit and an exit condition like any other tool (Section 62), and every state change it produces flows through the existing platform write paths — a draft pull request, or a workflow dispatch that the platform executes and records. Hermes proposes; the platform disposes (D71).

### 37.7 Output value measurement

The background layer is not throttled; it is measured, so that its output can be steered rather than limited. These measures feed the automation ledger (Section 57, Automation Value and AI Output Measurement).

| Metric | Definition | Response when poor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accepted-PR yield | Draft PRs merged ÷ draft PRs raised, by task class | Narrow or remove the task class from the whitelist |
| Review cost per accepted PR | Human review minutes ÷ accepted PRs, by task class | Improve the task template or prompt context |
| Net attention effect | Human hours saved by accepted output minus human hours spent reviewing rejected output | Negative for two quarters: retire the task class |
| Rework rate | Accepted background PRs later reverted or hotfixed | Add verification requirements for that class |
| Verification yield | Background-drafted test suites accepted by QA | QA feedback loop into the task template |

**Interpretation rule:** low yield in a task class is a signal about the task class, not about the volume. The correct response is to change what the background layer is asked to do, never to cap how much it does. Priority: P2, except the whitelist-narrowing response path, which is P1 because it is a safety behaviour.

Volume of AI-generated output is never individual productivity, and no individual receives credit or penalty proportional to background-layer volume; background-model output is a capacity layer (Section 91, Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart). A sustained poor task class is also a nominated failure-pattern candidate (Section 58, Failure Patterns and the Incident Learning Loop).

An AI-generated change that causes a production defect is handled identically to any other production defect — incident, rollback or flag disable, postmortem, permanent regression test — plus one additional question: which gate should have caught it, and why did it not?

### 37.8 The cage configuration contract

**Priority: P0.** Every Hermes Agent instance in the estate — the background worker harness first among them — runs under this contract (D69). It has two layers, and the order matters.

**The walls are outside Hermes.** The harness's own security doctrine states that the only security boundary against an adversarial LLM is the operating system; everything inside the harness's configuration is a heuristic, not containment. The load-bearing walls are therefore enforced at the OS and platform level, where no harness behaviour can reach them:

* **Host-level egress allowlist.** The whole agent process is Docker-wrapped and the host's network egress permits only GitHub, the package registries and the LAN inference endpoint — enforced by the Docker network egress override or the host firewall, not by harness configuration.* **The egress ledger, because the allowlist bounds destinations and not content.** GitHub is a read-write authenticated channel this host holds a Write credential for and uses by design, so exfiltration through it is indistinguishable from ordinary work at the firewall. Two things close the gap. The allowlist names endpoints, not vendors: the specific GitHub API and git hosts the queue needs, and the company's own mirror (Section 36.3) rather than the public package registries. And every connection out of the background host is recorded — destination, bytes out, time, calling instance — to storage the host cannot modify, alerting on shape as well as volume: a push to a repository not in the night's task queue, any repository touched outside the whitelist, and bytes pushed per night beyond the calibrated band (calibrated configuration, initial value 3× the trailing 14-night median, refitted at the Section 84.6 threshold review). The ledger is an operating control, not an audit artefact waiting for an auditor: it is the only instrument that can answer what left.
* **GitHub-side draft-PR-only enforcement.** The background worker's GitHub identity is a machine account restricted to draft pull requests on whitelisted repositories; branch protection and human-only CODEOWNERS (Section 11.3) enforce, GitHub-side, that machines never merge, never approve, never deploy.
* **Wall-clock hard stop.** The 07:00 weekday stop is a systemd-enforced shutdown of the background window, with a graceful drain — not a harness setting.
* **Separate instances.** Each deployment slot is a separate Hermes instance under a separate OS user with its own `HERMES_HOME` directory and its own sender allowlist. Within one instance all authorised callers are equally privileged, so privilege separation is instance separation — never two surfaces of one instance.* **The shared inference endpoint authenticates every caller.** One model server behind four slots is one shared surface, and instance separation does not survive an endpoint that serves anyone who can reach it. The endpoint sits behind an authenticating reverse proxy; each instance presents its own credential and carries its own rate and context limits; and the proxy writes a request record — calling instance, time, token counts — to storage the calling host cannot modify, so a compromised slot cannot edit its own trail. Machine instances hold their credential in the fifth secrets tier (Section 40.1); a personal seat holds a workstation-scoped endpoint token that grants inference and nothing else, so it adds no authority to the Section 40.3 workstation blast radius. The endpoint binds to the proxy, never to a bare LAN address any workstation can reach directly.
* **Two model processes, not one.** The slots that ingest untrusted repository text by design — the background worker and the PR-review engine (Section 36.1) — are served by a model process that shares no OS user and no volume with the process serving the Founder ops console and the personal seats. A parsing defect or a malicious model artefact reached through untrusted text must not land inside the request path that carries Layer A answers and every seat's prompts. Both processes are the estate's own local inference: nothing leaves the network and the Section 36.6 guarantee is unchanged.
* **Emergency stop.** The ESTOP sentinel file, honoured by the harness, pauses all new work fail-safe; it complements, and never replaces, the systemd stop.

**The configuration keys are the second fence.** With the walls in place, the harness is additionally locked down at the pinned commit's verified configuration surface. Mandatory on every instance, with slot-specific notes:

* Memory disabled: `memory.memory_enabled: false` (machine identities carry no memory).
* Background self-review disabled: `model.background_review.enabled: false` — the autonomous skill-and-memory writer never runs on any machine identity.
* Skills self-authoring nudges disabled; skills come only from reviewed, version-controlled, read-only directories.
* Unneeded toolsets removed via `agent.disabled_toolsets`, which overrides every per-job override.
* Messaging platforms not configured at all on the worker and PR-review instances; on the console instance, the gateway is locked: `GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=false`, sender allowlists set, and unauthorised-DM behaviour set to ignore (`unauthorized_dm_behavior: ignore`).
* Cron approvals default-deny: `approvals.cron_mode: deny`, with only registered no-agent jobs and whitelisted task classes scheduled; agents cannot schedule agents.
* Lazy package installation disabled: `security.allow_lazy_installs: false` — the dependency surface is the lockfile, nothing arrives at runtime.
* Where terminal sandboxes are used, sandbox egress goes through the harness's bundled allowlist proxy, so real credentials never enter a sandbox.
* The self-update command is never run. Pinning means never updating in place: updates arrive only by moving the pinned SHA through the normal dependency-update workflow (Section 36.3).

**Sensitive at rest.** The `HERMES_HOME` directory holds session trajectories — full transcripts of everything each instance read and produced — alongside logs and job state. It is classified sensitive-at-rest and lives on the encrypted volume, with the same handling discipline as any other sensitive operational store.

## Section 38. AI in the Product

The preceding sections govern AI as a build-time tool. This section governs products whose **runtime** behaviour depends on model inference — products where an LLM or speech model is part of what the customer buys. Such a product carries a dependency that can change behaviour without any deployment, consume metered spend, and be attacked through its own users. All three properties are declared and governed in the product contract.

### 38.1 The ai_runtime_dependency block

Every product whose runtime consumes model inference declares it in `product.yaml`:

```yaml
# product.yaml — excerpt
ai_runtime_dependency:
  providers:
    - name: <provider>
      role: primary
      models:
        - id: <model-id-with-version-snapshot>   # pinned snapshot, never a floating alias
          used_for: <capability, e.g. conversation, transcription>
    - name: <provider-or-model>
      role: fallback
  evaluation:
    suite: verification/ai-eval/            # required — Section 38.3
    run_on: [model_change, provider_change, release, scheduled]
    schedule: nightly                       # scheduled-run cadence — nightly is the default, Section 38.3
  keys:
    per_environment: true                   # separate provider keys per environment — required
    spend_attribution: per_key              # provider-side spend reported at key level
  cost:
    monthly_ceiling: <amount band>          # product COGS budget — Section 50
    provider_hard_cap: true                 # provider-side hard cap where the provider offers one — the declared ceiling actuator    daily_sub_cap: <amount>                 # daily ceiling inside the monthly one — a runaway is bounded at one day, not one month
    usage_reconciliation: hourly            # provider usage API read per key, reconciled against the product-side counter — Section 38.4
    eval_budget: <amount line>              # explicit budget line for scheduled evaluation runs, inside the cost band
    metrics_alert_fraction: 0.8             # product-side /metrics alert at this fraction of the ceiling — Section 38.4
    anomaly_alert: true                     # spend anomaly is a Red health signal
  fallback_behaviour: <degrade | queue | refuse>   # declared, tested behaviour when the provider fails
  injection_surface:
    end_user_text_reaches_model: true
    mitigations:
      - <instruction/data separation in prompts>
      - <output constraints and tool-permission limits>
      - <abuse rate limits>
```

A product with no runtime AI omits the block. Reconciliation flags a repository whose code imports a model-provider SDK in a product without the block.

Provider keys are issued **per environment** — production, staging and any development environment each hold their own key — and spend is attributed at key level in the provider console, with provider-side hard caps enabled wherever the provider offers them, as the declared ceiling actuator. The requirement is diagnostic as much as financial: with key-level attribution, a leaked key and a defect retry loop are distinguishable in one query — spend on a key no deployed environment should be using is a leak; spend concentrated on the production key is a product defect.

### 38.2 Model pinning and the change-without-deployment problem

The rest of the operating system assumes an error correlates with a deployment: `/version` identifies the artifact digest, the evidence chain ties behaviour to a reviewed change, and rollback restores a prior artifact. A hosted model breaks this assumption — the provider can silently retrain, re-route or deprecate a model, altering product behaviour while the artifact digest is unchanged.

Countermeasures:

* **Pin model snapshots, never floating aliases.** The pinned identifier lives in `ai_runtime_dependency` and in configuration, so a model change is a visible, reviewed change like any other.
* **A provider-forced model change is treated as a change,** not weather: it triggers the evaluation suite before the new pin is accepted, follows the product's progressive-delivery posture where the provider allows staged adoption, and is recorded as a deployment-class event even though no artifact was rebuilt.
* **A fifth defect category exists for this failure mode: "external model behaviour change"** — beside the four in the defect taxonomy (Section 41, Observability and the Defect Taxonomy). Classifying a defect here redirects the response: there is nothing to roll back; the responses are re-pinning, fallback activation, prompt or configuration adjustment, or a provider decision.
* Announced model deprecations enter the vendor deadline watch (Section 49, Operational Asset Inventory and Vendor Deadline Watch) with a named owner and alert lead time.

### 38.3 Evaluation suites under verification/

A product with AI-driven behaviour cannot be verified by exact-match assertions alone; its verification contract (Section 31, Verification Contract) therefore includes an evaluation suite under `verification/`:

* A maintained set of representative scenarios with graded expected behaviour — acceptance criteria expressed as properties and rubrics, not single exact outputs.
* Run on every model or provider change, on release, and on a schedule — the cadence is declared in `evaluation.schedule`, **nightly by default** — so silent drift is caught between deployments. Scheduled runs carry an explicit budget line (`cost.eval_budget`) inside the product's cost band, so evaluation spend is planned COGS, not absorbed noise.
* Results from every run — triggered or scheduled — are written to `records/eval/` like any other verification evidence; a regression against the suite blocks adoption of a new model pin exactly as a failing test blocks a merge.
* A regression detected by a scheduled run raises **SIG-42, AI-eval regression (Red, routed to the Primary Owner)** and auto-creates an incident classified in the fifth defect category, external model behaviour change (Section 38.2): the product changed without a deployment, so the incident flow, not the backlog, carries the response. The named responder is the product's **Primary Owner**, with a **same-day** response SLA — triage, fallback or re-pin decision, and the incident record opened the same working day the regression is detected.
**The arrival rate is planned, not absorbed.** A nightly suite across the AI-runtime products produces a standing weekday interrupt stream against a single Primary Owner, on a trigger — provider-side model change — outside that owner's control. Three rules bound it. A night's regressions on one product coalesce into **one** SIG-42 triage, never one per scored dimension, and the same-day SLA runs against that triage rather than against each finding. The triage has a named place in the day (Section 94.3), so it is planned load rather than silent displacement of committed delivery, and its hours are logged as Incident-category attention (Section 67.2) instead of being absorbed against the owner's commitment-achievement KPI. And the expected weekly arrival count per product is declared beside the tolerance in `os-health.yaml`: an observed rate above it is a signal about the tolerance or the provider, entering the Section 84.6 calibration review — never a signal about the owner.

Until a product's evaluation harness exists, SIG-42 is **unarmed — not yet instrumented** on that product under the Section 52.2 arming discipline: it cannot breach, and the affected behaviours are verified by structured human UAT against the same scenario list. Building the harness is funded assigned work with reserved hours, never an expectation carried on top of a full delivery plan.

**The eval-suite starter kit.** So that no product's first evaluation suite starts from a blank page, `verification/ai-eval/` follows a starter layout:

```
verification/ai-eval/
  scenarios/        # one file per scenario — schema below
  rubrics/          # acceptance rubrics — owned by the verification authority
  fixtures/         # audio clips, transcripts and prompt fixtures, referenced by scenario id
```

The scenario/rubric schema mirrors the `verification/uat.md` format (Section 31.1), so authoring an evaluation scenario feels like authoring a UAT step, not learning a new tool:

```yaml
scenario: refund-request-conversation
preconditions:
  - test tenant exists
  - fixture available: fixtures/refund-request-01.wav
steps:
  - open a conversation as an end user
  - request a refund with an ambiguous order reference
expected:
  rubric: rubrics/conversation-grounding.yaml
  properties:
    - agent asks a clarifying question before acting
    - no fabricated order details appear
    - fallback path is clean on provider timeout
```

Scenario drafting may ride the background layer's task whitelist (Section 37.2): the background worker harness may draft evaluation scenarios as draft pull requests, confirmed by a human before they enter the suite. The rubrics and the runner are unchanged by this — rubrics remain owned by the verification authority, and the scheduled eval runner remains CI machinery holding the product's environment-scoped provider keys, which never reside on any Hermes Agent host (Section 40).

Fixtures live under `verification/ai-eval/fixtures/` and are referenced by scenario id — never fetched from external URLs at run time, so a run is reproducible from the repository alone. The ownership split matches the rest of the verification contract: the product's AI specialist authors and maintains the scenarios (for Solvox.ai, Mansi as Voice AI Developer), and the verification authority (Saumit, QA) owns the acceptance rubrics and the recorded results — the builder describes behaviour; verification decides what passes.
**Fixture provenance is declared, and no fixture is a customer's data.** Invariant 111 (Section 101) holds here without exception: a real customer call recording or transcript never enters the tree, and git history is append-only, so this is the one prohibition with no rotation-equivalent remedy after the fact. Every file under `verification/ai-eval/fixtures/` therefore carries a declared provenance — `synthetic`, `consented-and-recorded` with the consent record referenced, or `de-identified` with the method named — recorded in a fixture manifest beside the scenarios. The verification-contract check validates the manifest: a fixture with no provenance declaration, or a manifest entry with no file, fails CI. The verification authority owns fixture provenance and reviews it on the verification-contract cadence, recorded as a policy entry in `policies.yaml` with that owner and that cadence, so the invariant has a detector rather than an intention. The same rule reaches incident evidence: an incident record references customer data by identifier, and any reproduction fixture attached to one is synthetic or de-identified before it is committed.

**Current configuration example:** the Voice AI evaluation harness for Solvox.ai — scenario coverage for conversation flows, transcription accuracy and agent behaviour acceptance — is a verification-contract requirement of that product, not merely KPI evidence. Until the harness exists, its absence is declared as an instrumentation gap and the affected behaviours are verified by structured human UAT against the same scenario list; the harness additionally supplies evidence for the Voice AI role's KPIs (Section 81, Role-Specific Evidence Models), but the product obligation stands on its own.

### 38.4 Cost ceilings and anomaly alerts

Metered inference is a runaway-spend surface: an abusive user, a retry loop or a prompt defect can multiply the bill silently. Every `ai_runtime_dependency` block declares a monthly cost ceiling within the product's `infrastructure.monthly_budget_band`, and a spend anomaly raises a Red health signal and a cost-incident classification — mechanics in Section 50 (Cloud Cost Observability). The ceiling is a monitored budget with an alert, and the declared response to breaching it (throttle, degrade, or founder decision) is part of the product's operational contract.

Provider billing consoles lag; the ceiling therefore has a near-real-time product-side counter as well. Every AI-consuming product exports a spend and token counter through its `GET /metrics` endpoint (Section 41.2) — cumulative tokens and estimated spend per provider key for the current billing month — and Prometheus alerts when the counter crosses the declared fraction of the monthly ceiling (`cost.metrics_alert_fraction`, initial calibrated value 0.8). The alert fires from the product's own counters, independent of billing lag, so a runaway is visible within a scrape interval rather than a billing cycle. Where the provider offers hard caps, the provider-side cap (`cost.provider_hard_cap`, Section 38.1) remains the declared ceiling actuator of last resort — it stops a runaway even when the product's own counters are the thing that is broken.
**The counter is blind to spend the product did not generate.** The product-side counter increments on the product's own request path, so it cannot see a key spent outside that path — which is exactly the leaked-credential signature of Section 50.3. The fast detector for that cause is divergence, and divergence is directly measurable. The provider's **usage API** — not its billing feed — is read per environment-scoped key on the declared cadence (`cost.usage_reconciliation`, calibrated configuration, initial value hourly) and compared against the product-side counter for the same key and the same window. Usage charged to a key that the product never accounted for is not a cost anomaly: it is **credential exposure**, escalated at Level 5 (Section 53.2) into the security incident flow of Section 43 immediately, because the provider access log that identifies the abuse expires. The alert fires on the divergence, never on the ceiling — a leaked key is detectable long before it reaches one.

Two bounds sit behind the detector. `cost.provider_hard_cap` is set wherever the provider offers a cap, and `cost.daily_sub_cap` declares a daily ceiling inside the monthly one, so an undetected runaway costs one day's ceiling rather than one month's. Where a provider exposes no usage API, that is a declared instrumentation gap on the product (Section 42.2) and the daily sub-cap carries the bound alone — an honest gap, never a silent one.

### 38.5 Provider fallback behaviour

`fallback_behaviour` declares — and the evaluation suite exercises — what the product does when its provider fails or degrades: fall back to a secondary provider or model, degrade to a reduced non-AI experience, queue work for later processing, or refuse the AI feature cleanly while the rest of the product serves. "The product hangs" is not a permitted answer. Provider outage for an AI-in-the-product dependency is handled through dependency health monitoring and the incident flow (Section 42, Incident Management and Detection), distinguished from a product fault exactly as any other external provider outage is.

### 38.6 End-user prompt-injection surface

The constitutional rule in Section 36 protects the engineering toolchain. A product whose runtime feeds end-user text to a model has its own injection surface: a customer, or an attacker using the product, can attempt to steer the model against the product's rules. Each AI-consuming product therefore declares its injection surface and mitigations in the `injection_surface` block: whether end-user text reaches a model, what instruction/data separation the prompts enforce, what the model's outputs are permitted to do (tool and action permissions are least-privilege), and what rate and abuse limits apply (Section 43's abuse classification covers exploitation). The evaluation suite includes adversarial scenarios for this surface. A successful end-user injection with material effect is a security incident.

### 38.7 Tooling versus product COGS

The fixed-cost rule is two rules, stated plainly:

* **Tooling: no metered spend.** Everything engineers use to build — runtimes, agents, CI, review tooling — is free, self-hosted, or a flat per-person subscription. No API keys in developer environments (Section 36.6).
* **Product COGS: metered inference is permitted, budgeted and monitored.** A product whose value proposition includes AI behaviour may buy metered inference as cost of goods sold, governed by this section's ceilings, anomaly alerts and the product's portfolio economics (Section 68, Product Load Model and Portfolio Economics).

The boundary is the product contract: metered spend exists only where an `ai_runtime_dependency` block declares it, and never for engineering tooling.

The Hermes Agent estate sits entirely on the tooling side and adds **zero metered spend**: the harness is MIT-licensed, every instance runs local inference on existing hardware, and no vendor key exists anywhere in the estate (Section 36.6). Its only costs are the background host's electricity and the maintenance attention-hours already carried by the background layer — both visible in the asset inventory and automation ledger, neither of them a new billing line.

### 38.8 The AI-exposure statement

When a customer or auditor asks "what AI touches my data in this product?", the answer must not require an engineer to reconstruct it. Each product therefore has an **AI-exposure statement**: a generated per-product view that support can hand to a customer or auditor directly. It states:

* whether the product has runtime AI (yes/no), and if yes, the providers and pinned model snapshots from `ai_runtime_dependency` (Section 38.1);
* the sub-processors involved, from the vendor data-handling checklist records (Section 35.6);
* the product's build-time code-processing status under its `ai_restrictions` declaration (Section 36.4) — whether, and under what restrictions, AI tooling processes the product's code;
* the vendor training-opt-out verification dates, from the recorded checklist runs (Section 35.6).

Every input is data the operating system already declares and records; the statement is **generated, never authored** — no new declaration exists only inside it, so it cannot drift from the contracts it summarises. It is regenerated whenever any input changes, and a product whose statement cannot be generated has a declaration gap, which is a reconciliation finding, not a documentation task.

## Section 39. AI Subscription and Seat Lifecycle

AI subscriptions are recurring, per-person, externally billed and easy to forget — exactly the profile the operational asset inventory exists for. This section makes seats a managed asset class and collects the activation triggers for conditional AI tooling.

### 39.1 Seats as operational assets

Every AI subscription seat is an entry in the operational asset inventory (Section 49, Operational Asset Inventory and Vendor Deadline Watch), with the same discipline as a certificate or a domain:

```yaml
# assets.yaml — excerpt
- asset: ai_subscription_seat
  vendor: <vendor>
  runtime: <approved runtime>
  holder: <person id>
  owner: <named owner of the vendor relationship>
  renewal_date: <date>
  billing_cycle: monthly | annual
  cost_band: <band>
  tier: <purchased tier>            # ties the Section 35.6 checklist to what is actually bought
  alert_days: 30
```

* Each seat has a named owner for the vendor relationship (by default the Founder, as billing holder), a renewal date with at least a 30-day alert, and a cost band so aggregate seat spend is visible against budget.
* Seat spend is reviewed quarterly alongside the automation ledger (Section 57): the seats are themselves a priced automation investment.
* A seat whose holder no longer appears active in the people registry is a reconciliation finding.

The three committed Hermes Agent instances are named entries in the same inventory: the **background worker harness** (on the dedicated background host), the **founder ops console**, and the **PR-review engine** runner — the PR-review instance shares the background host's asset entry, so the inventory carries two host entries and three `tools.yaml` entries. Each entry names an owner, the pinned commit, a fixed cost band (hardware and hosting only — no metered line exists for any of them, Section 38.7), a patch cadence for moving the pin, and an exit condition (D69). The personal-seat local-inference profile adds no new asset: it points at the shared inference host the inventory already carries, and a seat adopting it records `ai_runtime: hermes-agent` against the person like any other runtime choice.

### 39.2 Price increases and tier changes

A vendor price increase, tier restructure or terms change is an expected event, not an emergency:

* The seat owner updates the cost band; a material increase is a quarterly-review item, weighed like any tool cost against value.
* A tier change re-triggers the vendor data-handling checklist (Section 35.6) — the verified training-opt-out and retention terms are tied to the tier, and a "cheaper" tier that trains on input is not cheaper.
* If the vendor's offering degrades or the terms fail the checklist, the response is the standing one: the runtime list is configuration; update the approved list and people migrate at quarter boundaries. No workflow changes.

### 39.3 Seats on leave and exit

* **Exit:** the person-exit lifecycle (Section 12, Person Lifecycles) deactivates the AI runtime seat alongside access revocation — deactivation is a checklist item executed by reconciliation-verified state, not memory. The seat is cancelled or reassigned at the next billing boundary; an assigned seat with a departed holder is a drift finding.
* **Leave:** for approved leave longer than one billing cycle (leave records per Section 69 and the decision matrices in Section 85), the seat owner pauses or downgrades the seat where the vendor supports it; where pausing is unsupported, the cost of the idle seat is simply visible in the band. Nobody's seat is touched for ordinary short leave.
* **Suspension:** `access_status: suspended` (Section 43; Section 88) suspends AI runtime access with everything else.

### 39.4 Daily usage-window exhaustion

Subscription runtimes meter by usage windows. The planning assumption is roughly two subscription window cycles per working day, feeding the daily rhythm's two heavy-AI blocks (Section 94, Daily and Weekly Operating Picture); if observed behaviour differs, the assumption is adjusted after the first fortnight of measurement.

When a person's daily window is exhausted, the policy matches the outage stance (Section 35.4): **fall back to human work** — review, verification authoring, planning, documentation, UAT, debugging without generation. Window exhaustion is never a reason to: enter an API key (prohibited — Section 36.6), borrow another person's seat (one seat per person), buy metered credits, or stop working. Chronic exhaustion across the team is a capacity-and-tooling signal for the quarterly seat review, not an individual performance signal.

### 39.5 Conditional tooling activation triggers

**Priority: P2.** Each conditional tool has an explicit activation trigger. None are active at launch; a tool activates when its trigger fires, not before.

| Tool | Trigger |
| --- | --- |
| llama.cpp background layer | Benchmark passes (Section 37.6) and QA finds output usable |
| Issue-guard trust envelope | Owner: Team Lead. Detector: any GSD configuration that ingests issue or board bodies flips the trigger (Section 36.2); activation no later than support-intake activation |
| Evidence binding (cryptographically linking an agent-produced change to the evidence reviewed) | Before any reduction of human review below the gates defined in this specification (no such mode exists today) |
| Egress ledger | When the background layer is built (Section 37.6). A host that pushes to GitHub every night is the reason to hold a ledger, and the first time a client asks is too late to start one. A client or auditor question widens the ledger's scope; it never starts it |
| Designer / Doc Engineer / Release Manager personas | Roles with no human. Advisory PR comments only, never a gate |
| Terminal multi-repo tooling | If people want it, after GSD has landed |
| Roadmap layer above the execution boards | Around product 15, if portfolio initiatives outgrow boards |
| Automated PR review | Six adoption conditions below |
| Founder ops console | Only if free CI notifications prove insufficient |
| LLM gateway | Only if API keys are ever accepted |

**Automated PR review — the PR-review engine.** Server-side automatic review ordinarily requires a metered LLM key, which the fixed-cost constraint excludes; the review path is therefore a GitHub Action rather than a hosted service. The machine reviewer behind the existing machine-review step is **Hermes Agent**, pinned at commit `8e9459c97f707047be5915a5c8b4c503756daa9b`, running as its own instance (separate OS user, separate `HERMES_HOME`, no messaging platforms — Section 37.8) and triggered by the existing Action (D69). Its output is advisory comments only: it is non-blocking, it never approves, and the Code-Owner and CODEOWNERS walls (Section 11.3) are unchanged — no machine output can ever satisfy a gate. Six hard conditions bind, verified rather than hoped:

1. Pin to a full commit SHA, never a floating branch.
2. No default free provider pool is configured on any instance touching client code — the harness's bundled keyless and cheap provider pools stay unconfigured.
3. Its provider layer accepts a custom base URL — verified at the pinned commit — and points at the local model server, so this is automated review at zero marginal cost entirely inside the network.
4. The review job runs with read-only token permissions.
5. No base-repository secrets are exposed to the review job.
6. The organisation setting "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" is disabled, so no Action can ever cast a gate-satisfying approval.

Conditions 4–6 are verified with the same rigour as branch protection configuration (Section 11.3): continuously by reconciliation, not once at adoption. Such Actions commonly document a trigger running with base-repository secrets and a write token; that configuration fails conditions 4 and 5 and is not used — no external contributions are accepted, so a low-privilege trigger suffices.

**Runner posture.** All self-hosted runners — the PR-review engine's runner first among them — live in an organisation runner group restricted to named private repositories, with public-repository access off. The fork-pull-request code-execution attack applies to runners reachable from public repositories, so this posture is a stated rule of the estate, not an accident of current configuration (D80).

**Privileged-workflow isolation (Priority: P0).** The runner-group rule above closes the fork attack. It does not close the attack this estate actually has, which is the reverse: the estate accepts no external contributions, but it does grant the background machine account Write on whitelisted repositories, and a branch push executes CI (Section 40.3). The least-trusted identity in the organisation therefore executes code on a runner — and if that runner is long-lived and later runs a privileged workflow, anything the first job left behind on the host is present when production credentials materialise into the second. Persistence, not provenance, is the exposure (D87).

The **privileged workflows** are the closed set that handle production credentials or mutate production state: `deploy-production.yml`, `migrate.yml`, the rollback workflow and the per-product production-restore workflow. They are isolated from the branch-push execution surface by construction:

* **The default is a hosted runner.** Privileged workflows run on GitHub-hosted runners, which are destroyed after every job, so no host persists between an untrusted job and a privileged one. This is a recorded, deliberate exception to the self-hosted posture, and it does not weaken the fixed-cost rule of Section 35: D80's reasoning is that the self-hosted estate keeps *CI volume* inside fixed cost — every push, every product — and the privileged tail is a small, low-frequency set whose metered exposure is bounded, declared in the control-plane budget band (Section 50), and reviewed at the business review like any other line.
* **The declared exception is an ephemeral self-hosted runner.** Where a product's production plane requires a fixed egress address or a private network path that a hosted runner cannot reach, that product's privileged workflows run on a self-hosted runner registered `--ephemeral` — a fresh container or virtual machine per job, with no writable shared volume — in a runner group labelled `privileged` that never accepts a branch-push-triggered job. The exception is recorded per product in the contract with its reason, and it is the only sanctioned self-hosted path for a privileged workflow.
* **The separation is asserted in the workflow, not only in configuration.** Each privileged workflow fails closed unless the runner it resolved to carries the `privileged` label or is hosted; a privileged workflow that finds itself on a shared-pool runner does not proceed.

Reconciliation carries three Blocking rows for this posture (Section 53.1): a self-hosted runner in the `privileged` group registered non-ephemerally; a privileged workflow resolving to a shared-pool label; and a branch-push-triggered workflow admitted to the `privileged` group.

**Machine identities.** Wherever the mechanism allows it, a machine identity is a GitHub App, not a seat-consuming machine user account — Section 40.1 permits both, and the App is preferred. The draft-PR machine account remains an account because only an account can serve there: draft pull requests need a Git author identity.

**Founder ops console.** The console is a read-only conversational query surface over Layer A operational data, implemented as its own **Hermes Agent** instance at the pinned commit (D69). Free GitHub Actions notifications to a messaging channel are tried first; they cover most of the need at zero risk and zero attack surface, and the activation trigger in the table above is unchanged. On activation, the console's authority and data boundaries are fixed:

* It runs under a Layer A read-only credential and carries no write tools: it holds no merge, approval, deployment or production authority, and it never writes records, decisions or board state — every state change anyone wants after reading a console answer goes through the existing platform write paths (D71).
* It never holds people-intelligence: Layer B is never reachable by any Hermes instance — no credential, no folder scope, no exception — and Layer B content is never relayed over a messaging channel (Section 89.1).
* The messaging gateway accepts commands only from a sender allowlist bound to Founder identities, with unauthorised senders silently ignored and the caged gateway defaults of Section 37.8 applied.
* Memory and skills persistence is disabled per the cage configuration contract (Section 37.8).
* Every answer it gives carries links back to the boards and records it summarised — the console is a lens over the surfaces of record, never a surface of record itself.
* The host it runs on gets a `tools.yaml` entry with an owner, the pinned commit, a patch cadence and a trust-boundary statement (Section 62).
* Its local-model configuration exists only where the Section 37.6 hardware exists; otherwise the console is not activated — a metered console key is prohibited (Section 36.6).

**Machine-drafted digests and wait-surface aids (D72).** Alongside the console, an approved roster of auxiliary machine-drafted outputs may run as scheduled jobs on the caged instances: a morning portfolio digest, wait-state summaries, meeting-prep briefs, and similar wait-surface aids. Each is machine-drafted, each links back to the source surfaces it summarises, and none of them is a new surface of record. All of them are wait surfaces under the notification contract (Section 92.11): they never page anyone. Uses outside this roster and the task whitelist remain rejected regardless of harness capability.

### 39.6 The Hermes deployment estate

One harness, four deployment slots, each a separate instance (D69):

| Slot | Status | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Background worker harness | Committed | The agent harness inside the Subsystem J background execution cage on the dedicated background host (Sections 37.6, 37.8) |
| Founder ops console | Committed | Read-only conversational query surface over Layer A operational data, sender-allowlisted to Founder identities (Section 39.5) |
| PR-review engine | Committed | Advisory machine reviewer behind the existing machine-review step — non-blocking, never approving (Section 39.5) |
| Personal-seat local-inference profile | Adopted on demand | Optional per-person profile pointed at the shared local inference endpoint — adopted per person, never mandated (Section 35.2) |

The separate-instances rule is structural: each slot runs as its own Hermes instance under its own OS user with its own `HERMES_HOME` and its own allowlists, because within one instance all authorised callers are equally privileged — privilege separation is instance separation. Every instance runs local inference only (Section 36.6), under the cage configuration contract (Section 37.8), and under the one-write-path rule: Hermes proposes; the platform disposes (D71).

The harness's kanban plugin is disabled on every instance (D70). Its sole permitted use, if ever enabled, is a machine-internal dispatch queue inside Subsystem J that no human ever uses as a work surface, under the Section 62.5 preconditions — it is never execution truth and never a second board; the OS boards remain the only execution truth (D49, Section 62.5).

Layer B is absolutely never reachable by any Hermes instance — no slot, no exception (Section 89.1). And Hermes remains a registered external tool in the Section 62.5 sense: every slot carries an exit condition, and the estate must survive the harness's removal with the operating model intact.

# Part VI - Operations, Reliability and Security

Part VI defines how the portfolio stays up, how it fails safely, and how it recovers. It covers the credential architecture and the workstation trust boundary; observability and the taxonomy that separates "our code is broken" from every other kind of broken; incident and security-incident response; backup, restore testing and disaster recovery — including the loss of the GitHub organisation itself; the degraded modes under which engineering continues when a platform dependency is unavailable; the out-of-hours exception policy that protects both customers and people; supply-chain, licensing and compliance controls; the operational asset inventory and its vendor-deadline watch; cloud cost observability; and the data, privacy and control-plane stack rules that everything else in this part leans on.

Two principles run through every section. First, the control plane observes the products; the products never depend on the control plane — nothing in a product's runtime path touches the operations VM, GitHub, or any dashboard. Second, an untested recovery path is not a recovery path: backups, exports, failovers and rebuild procedures are all exercised on a declared cadence, and staleness fails loudly.

Where a rule in this part reads a criticality value, it names the field it reads: `classification.reliability_criticality` governs operational stringency (restore cadence, manual-rollback requirements, monitoring depth, verification depth); `business.criticality` governs business importance and never tightens or loosens an operational control. The escalation role referenced throughout resolves through the organisational topology of Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution): the domain lead where domains are active, otherwise the single portfolio Team Lead.

## Section 40. Secrets and Production Access

Priority: P0.

### 40.1 Five secret tiers

Secrets live in exactly five tiers, strictly separated:

| Tier | Location | Contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developer | `.env.local`, git-ignored | Local-only values. Never real production credentials |
| CI | GitHub Actions secrets | Build-time and scan credentials |
| Staging | GitHub Environment: staging | Staging-scoped credentials only |
| Production | GitHub Environment: production | Production credentials, accessible only to the production deployment workflow |
| Control plane | Machine-credential store on the hosts that use them | Machine credentials — the reconciler, the provisioning CLI, the organisation-export token, the records-writer credential, the Layer B backup credential. Each is a least-privilege GitHub App or fine-grained PAT (the backup credential, an append-only object-store credential), rotated on a schedule, and bounded by the behavioural envelope declared below |

A secret never moves down a tier. A production credential appearing anywhere below the production tier is a security incident under Section 43 (Security Incident Workflow), not a cleanup task.

**The records-writer credential.** Workflow-written records and events need a machine write path, because machines can neither push to protected branches nor merge pull requests — CODEOWNERS approval is human-only — and without one every generated record would require a human-reviewed pull request (D76).

**That path is a separate repository, not a scoped bypass (D89).** A ruleset bypass actor on GitHub bypasses the rule wherever the rule applies; bypass is not scoped by path. A credential described as writing "only `records/**` and `events/**` through a path-scoped ruleset bypass" is in fact an unscoped write credential on the repository holding `people.yaml`, `roles.yaml`, `exceptions.yaml` and `policies.yaml` — every file from which authority is resolved — and the Blocking-drift rule meant to catch misuse cannot fire, because there is no scope for a write to fall outside. The estate does not rely on a guarantee the platform does not provide.

The record stores therefore live in their **own repository**, separate from the control-plane repository:

| Repository | Holds | Protection | Machine write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control plane | Registries, contracts, policies, exceptions, platform configuration | Full branch protection per Section 11.3. **No bypass actor exists** | None, except the reconciler's declared repair scope (Section 26.4) |
| Records | `records/**`, `events/**` | No protection rules — the store is append-only by convention and by the write path, not by review | The records-writer credential: a GitHub App installation token whose fine-grained `contents: write` is scoped to this repository alone |

The property this buys is the one the specification prefers everywhere else: **the credential cannot reach a registry, so the violation the old rule tried to detect becomes impossible rather than merely observable** — the same reasoning that makes the background layer's prohibitions architectural rather than policy (Section 37.3). It also separates two stores with different retention shapes: records grow without bound and are pruned on their declared retention classes, while registries are small and permanent.

Consequences, binding: the records repository is part of the minimum reconstruction set and the organisation export (Section 45); CI checks that derive metrics from records read across both repositories, and a check that cannot reach the records repository fails closed rather than reporting zero; and the control-plane repository's protection is stated without exception — **no machine identity is a bypass actor on it**, which is now literally true rather than true-by-convention.

**Append-only is enforced, not merely asserted (D107).** Removing protection rules from the records repository is what lets the credential append without review, and it removes the mechanism that previously made history durable. Invariant 47 and Section 63.1 assert immutability for exactly these records, so the property is restored by controls that do not require review:

* **Rewriting is blocked, appending is not.** A repository ruleset on the records repository's default branch blocks force pushes, branch deletion and tag deletion, with **no bypass actor**. Ordinary appends are unaffected — they are fast-forward commits, which the ruleset permits. The credential can therefore write freely and cannot rewrite.
* **Commits are signed by the writing identity.** The records-writer signs every commit, and a commit on the default branch that is unsigned, or signed by any other identity, is Blocking drift. This is the same authorship discipline the Renovate bypass carries (Section 33.2): a scoped grant is a grant to one identity, and the store must carry that identity's work only.
* **History is anchored where it cannot be rewritten.** Once per reconciliation run, the reconciler records the records repository's default-branch head SHA and commit count into the **control-plane repository**, which is fully protected. Because git history is a hash chain, any rewrite of a past record changes every subsequent SHA, so a head that does not descend from the last anchored SHA is proof of rewriting rather than evidence of it. A non-descendant head is **Blocking drift, Level 5** — the reconciliation-instrument failure class of Section 53.2, not a routine finding.
* **The off-site anchor already exists.** The object-locked organisation export (Section 45.3) is immutable by construction and carries the records repository, so a rewrite that somehow passed every control above is still contradicted by the last export. The export is the slow anchor; the per-run SHA is the fast one.

The distinction this preserves is the one that matters: the records repository is unprotected against *review*, deliberately, and protected against *rewriting*, absolutely. A store nobody reviews and anybody can rewrite would not be a record of anything.
**The reconciler's check-run scope.** Blocking-class drift must be able to hold a product repository's deployment path closed (Section 53.2), so the reconciler credential additionally holds check-run write on product repositories, used for exactly one named check. That is not a further machine write path: a check run carries status only — it writes no repository content, approves nothing, and satisfies no gate a human is required to satisfy. A check run published under that name by any identity other than the reconciler is Blocking drift.

**Fifth-tier operations.** Each control-plane machine credential — the reconciler credential, the provisioning CLI credential, the organisation-export token, the records-writer credential, the Layer B backup credential — carries an entry in the operational asset inventory (Section 49) recording its rotation cadence (initial value: quarterly), its named rotator (a holder of the DevOps capability), a link to the rotation runbook, its declared behavioural envelope, and the named owner of that envelope's alert configuration — so the alert on a run outside the envelope is itself an owned control, not an unowned hope. A one-page rotation runbook lives in the control-plane repository. After any rotation, a manual reconciliation run must complete clean before the rotation is recorded as done — a credential that rotates but no longer reconciles has not been rotated, it has been broken. Should the operations VM be lost, the re-issue source for these credentials is the Section 14.4 escrow.

**The behavioural envelope.** "Outside its scheduled window" is not a boundary for a credential that fires nightly, on registry change and at least hourly for security-class checks: the complement is nearly empty, an attacker simply acts inside the hour, and an alert that cannot fire is a gate that appears to be working and is not. Each fifth-tier credential therefore declares a behavioural envelope in its inventory entry, and a run outside it is Blocking drift: a **required signed run record** naming the scheduled trigger, so any run without a matching trigger record raises immediately; a **run-count ceiling per day** (calibrated configuration, initial value: twice the scheduled run count, recalibrated whenever the schedule changes); an **expected source host**; and **published per-run API-call counts**, so read-side abuse — enumerating and cloning every private repository emits no webhook and no event-log entry, and the Team-plan detection path of Section 45.3 cannot see it at all — surfaces as a volume anomaly rather than as nothing. Each credential's exact permission set is published in its inventory entry and in this section, the way Section 11.1 publishes GitHub's permission semantics, so over-scoping is visible on the page rather than latent in the provisioning.

### 40.2 Boundary rules

* **No production database access from developer machines.** This is a P0 security boundary, and the architecture enforcing it is declared, not assumed. Each product declares an `infrastructure:` block naming the network boundary of its production datastore — which networks and which principals may reach it — validated by contract CI exactly as the `recovery:` block is (Section 44), with `security.production_db_access: ci-only` as its declared default. Human infrastructure access is **provider-SSO-federated with no long-lived key**: a DevOps-capability holder reaches a provider console through federated sign-in, never through a stored credential, which is why the five secret tiers of Section 40.1 remain exactly five. Migrations and operational tasks run as controlled CI jobs (Section 34, Deployment, Release and Database Migrations). Reconciliation compares declared state against GitHub state and never leaves it, so the provider side is verified by **attestation rather than reconciliation**: the declared boundary carries a named owner who records a dated attestation that actual provider state matches the declaration — **calibrated configuration**; initial value monthly, run with the asset-inventory sweep of Section 49, recalibrated if an attestation ever finds drift. An expired or failed attestation is Blocking drift (Section 53.1). Invariants 24 and 26 rest on this declaration, this federation rule and this attestation. Naming the mechanism is what makes them auditable; a security group opened to the world with nothing declared to compare it against produces no finding at all.
* **The background machine layer holds no production credentials, no deploy keys, and no environment access.** Enforced by the machine account's permissions, not by its task whitelist (Section 37, Background Machine Layer).
* **No API keys in developer environments.** `env | grep -i api_key` must return empty. Shell profiles and repository `.env` files are checked during onboarding and re-checked quarterly. Some AI tools silently prefer an API key over subscription authentication when one is present, producing metered billing with no warning — this check protects the fixed-cost rule of Section 35 (AI Runtime Contract) as well as the credential boundary.
* **Secret rotation is documented per product**: who rotates, where, whether rotation requires a deployment, and whether it causes downtime. Rotation requiring a code deployment is a design weakness to be removed over time.
* **OIDC reservation.** The architecture reserves the capability for OIDC federation to eliminate long-lived cloud credentials from GitHub secrets, even where not implemented at launch. New cloud integrations prefer OIDC where the provider supports it.

### 40.3 The workstation trust boundary — stated explicitly

> A fully compromised developer workstation must not yield production database access, production credentials, or the ability to deploy to production.

This is enforced technically, not behaviourally: production secrets exist only in the production GitHub Environment, accessible only to the production deployment workflow, which requires an approval from someone other than the actor (Section 27, Four Distinct Events: Approve, Merge, Approve for Production, Deploy). A compromised workstation yields source code, the ability to open a pull request, and the ability to push a branch — and, because a branch push executes CI, it also yields execution with CI-tier credentials. It does not yield production. The CI-tier exposure is bounded by compensating controls: the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` is read-only, scan and build credentials are environment-gated where the platform supports it, and a workflow-file change pushed by a machine identity is Blocking drift. A second boundary is stated with the same force, because the first is silent about the highest-privilege identity in the system (Section 99.6, risk 6):

> A fully compromised engineering workstation must not yield the control-plane machine-credential store.

The reconciler credential and the organisation-export token live in the fifth tier on the operations VM, so a cached session or key from a workstation to that host reaches organisation-admin-equivalent write across every repository without ever touching production — and does so from the host the credential is expected to be used from, which is why the behavioural envelope of 40.1 is host- and volume-aware rather than only time-aware. Enforcement is technical: the fifth-tier credentials sit under a separate OS user or secret agent that a passive root shell does not read; shell access to the operations VM requires a second factor on top of the private network path of Section 51.4; and the rotator of a fifth-tier credential and the holder of host root on the machine that stores it are separated where headcount permits — where it does not, the concentration is a recorded accepted risk with a named holder and a dated review, never an unstated default. Every control in this part — and every judgement about what an engineering agent, extension or tool may run on a workstation (Section 36, Untrusted Input and Agent Toolchain Supply Chain) — is calibrated against both boundaries.

## Section 41. Observability and the Defect Taxonomy

Priority: P0.

### 41.1 Two questions, both required

Engineering metrics answer "how is the team doing." They do not answer "is this product healthy for customers right now." Both are required, and neither substitutes for the other.

Per-product operational signals: availability, error rate, latency, application health endpoint, database health, queue health, external dependency health, and business-critical synthetic checks. Monitoring depth scales with `classification.reliability_criticality` — a product declared `critical` carries synthetic checks on its business-critical workflows; a `low` product may carry only the health endpoint and error rate.

Two further machine signals join the per-product set. First, wherever a product declares `abuse_controls` (Section 43.5), at least one abuse detection signal — a failed-login rate or a limit-trip counter — is wired to the alert channel, with thresholds scaled by the product's `classification.reliability_criticality`: an abuse posture that no machine watches is a declaration, not a control. Second, a product whose declared `conformance_profile` is `client-app` declares its crash-free-session thresholds and their SEV mapping in the operational contract (initial calibration: below 99.5% crash-free sessions in a rolling 24 hours is SEV-2; below 98% is SEV-1), and crash alerts join the machine-signal set — a crash spike during a staged rollout is a machine detection that alerts like any other signal, never a discovery made by visiting a dashboard.

### 41.2 The three required endpoints

Every product whose declared `conformance_profile` exposes the service interface — the `service` default, and `white-label` per deployment — implements exactly three runtime endpoints. They are the entire runtime interface the operating system requires of a served product; a product implementing them in any language, on any stack, conforms. A product declaring a different profile (`client-app`, `library`, `batch`, `customer-hosted`, `static-site`) meets the equivalent evidence of Section 15.7 instead, and is never failed for lacking an endpoint its shape cannot serve.

| Endpoint | Provides |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | Liveness plus dependency health, distinguishing internal from external failure |
| `GET /version` | Deployed artifact digest and build metadata |
| `GET /metrics` | Prometheus format |
The three endpoints are not a public surface. `/metrics` carries error rates, queue depths, internal topology and — for every AI-consuming product — cumulative tokens and estimated spend per provider key (Section 38.4), which is commercial data and precisely the view that distinguishes a leaked key from a retry loop. Each product therefore declares `observability.telemetry_exposure` (Section 15.1), and the estate's declared posture is `private-authenticated`: the endpoints are reachable only over the private path from the operations VM, with a per-product scrape credential, exactly as Section 51.4 already requires of every control-plane surface. `public` remains available and is a recorded Founder decision, never a default inherited from a framework. The private path is a scrape path only — it carries the operations VM no production credential, no deploy key and no environment access, so Section 51.5 stands unqualified — and because the field is required, a product cannot reach launch readiness without answering the question.

`/version` closes the production evidence chain (Section 32, Production Evidence Chain): the digest it reports must equal the approved digest, and any mismatch is a P0 investigation.

### 41.3 Dependency failure distinction

The system must separate "our code is broken" from "an external dependency is broken." Each product declares its critical dependencies and monitors them independently through the dependency section of `/health`. A payment provider outage must not read as a product failure, must not open a code-defect investigation, and must not consume a weekend exception (Section 47) as though it were one.

### 41.4 The defect taxonomy — five categories

At twenty products, misdiagnosis is expensive. Every production defect is classified into exactly one of five categories, and the classification determines the response path:

| Category | Signal | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Code defect | Error correlates with a deployment; reproducible in staging | Normal or emergency change flow |
| Configuration defect | Error appears in one environment only; parity check flags divergence | Configuration change, no code deployment |
| Customer-specific integration defect | Error affects one tenant; their integration or configuration differs | Customer configuration change, no code deployment |
| External dependency defect | Dependency health check failing; multiple products affected if shared | Status recorded, no code change, customer communication if material |
| External model behaviour change | Product behaviour changes with no deployment and no configuration change; a pinned or provider-side AI model has changed underneath the product | Evaluation suite run against the declared `ai_runtime_dependency`; provider fallback per Section 38 (AI in the Product); no code deployment unless the fallback requires one |

The fifth category exists because a product consuming a hosted model can change behaviour without any change the evidence chain can see: `/version` identifies the artifact digest, not the model behind an API. Section 38 (AI in the Product) defines the `ai_runtime_dependency` declaration, the evaluation suite, and the fallback behaviour this category relies on. Customer support triages inbound reports into this same taxonomy (Section 22, Customer Support Operating Contract), and the incident learning loop aggregates over it (Section 58, Failure Patterns and the Incident Learning Loop).

### 41.5 Configuration is not a release

**A product should not require a code deployment for every customer-specific configuration issue.** Where configuration must change per customer, it lives in configuration rather than in code, and changing it is not a release. A product repeatedly deploying code to fix customer configuration is carrying a design defect, and the pattern is raised through technical debt governance (Section 56, Technical Debt Governance).

## Section 42. Incident Management and Detection

Priority: P0.

### 42.1 Severity model

| Level | Definition | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEV-1 | Customer-wide outage, data loss, security breach, payment failure | Immediate from detection, including out of hours |
| SEV-2 | Major feature broken | Next business day, unless the product declares `support_model: extended` |
| SEV-3 | Limited customer impact | Next business day |
| SEV-4 | Minor defect | Normal backlog |

A shared service inherits the highest `classification.reliability_criticality` of its consumers for severity purposes (Section 20, Shared Services and the Dependency Graph): an outage of a shared service serving a critical product is classified as if it were that product's outage.

### 42.2 Detection honesty — the detection expectation

The severity model promises SEV-1 response "immediate". That promise is only honest if the system is equally explicit about when a SEV-1 is *noticed*. Each product's `support_model` therefore declares a detection expectation, and the SEV-1 clock is defined against it:

| `support_model` | `detection_expectation` | Detection expectation | Meaning of "immediate" |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `business-hours` | `next-business-morning` | Detection is best-effort outside working hours; an out-of-hours alert may not be seen until the next working morning | The SEV-1 "immediate" clock starts at **detection**, not at occurrence |
| `extended` | `rostered-window` | A staffed watch or paging path covers the declared `coverage_window` | Immediate within the declared coverage window |
| `24x7` | `continuous` | A funded, staffed rota with a paging path — an onboarding blocker without one (Section 47) | Immediate, around the clock |

`detection_expectation` is **derived, not authored**: this table is the mapping, its three tokens are the closed value set, and CI fails a contract whose declared value differs from the value its `support_model` implies — a product cannot declare a detection expectation its staffing does not honour. The worst-case undetected window that Section 21.4 checks an uptime SLA against is computed from the token and the declared working calendar (Section 6.4): for `next-business-morning`, the longest interval from any non-working minute to the start of the next working day, public holidays included; for `rostered-window`, the longest gap between the accepted rota windows covering the declared `coverage_window`; for `continuous`, zero. One definition, so the feasibility row of 21.4 and the `check-commitment` command compute the same number.

This is not a weakening of the response commitment; it is the honest statement of what is staffed. A `business-hours` product whose customer expects faster detection has a commitments conflict, surfaced before signature through Section 21 (Customer Commitments and SLA Registry), not discovered during an incident.

Two mechanisms make the expectation real:

* **A documented phone-escalation path exists from the alert channel.** Alerts route to a channel monitored by the Founder and the Team Lead (Section 47); either of them can reach any responder by direct phone call, and the numbers, order and fallback are written down — not reconstructed at 03:00.
* **Detection-to-response latency is a measured metric**: time from first alert (or first customer report, whichever is earlier) to a responder acknowledging the incident, recorded on every incident record and reviewed monthly (Section 103.3). A `business-hours` product persistently detecting SEV-1s many hours after occurrence is evidence for changing its support model or its monitoring, and the metric makes that decision empirical.

**Automated containment fires before any human wakes.** Where a product declares `automated_containment` (Section 15.1), the declared alert class triggers the declared action — halting writes or disabling the flag — the moment it fires; the action is armed by the Primary Owner at configuration time, verified during launch readiness, and every firing is recorded on the incident record as the first response step. It narrows blast radius during the honest detection gap of business-hours products; it never substitutes for the human response that follows.

### 42.3 Response flow

```
Alert → classify severity
     → in hours: Primary Responder leads, Backup Responder supports
     → out of hours: SEV-1, plus SEV-2 where the product declares
       support_model: extended (Section 47)
     ↓
Rollback possible? (pure redeploy of prior digest)
  YES → any holder of incident-response rolls back → smoke → observe   ← PREFERRED
        (rollback of an already-approved digest needs no fresh
         approval — the dedicated rollback workflow of Section 27.2)
  NO  → is a feature flag available?
          YES → disable the flag → observe                             ← NEXT BEST
          NO  → hotfix path:
                  incident issue created
                  minimal change only
                  automated tests still run
                  second reviewer still required
                  authorised by escalation role
                  deploy → smoke → observe
     ↓
Postmortem within 5 working days
     ↓
Every production bug becomes a permanent regression test
```

**The emergency path does not skip verification.** It reduces scope: reproducible incident, regression test where feasible, relevant automated tests, second reviewer, deployment record, rollback plan, postmortem. Weekend or night pressure does not remove independent review — the second-reviewer requirement survives every emergency (Section 47.6). Missing permanent tests become mandatory follow-up work in H2, not H3 (Section 29, Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change).

**The client-app response ladder.** Where the product's declared `conformance_profile` is `client-app`, digest rollback does not exist — the broken build is already installed on customers' devices. The ladder for such a product is: **halt the staged rollout** (this protects only users who have not yet updated); **trigger the remote kill-switch or feature flag** — the client-app conformance requirement of Section 15.7, cross-referenced here so the capability exists before the incident that needs it; **request expedited store review** for the corrected build; and **mitigate users stranded on the broken build** through server-side controls (API-side guards, degraded-but-safe responses) while the store review runs.
