The background machine layer does **not** run on the operations VM: it runs on its own dedicated host (Section 37), the two hosts share no credentials, and the background host carries the Section 37.8 network egress allowlist permitting only GitHub, the package registries and the LAN inference endpoint. Any pressure to make the VM load-bearing for a product runtime path is refused by the invariant in 51.3.

# Part VII - Operating System Governance

The operating system governs products, people and change. This part governs the operating system. It defines how the system observes its own health, detects and grades its own drift, records its own exceptions, prices its own automation, learns from its own failures, budgets its own change, versions its own contracts, and evolves its own structure — with the same rigour it applies to any product. The operating system must be at least as recoverable, at least as observable and at least as honestly measured as the products it manages.

## Section 52. Operating System Health

### 52.1 The question being answered

The Founder and Team Lead must be able to answer, without asking anyone: is the operating system itself healthy, degrading, or quietly accumulating debt that will surface as an incident later?

The output is a single generated Operating System Health Report, refreshed daily, with one headline state — Healthy, Degrading or Impaired — and drill-down into the signals below. It is a report, not a new dashboard product: it renders in the Grafana instance the platform already requires (Section 92, Dashboard and View Architecture).

The headline state is a triage entry point, not a score. Composite scores are prohibited everywhere in this system — for products, for people, and for the operating system itself (Section 92, Dashboard and View Architecture). The headline is computed from **budget consumption, not from the presence of a class**, and the rule is stated once, here: **Impaired** when any Blocking signal is open, or the flat portfolio-wide Red tolerance is exceeded; **Degrading** when any Red is open, or the portfolio-scaled Amber tolerance is exceeded; **Healthy** otherwise. The tolerances are the ones already declared in `os-health.yaml` (Section 53.4), so the headline is calibratable without a code change. The obvious alternative — worst open class wins — would read Degrading every day, because the drift budget deliberately tolerates up to two open Amber per product as routine remediation debt; a report that reads Degrading every day teaches its reader to skim, which is the failure the budget exists to prevent. Because the state is a maximum over budget breaches rather than a weighted sum, no blending occurs. The headline therefore never averages, weights or blends signals; it always names its top contributing signals so that the reader lands directly on the dimension that is actually breached. The correct action differs entirely depending on which signal is red, and any aggregation that hides the signal hides the action.

### 52.2 The unified signal table

Every operating-system health signal lives in this one table, with a single identifier space. There are exactly forty-seven signals. Signal definitions, thresholds, time windows, baselines, drift classes, expected interpretations, known limitations, owners and activation dependencies are declared in `os-health.yaml`; values are derived, never hand-maintained. The table below renders the operator-facing subset — the full eight-attribute declaration required by Section 84.6 lives in the file, and the table is a view of it, never a second copy.

**Arming discipline (D77).** Every signal row in `os-health.yaml` declares an `activation_dependency`: the record store, collector or build phase that feeds it. A signal whose source is not yet live renders as **unarmed — not yet instrumented**: it is excluded from drift-budget counts, cannot breach, and never renders as Amber or as missing data. A signal arms when its declared source is live **and** that source holds the full lookback window the signal's definition requires; until both hold it renders as **unarmed — insufficient history**, on the same terms. Every `os-health.yaml` row therefore declares a `lookback_window` beside its `activation_dependency`, and window fill is what the arming event records. Without that conjunction, the day DevLake connects SIG-40 evaluates every assigned cross-reviewer in the portfolio as having no participation in 180 days and SIG-04 computes a spread over three days of reviews — the wall of amber, produced by the instrument rather than by the system. The arming is itself an event, recorded like any other. This protects the instrument's credibility: a report that opens as a wall of amber teaches its reader to skim.

Near-duplicate signals have been merged deliberately: Team Lead bottleneck and Team Lead overload are one graded signal (SIG-07); QA bottleneck and QA overload are one graded signal (SIG-08); reviewer imbalance and review concentration are one signal (SIG-04); the two stale-assignment definitions are one signal (SIG-02). Orphan risk (SIG-05), role gap (SIG-27) and succession gap (SIG-26) remain three distinct signals with explicitly disjoint definitions, stated beneath the table.

| ID | Signal | Definition | Source | Default class on breach | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SIG-01 | Stale product contract | `product.yaml` not reviewed within 180 days, or `contract_version` behind the supported minimum | Control plane | Amber | Primary Owner |
| SIG-02 | Stale assignment or allocation | An assignment past `end_date` still present, an assignment referencing a departed person, an expired temporary assignment still active, or an allocation not reviewed within its configured window | Registries | Red | Team Lead |
| SIG-03 | Permission drift | GitHub Team membership, branch protection or environment reviewers differ from declared state | Reconciliation | Red; Blocking if it weakens a security control | Team Lead |
| SIG-04 | Review concentration | Gini-style spread of Gate 2 reviews across eligible reviewers over 90 days beyond the configured spread | DevLake | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-05 | Orphan risk | Any product with no active Primary Owner, no active Cross-Reviewer, or no named responder | Registries | Blocking | Team Lead |
| SIG-06 | Ready-queue misses | Ready Queue Miss events (Section 29, Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change), 30-day rolling count and trend | Planning board | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-07 | Team Lead bottleneck | Median time from plan submission to Gate 1 approval, and count of items waiting. Graded: Amber on breach; Red on sustained breach with delegation not in place ("sustained" is calibrated configuration, initial value 6 consecutive weeks) | DevLake | Amber, Red on sustained breach | Founder |
| SIG-08 | QA bottleneck | Median time in the Verify column and verification backlog by product; verification demand above sustainable capacity. Graded: Amber on breach; Red on sustained breach across multiple measurement windows (same calibrated "sustained" threshold) | DevLake | Amber, Red on sustained breach | Founder |
| SIG-09 | Platform migration backlog | Products on a platform version behind current, weighted by age of lag | Control plane | Amber, Red beyond two versions | Team Lead |
| SIG-10 | Transitional compatibility backlog | Products with `platform_compatibility: transitional` and days in that state | Control plane | Amber, Red beyond the declared transition window | Team Lead |
| SIG-11 | Stale feature flags | Progressive-delivery flags older than their declared removal target | Product repositories | Amber | Primary Owner |
| SIG-12 | Stale platform versions | Pinned GSD, reusable workflow or action SHAs behind current beyond the policy window | Control plane | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-13 | Failed reconciliations | Reconciliation job failures, or unresolved findings older than their class response time | Reconciliation | Red | Team Lead |
| SIG-14 | Failed canary deployments | Canary sets that failed or were abandoned without a closed manifest | Change manifests | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-15 | Repeated manual overrides | Count of admin bypasses, forced merges, manual deploys and skipped gates | Organisation webhook events plus the event log on the Team plan; the organisation audit log where the plan tier provides its API (Section 45.3). The manual audit-log review of 45.3 covers the override classes neither source can see | Red | Founder |
| SIG-16 | Break-glass usage | Count, duration and post-use review completion | Exception registry | Red if review overdue | Founder |
| SIG-17 | Restore-test currency | Products approaching or past their restore window — the rolling 90-day floor, or the tightened cadence their `classification.reliability_criticality` requires (Section 44, Backup, Recovery and Restore Testing) | Control plane | Amber approaching, Blocking past | QA |
| SIG-18 | Verification-contract coverage gaps | Requirements shipped without a mapped verification mechanism, or a contract whose seeded-defect case passed on its last run (Section 31.2) | Verification contracts | Red | QA |
| SIG-19 | Exception population | Open exceptions, expired-but-open exceptions, and exceptions renewed more than twice | Exception registry | Amber, Red on repeat renewal | Team Lead |
| SIG-20 | Policy currency | Policies past their review date | Policy register | Amber | Policy owner |
| SIG-21 | Control-plane SLO burn | Control-plane service-objective error-budget consumption | Control-plane SLOs (Section 51, Data, Privacy and the Control-Plane Stack) | Amber where burn is ahead of the elapsed period, Red on budget exhausted — an exhausted budget reduces that month's platform change budget (Section 51.2) | Team Lead |
| SIG-22 | Missing framework evidence | A KPI with no evidence source and no instrumentation plan at review time | Framework registry | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-23 | Outstanding framework mapping | A person or role whose performance-framework mapping is incomplete | Framework registry | Amber | Framework maintainer |
| SIG-24 | Stale performance evidence | An evidence bundle not refreshed within the review cadence | Layer B | Amber | Founder |
| SIG-25 | Capability gap unaddressed | A role-required capability at Learning or below with no development action, at medium or higher confidence | Capability matrix | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-26 | Succession gap | A critical product or role whose current holder is active, but for which no ready successor exists | Registries | Red | Founder |
| SIG-27 | Role gap | A required role with no active holder at all | Registries | Red | Founder |
| SIG-28 | Operational dependency risk | Single-point concentration of actual operational knowledge or practice on one person for a critical product or capability, even where declared ownership and succession are formally in place | Registries plus derived activity aggregates | Red | Founder |
| SIG-29 | High management intervention | Sustained elevated aggregate Management Attention across the team as a whole, never a single person | Layer B aggregate | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-30 | Sustained team overload | Team-level overload across multiple measurement windows (calibrated "sustained" threshold, initial value 6 consecutive weeks) | Capacity model | Red | Founder |
| SIG-31 | Sustained team under-utilisation | Team-level unused capacity with a diagnosed planning cause | Capacity model | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-32 | Signal override rate | A signal class overridden repeatedly — this signal applies to every instrument in this table, and to drift classes (Section 53) | Health report history | Amber | Owner of the overridden signal |
| SIG-33 | Sunset overstay | A product in Sunset beyond its declared window — half-retired products consume attention indefinitely (Section 18) | Product contracts | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-34 | Organisation export staleness | The scheduled GitHub organisation export (Section 45) missing, failed, or not restore-tested within its 90-day window | Export job telemetry | Red | Escalation role |
| SIG-35 | Cloud cost anomaly | Product infrastructure spend outside its declared `monthly_budget_band`, or aggregate control-plane spend outside the declared `control_plane_budget_band` (Section 50) | Provider billing telemetry | Red | Primary Owner; Founder for the control-plane band |
| SIG-36 | Control-plane patch staleness | Grafana, DevLake or operations-VM OS behind the declared patch cadence (Section 51) | Tool register | Amber; Red beyond twice the cadence | Team Lead |
| SIG-37 | Forecast accuracy degradation | A forecast class scored retrospectively wrong more often than right (Section 72) | Forecast scoring records | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-38 | Brownfield adoption health | A product in pre-onboarding mode past its deadline, or adoption signals regressing (Section 96) | Control plane | Amber; Red past deadline | Team Lead |
| SIG-39 | Bootstrap exception unclosed | A bootstrap-mode exception (Section 95) past its expiry with its gate still unarmed | Exception registry | Red | Founder |
| SIG-40 | Cross-review participation | An assigned cross-reviewer with no review, change or incident participation on that product within 180 days — the assignment is nominally satisfied and operationally hollow (Section 17) | DevLake plus registries | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-41 | Support-intake anomaly | A product's 7-day support-intake volume deviating from its trailing 28-day baseline beyond the calibrated threshold (initial value: 2× the trailing 28-day daily average, sustained across the 7-day window) | Support-intake records | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-42 | AI-eval regression | The scheduled evaluation suite regressing beyond its declared tolerance on any product with an `ai_runtime_dependency` (initial value: any scored dimension falling more than 5 percentage points below its recorded baseline) | `records/eval/` | Red | Primary Owner |
| SIG-43 | Founder operating load | Total Founder attention hours across all eight categories (Section 67) above the declared Founder operating-load ceiling, over a trailing window that is calibrated configuration with an initial value of 4 weeks. The ceiling is calibrated configuration; its initial value is recorded in the Section 103.14 pre-Phase-1 baseline capture and refitted at calibration review. This is a role-level measure of the Founder role and is never performance evidence | Attention ledger | Amber; Red on sustained breach (calibrated "sustained", initial value 6 consecutive weeks), routed to the escalation role | Team Lead |
| SIG-44 | Operating-system net value | The operating system's own standing ledger entry (Section 57.2) reading negative net value, or measured ritual hours above its declared quarterly attention-hours budget line | `economics.yaml` | Amber; Red on two consecutive quarters, which is the Section 57.1 simplify-or-retire trigger | Founder |
| SIG-45 | Change-budget breach | Platform changes or fleet migrations above the Section 59.3 change budget in the period, or net policy growth positive across a rolling two quarters | `platform-roadmap.yaml` plus the policy register | Amber | Team Lead |
| SIG-46 | Audit-log review staleness | The manual audit-log review of Section 45.3 missing, failed, or older than its declared cadence — the compensating control for a P0 accepted risk | `records/security-reviews/` | Red | Escalation role |
| SIG-47 | Unclosed learning-loop items | An open postmortem older than 30 days with unclosed generated items, or a closed production-bug incident with no linked regression-test item (Section 58.4) — the standing escalation behind invariant 2 | `records/postmortems/` plus `records/incidents/` | Amber | QA |

Disjoint definitions, stated once and binding:

* **Orphan risk (SIG-05)** is a *product-structure* condition: a product's declared ownership slots — Primary Owner, Cross-Reviewer, responder — are empty or held by inactive people.
* **Role gap (SIG-27)** is an *organisational* condition: a role the organisation requires has no active holder, regardless of any particular product.
* **Succession gap (SIG-26)** is a *forward-looking* condition: the role or product is currently held, but no ready backup exists if the holder becomes unavailable.

A single event can raise more than one of these — a departure can convert a succession gap into a role gap and an orphan simultaneously — but each signal answers a different question and drives a different action.

People-derived signals (SIG-22, SIG-23, SIG-24, SIG-25, SIG-26, SIG-27, SIG-28, SIG-29, SIG-30, SIG-31 and SIG-40) appear on the health report only as team-level and role-level aggregates. No per-person value, name or drill-down appears on this or any general surface; individual-level detail exists only inside access-controlled Layer B (Section 90, Access Control Architecture). One carve-out applies to SIG-40: the assignment-status fact underlying it — a stale cross-reviewer flag — is operational allocation data, and may appear, naming the assignee, on the reviewer-matrix view; the health-report rendering of SIG-40 remains team- and role-level aggregate.

### 52.3 Presentation discipline

The anti-pattern to avoid is presenting all forty-seven signals with equal weight. The report shows the headline state, then only the signals currently outside their class threshold, then everything else on demand. A signal within tolerance earns no screen space.

### 52.4 Signal priorities

* **P0:** SIG-02 (stale assignments), SIG-03 (permission drift), SIG-05 (orphan risk), SIG-13 (failed reconciliations), SIG-15 (repeated manual overrides), SIG-16 (break-glass usage), SIG-17 (restore-test currency), SIG-34 (organisation export staleness), SIG-39 (bootstrap exception unclosed), SIG-46 (audit-log review staleness).
* **P1:** SIG-06 (ready-queue misses), SIG-07 (Team Lead bottleneck), SIG-08 (QA bottleneck), SIG-09 (platform migration backlog), SIG-10 (transitional backlog), SIG-18 (verification coverage gaps), SIG-19 (exception population), SIG-26 (succession gap), SIG-27 (role gap), SIG-28 (operational dependency risk), SIG-30 (sustained team overload), SIG-35 (cloud cost anomaly), SIG-38 (brownfield adoption health), SIG-40 (cross-review participation), SIG-41 (support-intake anomaly), SIG-42 (AI-eval regression), SIG-43 (Founder operating load).
* **P2:** SIG-01 (stale contracts), SIG-04 (review concentration), SIG-11 (stale flags), SIG-12 (stale platform versions), SIG-14 (canary failures), SIG-20 (policy currency), SIG-21 (control-plane SLO burn), SIG-22 (missing framework evidence), SIG-23 (outstanding framework mapping), SIG-24 (stale performance evidence), SIG-25 (capability gap unaddressed), SIG-29 (high management intervention), SIG-31 (sustained team under-utilisation), SIG-32 (signal override rate), SIG-33 (sunset overstay), SIG-36 (control-plane patch staleness), SIG-37 (forecast accuracy degradation), SIG-47 (unclosed learning-loop items), SIG-44 (operating-system net value), SIG-45 (change-budget breach).

Tiers enumerate identifiers, never ranges: the CI check below reads identifiers, and a range that reads naturally to a human leaves the signals inside it in no tier at all.

A CI check validates that every SIG identifier in the signal table appears in exactly one priority tier; an unassigned or doubly assigned signal fails validation of `os-health.yaml`.

The first Phase G1 health report arms only the signals whose `activation_dependency` is already live; every other signal renders as unarmed — not yet instrumented, per the arming discipline of Section 52.2 (D77). P0 signals do not all arm at the same phase, and the report states which, rather than implying a coverage it does not have. SIG-15, SIG-16 and SIG-39 arm in Phase 1, from the GitHub audit log and the exception registry. SIG-02 and SIG-05 arm at Phase 3, when the assignment registries are populated. SIG-03 and SIG-13 arm when reconciliation goes live in early hardening (Section 98.3). SIG-17 arms at the first recorded restore test in Phase 6. SIG-34 arms when the organisation export job first runs. Because Phase G1 depends on reconciliation being operational (Section 98.5), every P0 signal is in fact armed by the time the first report is generated in the planned order — but the guarantee is the arming discipline and the per-signal `activation_dependency`, never a blanket claim, and any P0 signal still unarmed when the report generates is named on it as unarmed rather than counted as clean.

### 52.5 Calibrating the instrument itself

The health report is an instrument, and instruments are gamed unless they are calibrated by someone other than the party they measure. The following guards are binding:

* The calibration rule that governs KPIs — a repeatedly overridden signal is a suspect signal (Section 84, Performance Periods, Framework Evolution and KPI Calibration) — applies with identical force to every row of the signal table and to every drift class in Section 53. SIG-32 exists to make repeated overrides visible rather than silent.
* Signal definitions, thresholds and class assignments in `os-health.yaml` are reviewed at the same calibration cadence as KPIs. The review asks, per signal: has this signal ever changed a decision; has it been overridden, and why; is its threshold still honest?
* Threshold changes are recorded as decisions with rationale. A threshold loosened in the same quarter in which the signal breached is flagged on the next calibration review automatically.
* The Founder consumes this report; the Team Lead owns most of its thresholds. That separation of reporting party from consuming party is intentional, and the calibration review is where the Founder audits the instrument rather than only its readings.
* The Founder's own operating load is an instrument like any other, and SIG-43 is therefore owned by the Team Lead, not by the Founder: a party does not calibrate the instrument that measures it. Its sustained breach routes to the escalation role, so clearing it never depends on the person it measures noticing it. The quarterly review weighs the trend; the signal is the detector.

### 52.6 Registry of control-plane files

Every control-plane artifact is listed here with its owner and purpose. The inventory spans both control-plane repositories — the control-plane repository proper and the records repository (Section 40.1, D89) — and the row for each artifact names which one holds it where that is not obvious. This table is the complete inventory — thirty entries. Any proposal for a new control-plane artifact must state which existing file cannot hold the content; if an existing file can hold it, the proposal is rejected. All hand-maintained artifacts live in the control-plane repository, are version-controlled, CI-validated and schema-versioned by the versioned-contract mechanism of Section 60 (Platform Versioning, Versioned Contracts and Compatibility) — except the Layer B stores and the conduct-records store, whose durable homes are stated in their own rows and are never any org-readable repository. Everything else the operating system produces is a generated report, not a file a human edits.

## Section 53. Reconciliation and the Drift Budget

A declarative operating system without reconciliation degrades into documentation. A scheduled job compares declared state against actual platform state and grades the response.

### 53.1 Declared versus actual

| Declared in | Compared against | On mismatch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `people.yaml` | GitHub organisation membership | Alert; block on removal drift |
| `people.yaml` capabilities | Team membership implying authority | Alert |
| `product.yaml` assignments | GitHub Team membership | **Fail CI on the affected repository** |
| `product.yaml` assignments | CODEOWNERS | Regenerate; alert if hand-edited |
| Branch protection template | Actual branch protection | **Alert immediately; block deployment on the affected repository** |
| Workflow template version | Actual workflow file | Alert; flag `platform_compatibility` as drifted |
| Environment configuration template | Actual environments | Alert |
| Environment deployment branch and tag policy | Actual environment configuration | **Alert immediately; block deployment on the affected repository** |
| Declared `infrastructure:` boundary (Section 40.2) | The latest provider-side attestation record | **Blocking past its attestation window** |
| `product.yaml` lifecycle | Renovate, monitoring and CI configuration | Auto-repair where safe; alert otherwise |
| Assignment `end_date` | Current Team membership | **Auto-revoke expired access** |
| Declared dependency | Shared service registry | Fail CI on unknown dependency |
| `platform.yaml` workflow versions | The commit SHA each `workflows/*` tag currently resolves to | **Blocking on any change — a moved tag reaches every consumer with no reviewable diff** |
| Renovate bypass ruleset | The ruleset carrying the diff-path status check | **Blocking where that ruleset names any bypass actor** |
| Declared write-freshness window per record store (Section 97.2) | Latest commit timestamp on the store's path | Amber; **Blocking for `events/`, `records/deployments/` and `records/uat/`** |
| Production-restore record (Section 44.5) | Recorded `integrity_check` result and named verifier | Red where either is absent |
| `product.yaml` `restore_tested` | Newest passing record in `records/restore-tests/` | **Blocking**: a declared date with no matching record is an unevidenced reliability claim, not a scheduling question |

A workflow-file change pushed by a machine identity is Blocking-class drift, regardless of the change's content: workflow files define the enforcement path itself, and no machine credential is authorised to alter it.

A commit authored or committed by any identity other than the declared bypass actor, on a branch that merges under that actor's bypass, is Blocking-class drift for the same reason: a bypass is a grant to one identity, and a branch merging under it must carry that identity's work only (Section 33.2).

Silent drift is not permitted. Every reconciliation run writes its result, and a clean run is recorded as clean.

**The seeded-canary rule.** A permanent seeded drift record — a deliberately planted, clearly labelled mismatch in the comparison set — exists at all times, and every reconciliation run MUST find it. A run that reports zero findings, including the canary, is a FAILED run, not a clean one: it proves the instrument stopped looking, not that nothing drifted. Every run additionally records its per-registry comparison counts — how many rows of each registry it actually compared — so that a silently narrowed comparison is itself visible drift. This is the negative-test philosophy of Section 95.4 applied to the instrument itself.

**The independent control verifier.** Reconciliation regenerates CODEOWNERS and re-applies branch protection, and is also the only thing that checks them — an instrument that can rewrite the wall it inspects and then report the wall intact. The seeded canary catches an instrument that stopped looking; it does not catch one that reports falsely. A second verifier therefore runs **off the operations VM and under a different credential**: a scheduled workflow in the control-plane repository, holding its own read-only fine-grained credential, asserting that no machine identity appears in any CODEOWNERS file in any repository, that branch protection and ruleset JSON match the committed template, and that the ruleset bypass-actor list is exactly the set Sections 40.1 and 33.2 declare, with their declared scopes. It writes its result to a surface the operations VM cannot write to, and its own absence for one cycle is Level 5. CODEOWNERS and branch protection are the two files that constitute the machine-authority wall (Section 37.3); no control that can be rewritten by the credential it is checking is a control.

A reconciliation failure caused by an acknowledged external outage — a GitHub or provider incident confirmed on the vendor's status channel — is annotated `external-cause` on the run record rather than raised as raw Red; the annotation names the outage, and the run is re-executed once the dependency recovers.

Every drift finding carries an `acknowledged_by` and `acknowledged_at` field, written by the first responder who claims it, so that a second responder can see at a glance that the interrupt is already claimed rather than duplicating the response.

Priority: P1 for the reconciliation job and the comparison set; P0 for the blocking rows, which are security controls.

### 53.2 The five reconciliation levels

| Level | Behaviour | Applies to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level 1 — Detect | Record the finding with evidence and age. No notification. | Green-class drift: display names, documentation links, non-blocking metadata |
| Level 2 — Warn | Raise on the health report and notify the owner. No block. | Amber-class drift: stale contracts, stale flags, review concentration |
| Level 3 — Auto-repair | Reconcile actual state back to declared state automatically, then record the repair. | Safe, idempotent, reversible repairs only: Team membership sync from registries, CODEOWNERS regeneration, label and board field sync, re-applying declared branch protection, removing expired assignments and expired access |
| Level 4 — Block | Fail CI or block the deployment path until resolved. | Blocking-class drift: orphaned product, expired non-employee access still provisioned, restore test overdue, security control weakened, artifact digest mismatch, workflow-file change pushed by a machine identity |
| Level 5 — Escalate | Create an incident and notify the escalation role, then the Founder if unresolved within its response time. | Production environment drift, credential exposure, repeated failed auto-repair, a repair class discovered to have written incorrect state (53.7), the reconciliation job itself failing |

### 53.3 The auto-repair rule

Binding: a repair is permitted only when it moves the system toward the declared state **and** the declared state is at least as restrictive as the actual state. Reconciliation never loosens a control automatically, never modifies production runtime configuration, never modifies data, and never rotates or writes secrets. Where actual state is stricter than declared state, reconciliation raises Level 2 for human judgment rather than relaxing the control.

### 53.4 Drift classes and the drift budget

Not all deviation is equally urgent, and treating it as such produces alert fatigue — which is itself a failure mode of the operating system. There is exactly one drift severity scale, used everywhere:

| Class | Meaning | Response time | Who acts | Blocks work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Green | Within tolerance; recorded only | None | Nobody | No |
| Amber | Real but non-urgent; scheduled remediation | Next planning cycle, H2 | Owner | No |
| Red | Material risk to security, reliability or continuity | Within 2 business days | Owner plus Team Lead | No, but visible on the Founder view (Section 93, The Founder View) |
| Blocking | Unsafe to proceed | Immediate | Team Lead or escalation role | Yes — CI or deployment path blocked |

Older vocabulary is retired and maps onto this scale exactly once, here: *dangerous* drift is **Blocking**, *correctable* drift is **auto-repairable** (Level 3), *informational* drift is **Level 1**. No other severity vocabulary exists anywhere in this system.

Budget rules:

* Each class has a tolerance declared in `os-health.yaml`. The two middle classes are budgeted on deliberately different bases, and the difference is the point: **Amber scales with the portfolio** — up to 2 open Amber per product, so the ceiling reads 16 at eight products and 40 at twenty — because Amber is routine remediation debt and a fixed ceiling would tighten silently as products are added. **Red is deliberately held flat at 3 portfolio-wide**, and does *not* scale, because Red is the volume of material unremediated risk the team can actually hold in attention at once; that number is a property of the team, not of the portfolio. A growing portfolio therefore makes the Red budget bind harder, and that is the intended pressure: it forces remediation capacity or portfolio lifecycle decisions rather than absorbing risk quietly. Green is unlimited; Blocking has no budget. Initial calibrated values are set at eight products, and any change in portfolio size automatically prompts a recalibration of these tolerances at the next calibration review — for Red, that review asks whether team remediation capacity has changed, never merely whether the product count has.
* Exceeding an Amber tolerance is itself an Amber signal about the operating system, not about any individual product. It means remediation capacity is under-allocated.
* Security drift and production environment drift are never classified below Red, regardless of apparent impact.
* Class assignment lives in configuration and is reviewable; it is not decided ad hoc during an incident.

### 53.5 Reclassification authority

Reclassifying a finding downward requires the same authority as approving an exception for it (Section 54), and is recorded as a decision. There is no informal path from Red to Amber.

### 53.6 Calibration and closure quality

The drift budget is a target, and targets attract gaming: tolerances can be kept under ceiling by widening Green definitions or slow-walking detection. Two guards are therefore binding:

* **Class definitions and tolerances are themselves calibration-reviewed.** Drift class definitions, thresholds and tolerances in `os-health.yaml` go through the same calibration review as health signals and KPIs (Section 52.5; Section 84, Performance Periods, Framework Evolution and KPI Calibration). A drift class whose findings are repeatedly reclassified or overridden is a suspect class, and the review says so explicitly.
* **Closure quality is auditable.** Every closed drift finding records what changed and links its evidence. A sample of closed findings is audited at the quarterly review; a finding closed without evidence of remediation, or a finding that recurs in the same scope shortly after closure, is reopened and counted as a closure-quality defect, not as new drift. Fast-closing findings to keep counts pretty therefore fails the audit rather than passing the budget.

### 53.7 The control-loop gap procedure

The control loop can fail in two directions. It can go dark — a reconciliation gap, an export gap, or a health-report gap. It can also run and repair against a wrongly-computed declared state, which completes, records clean, and is therefore invisible to every check that asks only whether the loop ran. When any such gap closes, the escalation role runs the gap procedure, mirroring the recovery list of Section 46.1:

* **Replay expiries** that should have fired during the gap — assignment `end_date`s, temporary access, exception expiries — and revoke or revert anything now overdue.
* **Diff-audit** every access grant, merge and production approval made during the gap window against declared state, treating the gap window as unverified rather than presumed clean.
* **Re-run all standing checks** — reconciliation, export verification, health-report generation — and confirm clean results, including the seeded canary.
* **Record the gap as an incident** at Level 5, with a postmortem on the standard cadence (Section 58.4).
* **Mark interim records `gap-window`.** Every record produced during the gap window carries the `gap-window` mark until re-verified; a gap-window record is not evidence for any gate until re-verification clears the mark.
**When the loop ran wrong.** A repair class discovered to have written incorrect state is a Level 5 escalation in its own right (53.2), and the same window discipline applies: freeze that repair class, enumerate its repairs in the affected window from the repair records of Section 26.4, revert or human-confirm each against the compensating action its change plan was required to name and test (Section 28.1), and mark every record produced in the window `gap-window` until re-verified. A loop that completed is not thereby a loop that was right, and without this branch the window's repairs stand as valid gate evidence for as long as nobody asks.

## Section 54. Exception Registry and Break-Glass

Several exception mechanisms exist across this system — break-glass, weekend authorisation, support extensions, temporary access, platform compatibility waivers, emergency production paths, policy waivers, bootstrap exceptions. Their records unify into one registry so that the question "what is currently true about this system that is not supposed to be true?" has a single answer.

### 54.1 The registry

```yaml
# exceptions.yaml — control-plane repository
registry_version: 1

exceptions:
  - id: EXC-2026-041
    type: platform_compatibility   # break_glass | weekend_work
                                   # | platform_rollback
                                   # | founder_intervention
                                   # | support_extension | temporary_access
                                   # | platform_compatibility
                                   # | emergency_production | policy_waiver
                                   # | bootstrap
                                   # | founder_standing_delegation_activation
    reason: "Product 12 blocked on Node 22 upgrade pending vendor SDK release"
    requester: dev-b
    authority: lead-1              # must hold the mapped capability
    affected:
      products: [product-12]
      repositories: [org/product-12-api]
    scope: "Remain on workflows@v3 for CI only; deployment path unchanged"
    start: 2026-05-02
    expiry: 2026-06-30             # mandatory
    compensating_control: "Weekly manual dependency scan; owner-confirmed"
    compensating_control_record: records/security-reviews/  # where execution lands
    compensating_control_cadence: weekly   # weekly | monthly | per-push | none
    owner: lead-1                  # accountable for the compensating control
    review_date: 2026-06-01
    renewals: 0
    became_permanent: false
    closure: null                  # expired | remediated
                                   # | promoted_to_policy | trigger_satisfied
    deactivation_trigger: null     # mandatory for types that close on an event
```

### 54.2 Rules

* **Expiry is mandatory.** CI rejects any exception without one. An exception with no expiry is not an exception; it is undocumented policy.
* **Automatic expiry where technically possible.** Temporary access, temporary assignments and platform compatibility waivers are revoked or reverted by reconciliation at expiry, not by memory. Where automatic revocation is not possible, the exception becomes Blocking-class drift on its expiry date.
* **Renewal is visible and rate-limited.** A second renewal raises Amber. A third renewal raises Red and forces one of three outcomes at the next quarterly review: remediate; promote to a policy with an owner and a review date; or, where the closing condition is a declared non-discretionary precondition rather than work the owner could do, **re-affirm by recorded Founder decision** naming the unmet precondition, the compensating controls now in force and the next review date. The third branch is available only to exception types whose `deactivation_trigger` is declared non-discretionary — `bootstrap` and `founder_standing_delegation_activation` — it is reviewed again every quarter, and each re-affirmation raises the compensating-control requirement, so it is not a quiet renewal under another name. Perpetual renewal is not an option; neither is forcing a Founder who cannot hire on demand to promote "unreviewed changes reach the default branches" into standing policy, which is the inversion Bootstrap Mode exists to prevent.
* **Same scope, new ID, still a renewal.** An exception opened for a scope substantially matching one closed within the preceding two quarters counts as a renewal of the closed exception, inherits its renewal count, and links to it. Pattern detection (Section 58) matches exceptions on scope and reason, not on identifier, precisely so that closing EXC-041 and opening EXC-052 for the same waiver gains nothing.
* **Every exception names a compensating control, and the control is verified like a restore test.** If the honest answer is "none", that must be written, because it changes the class. Where there is one, the record names the store its execution lands in and the cadence it runs on, and reconciliation compares expected executions against that store; on a missing execution the exception itself becomes **Blocking**-class drift — the pattern SIG-17 already applies to restore currency. A fictional weekly scan and a real one must not produce identical records and identical signal readings, because the compensating control is the entire reason an exception is acceptable rather than a silent policy breach.
* **Same-scope nomination is binding by default.** A same-scope match nominated by reconciliation inherits the closed exception's renewal count automatically; dismissing a nomination is a recorded Founder decision, never a judgement by the registry's owner, who is usually the party that granted the exception. The lookback is two quarters or the closed exception's own longest prior lifetime, whichever is longer, so a waiver re-opened in the third quarter does not restart at zero.
* **Post-use review is mandatory** for break-glass and emergency production exceptions, within 5 working days. An overdue review is a Red signal on the Founder view.
* **Exception records are never deleted.** They close with an outcome: expired, remediated, promoted to policy, or trigger satisfied. `trigger_satisfied` is available only to types that declare a `deactivation_trigger` — `bootstrap` and `founder_standing_delegation_activation` — and it records that the stated precondition was met, which `remediated` does not, because nothing was remediated.
* **An unknowable end date is bounded, not omitted.** Where the closing condition is an event rather than work — the Founder becoming reachable, a second context-holding engineer onboarding — the exception still takes a bounded expiry at open and renews, exactly as break-glass does under Section 54.4 for a SEV-1 whose resolution time is equally unknown. Renewal is the pressure that is wanted: it forces the Section 14.4 successor arrangement, or the hire, onto a clock.

### 54.3 Exception authority mapping

Exception governance introduces no new capabilities. Authority resolves through the Capability Model (Section 9, Capability Model).

| Exception type | Required capability |
| --- | --- |
| `break_glass` | `platform-admin`, plus Founder notification within 1 hour |
| `emergency_production` | `production-approval` held by someone other than the deploying actor, plus escalation authorisation |
| `platform_rollback` | `platform-change-approval` or `escalation`, whichever holder is reachable first; recorded either way (Section 61.2) |
| `founder_intervention` | `strategy` |
| `weekend_work` | `exceptional-approval`, in advance, per Section 47 (Weekend and Out-of-Hours Exception Policy); SEV-1 restoration requires no prior authorisation |
| `support_extension` | `lifecycle-decision`, plus Founder for any commitment implying cost |
| `temporary_access` | `reviewer-matrix-change` for assignment scope; `platform-admin` for organisation scope |
| `platform_compatibility` | `platform-change-approval` |
| `policy_waiver` | The policy's declared owner capability, or `exceptional-approval` for Founder-owned policies |
| `bootstrap` | `exceptional-approval`, per Section 95 (Bootstrap Mode and the Solo-Founder Build) |
| `founder_standing_delegation_activation` | Declared by the Team Lead when the Section 14.3 trigger fires, countersigned by the successor custodian (Section 14.4); the record captures activation time, trigger evidence and the scope granted, and closes automatically the moment the Founder is reachable again |

### 54.4 Break-glass governance

* **Who:** only holders of `platform-admin`, enumerated in the registry — a deliberately small set.
* **Trigger:** only a SEV-1 in progress, or a control-plane failure preventing normal execution. Convenience, deadline pressure and reviewer unavailability are not triggers; reviewer unavailability routes to the escalation role instead.
* **Logging:** the GitHub audit event, the exception record, the affected repositories or environments, the actions taken, and the state at open and at close.
* **Duration:** bounded at open — default 4 hours, maximum 24 — and revoked automatically by reconciliation.
* **Post-use review:** mandatory within 5 working days, owned by the escalation role, answering one question: what would have made break-glass unnecessary?
* **Repeat detection:** three or more uses in a quarter is a failure pattern candidate (Section 58), not an accepted operating mode. Break-glass must not become an alternate normal workflow.

### 54.5 Bootstrap exceptions

While fewer humans exist than gate independence requires, gates run under declared, expiring `bootstrap` exceptions recorded in this registry, with the activation checklist that arms each gate as headcount allows (Section 95, Bootstrap Mode and the Solo-Founder Build). Bootstrap exceptions follow every rule in this section — mandatory expiry, visible renewal, compensating controls — and are the registry's first production use. They carry `type: bootstrap` and the field names of Section 54.1, so the week-one validator and the full Phase G2 validator read one schema and not two. They close as `trigger_satisfied` when their deactivation trigger fires. And at a third renewal they take the re-affirmation branch of Section 54.2, because their closing condition is headcount — a precondition, not work the owner could perform.

## Section 55. Policy Lifecycle and Gradual Enforcement

This system states many of its rules as policies: the Friday deployment freeze, the no-evening-obligation rule, restore cadence, pinning rules, freeze windows, the AI runtime quarter-hold, and others. Every such rule has a lifecycle so that it can be evidenced, reviewed and retired.

### 55.1 The policy register

```yaml
# policies.yaml — control-plane repository
registry_version: 1

policies:
  - id: POL-DEPLOY-FRIDAY
    title: "No production deployment after 15:00 Friday"
    owner: lead-1
    purpose: "Avoid consuming weekend exception capacity on avoidable failures"
    origin: "Section 34 (Deployment, Release and Database Migrations)"
    version: 1
    effective_date: 2026-01-06
    enforcement_stage: enforce     # observe | warn | pilot | enforce
                                   # full adoption is enforce with
                                   # exception_window_closes in the past
    min_dwell: { warn: 14, pilot: 1 }   # days at Warn; delivery cycles at Pilot
    pilot_products: []             # required non-empty while stage is pilot
    entered_at_enforce_directly: false  # true only for a critical security
                                        # control; the label is auditable
    justification: null            # required when entered_at_enforce_directly
    exception_window_closes: 2026-04-06
    supersedes: null               # the policy ID this one replaces (55.2)
    enforcement_mechanism: "deploy-production.yml time gate; override requires
      an emergency_production exception"
    evidence:
      metric: "incidents opened Sat/Sun attributable to Fri >15:00 deploys"
      baseline: "4 in the preceding 2 quarters"
      current: "0 since effective_date"
    review_date: 2026-07-06
    retirement_condition: "Zero attributable weekend incidents over 4
      consecutive quarters AND rollback median under 10 minutes"
    exceptions_open: 0             # DERIVED — reconciliation computes it from
                                   # exceptions.yaml; never hand-edited
    status: active                 # proposed | active | superseded
                                   # | withdrawn | retired
```

### 55.2 Rules

* Every policy has an owner. An unowned policy is retired at the next quarterly review by default.
* Every policy has a review date — at most 12 months out, and 6 months for any policy that blocks work.
* Every policy states its evidence. If the metric that justified it cannot be produced, that is recorded honestly and the policy is a candidate for retirement or replacement.
* Retirement is a first-class outcome, with a stated condition written when the policy is created. A policy created without a retirement condition must justify permanence explicitly.
* Superseding is explicit. A replacing policy names what it replaces; the old record is retained.

### 55.3 Gradual enforcement

New policies do not begin by blocking the fleet.

```
Observe   → measure current behaviour; no signal to anyone but the owner
    ↓
Warn      → non-blocking notice on the health report and in CI output
    ↓
Pilot     → enforced on a named pilot set of products only
    ↓
Enforce   → fleet enforcement, with a stated exception window
    ↓
Exception window closes → full adoption; remaining gaps become Red drift
```

* Minimum dwell time per stage is declared per policy in `min_dwell`; the default is two weeks at Warn and one full delivery cycle at Pilot. A stage transition recorded before its dwell has elapsed fails CI.
* Critical security controls may enter directly at Enforce. This is the only permitted skip, it is recorded as `entered_at_enforce_directly` with its required `justification`, and the label is auditable.
* Pilot names its products in `pilot_products`, and Enforce names the date its exception window closes in `exception_window_closes`. A ladder whose stages cannot be checked against the record is a hand-edited string, not gradual enforcement.
* **Every stage transition names its decider.** The policy's declared owner advances a policy one stage. Declaring pilot failure, withdrawal, or a direct entry at Enforce is the `policy_waiver` authority of Section 54.3 — the policy's declared owner capability, or `exceptional-approval` for Founder-owned policies. A stage machine with no decider stalls at the stage nobody is named to leave.
* A policy that fails at Pilot returns to Observe or is withdrawn — `status: withdrawn`, its own first-class outcome, because recording a withdrawn policy as `retired` erases the distinction this rule exists to draw. Failure at pilot is a successful outcome of piloting, not an embarrassment.

### 55.4 Policy count as a churn signal

Policy count is itself a health signal (SIG-20 tracks currency; net growth feeds churn detection in Section 59). Growth in active policies without corresponding retirement is a process-churn indicator, and merging several policies into fewer, fatter ones to flatter the count is caught by the churn review reading policy *scope*, not only policy *number*.

## Section 56. Technical Debt Governance

No new tracker, no new board, no debt committee. Debt items are ordinary work items in the existing planning system (Section 29, Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change), carrying additional structured fields, and they compete for the same capacity as feature work — because that is the honest situation.

### 56.1 Fields on a debt-labelled work item

* **Severity:** cosmetic, friction, risk, blocking.
* **Business impact:** which product, which customers, what it prevents.
* **Reliability impact:** linked incidents or near-misses.
* **Security impact:** linked findings, if any.
* **Cost:** estimated cost to remediate, and estimated cost of continuing to carry it per quarter where it is measurable in attention hours.
* **Owner.**
* **Recurrence:** does this item generate repeated incidents, repeated exceptions or repeated manual work?
* **Blocking relation:** which planned or roadmap work it prevents or slows.

### 56.2 Governance rules

* Debt items enter H1, H2 or H3 by the same rules as any other work. Debt that blocks committed work is H1 by definition, not by negotiation.
* The Team Lead sees a generated Portfolio Debt Inventory grouped by product and by severity, derived from labels and fields — nothing is maintained twice.
* **Recurrence is the escalation trigger.** A debt item linked to three or more incidents or exceptions becomes a failure pattern candidate (Section 58) and receives an architecture decision rather than another remediation ticket.
* **Emergency debt is recorded at the time.** Debt created deliberately during an incident carries the incident reference and appears in the postmortem's tracked work.
* A product entering Maintenance or Sunset has its debt **reclassified rather than remediated**. Paying down debt on a product being retired is a real and common waste. The reclassification reads `business.criticality` and lifecycle state, not reliability stringency.

Priority: P1.

## Section 57. Automation Value and AI Output Measurement

### 57.1 The automation ledger

Every significant automation — an internal tool, a scheduled job, a bot, a generated report, a reconciliation routine — has a ledger entry in `economics.yaml`.

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Build cost | Attention hours to create |
| Maintenance cost | Attention hours per quarter, measured, not estimated |
| Failure cost | Incidents, false alerts, blocked work attributable to it |
| Human time saved | Measured before-and-after on the specific task it replaced |
| Adoption | Distinct invoking roles or teams per quarter, derived from the event log — workflow-dispatch and job-run events — never named individuals, because per-person tool-usage tracking is banned outright by Section 91.2 |
| Net value | Saved minus maintenance minus failure cost, per quarter |
| Verdict | Keep, improve, simplify, retire |

Every ledger entry names its owner, and every field names the record store it derives from, on the same discipline Section 84.6 applies to any other metric — `economics.yaml` being Founder-owned gives the file an owner, not the entry. Adoption and Human time saved are the two fields that keep the quarterly verdict honest against a builder's self-reported saving, so an entry whose Adoption field cannot name a store is not scored that quarter; it is recorded as unbaselined and the verdict says so.

Human attention saved is stated as a measured before-and-after pair, for example: portfolio status gathering, 2 hours per week before, 15 minutes after, net 1.75 hours per week, against 0.5 hours per quarter maintenance. Attention hours use the single taxonomy of Section 67 (Human Attention Economics). This is the primary evidence that the operating system is succeeding, and it is also the primary defence against building automation that costs more than it returns. Because "hours saved" is typically reported by the automation's own builder, the quarterly review checks the claimed saving against the attention ledger's observed composition rather than accepting the claim at face value.

**Rule:** any automation with negative net value for two consecutive quarters is simplified or retired. Retirement of an automation follows the tool retirement path (Section 62, Tool Register and Platform Exit).

Each Hermes Agent deployment (D69) — the background worker harness, the founder ops console and the PR-review engine — carries its own ledger entry in `economics.yaml`, measured on exactly the fields above and subject to the same two-consecutive-quarters rule; machine-drafted digest and drafting-aid jobs (D72) are ledgered per job class in the same way. Beyond the quarterly economics, every Hermes instance's sessions are recorded as machine-activity entries in the existing ledger vocabulary: background worker task executions, ops-console query sessions — who asked, and what was read — and PR-review runs. The session trajectories the harness writes to its `HERMES_HOME` directory are the raw evidence backing those entries; they are classified sensitive-at-rest, live on the encrypted volume, and are retained under the same retention rules as the entries they evidence.

### 57.2 The operating system's own ledger entry

The operating system prices itself. A standing ledger entry exists for the operating system as a whole: its build phases, its ritual cost (reviews, reconciliation attention, calibration sessions, report reading) and its measured savings in coordination and status-gathering time. **The standing entry is authored in Phase 1, not at Phase G6.** It is a hand-authored block in `economics.yaml` carrying the seven investment-gate answers per phase (Section 59.2), the predicted saving and a dated commitment to score it — a file, not a scenario calculator, depending on nothing G6 builds. G6 automates an entry that already exists. A gate answered into a register that does not yet exist is an unrecorded intention, and the whole period during which abandoning a bad phase is still cheap is the period that register would otherwise be missing. On the same rule, the quarterly review of this entry runs from the end of the first quarter on whatever data exists, with every figure that has no baseline marked unbaselined (Section 103.14); its first end-to-end run from a generated review pack is a Phase G8 exit criterion, not its first run at all. The quarterly review weighs the operating system's ritual cost against its value with exactly the same fields and the same honesty as any other automation, and the platform investment gate (Section 59) applies to the operating system's own implementation phases (Section 98, Implementation Phases and Roadmap). The system is not exempt from its own economics.

The standing quarterly ritual inventory is enumerated so that the ritual cost is priced completely, not impressionistically. It comprises: the quarterly operating-system review topics; the AI seat review; the automated bus-factor scenario and its outputs; the dependency review; control-plane restore drills; workstation checks; the PLU weight refit; the canary-set review; the product lifecycle review; closure-quality audits; calibration reviews; the per-review-period performance review cycle — pack reading, per-KPI assessment entry into the governed rating aid and the review conversation, per person (Section 89); the monthly Layer B operating session (Section 94.8); and the monthly encrypted self-view delivery, per person. The last three are the Founder's largest recurring obligation and are non-delegable in substance (Section 74.1), which is exactly why they are priced here: the review cadence is a Founder-set operational parameter with an initial value of quarterly (Section 77.1), and a cadence cannot be chosen honestly without its cost in front of the person choosing it. The ledger entry carries an attention-hours budget line for this ritual layer as a whole — budgeted hours per quarter against measured hours — reviewed at the same business review, so that ritual growth is a priced decision rather than an accretion. Beside it the entry carries a cash line: aggregate control-plane spend against the declared `control_plane_budget_band` (Section 50.1), so the operating system's net value is net of money as well as of hours.

### 57.3 Background layer output value

The background machine layer (Section 37, Background Machine Layer) is not throttled. It is measured, so that its output can be steered rather than limited.

| Metric | Definition | Response when poor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accepted-PR yield | Draft PRs merged ÷ draft PRs raised, by task class | Narrow or remove the task class from the whitelist |
| Review cost per accepted PR | Human review minutes ÷ accepted PRs, by task class | Improve the task template or prompt context |
| Net attention effect | Human hours saved by accepted output minus human hours spent reviewing rejected output | Negative for two quarters: retire the task class |
| Rework rate | Accepted background PRs later reverted or hotfixed | Add verification requirements for that class |
| Verification yield | Background-drafted test suites accepted by QA | QA feedback loop into the task template |

**Interpretation rule:** low yield in a task class is a signal about the task class, not about the volume. The correct response is to change what the background layer is asked to do — never to cap how much it does. These are portfolio- and task-class-level measures; they are never individual performance evidence (Section 91, Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart).

Priority: P2, except the whitelist-narrowing response path, which is P1 because it is a safety behaviour.

## Section 58. Failure Patterns and the Incident Learning Loop

A single failure is an incident. A repeated failure is a property of the system.

### 58.1 Pattern detection

Detection runs over incident records, deployment records, migration outcomes, review comments, exception records and reconciliation findings, and proposes candidates. **Humans confirm patterns; the machine only nominates.**

The pattern class table has nine classes:

| Pattern class | Example trigger | Expected remediation type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated migration failure | The same migration failure case (Section 34, Deployment, Release and Database Migrations) three times in 90 days across any products | Architecture change or migration tooling, not another checklist |
| Repeated rollback on one product | Three rollbacks in 90 days on the same product | Verification depth increase, or reassessment of `classification.reliability_criticality` |
| Repeated review finding class | The same reviewer raises the same defect class repeatedly | Automated check, lint rule or template change — encode the knowledge |
| Poor AI task class | A background or agent task class with sustained low yield or high rework | Task whitelist change, plan-checker rule |
| Recurring external dependency failure | The same external dependency causes three incidents | Architecture change: circuit breaker, fallback, or vendor decision |
| Recurring exception | The same exception type renewed repeatedly on the same product — matched on scope and reason, not identifier (Section 54.2) | Policy change or permanent remediation |
| Recurring Ready-queue miss on one product | The same product starves repeatedly | Planning capacity or priority clarity, not developer behaviour |
| Recurring break-glass | Three uses in a quarter | Control-plane gap; fix the workflow that forces bypass |
| Vendor deprecation | A vendor API sunset, store policy deadline or OAuth change reaches its alert window unactioned, or forces emergency work (Section 49, Operational Asset Inventory and Vendor Deadline Watch) | Deadline-watch entry with owner and lead time; migration scheduled as planned work, not incident response |

### 58.2 The pattern record

Confirmed patterns are recorded in `patterns.yaml` with: occurrence evidence, the confirmed root class, the chosen remediation type, the linked work item, and a closure condition expressed as a measurable absence — for example, zero recurrences over two quarters.

### 58.3 The third-occurrence question

The governing question for every third occurrence: is this an isolated incident or a systemic pattern? A confirmed pattern must resolve into exactly one of:

* architecture change
* automation
* permanent test
* policy change
* product lifecycle decision
* staffing decision

**"Be more careful" is not a permitted remediation.**

### 58.4 The incident learning loop

Postmortems are due within 5 working days of incident closure, and every production bug becomes a permanent regression test (Section 42, Incident Management and Detection). The downstream chain is tracked and closable:

```
Incident closed
    ↓
Postmortem (Section 42)
    ↓
Root cause classified: code | configuration | customer integration
  | external dependency | external model behaviour change
  | process | knowledge | capacity
    ↓
Generates, where applicable, tracked items:
  • permanent regression test          → H1 or H2, verification-owned
  • architecture remediation           → H2 or H3, debt-linked
  • monitoring or alerting improvement → H2
  • product contract change            → immediate, contract-owned
  • policy change or new exception     → policy register / exception registry
  • pattern candidate                  → patterns.yaml
    ↓
Each item verified on completion
    ↓
Postmortem closes only when all generated items are closed or explicitly
deferred with a named owner and a date
```

An open postmortem older than 30 days with unclosed items is an Amber operating-system signal. Postmortems that generate no tracked work are permitted — but three in a row is itself a signal that postmortems have become documentation rather than learning.

Priority: P1.

## Section 59. Platform Roadmap, Investment Gating, Change Budget and Churn Control

### 59.1 Two roadmaps

Two roadmaps, coordinated, never merged into one undifferentiated list:

| Product roadmap | Platform roadmap |
| --- | --- |
| What products need for customers | What the company needs in order to operate products efficiently |
| Owned per product | Owned by the Team Lead at portfolio level |
| Example: customer billing | Example: reusable migration verification workflow |
| Competes for engineering attention hours | Competes for the same attention hours, and must be allocated explicitly |

The reason for the separation is empirical: platform work with no separate visibility disappears behind feature work until it resurfaces as an incident or a migration crisis. The remedy is an explicit standing allocation of portfolio attention hours to platform work — a declared percentage band of portfolio attention hours (Section 71.5), reviewed quarterly against the hours actually spent as measured by the attention ledger (Section 67). The band is calibrated configuration, recalibrated at that review against measured spend.

The platform roadmap contains: platform evolution, security evolution, shared services, architecture investment, technical debt above a severity threshold, operating-system improvements including this system's own implementation phases (Section 98, Implementation Phases and Roadmap), and tooling changes.

### 59.2 Investment gating

Before any major platform initiative is committed, seven questions are answered in `platform-roadmap.yaml`. Short answers are fine; missing answers are not.

1. What human attention will it save, measured in hours per quarter, against what baseline?
2. Which diagnosed bottleneck does it remove? Name it from the bottleneck taxonomy (Section 73, Workforce Staffing Diagnosis and Rebalancing).
3. Which products benefit, and how many are unaffected?
4. What is the migration cost across the fleet, in attention hours?
5. What is the failure risk, and what breaks if it half-lands?
6. What is the rollback path?
7. When does it pay back? If the payback exceeds four quarters, why is it still the best use of that capacity?

**Rule:** internal infrastructure is not built because it is technically interesting. An initiative that cannot answer questions 1, 2 and 7 goes back to H3 as a candidate, not forward into H2.

**The gate applies to the operating system itself.** Every phase of this system's own build (Section 98) answers the same seven questions before it is committed, and its answers land in the operating system's standing ledger entry (Section 57.2). The operating system earns its next phase the same way any platform initiative does.

Priority: P1 for the roadmap split; P1 for the gate, which is cheap and prevents expensive mistakes.

### 59.3 Change budget

The operating system must be able to evolve. It must also not become a source of the very context-switching it exists to eliminate. Those two requirements conflict, and the resolution is a budget.

```yaml
# platform-roadmap.yaml
change_budget:
  period: month
  max_platform_changes: 4        # tunable, portfolio-wide scope
  max_fleet_migrations: 1        # changes requiring action in every product
  freeze_conditions:
    - "two or more failed platform changes in the trailing 60 days"
    - "migration backlog Red for 2 consecutive weeks"
    - "developer disruption hours above threshold in trailing month"
```

Tracked: platform changes per month, migration burden in attention hours, developer disruption hours, failed platform changes and their causes, and improvements deferred because the budget was full.

Exceeding the budget is not forbidden; it requires the Team Lead to defer something else, and the deferral is recorded. Critical security changes are outside the budget entirely and are never deferred by it.

### 59.4 Process-churn detection and the stabilisation rule

Measured over a rolling two quarters:

* Number of operating rules changed (policy register version increments)
* Frequency of change per rule — a rule changed three times in two quarters is unstable and is reverted to its last stable form or redesigned
* Number of products required to migrate, and how many times the same product migrated
* Human time consumed by migrations
* Net policy growth: policies added minus policies retired — read alongside policy scope, so consolidation into fewer, broader policies does not masquerade as retirement

**The stabilisation rule:** when churn exceeds threshold, the system recommends a stabilisation period during which only critical security changes and in-flight rollbacks proceed. This recommendation goes to the Founder, because it is a business-tempo decision, not an engineering preference.

The operating system itself must not become a source of context switching. This section is the mechanism that enforces that claim rather than merely asserting it.

Priority: P1.

## Section 60. Platform Versioning, Versioned Contracts and Compatibility

The operating system is versioned. The team does not silently modify it in production.

### 60.1 The platform record

```yaml
# platform.yaml — control-plane repository
platform_version: 4.0

supported_contract_versions:
  product: [1, 2]
  verification: [1]
  people_registry: [1]
  service: [1]

reusable_workflow_versions:
  current: v4
  supported: [v3, v4]
  deprecated: [v2]
  deprecation_deadline:
    v2: 2026-08-01
    v3: 2026-12-01

canary_set:                      # configurable, reviewed quarterly
  - product-3                    # simple web
  - product-7                    # backend-heavy, high volume
  - product-12                   # mobile
  - product-1                    # high reliability criticality
```

The platform carries a version, a changelog, a compatibility statement, a migration process, a rollout process and a rollback process — exactly as a product does. **The operating system must be at least as recoverable as the products it manages.** Changes to this specification itself follow the platform-change process of Section 61.

### 60.2 Versioned contracts

Every contract schema carries a version. **Simultaneous fleet migration is never required.**

| Contract | File | Version field |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Operating Contract | `product.yaml` | `contract_version` |
| Verification Contract | `verification/contract.yaml` | `contract_version` |
| People Registry | `people.yaml` | `registry_version` |
| Role Registry | `roles.yaml` | `registry_version` |
| Shared Service Contract | `service.yaml` | `service_version` |
| Reusable workflow interface | workflow tag | tag version |
| Operational record envelope | `records/**` | `record_schema_version` |
| Event envelope | `events/**` | `event_schema_version` |
| Event-type enum | `platform.yaml` | `platform_version` |

The migration flow for any schema change:

```
Schema change proposed
    ↓
Write the v2 schema alongside v1 — do not replace
    ↓
Validator supports BOTH v1 and v2
    ↓
Write the migration — automated where possible
    ↓
Canary products migrate first
    ↓
Verify
    ↓
Fleet migrates gradually, each product on its own schedule
    ↓
v1 deprecation deadline set and published
    ↓
v1 support removed only after every product has migrated
```

* Products may temporarily remain on an older supported version. This is `platform_compatibility: transitional`.
* A contract version below the supported floor is `unsupported` and blocks deployment until migrated.

### 60.3 Compatibility states

```yaml
platform_compatibility: transitional
platform_migration:
  target_contract_version: 2
  target_workflow_version: v4
  owner: dev-b
  deadline: 2026-07-15
  reason: "Awaiting Node 22 upgrade; blocked on vendor SDK"
```

| State | Meaning | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supported` | On current or supported contract and workflow versions | Normal operation |
| `transitional` | On an older supported version, migration planned | **Requires a named migration owner, a target version and a deadline.** Visible on the platform rollout view |
| `unsupported` | Below the supported floor | **Deployment blocked.** Escalates automatically |

**"Transitional" must not become permanent.** A transitional product without an owner or past its deadline appears on the Founder's product-attention dimension as Action Required, and feeds SIG-10. This is the enforcement that prevents a slow accumulation of products nobody can safely change.

Priority: P1 throughout this section — platform versioning, versioned contracts and compatibility states are all P1.

## Section 61. Platform Change, Canary and Rollback

### 61.1 What a platform change is

A platform change is any change to shared CI workflows, the reviewer matrix validator, branch protection templates, contract schemas, the verification engine, the GSD version, dashboard schemas, shared automation, or scaffolding templates. Changes to this specification's own rules are platform changes and follow this section.

### 61.2 The platform change flow

```
PLATFORM CHANGE PROPOSED
    ↓
IMPACT ANALYSIS (generated, not hand-written)
  affected products · repositories · stacks · lifecycle states · risk
    ↓
CHANGE MANIFEST created in git (Section 25, Change Manifests)
    ↓
CANARY SET SELECTED
  from platform.yaml, adjusted for this change's characteristics
    ↓
CANARY ROLLOUT — 1 to 3 representative products
    ↓
VERIFY on canaries
  CI green · deployment succeeds · parity clean
  · no unexpected failures · observe for at least one full working day
    ↓
    ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
  FAIL                        PASS
    ↓                           ↓
PLATFORM ROLLBACK           APPROVAL (platform-change-approval)
  stop rollout                  ↓
  revert workflow tag       FLEET ROLLOUT
  restore prior version     in waves, not all at once
  validate canaries             ↓
  record in manifest        VERIFY each wave
  fix and re-canary             ↓
                            MANIFEST closed: complete
```

**The rollback branch names its authority too.** Platform rollback is initiated by a holder of `platform-change-approval` or of `escalation`, whichever is reachable first, and is filed as a `platform_rollback` exception (Sections 26.3, 54.3). The branch that stops a failing rollout cannot be the one branch of this flow with no recorded basis to act.

### 61.3 Canary selection criteria

The canary set is configurable in `platform.yaml` and covers representative categories — a simple web product, a backend-heavy product, a mobile product, a product of high `classification.reliability_criticality`, and a high-customer-volume product. It is reviewed quarterly and adjusted as the portfolio changes. **Do not hard-code specific products as permanent canaries.**

Adjust the set per change: a Node-only change canaries on Node products; a mobile-affecting change must include a mobile product.

**A canary must be exercised, not merely observed.** During its observation window, every canary product runs a synthetic exercise: a `workflow_dispatch` run of `ci.yml` and `build.yml`, and a staging deploy, each recorded on the change manifest. An unexercised canary is not a passed canary — a product that happened to have no activity during the window has verified nothing, and its silence must not be mistaken for a pass.

### 61.4 Pilot, rollout, fleet

Every new platform capability progresses through three stages, recorded on the existing change manifest rather than in a new artifact:

| Stage | Meaning | Exit criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pilot | Enabled on a named, deliberately small product set chosen for representativeness, not convenience | Verification passed on every pilot product; no unresolved Red drift attributable to the change; pilot owner sign-off |
| Rollout | Expanding set, in waves, with each wave verified | No wave regression; migration burden within estimate |
| Fleet | Organisation-wide; becomes the default for new products | Manifest closed; old path deprecated with a date |

Rules: an experimental capability is never mandatory immediately. Pilot products are selected using capability and stack declarations so that the pilot set covers the relevant technology diversity. A capability stuck between stages for more than a quarter is either finished or abandoned; lingering half-rollouts are the origin of most transitional compatibility backlog (SIG-10).

**Default wave rule:** fleet rollout proceeds in waves of at most one-third of the fleet, ordered ascending by `classification.reliability_criticality` — the least critical products migrate first — and each wave is verified before the next begins. A change manifest may declare a different wave plan with rationale, but the default binds where none is declared.

**Routine-class pinned-tag bumps and the bulk-PR script.** A pure pinned-tag bump raised under an open, approved change manifest is routine-class review: the manifest already carries the risk decision, and the per-product PR needs only routine confirmation that the diff is the tag bump and nothing else. For fleet migrations, the bulk-PR script that raises those bumps across products is a named build-surface tool with its own `tools.yaml` entry; it is run by a human under that human's identity — never under a machine account, which the Section 53.1 rule on workflow-file changes would in any case block — and each run is recorded on the manifest.

Operating-system changes use the same mechanisms products already use: compatibility flags via pinned tags, migration flags via `platform_compatibility`, rollout percentage expressed as the named product set, and canary products. No dedicated flag platform is introduced unless the fleet genuinely outgrows pinned tags, which at the scale contemplated it will not.

### 61.5 Never fleet without canary

**Never roll a shared change across the fleet automatically.** No shared workflow change goes to every product in one action, regardless of how safe it appears.

Priority: P1.

## Section 62. Tool Register and Platform Exit

### 62.1 The tool register

```yaml
# tools.yaml — control-plane repository
tools:
  - id: gsd
    purpose: "Plan/execute/verify workflow"
    owner: lead-1
    current_version: v1.11.0
    upgrade_policy: "platform change process; canary set required"
    replacement_candidates: []
    exit_condition: "Workflow can be executed without it via documented
      fallback; .planning artifacts remain readable"
    last_reviewed: 2026-07-01
    criticality: high

  - id: hermes-background-worker
    purpose: "Hermes Agent harness inside the Subsystem J background
      execution cage; drafts whitelisted-class output as draft PRs only"
    owner: lead-1
```
