# Part IX - People, Performance and Management Intelligence

This part defines how the operating system supports people decisions: who holds authority over them, the conceptual model that keeps people analytics fair, the dynamic architecture that survives organisational change, the performance framework registry and its current content, the evidence pipeline that feeds it, the mandatory systemic-context safeguard, the role-specific evidence models, and the capability matrix. Throughout this part one rule dominates: the system provides evidence, context and options; formal people decisions belong to the Founder and are never made, initiated, scheduled or executed by the system.

## Section 74. People Decision Authority

This section is authoritative for people decisions and overrides any looser wording elsewhere in this specification.

### 74.1 The Founder is the final decision-maker for formal people decisions

The following are formal people decisions. Each belongs to the Founder alone.

* Promotion
* Formal warning
* Formal performance concern escalation
* Performance Improvement Plan
* Compensation decision
* Role change where it materially affects employment responsibility or status
* Termination or exit
* Permanent headcount increase
* Headcount reduction
* Creation of new permanent roles
* Major people restructuring or reorganisation

The operating system assists the Founder with evidence, context, trends, capacity, team health, options and confidence. It never makes, initiates, schedules or executes any of these decisions. No configuration enables it to.

### 74.2 Team Lead operational authority

The Team Lead owns engineering execution and holds real, substantial authority within it. The Team Lead may:

* assign tasks and sequence work
* rebalance engineering work within the team
* assign and reassign products within the team
* change cross-review routing within reviewer-matrix rules (Section 23 (Review Routing - the Single Authoritative Model))
* execute product-ownership and reviewer-matrix changes, temporary and permanent, under the reviewer-matrix-change capability, each recorded as a decision (Section 17 (Ownership and the Cross-Review Network))
* prepare and maintain the H1, H2 and H3 planning horizons (Section 29 (Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change))
* manage the Ready queue and future work preparation
* unblock engineers and remove impediments
* mentor, pair and coach technically
* provide normal work feedback and explain expectations
* identify blockers, capacity problems, capability gaps and operational team issues
* request QA capacity and architecture support
* request a temporary specialist
* recommend hiring, and prepare the engineering case for it
* prepare performance evidence for Founder review
* prepare development recommendations

None of this requires Founder involvement. Every permanent ownership change generates a Founder-view notification: visibility, not approval. Operational engineering autonomy is preserved in full.

### 74.3 What the Team Lead must never do independently

The Team Lead must never, on their own authority:

* terminate or initiate an exit process
* issue a formal warning
* initiate a formal Performance Improvement Plan
* approve a promotion
* approve or change compensation
* approve permanent headcount
* approve a role change affecting employment responsibility or status

Where the Team Lead identifies an individual concern, the path is fixed:

```
Signal
  → evidence
  → systemic context analysis (Section 80)
  → Team Lead observation and operational context
  → Founder review
  → Founder decision
```

### 74.4 Normal work feedback is not a formal personnel decision

These two things must never be conflated.

| Normal work feedback - Team Lead | Formal personnel decision - Founder |
| --- | --- |
| "This needs better test coverage before QA." | A documented formal warning |
| "Let's pair on this module next week." | A Performance Improvement Plan |
| "I'm moving this product to you for two sprints." | A role change affecting employment responsibility or status |
| "You're ready to own this module." | A promotion |
| "I think we need another QA engineer." | Approving a permanent QA hire |
| "Your estimates have been drifting; let's look at why." | A formal performance rating decision |

The left column is daily engineering management and requires no escalation. Product-ownership moves - including permanent ones - also sit on the operational side: the Team Lead executes them under the reviewer-matrix-change capability with a recorded decision, and permanent moves surface as Founder-view notifications. The right column is Founder authority and cannot be reached from the left column without an explicit Founder decision. The dividing line for role changes is employment responsibility or status: only changes that affect it are Founder decisions.

### 74.5 Authority matrix

| Decision | System can signal | Team Lead | Founder final authority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Task assignment and sequencing | Yes | Executes directly | Not required |
| Within-team rebalance, temporary, with expiry | Yes | Executes directly | Not required |
| Cross-review routing within matrix rules | Yes | Executes directly under the reviewer-matrix-change capability | Not required |
| Product-ownership change, temporary or permanent | Yes | Executes directly under the reviewer-matrix-change capability; recorded as a decision | Not required; every permanent change generates a Founder-view notification |
| Coaching need | Yes | Delivers normal coaching | Required for any formal action |
| Recognition | Yes | Recommends | Yes |
| Promotion candidate | Signal only | Recommends | Yes |
| Role change affecting employment responsibility or status | Signal only | Recommends | Yes |
| New permanent hire | Signal only | Recommends and prepares the case | Yes |
| Temporary specialist | Signal only | Recommends | Yes |
| Leave approval | Yes, calendar and capacity impact | Coordinates delivery around approved leave | Founder or a named delegate (Section 85 (Decision Matrices and the Performance Concern Protocol)) |
| Formal warning | Evidence only | Provides evidence | Yes |
| Performance Improvement Plan | Evidence only | Provides evidence | Yes |
| Exit consideration | Evidence only | Provides evidence | Yes |
| Compensation | No signal of any kind | Input only | Yes |
| Permanent headcount change | Signal only | Recommends | Yes |
| Layer B access delegation | No | No | **Not delegable** (D109). The Founder holds `people-intelligence`; continuity runs through the Section 14.4 sealed contingency credential as a recorded break-glass event |

Ordinary within-team allocation authority granted to the Team Lead by the assignment model (Section 10 (Assignment Registry and Delegation)) is preserved in full. Operational assignment must never be confused with a formal employment decision.

---

## Section 75. The Fundamental People Model

Nine concepts. They are related and they are not the same thing. Collapsing any two of them is the most common way a people-analytics layer becomes unfair and then becomes ignored.

| Concept | Definition | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity | Realistically available productive attention for a period | Not hours at desk, not headcount |
| Utilisation | Share of capacity currently committed or consumed by useful work | Not performance, not effort, not commitment |
| Bandwidth | Remaining safe capacity after commitments and reserve | Not idle time |
| Workload | The specific composition of work a person carries | Not a single number |
| Performance | Role-appropriate outcomes and quality sustained over time, in context | Not activity volume |
| Capability | Demonstrated technical and professional competence | Not authorisation, not seniority label |
| Potential / readiness | Evidence of sustained next-level behaviour already occurring | Not a prediction, not a personality judgment |
| Team health | Structural properties of how the team's work is distributed and flowing | Not the average of individual scores |
| Organisational constraint | A limit imposed by process, architecture, platform, priority or staffing | Not an individual failure |

Capacity, utilisation and bandwidth are defined and measured in Sections 69 (Capacity and the Capacity Profile) and 70 (Utilisation, Bandwidth and Sustainable Utilisation); this section fixes what the words mean so no later section can quietly repurpose them.

Prohibited constructs, binding:

* No "Employee Productivity Score".
* No "Developer Score".
* No composite index that collapses capacity, utilisation and performance into one number.
* No single-number team score that hides which dimension is failing. This mirrors the prohibition on composite product health scores (Section 92 (Dashboard and View Architecture)): the correct action differs entirely depending on which dimension is red.

---

## Section 76. Dynamic People Architecture

This section makes the people layer survive organisational change without redesign.

### 76.1 The core principle

The people layer is designed around entities and relationships, not around today's individuals:

```
Person → Role → Expectation Profile (from the framework in force) → Evidence → Performance Period
Person → Capability Profile → Assignments → Capacity Profile → Allocation
```

It is not designed around a person permanently bound to a fixed KRA set, a fixed product and a fixed role. A person may join, leave, change role, change products, gain capabilities, shed responsibilities, take a temporary assignment, become acting Team Lead, become Team Lead, move into QA, move into engineering, or become a specialist. None of these requires architectural change. All of them are registry operations with effective dates (Section 12 (Person Lifecycles)).

### 76.2 Person record

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Person ID | Stable internal identifier; the only thing other records reference |
| Name | Display only; never a logic key |
| Current role | Reference to a Role Profile, effective-dated |
| Capability profile | Authorisation capabilities plus observed maturity, per Section 82 |
| Employment type | One of `employee`, `contractor`, `intern`, `temporary_specialist`, `consultant`, matching the Section 7 (People Registry) enumeration exactly |
| Working calendar | Declared working days and hours |
| Leave records | Approved leave, held as control-plane records (Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions)); approval authority is the Founder or a named delegate per the decision matrices (Section 85). Leave is a load-bearing capacity input (Section 69) |
| `availability` lifecycle state | The lifecycle enum of Section 6.4 - `active`, `on_leave`, `departing`, `departed` - transitioned by reconciliation against calendar and leave records; consumed by capacity, allocation and succession logic, and an input to `allocation_state` (Section 90.5) - never hand-maintained separately |
| Status | Active or inactive |
| Assignments | References to products and scopes, effective-dated |
| Effective dates | Join date, role change dates, departure date |

Binding rule: performance expectations are never embedded in the person record. A person resolves to expectations through their role and the framework version in force. This is what makes a framework replacement a configuration change rather than a migration project.

Non-employee employment types carry no performance-framework mapping by default: their framework field is marked exactly Not defined in framework, and mapping-completeness signals do not fire on them.

### 76.3 Role Profile

A Role Profile is configuration and contains:

* role ID and role name
* role purpose
* primary and secondary responsibilities
* required capabilities
* optional capabilities
* performance dimensions
* applicable performance framework and framework version
* capacity dimensions relevant to the role
* typical workload model

A Role Profile must never contain a hard-coded person, a hard-coded product, or an assumption that exactly one person holds it. Roles may have zero, one or many holders.

### 76.4 Prohibited hard-coding

The implementation must contain no logic of the form:

* `if person == "<name>"`
* `if role_count == 1`
* `developers = [A, B, C]`
* any assumption of exactly one Team Lead, exactly one QA engineer, exactly one mobile engineer or exactly one specialist
* any assumption of a fixed number of people, products, KRAs or KPIs

Names appear in this specification only in clearly-labelled current-configuration snapshots (Section 78) and in illustrative worked examples. They are never schema entities and never branch conditions.

### 76.5 Scaling requirements

The model must remain valid without architectural change at 7, 10, 15, 20, 30 and more people; at 8, 20, 30 and 50 or more products; and across topology changes.

Supported topology evolution:

```
Founder → Team Lead → Developers

then, when justified:

Founder → Team Lead A, Team Lead B → product domains
```

Domains are activated only when the delegation and second-Lead conditions in Section 13 (Team Lead Succession and Delegation) and Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution) are met. Activating a domain is a configuration change: new role instance, new assignments, new capacity aggregation grouping. The people layer is not rewritten.

### 76.6 History versus current configuration

This distinction prevents both of the common failure modes - losing history, and freezing the future.

| Property | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Current team membership | Mutable configuration |
| Current roles and assignments | Mutable configuration |
| Current framework version | Mutable configuration |
| Who was assigned, when, to what | Immutable history |
| Which role a person held during a period | Immutable history |
| Which framework version governed a period | Immutable history |
| Which targets applied during a period | Immutable history |
| Evidence gathered for a period | Immutable history |
| Decisions made, by whom, on what basis | Immutable history, append-only |

All records are effective-dated. Changing current configuration never overwrites history. A person who leaves does not have their past evidence deleted; their record becomes inactive and their history remains intact and access-controlled (Section 91 (Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart) governs retention). A retired KPI does not erase the periods it governed.

Where a role, person or framework element is no longer part of the active configuration, it moves conceptually to Historical / Inactive Configuration. It is never destroyed.

---

## Section 77. Performance Framework Registry

The registry pattern that governs products and assignments also governs performance frameworks. This is the mechanism that makes the KRA/KPI layer fully replaceable.

### 77.1 Registry structure

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| Framework version | v1, v1.1, v2.0, and so on |
| Status | Draft, Pilot, Active, Deprecated, Retired |
| Effective date | The date from which it governs |
| Retirement date | Set when superseded; never deleted |
| Affected roles | Which Role Profiles it applies to |
| KRAs | Titles, weights, definitions |
| KPIs | Titles, weights, definitions, targets, verbatim from the framework source |
| Stretch targets | Per KPI, verbatim from the framework source |
| Rating scale | The framework's own rating bands, recorded verbatim; the registry imposes none of its own |
| Evidence sources | Per KPI |
| Human judgement areas | Per KPI |
| Review cadence | As defined by the framework; where the framework in force defines none, the field records exactly Not defined and the Founder sets an operational cadence at registry activation |

Exactly one framework version is Active for a given role at a given date, unless multi-framework operation is explicitly configured for a transition period.

### 77.2 Variable structure per role

The number of KRAs and KPIs is configuration, not architecture. The registry must support a role with three KPIs, a role with six, a role with ten, and a role with an entirely custom evaluation structure that does not use KRA/KPI vocabulary at all. Nothing in the capacity engine, the team health model, the evidence pipeline, the dashboards or the decision support depends on the count or the naming convention.

### 77.3 Framework replacement without system rebuild

Worked example of a KPI rename and reweight:

```
Framework v1:  "Delivery Commitment Achievement", weight 25
Framework v2:  "Verified Delivery Reliability", weight 20
               plus "Quality", weight 30

Result:
  - v1 evidence remains attached to v1 periods, unchanged
  - v2 activates on its effective date
  - v2 receives a new evidence mapping
  - the people layer, capacity engine, dashboards and decision flow are untouched
```

The requirement this satisfies: a future organisation may discard the entire framework, including the rating scale, the review frequency and the role taxonomy, without breaking capacity measurement, utilisation composition, team health, the evidence pipeline, the dashboards or Founder decision support. This is acceptance test AT-014 (Section 100 (Acceptance Tests)).

### 77.4 Change authority

Routine configuration maintenance - correcting a typo, attaching a newly available evidence source to an existing KPI, adjusting a calibration threshold - does not require Founder involvement and is owned by the framework maintainer.

Changes to formal company-wide people-performance policy - adding or removing a KRA or KPI, changing a weight, changing a target or stretch target, changing the rating scale, changing review cadence, activating a new framework version - require Founder approval. The Team Lead provides engineering input. The system may recommend. The system never activates a framework change on its own authority.

Captured framework content changes only through this change authority. Where a field genuinely does not exist in the framework in force, it is marked exactly: Not defined in Framework v1. No value is invented to fill it.

### 77.5 Revision integrity audit

Whenever the framework registry or the people-layer configuration is revised, an integrity audit compares the prior state against the new state and verifies that nothing was lost unintentionally:

* no person, role, KRA, KPI, weight, target, stretch target or rating-scale detail was unintentionally deleted or changed;
* no acceptance test, invariant or access rule was deleted or weakened;
* no Founder authority was weakened, and no Team Lead authority was accidentally expanded into formal people authority;
* no historical record was overwritten (effective-dated records supersede; they never destroy — Section 63).

Where a person, role, KRA or KPI is intentionally retired from active configuration, its history moves to inactive configuration with a retirement date and remains queryable for the periods it governed. Unintentional loss of detail is a defect and is restored from the prior version.

The audit is implementable in two parts, and runs as part of CI on the control-plane repository whenever these files change. CI generates the diff of removed or changed protected entities — people, roles, KRAs, KPIs, weights, targets, stretch targets, rating-scale details, acceptance tests, invariants and access rules — and blocks the change until every removal carries an intentional-change marker referencing a decision record. Semantic judgments — whether a Founder authority was weakened, or a Team Lead authority accidentally expanded into formal people authority — are a human review step performed on that flagged diff; CI flags, it does not adjudicate.

## Section 78. Framework v1 - Current Configuration Snapshot

### 78.1 Status of this section

Everything in this section is a current configuration snapshot, not architecture. It records the performance framework currently in force - Framework v1, the Lumiverse Engineering KRA/KPI workbook - exactly as registered in the Performance Framework Registry (Section 77). Role purposes, primary and secondary responsibilities, KRA titles, KRA weights, KPI titles, KPI weights, definitions, targets, stretch targets and the rating scale are preserved verbatim. The operating system adds an evidence layer beside each KPI (Section 79); it changes nothing inside the framework.

Terminology preservation, binding: the framework's own names are used throughout. "Team Delivery & Execution", "Engineering Quality & Reliability", "Beyond KRA/KPI", "Client Demo & Presentation", "Work Management & Reporting Discipline" and all other titles appear exactly as written. Where two people have similarly named KRAs or KPIs with different weights or wording, both are preserved separately rather than merged.

Framework v1 is the current configuration. It is not a permanent constraint. Section 77 defines how it is replaced. If the team changes tomorrow, the same operating system continues with a different roster.

The framework review cadence is Not defined in Framework v1. The Founder sets the operational cadence at people-tier Phase P2 registry activation; the initial value is quarterly.

### 78.14 The 1-5 Scoring Guide

Framework v1's rating scale, recorded verbatim as registry content (Section 77.1).

| Score | Rating | Meaning | Guidance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Far Below Expectations | Performance materially below role expectations. | Requires immediate corrective action and a documented improvement plan. |
| 2 | Below Expectations | Some important expectations are not consistently met. | Requires focused coaching and improvement actions. |
| 3 | Meets Expectations | Consistently delivers the expected standard for the role. | This is a successful/fully satisfactory performance level. |
| 4 | Exceeds Expectations | Frequently performs above the expected level with clear positive impact. | Evidence should show proactive ownership or measurable improvement. |
| 5 | Exceptional | Sustained, exceptional performance with significant measurable impact. | Reserved for genuinely exceptional contribution; not simply high effort or long hours. |

### 78.15 Framework v1.1 - Founder-approved edits

Framework v1.1 consists of Framework v1 plus exactly three Founder-approved edits, registered through the change authority in Section 77.4. The v1 wording above is preserved verbatim as the v1 record; v1.1 applies from its effective date.

Framework v1.1 carries status Active, with an effective date of people-tier Phase P2 registry activation (Section 98). Until that activation the v1 wording governs operationally, and the v1.1 edits stand approved-pending-activation.

1. **Work-management wording.** Every KPI naming "Bitrix24" is reworded to "the designated work-management system", matching the Team Lead KPI wording already used in the framework. The designated work-management system is the operating system's own execution-truth boards (Section 29 (Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change); Section 5 (Source of Truth Hierarchy)). Affected KPIs:
   * Bhushan - "Bitrix24 Work Management & Reporting Discipline" (Work Management & Process Discipline): title becomes "Work Management & Reporting Discipline"; definition reworded.
   * Mansi - "Work Management & Reporting Discipline" (Work Management & Collaboration): definition reworded.
   * Harshal - both "Work Management & Reporting Discipline" KPIs (CI/CD & Deployment Automation; Engineering Collaboration & Continuous Improvement): definitions reworded.
   * Unmesh - "Work Management & Reporting Discipline" (Work Management & Collaboration): definition reworded.
   * Aarti - "Work Management & Reporting Discipline" (Work Management & Professional Discipline): definition reworded.
2. **Deployment Automation Coverage evolution.** Once deployment is 100% pipeline-executed by construction under this operating system (Section 34 (Deployment, Release and Database Migrations)), the DevOps KPI "Deployment Automation Coverage" ceases to discriminate. It evolves into a pipeline and rollback reliability measure - pipeline availability, deployment success rate and rollback exercise success - drawing on the same deployment records.
3. **Management Reporting redefinition.** The Team Lead KPI "Management Reporting" is redefined as the accuracy and currency of system-carried state: the operating system replaces status reports, so the KPI measures whether boards, records and dashboards faithfully reflect reality without repeated management follow-up, not whether reports are written.

Context: Bitrix24 is not part of the operating system estate; execution truth lives in the operating system's own boards, and any future Bitrix24 integration is an optional, registered external integration with a declared exit condition (Section 62 (Tool Register and Platform Exit)).

## Section 79. Evidence Mapping and Instrumentation Status

### 79.1 Purpose and conventions

Every KPI in the framework in force carries an evidence mapping: where the evidence comes from, how much of it the system generates, where human judgement is required, and how instrumented the source currently is. The canonical mapping is maintained in the control plane and generated into review packs (Section 89 (Evidence Bundles, Review Packs and Auditability)) rather than hand-copied; the tables below record the mapping for Framework v1.

Conventions, binding:

* **Targets are quoted verbatim from Framework v1** (Section 78) and are not restated in any other wording. If a discrepancy with the framework source is found, the source wins and the mapping is corrected through the registry (Section 77.4).
* **Instrumentation status values**: Available now; Available after instrumentation; Requires human input; Not measurable reliably; Not yet instrumented. Where a KPI is assessed against qualitative target wording, the status says so; no numeric proxy is substituted.
* **One row per distinct KPI pattern.** A KPI whose definition and evidence pipeline are materially identical across role instances appears once, annotated with the people it covers; the applicable target for each person is the one recorded in Section 78. KPIs with role-specific evidence appear in their role's table.
* **Independent-problem-solving evidence rule.** The Development KPI "Independent Problem Solving" - and every progressive-independence KPI of the same shape - takes its evidence from escalation records and review outcomes, never from Management Attention signals. Management Attention (Section 86 (Recognition, Promotion and Management Attention)) is diagnostic-only and feeds exactly one decision use; it is not KPI evidence.
* **No-proxy rule.** Where no reliable evidence exists, the status is stated and no proxy is substituted. No KPI is forced into automation. A partially automated KPI presents its machine component and its human component separately, never blended into a single computed score.* **Board-hygiene evidence rule.** The Work Management & Reporting Discipline family is measured over fields humans write, so its machine reading proves tidiness, not truth. It is scored only alongside the board-versus-reality accuracy spot-checks of the Team Lead's Management Reporting KPI (Section 79.3), and a board made tidy by curation — retroactive cards, reopened work re-entered as new cards, the curation signals of Section 96.4 — **fails this KPI rather than passing it**. A hygiene percentage rising while those curation signals rise is evidence about the metric, not about the person, and enters the calibration review (Section 84.5).
* All derivations respect the individual-metrics invariant (Section 101 (Non-Negotiable Invariants)): attention hours, utilisation, PLU and output volume are never KPI evidence; only role-specific outcome and quality evidence feeds this mapping, and it feeds a Founder-owned review with mandatory context adjustment (Section 80).

### 79.12 Automation classification

Every KPI is classified into one of four automation classes.

* **Fully machine measurable**: review coverage, deployment success, pipeline availability, defect reproducibility, verification coverage, estimation variance, restore-test currency, incident acknowledgement latency, board task hygiene.
* **Partially machine measurable**: delivery commitment achievement (requires approved-scope-change validation), production defect rate (requires attribution), rework rate (requires legitimacy judgment), automation coverage (requires meaningfulness judgment), AI output validation (requires adequacy judgment).
* **Human judgement required**: technical decision quality, architecture quality, mentoring quality, requirement understanding, exceptional contribution, conflict resolution, code understanding and ownership, professional discipline.
* **Currently not instrumented**: Voice AI agent behaviour acceptance, scenario evaluation coverage, demo readiness, several Continuous Improvement KPIs.

No KPI is forced into automation. A partially automated KPI presents its machine component and its human component separately, never blended into a single computed score. Where no reliable evidence exists, the status is stated and no proxy is substituted.

### 79.13 Metric decision-use register

Every metric that can inform a people or management decision is classified into **exactly one** decision use: **Diagnostic only**, **Performance evidence**, **Planning input**, or **Management decision support**. A metric with two decision uses is split or removed. This register is scoped to those metrics. Section 103's tables carry no decision-use column of their own, so their decision use is assigned here, by default: **every Section 103 measure is Planning input where it feeds a staffing, capacity, lifecycle or investment decision, Management decision support where Section 103.11 or Section 73.2 attaches a remedy ladder to it, and Diagnostic only otherwise. No Section 103 measure is ever Performance evidence** — the blanket exclusion its own preamble states. The one-decision-use rule applies to Section 103 equally: a Section 103 measure that any decision in practice reads as evidence about a named person is dual-use, and is entered in this register as its own named row with a single decision use, or split or removed at the next calibration review (Section 84). A default assigned here is checkable; a column asserted to exist elsewhere is not. The reporting level for each metric is portfolio, team, role or individual as stated, and individual-level rows are Layer B (Section 90).

## Section 80. Systemic Context Adjustment and Variance Classification

This section is mandatory and is the single most important safeguard in the people layer. It runs before any individual-level interpretation of any KPI variance and before any Founder-facing performance concern is generated.

### 80.1 Context checks

Before interpreting a person-level KPI variance, the system checks and presents:

1. requirements changed during the period
2. scope changed, approved or unapproved
3. architecture blocked or an architecture decision pending
4. QA blocked, verification environment unavailable, or verification backlog
5. environment failure, CI failure, deployment platform failure
6. dependency failure, internal shared service or external provider
7. incident load during the period
8. product complexity and criticality - business.criticality and reliability_criticality alike (Section 15 (Product Operating Contract)) - including changes to either
9. new technology or new product onboarding
10. approved leave (Section 76.2)
11. role transition or role change mid-period
12. team composition changes
13. customer escalation or reprioritisation
14. freeze windows, platform migrations, or fleet change burden (Section 59 (Platform Roadmap, Investment Gating, Change Budget and Churn Control); Section 61 (Platform Change, Canary and Rollback))
15. external events

### 80.2 Variance classification

Every variance is classified as exactly one of:

| Classification | Meaning | Default owner of the response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Person-driven | Evidence points to individual execution after other causes are examined and excluded | Team Lead operationally; Founder for any formal action |
| Team-driven | Team process, planning, allocation or coordination caused it | Team Lead |
| Product-driven | Product complexity, debt, requirements volatility or either criticality field (Section 6.1) caused it | Primary Owner and Team Lead |
| Platform-driven | CI, environments, infrastructure, tooling or the operating system caused it | Team Lead, DevOps |
| External | Customer, vendor, provider or market event caused it | Founder |
| Mixed | Multiple material causes, none dominant | Team Lead, with Founder if structural |
| Insufficient evidence | Not enough evidence to classify | Nobody - no signal is emitted |

Rules, binding:

* A variance may not be presented as person-driven until the other classes have been examined and the examination is visible in the evidence bundle (Section 89).
* Mixed is a legitimate and common outcome. The system must not force a single attribution for tidiness.
* Insufficient evidence is a legitimate outcome and produces no management signal at all. No negative people signal may be generated from insufficient evidence.* **Who classifies.** The generator proposes; a human confirms. The evidence-bundle generator (Section 89) emits a proposed classification restricted to the classes its machine sources can evidence — Platform-driven, Product-driven, External, Insufficient evidence — from the Section 80.1 checks that have machine sources, and shows on the bundle which checks it could not evaluate. The Team Lead proposes Team-driven and Mixed at the monthly judgment-capture ritual (Section 84.7), at team and product level only, which stays inside the Team Lead's minimum-necessary access because team- and product-level attribution is not individual evidence (Section 90.5). **Only the Founder confirms Person-driven**, in the Layer B session where the bundle is read — that is the one transition the person-driven rule above gates, and no other class needs Founder time. A variance nobody confirms stands as Insufficient evidence and emits no signal.
* **The classification act is budgeted.** The Founder's person-driven confirmations are calibrated configuration with an initial value of fifteen minutes per month for the whole team, carried as an operating-system ritual cost in the attention ledger (Section 103.13) and recalibrated at the quarterly operating-system review. If the measured cost exceeds the initial value for two consecutive quarters, the response is to widen what the generator may propose — never to skip the confirmation, and never to move it to the Team Lead.

### 80.3 The diagnostic hierarchy

The variance classification is applied through a fixed diagnostic hierarchy. It exists to prevent unfair attribution, and every decision matrix in Section 85 applies it before any row is read as an individual signal.

| Situation | Correct output |
| --- | --- |
| Three engineers show the same difficulty on the same product | System or product investigation |
| One engineer shows the same difficulty across three products | Individual performance signal, subject to context and confidence |
| The whole team misses delivery because the QA environment failed | Platform or system issue |
| One developer repeatedly falls short after environment, requirements and team causes are examined and excluded | Stronger individual signal, still requiring Founder judgment |
| Everyone's estimation accuracy degrades in the same period | Planning or requirements-quality issue |
| One person's estimation accuracy degrades while carrying a newly critical product (`reliability_criticality` raised) | Product complexity context, not an individual signal |

## Section 81. Role-Specific Evidence Models

There is no universal developer performance framework. Each model is anchored to the role purpose and responsibilities recorded in the framework in force (Section 78.3 for the current snapshot), and each names its KRA/KPI parent. Where the framework is the authority, this specification does not add generic expectations on top. Role models are configuration instances; current incumbents are noted as the current snapshot only.

### 81.1 Development role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: develop, test, maintain and improve software applications according to requirements while delivering reliable, maintainable code and progressively increasing independent engineering capability (current snapshot: Swati).

Evidence dimensions: delivery reliability against committed work, context-adjusted; engineering quality (defects, rework, DoD compliance); ownership of assigned modules; debugging and root-cause depth; developer testing before QA handoff; review quality given and received; reliability contribution; increasing autonomy over time, evidenced by escalation records and review outcomes (Section 79.1); collaboration with QA, DevOps and peers; product knowledge growth.

### 81.2 AI-assisted development emphasis

The development role variant that carries the AI-Assisted Development & Engineering Productivity KRA (current snapshot: Unmesh; role purpose: develop and maintain software solutions using modern development practices and AI-assisted coding tools while ensuring AI-generated implementations are understood, tested, secure, maintainable and aligned with requirements) adds one emphasis to the development model, and only one:

* Evidence concerns the understanding, testing, security and maintainability of AI-generated implementations - whether the person can explain, validate, correct and own what the tools produced.
* Volume of AI-generated output is never evidence, for this role or any other.
* Rework arising from AI-generated work is a task-class quality signal first (Section 57 (Automation Value and AI Output Measurement)); it reaches an individual reading only through the variance classification of Section 80.
* Every engineer uses AI coding tools under the AI Runtime Contract (Section 35); this role model differs only in that the framework in force makes disciplined AI-assisted engineering an explicit, weighted expectation.

### 81.3 Senior / advanced development role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: deliver high-quality software across assigned Lumiverse products, take technical ownership of important modules, solve complex engineering problems, support other developers and ensure reliable, maintainable and production-ready outcomes (current snapshot: Bhushan).

Additional evidence beyond the development model: architecture and technical decision quality; mentoring and enablement of other developers; complex problem resolution with low recurrence; cross-product engineering impact and ramp-up speed on new products; technical risk and dependency identification ahead of impact; continuity of ownership, meaning whether another developer can take over routine maintenance.

### 81.4 QA role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: ensure the quality, reliability and release readiness of Lumiverse software through systematic manual and automated testing, effective defect identification, regression validation and continuous QA improvement (current snapshot: Saumit).

Evidence dimensions: verification throughput against verification demand, capacity-adjusted; escaped defect prevention and leakage analysis; UAT quality and defect report quality; automation coverage, reliability and maintenance burden; release confidence and release recommendation accuracy; risk identification ahead of release; verification backlog trend, reported as a capacity signal before it is read as a performance signal; regression effectiveness.

Binding rule: QA verification depth must never be traded for throughput. If verification demand exceeds verification capacity, that is a staffing or automation signal per Section 73 (Workforce Staffing Diagnosis and Rebalancing) - and feeds the QA single-point-dependency mitigation ladder - not a QA performance signal.

### 81.5 Mobile role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: independently design, develop, test, release and maintain reliable Android/iOS applications using Flutter while taking end-to-end ownership of assigned mobile features and products (current snapshot: Prathamesh).

Evidence dimensions: mobile delivery against commitments; application stability (crash-free sessions, ANRs where applicable); release reliability and store submission execution; performance and resource efficiency; device and OS compatibility; API integration and backend collaboration; platform-specific quality and security.

Context note: mobile carries a heavier manual UAT mix by declaration in the verification contract (Section 31), and external review latency in store submission. Both are context inputs, not performance deductions.

### 81.6 Voice AI / specialist role

The framework in force is the authority for this role. This specification adds no generic engineering expectations to it.

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: develop, integrate, test and continuously improve Voice AI capabilities across Lumiverse products, with Solvox.ai as the current primary assignment and scope extending to other Lumiverse products based on business priorities (current snapshot: Mansi).

Evidence dimensions are exactly those recorded in Framework v1: Voice AI Feature Delivery & Execution; Voice AI Quality & Reliability; AI Voice Integration & Technical Excellence; Testing & Voice AI Validation; Work Management & Collaboration; Technical Growth & Continuous Improvement; Beyond KRA/KPI; Client Demo & Presentation.

Instrumentation note: several of these KPIs are Not yet instrumented, notably agent behaviour acceptance and scenario evaluation coverage. The Voice AI evaluation harness that instruments them is a verification-contract requirement for products with an AI runtime dependency (Sections 31 and 38), scheduled in the implementation phases (Section 98 (Implementation Phases and Roadmap)). Until it exists, these KPIs are assessed by human judgement against the framework's target wording, and the evidence bundle states this rather than presenting a proxy.

Background LLM variability is a context factor (Section 80), not a performance factor; an external model behaviour change is a product defect category (Section 41), not a person signal.

### 81.7 DevOps / Infrastructure / CI role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: build, maintain and improve Lumiverse's CI/CD, deployment and infrastructure environment so applications can be delivered reliably, securely and efficiently across environments (current snapshot: Harshal).

Evidence dimensions: CI reliability and pipeline availability, mapping directly to the platform SLOs (Section 51); deployment reliability and automation coverage; infrastructure reliability and availability; recovery readiness and restore-test execution (Section 44); observability quality; infrastructure security and access governance; automation that measurably reduces recurring effort (Section 57); platform change safety (Section 61).

Context note: platform SLO breaches caused by fleet migration burden or change-budget overrun are platform-driven (Section 80.2), not person-driven.

### 81.8 Foundational development role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: develop foundational software engineering capability by completing assigned development tasks under appropriate guidance, following engineering standards and progressively increasing independence and ownership (current snapshot: Aarti).

Evidence emphasis: completion of assigned work to standard with appropriate guidance; learning trajectory and application of feedback; developer-level testing and debugging discipline; code-review participation; documentation and disciplined work management; progressive independence over time.

Binding fairness rules:

* Guidance consumption is expected in this role. Management Attention signals (Section 86) for a person in a foundational role are read as onboarding and development context, never as a performance concern by default.
* No comparison with senior developers on any shared raw metric.
* Targets for this role are exactly those recorded in Section 78.12; nothing stricter is assumed.

### 81.9 Team Lead role

Anchored to the Framework v1 role purpose: ensure effective execution of the technical team's work through planning, coordination, technical leadership, quality control, blocker removal, mentoring and continuous process improvement, with hands-on development on selected small or critical tasks as secondary responsibility (current snapshot: Nimesh).

Evidence dimensions: Ready-queue health and future work readiness; planning latency and Gate 1 queue depth (Section 26); blocker removal effectiveness; architecture decision quality; team capacity balance and allocation quality; review distribution health, never concentrating review on themselves (the review concentration signal, Section 52); knowledge redundancy across the portfolio; engineering health trend; strategic technical roadmap contribution including the platform roadmap (Section 59); delegation effectiveness; hiring diagnosis quality.

Binding rule: Team Lead overload is a topology and delegation signal before it is a performance signal. Sustained Gate 1 latency triggers the delegation and second-Lead paths in Section 13 (Team Lead Succession and Delegation) and Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution), not a coaching conversation about working harder.

Team Lead fairness rules. The Team Lead must not be evaluated adversely for:

* Ready-queue misses caused by product reprioritisation
* architecture workload caused by portfolio growth
* incident load caused by critical products
* QA backlog caused by portfolio expansion
* Founder-directed priority changes

The Team Lead is evaluated on whether they diagnose constraints, protect flow, prepare work, delegate, balance capacity, escalate structural problems and build team resilience.

### 81.10 Founder

No employee productivity score is created for the Founder. Founder effectiveness sits outside the ordinary engineering performance framework unless separately and explicitly defined by the Founder. The system measures Founder coordination hours only as a portfolio goal metric - the founder-protection objective (Section 67 (Human Attention Economics)) - and Founder-decision latency only as a system bottleneck diagnostic (Section 67), never as personal performance.

### 81.11 Extensibility

A new role is added by creating a role evidence model in the control plane naming: the role purpose from the framework version in force; the KRAs and KPIs that apply; evidence sources; instrumentation status per KPI; capacity dimensions; and confidence rules. No core system change is required. Roles may be added, retired or held by multiple people. This is covered by the acceptance tests in Section 100 (Acceptance Tests).

## Section 82. Capability Matrix and Maturity

This section extends the Capability Model (Section 9) with observed maturity.

### 82.1 The separation

Two distinct things, never merged:

* **Authorisation capability**: what a person is permitted to do. This is the Capability Model of Section 9, unchanged. Authority checks read authorisation capability, never observed maturity.
* **Observed capability maturity**: what the evidence suggests a person can currently do well.

Worked example of the intended shape:

| Domain | Authorisation | Observed maturity | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Backend | Granted | Strong | High |
| Architecture | Not granted | Developing | Medium |
| Migration review | Not granted | Learning | Low |
| Mobile release | Granted | Working independently | High |

Binding rule: capability assessment never automatically grants a permission. Permission and competence remain separate decisions, and permission changes go through the registry process (Sections 9 and 10) with the appropriate capability. This is verified by an acceptance test (Section 100).

### 82.2 Maturity levels

Not observed; Learning; Working independently; Strong; Expert / enablement, meaning able to teach and unblock others.

Evidence sources: completed work, review outcomes, architecture contributions, incident participation, mentoring, technical decisions, verification work, and explicit manager observation.

### 82.3 Confidence

Every maturity assessment carries a confidence level: high, medium, low, or insufficient evidence. The system does not pretend it can measure technical skill precisely. Low confidence is displayed prominently rather than hidden, and a low-confidence assessment may not be used as the basis for a role-fit conclusion.

### 82.4 Refresh by routing real work

The correct remedy for stale capability evidence is to deliberately route the next suitable piece of work or review to that person, not to create a documentation task. Capability evidence refreshes as a by-product of real work flowing through the review network (Section 17).

### 82.5 Visibility

Capability information is split by purpose. The capability requirements needed to assign work safely are operational and available to the Team Lead. Capability maturity assessments used as input to people decisions - promotion readiness, role fit, development planning - are Founder-only, inside Layer B (Section 90 (Access Control Architecture)). A person always sees their own full capability matrix.

## Section 83. Individual Workload Health, Overload and Under-Utilisation

### 83.1 Computed per-person fields

For each person the system computes, continuously and from machine-derived sources wherever they exist:

* current workload and its composition, expressed in the eight-category attention taxonomy of Section 67 (Human Attention Economics);
* capacity for the period, net of approved leave and calendar (Section 69 (Capacity and the Capacity Profile));
* utilisation by category (Section 70 (Utilisation, Bandwidth and Sustainable Utilisation));
* review share;
* incident share;
* coordination share;
* product complexity carried, PLU-weighted as context only (Section 68 (Product Load Model and Portfolio Economics));
* number of active products;
* context-switching rate;
* unplanned work share (entries carrying the unplanned flag);
* remaining safe bandwidth (Section 70).

These fields are diagnostic and planning inputs. None of them is individual performance evidence — the invariant of Section 75 (The Fundamental People Model) applies to every field in this list.

### 83.2 The six workload states

| State | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Healthy | Utilisation within the sustainable band, operational reserve intact, no quality or aging signals |
| Busy | Near the sustainable band, reserve thin — with or without adverse quality signals, which are carried as the state's named cause and enter Section 83.3 as candidate signals |
| Overloaded | Sustained above the sustainable band with reserve consumed, per Section 83.3 |
| Unsustainable | Overloaded plus adverse quality, aging or defect signals across multiple windows |
| Underutilised | Sustained unused capacity, cause diagnosed per Section 83.4 |
| Blocked | Capacity available but work cannot proceed due to dependency, environment, review or decision wait |

Binding rules:

* Underutilised is never rendered, exported or described as underperforming. The two are different states with different causes and different responses. Any implementation that conflates them is a defect.
* Full individual workload detail is Founder-only per Section 90 (Access Control Architecture). The Team Lead receives only the three-state `allocation_state` field defined in Section 90.5.
* "Sustained", wherever it appears in this section, is calibrated configuration with an initial value of six consecutive weeks. The value is reviewed at calibration (Section 84.5) and may be changed without code change.
* **This table is the authoritative individual state machine.** The four-state Remaining Safe Bandwidth reading of Section 70.3 is its bandwidth projection for an individual, and the three-state operational field of Section 90.5 is its allocation projection. No other set of workload states exists anywhere in this operating system, and neither projection defines a state of its own.
* **The six states are exhaustive and mutually exclusive**, resolved in this precedence order, highest first: Unsustainable, Overloaded, Blocked, Busy, Underutilised, Healthy. Blocked therefore outranks Underutilised — a person idle because a dependency, environment, review or decision is outstanding is Blocked, which is a dependency finding, never an unused-capacity one.
* **Leaving a state is as defined as entering it.** A person leaves Overloaded when fewer than three of the Section 83.3 signals are concurrent across the same number of consecutive windows their emission required, and leaves Unsustainable when the adverse quality, aging and defect signals clear across that same span, falling to Overloaded or below. The symmetry is deliberate hysteresis: one quiet window never clears either state, and a state that can be entered but not exited is a defect.

### 83.3 Overload detection

Overload is detected from sustained multi-signal patterns, never from a single condition and never from a single week.

Candidate signals:

* utilisation above the configured sustainable threshold across multiple consecutive windows;
* operational reserve repeatedly exhausted;
* review backlog attributable to this person rising;
* incident load rising;
* context switches rising;
* delivery quality falling through rework, reopened tasks or QA rejection;
* defect rate increasing;
* work aging in In Progress or In Review;
* Ready-queue items being pulled before preparation is complete.

Binding rules:

* No single condition classifies a person as overloaded.
* A minimum of three concurrent signals must hold across at least two consecutive measurement windows **and** the pattern must persist for the calibrated sustained window before the Overloaded state is emitted. The measurement window is one week. "Sustained" here is the same calibrated configuration as everywhere else in this section and in Section 84.6 — initial value six consecutive weeks — and one clean week resets the count. Signal counts and the number of concurrent windows are configurable and calibrated per Section 84.6; the sustained window is not separately configurable here, because a people-layer sustained threshold has exactly one value.
* The allocation-problem-first rule: overload of a person is first examined as a team allocation problem. Individual overload with team bandwidth available is an allocation signal for the Team Lead, who may generate a rebalance candidate per Section 73 (Workforce Staffing Diagnosis and Rebalancing).
* Overload of the whole team with no internal bandwidth is a capacity signal that enters the staffing diagnosis chain of Section 73.

### 83.4 Under-utilisation detection

Sustained unused capacity is detected and then diagnosed. Diagnosis comes first, always.

Possible causes the system attempts to distinguish:

* insufficient Ready work, which is a Team Lead planning-capacity signal (a Ready Queue Miss, Section 29 (Work Tracking, Planning Horizons and Material Requirement Change));
* dependency blocking;
* product deprioritised or paused;
* onboarding or ramp;
* role transition;
* approved leave;
* waiting for review;
* environment or platform issue;
* poor allocation;
* genuine low workload with no structural cause.

Binding rules:

* The first response to low utilisation is diagnosis, never a performance conversation.
* Low utilisation alone is never a performance failure and never appears in a performance evidence bundle as a performance measure.
* Where the cause is Ready-queue starvation, the signal routes to the Team Lead as a planning-capacity signal and the individual receives no negative signal at all.
* A utilisation figure such as 50% may mean no Ready work, an external dependency, onboarding, a paused product, approved leave or a review wait. It may have nothing whatever to do with performance, and the system must not present it as if it did.

### 83.5 Visibility and downstream use

Workload states feed three consumers only: the allocation view available to the Team Lead (as the three-state field of Section 90.5 plus team aggregates), the capacity and forecasting machinery of Sections 69–72, and the Founder's Layer B views (Section 90). Individual workload states appear on no general dashboard (Section 92 (Dashboard and View Architecture)). Individual-level forecast resolution — where one person is the constraint — is defined in Section 72 (Forecasting and Scenario Planning); forecasts create decision prompts and never trigger automatic personnel actions of any kind.

## Section 84. Performance Periods, Framework Evolution and KPI Calibration

### 84.1 Period resolution

Each performance period resolves, from effective-dated records:

```
Person
  + Role held at that date
  + Framework version active for that role at that date
  + Applicable expectations, KRAs, KPIs, targets and rating scale
  + Evidence accumulated within the period
  + Context for the period
```

Worked example of a mid-year role change:

```
January–June:   Role = Development,        Framework = v1
July–December:  Role = Senior development, Framework = v2
```

Both segments remain valid. Each is evaluated against what was actually in force at the time. Neither is mutated by the other.

### 84.2 Boundary rules

* At period start: the applicable expectations are fixed for that review period unless explicitly and documentedly amended.
* During the period: evidence accumulates continuously.
* At period end: the review is conducted against the expectations in force at period start.
* On role change mid-period: the new expectations apply from the effective date forward. The prior portion is evaluated against the prior expectations, and the review pack presents both segments separately.
* Retroactive judgment against newly introduced expectations is prohibited. Any exception requires documented Founder approval recorded on the framework version record.

These boundary rules are covered by acceptance tests (Section 100 (Acceptance Tests)).

### 84.3 The evolution loop

```
Framework in force
   ↓
Operating-system evidence accumulates
   ↓
Real observed patterns across roles, products and periods
   ↓
KPI calibration review (Section 84.5)
   ↓
Revision proposal, with reason and evidence
   ↓
Pilot, where appropriate
   ↓
Founder approval
   ↓
New framework version, with effective date
   ↓
Prior version deprecated, retained, never deleted
```

Legitimate reasons for change, none of which the system may apply on its own authority:

* a KPI is consistently too easy and no longer discriminates;
* a KPI is not achievable given operating reality;
* a KPI measures the wrong thing relative to its KRA's intent;
* a KPI is obsolete because the process changed;
* a KPI is duplicated;
* a KPI is missing;
* a weighting is wrong;
* a target is incorrect;
* a new role requires different KPIs;
* product complexity differences make a target unfair between people holding similar roles;
* a manual KPI can be replaced by system-derived evidence of equal or better validity;
* one KPI should be split because it measures two different things.

The system recommends. The Founder decides. The system never silently rewrites the framework.

### 84.4 Versioning rules

* Framework versions are numbered v1, v1.1, v2.0 and so on. The version currently in force, and its content, are recorded in the Performance Framework Registry (Section 77) with the current configuration snapshot in Section 78 (Framework v1 - Current Configuration Snapshot).
* Every version change records: reason, supporting evidence, effective date, affected roles and people, migration approach, and communication plan.
* Old versions are retained, never overwritten, per the append-only history rule (Section 63 (Immutable History and Decision Quality)).
* A person's evaluation for a period is performed against the version in force for that period.
* Targets are never retrospectively moved during an active review period without an explicit documented exception.

### 84.5 KPI calibration review

For every KPI, the calibration review measures:

| Dimension | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Usefulness | Does it change any decision? |
| Reliability | Is it measured consistently and correctly? |
| Gaming risk | Can it be improved without improving the outcome? |
| Data availability | Is evidence actually obtainable? |
| Context burden | How much human context is needed to interpret it fairly? |
| Founder disagreement rate | How often is the signal overridden at review? |
| Employee disagreement rate | How often does the person contest the evidence? |
| Predictive usefulness | Does it correlate with outcomes that matter? |

The override-rate rule, binding: if a KPI is repeatedly overridden at review, the KPI is treated as suspect, not the reviewer. A high override rate is evidence that the metric is wrong, mis-specified or missing context. The response is to review, revise or retire the KPI. Blaming the reviewer for overriding a bad metric destroys the feedback loop that keeps the framework honest.

The same rule applies to the operating system's own instruments. An operating-system health signal (Section 52 (Operating System Health)) or a drift class (Section 53 (Reconciliation and the Drift Budget)) that is repeatedly overridden, repeatedly waived or repeatedly argued down is a suspect signal, and enters this same calibration review with the same eight dimensions. The full statement of Goodhart discipline for the operating system's own instruments is Section 91.7.

### 84.6 Metric calibration discipline

Every capacity, health and performance-evidence metric declares: definition; source; time window; baseline; expected interpretation; known limitations; owner; and defined action on breach. This is the only list of required metric attributes in this system, and no section states a shorter one.

The declaration has a carrier, or the rule is decoration. `time_window` and `known_limitations` are required fields wherever the metric is registered: on every signal row in `os-health.yaml` (Section 52.2), on every Section 103 success metric declared in that same file, and on every framework KPI in the evidence-mapping register of Section 79. The rendered tables in those sections show the columns an operator reads; the full eight-attribute declaration lives in the register, and the table is a view of it, never a second copy.

`known_limitations` is never empty. It is the attribute the rest of this system leans on hardest — Sections 52.5, 84.5 and 91.7 all rest on an operator knowing when an instrument is lying to them — so a metric with no known limitation declares `none-known`, which is a claim a named owner made and can be shown wrong, rather than a blank that could mean either.

* A metric with no owner and no defined response is deleted. Section 103's measures take their owner and their default response from the wholesale grant in Section 103.13, so this limb never reaches them — a missing owner there is assigned, not treated as grounds for removing the instrument.* A metric with no declared `time_window` and no declared `known_limitations` is not calibrated: it is completed at the next calibration review, or deleted under the rule above.
* Thresholds are reviewed every six or twelve months and refitted against observed data. No first threshold is assumed correct.
* Threshold calibration must be possible through configuration without code change.
* Every "sustained" threshold in the people layer (overload, under-utilisation, staffing) is calibrated configuration with an initial value of six consecutive weeks.

### 84.7 The monthly judgment-capture ritual

Fifteen minutes, monthly. The ritual activates at people-tier Phase P2 registry activation — one review period before the first evidence-bundle generation — not at platform launch; until then the unclassified-honestly rule below covers the gap. A standing ritual with no consumer teaches that rituals are skippable (D79). The Team Lead classifies the month's judgment-bearing events while the context is fresh: scope-change events (approved scope change or not), rework-legitimacy calls (legitimate iteration or requirements miss), and misunderstanding-cause events (requirement ambiguity, communication gap or capability gap). The Team Lead also proposes, in the same ritual, the team-driven and mixed variance classifications of Section 80.2 — at team and product level only, never at person level. Person-driven is confirmed by the Founder alone. The classifications are written into the stores the evidence bundles later read (Sections 79 and 89), timestamped to the month they describe. The ritual's duration is calibrated configuration with an initial value of fifteen minutes; where the month's events do not fit, the duration is refitted at the calibration review (Section 84.5) rather than the classification being deferred to period end.

These judgments are never reconstructed at period end. A classification made months after the event is memory, not evidence; a period whose events were not captured in-month carries them as unclassified, honestly, rather than back-filled.

## Section 85. Decision Matrices and the Performance Concern Protocol

### 85.1 Signal-to-action matrix

| Signal | Evidence requirement | Operational action (Team Lead) | Founder decision | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overloaded | Sustained capacity mismatch across multiple signals and windows | Rebalance within team | Hire if structural, after remedies | Re-measure at next window |
| Underutilised | Sustained unused capacity with cause diagnosed | Improve allocation or unblock | Role review only if allocation is demonstrably adequate | Re-diagnose after allocation change |
| Capability gap | Repeated blocked or reworked work in a domain, medium or higher confidence | Coaching, pairing | Training investment, specialist engagement, role decision | Maturity reassessment |
| Strong sustained evidence | Role criteria met across multiple periods and products | Increase responsibility within role | Recognition, promotion decision | Next review period |
| Performance concern | Multiple periods, context examined, other causes excluded | Coaching with clear expectations, normal feedback | Formal action if warranted | Observation period, then reassessment |
| Persistent concern after documented support | Documented expectations, support, observation period | Prepare evidence package | Formal improvement plan or exit consideration | Founder-set review date |
| Team capacity gap | Sustained forecast breach after non-hiring remedies | Rebalance, automate, reprioritise | Hire, with evidence pack | Forecast re-run |
| Team Lead overload | Sustained planning or architecture queue breach | Delegate per Section 13 (Team Lead Succession and Delegation) | Add leadership capacity, second Team Lead per Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution) | Gate 1 latency re-measure |
| QA overload | Sustained verification demand above capacity | Automate regression, rebalance verification support | QA hire, with evidence pack | Verification backlog trend |
| Review concentration | Review distribution beyond threshold | Reviewer matrix rebalance | None required | Distribution spread re-measure |
| Knowledge concentration | Single-point recent knowledge on a product | Route work and review to a second person | Backup owner assignment if structural | Knowledge age re-measure |
| Management attention high | Repeated unblocking, clarification or follow-up | Diagnose onboarding, requirement clarity, capability | Role or expectation change if structural | Attention trend |

No row may produce an automatic final people action. Every row produces a proposed action, an evidence reference and a confidence level. The systemic-versus-individual diagnostic hierarchy of Section 80 (Systemic Context Adjustment and Variance Classification) is applied before any row is read as an individual signal.

### 85.2 Founder decision matrix

| Decision | When | Evidence required | Confidence needed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rebalance with permanent effect | Allocation uneven, internal bandwidth exists | Allocation view, both utilisations, capability fit | Medium |
| Coach formally | Individual pattern needs improvement, context examined | Evidence bundle with variance classification person-driven or mixed | Medium or high |
| Recognise | Sustained strong contribution or exceptional event | Recognition signals with specific instances | Medium |
| Promote | Sustained next-level behaviour already occurring | Promotion evidence per Section 86.3 | High |
| Hire | Capacity gap persists after alternatives | Hiring Decision Evidence Pack (Section 73) | Medium or high |
| Engage specialist | Capability gap narrow or temporary | Capability matrix with confidence, scenario comparison | Medium |
| Role change affecting status | Sustained mismatch or opportunity | Role fit evidence, capability maturity, context | High |
| Formal warning | Persistent concern with documented context | Full documented timeline | High |
| Performance Improvement Plan | Persistent concern after documented coaching and support | Full documented timeline plus prior interventions | High |
| Exit consideration | Persistent documented underperformance after proper process | Full documented timeline, support provided, improvement absent | High |
| Approve leave | On request; leave records in the control plane are the source of truth (Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions)) | The leave record itself; capacity effect visible in the planning view | Not applicable |
| Compensation change | Per company process | Founder judgment; system provides no signal | Not applicable |

Every row specifies evidence, context, the Founder as decision-maker, and confidence. No row is executable by the system. Leave approval may be delegated to a named delegate through a dated delegation assignment, or held under the standing leave-approval delegation of Section 10.3 (Section 10 (Assignment Registry and Delegation)); approved leave is a load-bearing capacity input (Section 69).

### 85.3 Team Lead decision matrix

Available without Founder involvement:

* assign; sequence; rebalance within the team, including temporary reassignment with an expiry;
* coach; delegate; mentor; pair;
* execute reviewer-matrix and product-ownership changes, temporary and permanent, under the reviewer-matrix-change capability — each recorded as a decision, with every permanent ownership change generating a Founder-view notification (visibility, not approval);
* adjust H1/H2/H3 sequencing;
* request QA support; request architecture help;
* approve leave, only where a dated delegation assignment — or the standing leave-approval delegation of Section 10.3 — names them as the leave-approval delegate;
* escalate a hiring diagnosis; prepare evidence for Founder review.

Reserved to the Founder:

* major staffing decisions; budget; new permanent roles; compensation;
* formal warnings; formal improvement plans; exit decisions;
* role changes affecting employment responsibility or status;
* any commitment implying cost.

### 85.4 The concern progression

```
Signal detected
   ↓
Validate — is the data correct, complete and attributable?
   ↓
Context analysis — full systemic check (Section 80)
   ↓
Systemic vs individual diagnosis (Section 80)
   ↓
Team Lead observation and operational context
   ↓
Founder review
   ↓
Founder decision: no action, coaching, recognition, promotion,
   role change, formal warning, improvement plan, or exit consideration
   ↓
Decision recorded
   ↓
Observation period with defined length and defined evidence
   ↓
Reassessment
   ↓
Further Founder decision if warranted
```

### 85.5 The prohibited construct

The system must never implement, and must never appear to implement, the pattern "metric below threshold triggers warning or termination". There is no configuration in which this is permitted. This is a hard invariant (Section 101 (Non-Negotiable Invariants)) and an acceptance test (Section 100).

### 85.6 Language rules

The system never produces "Warn employee X" or any directive about a person. It produces:

"Performance concern requiring Founder review."

Accompanied by: the evidence; the trend; the context; the repeated pattern; the comparison to role expectations in the framework version in force; prior coaching if any; and the confidence level. The Founder decides whether coaching, a formal conversation or any further action is appropriate.

### 85.7 Improvement plan and exit decision support

The system may prepare an evidence bundle for a formal process. It must not initiate a formal improvement plan, a termination, a demotion or a compensation change, and it must not schedule one.

Every such bundle carries: "Evidence for Founder review. Human decision required."

The bundle shows: expectations in force and their framework version; observed pattern with dates; context and variance classification for each period; previous support provided; agreed support and its delivery; the observation period; the timeline of interventions; and improvement or absence of improvement, with evidence.

Exit consideration must never be generated from a single metric, a single incident, low utilisation, low PR count, AI usage or hours logged.

### 85.8 The management-note and concern-closure records

The concern flow produces two defined record types, so that neither observation nor closure lives in anyone's memory or private notes.

The **management-note record** captures Team Lead observations and coaching delivery within the concern flow: what was observed, what feedback or coaching was delivered, when, and with what agreed expectation. It is authored by the Team Lead through a defined intake and, on submission, is written into the Founder's Layer B store — the Team Lead retains no copy, and authoring a management note grants no Layer B access (Section 90). Evidence bundles (Section 89.1) reference management-note records as the "previous feedback, previous commitments and previous management actions" evidence; a coaching step that produced no management-note record is, for bundle purposes, undocumented.

The **concern-closure record** is a Founder decision record that ends a concern, with an outcome of resolved or closed. Writing it removes the concern from the people-tab open list, and the closure — outcome, duration and whether the originating signal proved sound — feeds the KPI calibration review (Section 84.5). A concern is never left to fade: it is open on the people tab until a concern-closure record closes it.

## Section 86. Recognition, Promotion and Management Attention

### 86.1 Recognition signals

The system must not be only a failure detector. It actively detects:

* unusually strong ownership of a difficult problem;
* incidents prevented by foresight rather than resolved after the fact;
* mentoring that produces observable capability improvement in others;
* cross-product enablement;
* architecture improvements that reduce recurring effort;
* automation that materially saves human attention, evidenced by the automation ledger (Section 57 (Automation Value and AI Output Measurement));
* difficult recovery executed well;
* knowledge-sharing that reduces dependency concentration;
* repeated high-quality delivery with low rework.

These become Recognition Signals with specific referenced instances. They map naturally to the "Beyond KRA/KPI → Exceptional Additional Contribution" KRA present for every person in the framework, and to the mentoring and knowledge-sharing KPIs in the framework (Section 78).

### 86.2 Promotion readiness

Promotion readiness is detected as a pattern of next-level behaviour already occurring, not as a threshold crossing.

Illustrative pattern for a developer moving toward senior or advanced scope:

```
Sustained strong delivery
   → increasing complexity handled
   → strong review contribution
   → genuine module ownership
   → mentoring others
   → increasing architecture involvement
   → capability maturity demonstrated
   → next-level work already occurring routinely
```

Output: a Promotion Candidate signal, never a promotion.

### 86.3 Promotion decision support

Evidence presented to the Founder: current role and its expectations; next-role expectations from the applicable role profile in the framework version in force; capability evidence with maturity levels and confidence (Section 82 (Capability Matrix and Maturity)); ownership evidence; leadership and mentoring evidence; complexity of work handled; cross-product contribution; independence; technical impact; sustained trend across periods and, ideally, across products; and context, including whether the evidence came from a favourable or an adverse period.

Promotion is a Founder decision. Nothing is automatic. The Team Lead may recommend.

Promotion prerequisite, binding: a framework mapping for the new role instance must exist before the role change lands. The mapping is a Founder-approved framework edit (Section 77.4), effective-dated to the role change, and is sequenced before the change takes effect — a person is never moved into a role whose expectations are Not defined in the framework in force. The same requirement appears as a role-transition checklist item (Section 12 (Person Lifecycles)), so the sequencing is enforced by the checklist, not remembered.

### 86.4 Management Attention

Management Attention tracks how much intervention a person currently requires: repeated unblock requests; repeated clarification requests; repeated follow-up needed to obtain status; review escalations; repeated rework after review; incident support required from others; ownership reminders.

This is not a performance score and must never be displayed as one. It is a signal about autonomy, role readiness, onboarding need, requirement clarity, management burden, or possible role mismatch.

Binding classification: Management Attention is Diagnostic-only. It carries exactly one decision use in the metric register (Section 79 (Evidence Mapping and Instrumentation Status)) and never enters a performance evidence bundle. The Development KPI "Independent Problem Solving" takes its evidence from escalation records and review outcomes, not from Management Attention signals.

Interpretation rules, binding:

* High attention for a person in a foundational or onboarding role is expected and is read as development context.
* High attention concentrated around one product is a product-clarity or product-complexity signal, not a person signal.
* High attention across all people simultaneously is a requirements-quality or planning-quality signal, pointing at the planning process, not at the team.

Visibility rules, binding:

* Management Attention concerning an identified individual is Founder-only (Section 90).
* Team-level aggregate intervention load may remain operationally visible.
* The Team Lead must never receive a ranking of employees by management burden. No surface, export or report ranks people by management burden.

## Section 87. Succession Readiness and Operational Dependency Risk

### 87.1 Succession readiness fields
