For every critical role, and for every product whose `classification.reliability_criticality` is high or critical, the system maintains:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Primary | Current Primary Owner or role holder |
| Secondary | Cross-Reviewer or second knowledgeable person |
| Backup | Named Backup Owner or acting role holder |
| Readiness | Ready now, ready with support, developing, not ready |
| Knowledge age | Days since the backup last did real work or review on it |
| Capability confidence | High, medium, low, insufficient evidence |

Single-point dependency is flagged explicitly. Backup ownership itself is defined in Section 17 (Ownership and the Cross-Review Network).

### 87.2 Team Lead succession dimensions

For Team Lead succession specifically, readiness is measured on six dimensions: acting candidate identified; architecture capability; planning capability; incident leadership; portfolio understanding; delegation capability.

The acting Team Lead role and partial delegation are defined in Section 13 (Team Lead Succession and Delegation). Succession readiness measures whether those mechanisms would actually work if invoked — a named successor who has never planned a horizon or led an incident is a succession gap, not a succession plan.

### 87.3 Operational Dependency Risk

The system does not attempt to predict whether a person will resign. Behavioural resignation prediction is speculative, invasive and prohibited by Section 91.2.

What is measured instead:

* number of products dependent on one person;
* unique capabilities held by only one person;
* critical infrastructure known by only one person;
* unresolved ownership concentration;
* succession readiness gaps;
* knowledge staleness in the designated backup.

This is named Operational Dependency Risk. It is never named or framed as attrition prediction, flight risk or retention risk.

The quarterly bus-factor scenario (Section 72 (Forecasting and Scenario Planning)) is the primary input. Its output is a remediation plan — deliberate work routing, review routing, backup activation — not a personnel action.

### 87.4 The QA single-point dependency

The portfolio currently carries verification capability in a single QA role. This is recorded as a standing risk decision record (Section 97), surfaced through SIG-28, with a mitigation ladder applied in order:

1. Developer-authored verification with QA review — developers write automated verification under the verification contract (Section 31 (Verification Contract)); QA reviews coverage and quality rather than executing everything personally.
2. Regression automation — background-drafted and human-reviewed test suites reduce per-release manual verification demand.
3. Verification support rebalance — temporary verification support assignments with expiry dates.
4. A second QA hire — triggered by measured verification demand exceeding sustainable capacity across the calibrated sustained window (Section 73), never by product count alone.

The trigger discipline is binding: "we have twelve products" is not a QA hiring case; "verification demand has exceeded sustainable QA capacity for the sustained window after automation and rebalancing were applied and measured" is.

The same treatment applies to every other single-holder specialist capability. Standing single-holder risk decision records, each surfaced through SIG-28, exist for:

* **Mobile — single Flutter role.** Ladder: cross-training a second developer on routine Flutter maintenance; store-release and signing runbooks executable by another engineer; temporary specialist support with an expiry date; a second mobile hire, triggered by measured mobile demand exceeding sustainable capacity across the calibrated sustained window (Section 73).
* **Voice AI — single Voice AI role.** Ladder: evaluation-harness automation so agent behaviour is verifiable without the specialist; documented prompt, configuration and provider-integration runbooks; temporary specialist support with an expiry date; a second Voice AI hire, triggered by measured demand exceeding sustainable capacity across the calibrated sustained window, never by product count alone.
* **DevOps — single DevOps role.** Ladder: infrastructure-as-code and runbook coverage so another authorised engineer can perform common operations and recovery, evidenced by restore drills (Section 44); paging and escalation paths that do not terminate solely in one person; temporary specialist support with an expiry date; a second DevOps hire, triggered by measured demand exceeding sustainable capacity across the calibrated sustained window.

The trigger discipline above applies to each ladder identically.

---

## Section 88. Conduct Concern Protocol

### 88.1 Scope

This protocol covers conduct concerns: harassment, discrimination, grievance, insider misconduct, breach of trust, and comparable behavioural matters. Conduct is distinct from performance. A conduct concern is never routed through the Performance Concern Protocol (Section 85), never appears in a performance evidence bundle, and is never mixed into review packs. The two record classes are separate by construction.

The operating system's role in a conduct matter is deliberately narrow: intake routing, operational containment, evidence preservation and record-keeping. Adjudication, investigation judgment, disciplinary outcomes and legal process are human and, where necessary, external.

### 88.2 Intake paths

A complaint path exists for every possible subject, including the two people who otherwise sit at the top of every escalation chain:

| Subject of the concern | Intake path |
| --- | --- |
| A peer or any employee | The Team Lead or the Founder, at the reporter's choice |
| The Team Lead | The Founder directly, bypassing the Team Lead entirely |
| The Founder | The designated external route: the company's external HR or legal adviser, whose current contact is recorded in the people registry configuration and communicated to all staff at onboarding; the pre-designated successor arrangement of Section 14 (Founder Continuity and Absence) names the same external party |

Binding rules:

* No intake path may require the reporter to notify the subject of the concern.
* An anonymous intake route exists: the external adviser accepts anonymous reports, whoever the subject is. Anonymity may limit the investigative and feedback steps available; it never disqualifies a report from being acted on.
* Where the Founder is the complainant against an employee, the external adviser conducts the investigation, so that no matter is investigated by its own complainant.
* The external route is a standing arrangement, not something arranged after a complaint arises. Its existence and contact details are part of onboarding.
* A reporter is never required to raise a conduct concern through the work-management system, and conduct concerns never appear on any board.

### 88.3 Operational containment

Where containment is required pending investigation, the system reuses existing mechanisms rather than inventing new ones:

* Suspension pending investigation reuses `access_status: suspended` in the people registry — including its exit: reinstatement on this path is a recorded Founder decision against the review-by date every suspension carries (Section 7.1), and the alternative is a suspension that ends by nobody ending it (Section 7 (People Registry)), with the same access-revocation propagation as any suspension (Section 11 (Organisation and Access)). The registry records that access is suspended; it does not record why on any generally visible surface.
* Evidence preservation follows the security-incident preservation pattern (Section 43 (Security Incident Workflow)): relevant logs, records and artifacts are preserved before any remediation or clean-up, timestamps intact, chain of custody noted.
* Where the concern involves a compromised or misused account, the security incident workflow runs in parallel under its own rules.
* Ownership and coverage effects of a suspension (orphaned products, gate coverage) are handled by the normal succession and delegation mechanisms of Sections 13 and 17, without those surfaces disclosing the reason.
* Interim reporter–subject insulation is the middle option between no action and suspension: pending investigation, the Founder may quietly reroute the reporter's plan approvals and review routing away from the subject using the existing dated delegation and routing assignment types (Sections 10 and 23), with the reason withheld from all surfaces. The change appears as an ordinary recorded routing event; no surface links it to a conduct matter, and neither the reporter nor the subject is thereby exposed.

### 88.4 Records and confidentiality

* Conduct records are stored separately from performance records and from all Layer B performance evidence (Section 90). No conduct record enters an evidence bundle, review pack or calibration dataset.
* Conduct records live in a sealed conduct store: primary custody sits with the external adviser, and a minimal Founder-held encrypted copy exists. The store is absent from all backups except its own sealed copy.
* The sealed conduct store carries its own sealed contingency credential in the Section 14.4 escrow, distinct from the Layer B credential. This is the incapacity path: where the Founder is incapacitated, the escrow procedure of Section 14 reaches the Founder-held copy without exposing Layer B, and the external adviser's custody continues regardless.
* Access to conduct records is restricted to the Founder — or, where the Founder is the subject, to the external route — and is not delegable through the people-intelligence delegation of Section 90.4.
* Conduct records are append-only and retained access-controlled for their full retention life (Section 91.1).
* Confidentiality is default: the existence of a concern, the identity of the reporter and the content of the record are disclosed only to those who must act on them.
* Retaliation against a reporter is itself a conduct concern of the highest seriousness.

### 88.5 What the operating system does not do

The operating system does not adjudicate conduct. It does not score, classify, rank or infer anything about a conduct matter. It provides no "conduct signal", no risk model and no automation. It contains, preserves and records — and it hands the matter to humans, with external professional support where the matter warrants it. Employment-law process, mediation and disciplinary judgment are outside its scope by design.

---

## Section 89. Evidence Bundles, Review Packs and Auditability

### 89.1 The Evidence Bundle

The Evidence Bundle is the unit of individual evidence. It is generated, never hand-assembled. It is Founder-only per Section 90, plus the person's own access to their own bundle.

Generation runs in the Layer B operating session: bundle, review-pack and self-view generation executes as a script under the Founder's own identity in a credentialed session on the operations VM, on a monthly cadence. Machine identities continue to hold no Layer B access under any configuration — the session is the Founder, not a bot. Every generation run is logged in the Layer B access log (Section 90.3).

Structure:

```
Role → KRAs → KPIs → expected evidence → observed evidence
     → workload context → product complexity → system constraints
     → trend → interpretation
```

Required contents:

* role and the framework version in force
* the relevant KRA and its weight
* the relevant KPI, its weight, its definition and its target, quoted
* measurement period
* actual result where measurable, with instrumentation status (Section 79)
* target comparison, presented without an automatic verdict
* trend across prior periods
* complexity and context: products, both criticality fields, PLU weighting as context only
* workload context and capacity during the period
* system constraints active during the period
* leave, ramp and role-transition context
* blockers encountered, with duration
* review quality evidence, given and received
* reliability impact
* ownership evidence
* collaboration evidence
* role-specific evidence per Section 81 (Role-Specific Evidence Models)
* previous feedback, previous commitments and previous management actions
* improvement trend
* variance classification per Section 80
* confidence level

The bundle informs the Founder. The bundle does not make the decision, does not compute a rating, and does not rank. No signal is emitted from a bundle whose evidence is insufficient.

### 89.2 The Performance Review Evidence Pack

Generated per person per review period from the evidence bundles:

* current expectations and framework version;
* measured evidence per KPI with instrumentation status shown honestly;
* context and variance classification;
* trend;
* role-specific outcomes;
* capacity and load during the period;
* major contributions;
* development areas;
* specific review examples;
* incidents where relevant, with the person's role in them;
* mentoring and enablement evidence;
* previous commitments and their outcomes;
* improvement trends;
* capability maturity with confidence.

Every pack ends with: "Evidence for Founder review. Human decision required."

No final score is assigned by the system.

The governed rating aid: a Founder-only calculator inside Layer B computes the framework's weighted roll-up from the Founder's entered per-KPI assessments, using the weights and rating scale of the framework version in force. Its output is labelled EVIDENCE FOR REVIEW and is never stored as a rating. The aid exists so the arithmetic the framework requires happens inside the governed boundary — eliminating the shadow spreadsheet that would otherwise carry performance data outside Layer B.

### 89.3 Signal confidence

Every individual-level signal in any bundle, pack or matrix carries one of: **High**, **Medium**, **Low**, or **Insufficient Evidence**. Minimum evidence requirements depend on role, period length and signal type, and are declared in the role evidence model in the control plane (Section 81.11) — the one place confidence rules live. They are countable, and the predicate is stated so that two implementations compute the same value. Confidence reads three counts already available in the event log and the framework registry: distinct review periods the signal is evidenced in, distinct products it is evidenced across, and independent evidence sources behind it (Section 79). Initial calibrated values: **High** at three or more periods and two or more independent sources; **Medium** at two or more periods and two or more sources, or three or more periods on a single source; **Low** at one period or one source; **Insufficient Evidence** where the underlying KPI carries no instrumented evidence source at all, or where the new-joiner window below has not elapsed. The thresholds are recalibrated at the same review as any other threshold (Section 84.6). Where the vocabulary is human-assigned rather than derived — capability maturity (Section 82.2) and succession readiness (Section 87.1) — the record names the assessor and the date, and these same three counts bound what confidence that assessor may record. A guardrail that gates on a value nothing computes is a formality, and these guardrails are what make the people layer safe to build.

Binding rules:

* A new joiner produces Insufficient Evidence for individual performance signals until the declared evidence window has elapsed. Capacity and ramp signals still function. The initial value of the new-joiner evidence window is one full review period, or 90 days where review periods are longer.
* A person with a single complex incident or a single difficult period produces Insufficient Evidence for a performance conclusion.
* Persistent patterns across multiple products and multiple review periods produce higher confidence.
* A Low-confidence signal may not be used as the sole basis for **any** management action, and may not appear in a formal improvement or exit evidence bundle as a primary item.
* Insufficient Evidence produces no decision signal at all. It is not a neutral score; it is an absence, and it is displayed as an absence.
* No negative individual signal may be produced when confidence is insufficient.

### 89.4 Review draft generation

Where the system generates review text, its output is labelled "EVIDENCE FOR REVIEW". It is never labelled, exported or stored as "FINAL PERFORMANCE RATING". The Founder may modify interpretation, rating, context and development plan, and owns the final review. The record shows that the Founder owns it.

### 89.5 Decision auditability

If a formal action is taken — coaching, formal warning, improvement plan, promotion, role change, exit consideration, compensation change — the record captures:

* the decision;
* the Founder as decision-maker;
* the date;
* evidence references as pointers, not copies;
* context and variance classification at the time;
* prior interventions;
* the resulting change;
* the next review date.

These records follow the production evidence chain traceability pattern (Section 32 (Production Evidence Chain)) and the append-only rule (Section 63). They are access-controlled per Section 90 and never exposed on general dashboards. A person may access information appropriate to their own formal process through the management process.

---

## Section 90. Access Control Architecture

People performance data is sensitive. This section is implementation-level and binding.

### 90.1 Two layers, not one

There are two distinct data layers with different storage scope, different credentials and different surfaces.

Layer A — Engineering Operating View. Operational engineering information, available to the appropriate engineering users:

* product work, product assignment, product demand
* Ready queue and current work
* blockers
* review routing and reviewer distribution
* team-level and role-level operational capacity
* QA backlog and verification demand
* architecture backlog
* operational incidents and production health
* engineering constraints and bottlenecks
* team-aggregate health dimensions

GitHub-native per-person activity — PRs, reviews, commits, already visible to every organisation member in GitHub itself — is Layer A raw data; the Layer B boundary protects derived people-evidence, not what GitHub already shows. Permitted Layer A renderings of that data are the operational distributions needed to run the review network: reviewer load and turnaround per reviewer. Prohibited on Layer A: trends presented as performance, rankings, and any performance framing of the same data.

Layer B — People and Performance Intelligence. Visible only to the Founder unless explicitly delegated per Section 90.4:

* individual capacity
* individual utilisation and utilisation history
* individual bandwidth
* individual workload composition
* individual attention breakdown
* individual KRA/KPI evidence and trends
* individual performance evidence and evidence bundles
* performance concern signals
* recognition signals
* promotion signals
* individual capability maturity where used for people decisions
* management-attention signals for an identified individual
* improvement plan evidence
* formal warning evidence
* exit consideration evidence
* compensation-related analysis
* comparative individual analysis
* individual historical performance data
* individual staffing and replacement implications
* Founder management notes
* person-specific succession risk
* Founder decision records

General dashboards aggregate at product and portfolio level; no general surface carries a per-person raw-activity drill-down. Individual activity data lives only in Layer B.

Decision-record routing rule, binding: people-related Founder decisions are written to the Layer B decision store; all other Founder decisions are written to `records/decisions/` in the control plane (Section 97). The decision-latency metric reads both stores, so people decisions are neither invisible to latency measurement nor exposed by it. When a decision prompt is issued, a pending entry is opened at issuance in `records/decisions/pending/` — or in its Layer B counterpart for people-related decisions — so an unanswered prompt is a visible open record, not a silence.

### 90.2 The permission matrix

| Data category | Founder | Team Lead | Employee | Peer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| People capacity aggregate | Yes | Yes | Team-level operational view | Team-level operational view |
| Individual utilisation detail | Yes | No | Own only | No |
| Individual utilisation history | Yes | No | Own only | No |
| Individual workload detail | Yes | Minimum-necessary operational field only | Own | No |
| Individual KRA/KPI | Yes | No, unless explicitly delegated | Own | No |
| Individual performance evidence | Yes | No by default | Own evidence | No |
| Individual performance trend views | Yes | No | Own | No |
| Capability required to assign work | Yes | Yes | Own | No |
| Capability maturity used for people decisions | Yes | No | Own | No |
| Recognition signal | Yes | No | Own feedback only | No |
| Promotion signal | Yes | No | No | No |
| Coaching or performance concern | Yes | No | Only feedback actually shared through the management process | No |
| Improvement plan evidence | Yes | No | Only through the formal management process | No |
| Exit consideration | Yes | No | No | No |
| Compensation information | Yes | No | Own formal information only | No |
| Management attention, individual | Yes | No | No | No |
| Management attention, team aggregate | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Comparative individual analysis | Yes | No | No | No |
| Founder management notes | Yes | No | No | No |
| Founder decision records | Yes | No | Own formal process only | No |
| Team operational health | Yes | Yes | Appropriate team-level view | Appropriate team-level view |
| Product health | Yes | Yes | Relevant operational data | Relevant operational data |
| Ready queue | Yes | Yes | Own work and product | Relevant product |
| Review routing | Yes | Yes | Own assignments | Relevant product |
| Succession and dependency risk, person-specific | Yes | No | No | No |
| Succession readiness, product-level operational | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| Every people-related category above, for machine identities (reconciler, provisioning CLI, ops console, background agents) | No | No | No | No |

The machine-identities row is absolute: no machine identity holds any people-related data category, receives a Layer B credential or folder scope, or holds the people-intelligence capability, under any configuration. People intelligence is never relayed over messaging surfaces. The Layer B operating session (Section 89.1) does not breach this row: generation runs under the Founder's own identity in a credentialed session, never under a machine identity.

### 90.3 Datasource-level enforcement

Dashboard-level hiding is not access control. Neither, in Grafana OSS, is folder membership: datasource-level query permission is an Enterprise feature Grafana OSS does not have, so in a single OSS instance any editor can point Explore or a new panel at any registered datasource — which is exactly the leakage this section rules insufficient. The following are binding:

* The people-performance datasource is separately credentialed from the general engineering datasource.
* Any user able to query the people datasource is considered to have full access to it, regardless of which panels they can see.
* Layer B renders in a second, Founder-only Grafana instance on the operations VM — the same JSON-provisioning discipline as the shared instance, its own credential and its own authentication restriction (D75). The people datasource is never registered in the shared instance; the Layer B boundary is instance separation, not folder membership. Folder ACLs in the shared instance remain defence in depth for Layer A views only. Access to the Founder-only instance derives from the people-intelligence capability (Section 90.4).
* Sensitive people data must not be present in the general engineering datasource at all, not merely hidden from its panels.
* The individual self-view (Section 90.6) is delivered as a generated per-person document, not as a dashboard. This closes the last leakage path — a shared dashboard stack never holds per-person sensitive data for non-Founder viewers — and means no enterprise dashboard licence and no bespoke web application is required for the people layer.
* Layer B's durable home is the separately credentialed people-data store on the operations VM — the database plus its generated documents — encrypted at rest, with encrypted backups protected by a restricted backup credential, and never present in any org-readable repository. Host-level administrative access to that host — VM-root and Grafana-admin — is a **named, recorded accepted risk**, never a capability grant, and the acceptance is stated in full or it is not an acceptance. It names its holder in the operational asset inventory (Section 49); it states that the holder does not thereby hold `people-intelligence` and may not query, read, copy or render Layer B content; it carries a compensating control the holder cannot silently defeat — host-level file-access auditing on the store path, shipped to a destination the host holds no credential to alter, the same write-only discipline the organisation export uses (Section 45.3); and it carries a dated review on the calibration cadence (Section 84.5), calibrated configuration, initial value quarterly. The Layer B access log below is application-level and does not see a root-level file read, which is precisely the gap the host-level audit trail covers. An accepted risk with no named holder, no compensating control and no expiry is undocumented policy (Section 54.2).
* Every Layer B access is logged: who accessed, whose data, and when. The access log is reviewed on the calibration cadence (Section 84.5). Layer B sessions carry declared session-lifetime limits and expire; standing unattended sessions are prohibited.
* No Layer B evidence may be generated before this separation exists. This gates the corresponding implementation phase (Section 98 (Implementation Phases and Roadmap)).

The control-plane stack that hosts Layer B carries an elevated patch priority for exactly this reason (Section 62 (Tool Register and Platform Exit)).

### 90.4 The people-intelligence capability

Access to Layer B is gated by the `people-intelligence` capability in the capability model (Section 9 (Capability Model)).

* The Founder holds it by default.
* **It is not delegable** (D109). No assignment type grants it, and none may be introduced to do so: at this scale no holder exists for such a delegate, since the Team Lead is barred from the data by 90.2 and 90.5 and the design test of 90.5 depends on that. Access under Founder incapacity runs through the sealed contingency credential of Section 14.4.
* Delegation is a Founder decision, recorded as a decision.
* Access to the Founder-only Layer B instance (90.3, D75) — its credential and its authentication allowlist — derives from this capability and from nothing else; reconciliation (Section 53) verifies that the holders of Layer B access exactly match the holders of the capability. The comparison's scope is written down rather than assumed: it covers the instance credential, the authentication allowlist, and the host's named OS accounts, sudoers entries, SSH authorised keys and backup-store read list — compared against the capability holders and against the named accepted-access record of 90.3. A holder appearing in neither list is Blocking drift. A check scoped narrower than the access it exists to verify reports clean for the wrong reason.
* Conduct records (Section 88) sit outside this delegation: delegating people-intelligence does not grant conduct-record access.

### 90.5 Team Lead minimum-necessary access

Where individual capacity information is genuinely required to allocate work, the Team Lead receives only the minimum operational state — one field per person, named **`allocation_state`** everywhere it appears. The word `availability` is reserved for the person-record lifecycle state (Section 6.4) and never names this field:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Available | Can take additional work of the class being assigned |
| Constrained | Only small or low-risk work fits; assign with an explicit trade-off |
| Unavailable | Should not receive additional work in this window |

The field is **derived, never entered**. It is the projection of the Section 83.2 workload state, which is authoritative:

| Workload state (Section 83.2) | Operational field |
| --- | --- |
| Healthy, Underutilised | Available |
| Busy | Constrained |
| Blocked | Constrained, with the blocking class named |
| Overloaded, Unsustainable | Unavailable |

Blocked renders Constrained rather than Available because assigning fresh work to a blocked person converts a dependency problem into a context-switch problem; the blocking class travels with the field so the Team Lead's first response is to clear the block rather than to allocate around it. Underutilised renders Available and carries no cause, because cause here is diagnosis (Section 83.4) and diagnosis is not allocation input.

This field carries no history, no percentage, no composition, no trend and no evidence. It is sufficient for allocation and insufficient for evaluation, which is precisely the design intent.

`allocation_state` is derived, never hand-maintained. It collapses the person's remaining safe bandwidth (Section 70.3): Available and Constrained pass through unchanged, and Overloaded and Unsustainable both present as Unavailable — the Team Lead needs to know that no more work fits, not how badly. Any person whose person-record `availability` is not `active` presents as Unavailable for the duration. The lifecycle state is an input to the allocation state, never the same field, and never a second column.

The design test: the Team Lead must be able to answer "how should I allocate engineering work?" without being able to answer "who is being considered for promotion or exit?"

Single-holder-role honesty: where a role has exactly one holder, role-level operational views necessarily identify that person, and pretending otherwise would be false anonymity. This visibility is deliberate and bounded: single-holder role surfaces carry operational queues and demand only — never KPI evidence, never trends presented as performance, never management signals. The boundary is what is shown, not who can be inferred.

### 90.6 Own-data transparency

Transparency of one's own evidence and privacy of other people's management records are different things, and both are required.

An employee may see, through their generated per-person self-view document:

* their own role and responsibilities;
* their own active framework version;
* their own KRA/KPI;
* their own evidence;
* their own workload, capacity and assignments;
* their own capability matrix with confidence;
* their own trends;
* their own feedback;
* their own development goals and next development priorities;
* their own review history.

The self-view is generated into the people-data store (Section 90.3) and delivered in exactly one of two ways: as an encrypted per-person document whose key is exchanged directly with the person, or read in a Founder-granted session. It is never stored unencrypted outside the store.

Self-view operations are fixed: generation runs on the monthly Layer B operating-session cadence (Section 89.1), plus on demand when the person requests it. The key material is **per-person public-key material**: the person holds the private half — their existing hardware key or an equivalent personal identity — and only the public half is registered at onboarding, a named onboarding checklist item. The Founder session therefore holds nothing that decrypts anyone's self-view, which is what stops root on the operations VM (Section 51.4) being a path to every person's performance history, and what makes departure clean: the company never held the decrypting half. Registered material is **re-keyed annually**, and immediately on a lost-device or compromised-workstation report under Section 43.4, each re-key recorded as a decision — a static secret protecting a whole tenure of documents sitting in a messaging archive is one compromise away from retroactive *and* prospective exposure, with no event, no signal and nothing to detect. The deliverer is the Founder session, which sends the encrypted document over the existing team channel; the encryption is what makes that channel acceptable.

The evidence-contest path is part of the self-view: a person may attach a contest note to any item in their self-view. The note is routed to the Founder and is captured as data feeding the employee-disagreement dimension of the KPI calibration review (Section 84.5). Contesting evidence is never penalised; a frequently contested item is a suspect item, per the override-rate rule.

An employee may not see: another person's utilisation, capacity, bandwidth, workload, performance evidence, KRA/KPI trends, performance concern, promotion signal, improvement plan or exit consideration; compensation analysis; Founder management notes; comparative rankings; or private staffing decisions involving another employee.

No employee leaderboards are built. This is a design requirement, not a courtesy: a people layer visible only to management is an asymmetry that erodes trust and, over time, degrades the honesty of the underlying data.

The Team Lead, as an employee, always sees their own KRA/KPI, workload, evidence and development feedback, received through the same self-view mechanism — an encrypted document delivered by the Founder session over the team channel, exactly as for every other employee; their own evidence never appears on any Layer A view. They do not see Layer B information about anyone else.

### 90.7 Founder override

The Founder may override any system signal. An override records: the decision; the reason; the evidence or context relied on; the decision-maker; and the date.

Overrides are evaluated in aggregate, without blame, in the same spirit as decision-quality review (Section 63) and KPI calibration (Section 84.5). A signal class overridden repeatedly is a defective signal, not a defiant decision-maker. The response is to fix or retire the signal. An override never breaks the system.

---

## Section 91. Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart

### 91.1 Retention principles

* Retain what supports fair review, auditability and continuity: review evidence; framework versions; decisions with their decision-maker, context and period; performance summaries; and the supporting data those reference.
* Append-only history applies to state, decisions, approvals and records (Section 63). Raw activity telemetry is different: it may be aggregated or discarded after its declared diagnostic window has passed, unless referenced by an open decision record.
* Do not retain indefinite raw behavioural telemetry without a stated purpose.
* Retention operates on granularity, not on erasing decisions. Historical records are never silently overwritten; effective-dated records supersede, they do not destroy.
* Sensitive management records remain access-controlled for their full retention life.
* Retention classes per data class are declared in the control plane, reviewed at the annual metric review, and owned by the Founder.

The stated intent: the system must not become a surveillance archive.

### 91.2 No-surveillance design

Explicitly banned, with no configuration option to enable any of them:

* keystroke logging
* screen monitoring or screenshots
* arbitrary activity surveillance
* webcam or presence detection
* "hours online" or "hours at desk" as a performance measure
* AI token usage as a performance measure
* IDE active time as a performance measure
* resignation or flight-risk prediction from behavioural signals
* inference of emotional state, motivation, engagement, wellbeing or mental health from system telemetry
* surveillance scoring of any kind

The purpose of this layer is engineering management, not employee monitoring.

### 91.3 Team health versus employee health

The system may state: "workload risk high", "sustained overload detected", "reserve exhausted".

The system must never state: "employee is burned out", "employee is disengaged", "employee is likely to leave", or any equivalent inference about a person's internal state.

Wellbeing is a human conversation. The system's role is to make the workload facts available so that conversation is informed. It has no further role.

### 91.4 Fairness rules

The system must account for, and visibly present, the following whenever individual evidence is interpreted: role differences; product complexity and criticality (both fields, Section 15); experience level and role seniority; onboarding and ramp periods; temporary assignments; approved leave; incident load; architecture constraints and technical debt carried; platform and environment failures; customer-driven scope changes; role transitions mid-period.

Prohibited comparisons:

* a foundational developer against a senior developer on any single raw value;
* a developer against QA on any single value;
* a Team Lead against a developer on any single value;
* a person carrying a critical, high-complexity product against a person carrying a low-complexity internal tool, on any value not complexity-adjusted and context-annotated.

Anti-leaderboard rule: the system produces no ranked list of people by commits, PR volume, code volume, AI usage, hours, tickets or any composite of these. This is a hard invariant and a defect if implemented.

### 91.5 Prohibited incentives and design responses

The system must not create incentives to:

* split pull requests artificially;
* close trivial tickets to inflate completion counts;
* inflate estimates to improve estimation accuracy;
* avoid difficult work;
* avoid risky ownership;
* avoid mentoring because it does not show in a count;
* avoid review because it does not show in a count;
* generate AI output merely to increase apparent activity;
* stay online longer to improve utilisation optics;
* reduce verification depth to improve throughput.

Design responses:

* Outcomes and responsible ownership are what the evidence models weight.
* Mentoring, review quality, knowledge sharing and enablement are explicit evidence dimensions and explicit recognition signals, because work that is invisible in metrics is the first thing rationally abandoned when metrics matter.
* Difficult and high-risk ownership is recorded as complexity context and appears in promotion evidence.
* Volume metrics are diagnostic only and never appear as performance evidence.

### 91.6 The anti-Goodhart response sequence

When a metric becomes a target, its behaviour is monitored for gaming and for decoupling from the outcome it was meant to represent. If evidence of gaming appears:

1. Detect and document the gaming pattern.
2. Stop using the metric as a primary signal or target immediately.
3. Retain it as diagnostic evidence only, if it remains useful at all.
4. Revise or retire the KPI through the framework versioning process (Section 84).
5. Update the framework version with the reason recorded.

The sequence to be prevented is explicit: KPI becomes target, target drives behaviour, behaviour games the metric, management decides on gamed data. The organisation is never optimised around metric volume.

### 91.7 Goodhart discipline for the operating system's own instruments

The discipline above protects people from bad metrics. The operating system's own instruments — health signals, drift classes, maturity criteria, exception limits, budget ceilings, the attention-hour derivation rules (Section 97.4) and the automation ledger's own savings claims (Section 57) — are metrics too, and several of them are owned by the parties they measure. They receive the same discipline, explicitly:

* The override-rate rule extends to the operating system. A health signal (Section 52), a drift class (Section 53) or a maturity criterion (Section 65 (Operating Maturity Levels)) that is repeatedly overridden, waived or argued down at review is a suspect signal, not evidence of a defiant operator. It enters the calibration review of Section 84.5 and is revised or retired there.
* Exception identity is scoped, not numbered. An exception re-opened for the same scope after closure counts as a renewal of the original exception and inherits its renewal count (Section 54 (Exception Registry and Break-Glass)). Closing one exception ID and opening a fresh one for the same waiver does not reset the renewal clock; reconciliation matches exceptions on scope, not on ID.
* The weekend-activation metric targets zero undeclared activations, not zero activations (Section 47 (Weekend and Out-of-Hours Exception Policy)). Declaring a genuine SEV-1 activation is never penalised, never counted against anyone, and never reviewed with names attached as a fault. The metric exists to catch silent out-of-hours work, not to discourage honest incident response — and it is measured in a way that can actually return a non-zero reading: the residual of out-of-hours state-changing events against the exception registry (Section 103.3). That is record-to-record reconciliation of two stores the system already keeps, not arbitrary activity surveillance and not an hours-online measure (Section 91.2). A target of zero read from the register of declarations would be unfalsifiable, and an unfalsifiable guard is not a guard.
* Drift-finding closure quality is auditable. A sample of closed drift findings is reviewed at the quarterly operating-system review for whether the closure fixed the cause or merely cleared the count (Section 53). Fast-closing findings to protect a drift budget or a maturity level is itself a drift finding.
* Retirement and growth quotas are reviewed for substance. Where a review requires that a policy, metric or automation be retired, the retirement must name what burden it removes; token retirements of already-dead items are recorded as non-compliant with the quota's intent.
* **Derived attention hours are audited against the work they claim to measure.** Engineering hours are derived from authored commits and pull-request activity windows (Section 97.4), and a rising share of agent-directing work produces the same real effort inside a narrower observable window — so the derived figure can fall while carrying cost does not. Nobody games anything; the instrument drifts in the flattering direction on its own. A falling derived-hours figure is therefore never read as leverage unaided. The control is a banded self-report of the same period's hours from a rotating one-person sample, aggregated only and never attributed to a person on any surface, and a widening gap between derived and self-reported hours is a calibration finding against the instrument (Section 84.5), not progress on the goal it feeds. Sample size and cadence are calibrated configuration with an initial value of one person per quarter, recalibrated at the quarterly review against the measured gap. The same discipline binds the ledger's "human attention saved" pair and the operating system's own standing ledger entry (Section 57.2): a saving that appears because the work moved off the observable surface is instrument drift, and it is recorded as drift.

The principle generalises: any instrument whose reading benefits its own operator gets a calibration loop owned by someone else. For people metrics that is the Founder; for the operating system's instruments it is the quarterly review, on evidence, with overrides evaluated in aggregate and without blame.

### 91.8 Ex-employee data rights

When a person leaves, their records divide into two classes with different treatment:

* **Retained under a stated lawful basis**: approvals, decisions, the evidence chain and the records those reference. These are load-bearing for auditability and continuity; they are retained access-controlled for their declared retention life (Section 91.1), with the lawful basis stated in the retention class declaration.
* **Pseudonymised or deleted on request, where applicable law grants erasure**: display names, self-reports and non-load-bearing telemetry.

**What the mechanism actually achieves, stated honestly (D88).** Records carry stable person IDs, never names — that rule is real, it is enforced at schema validation, and it is what keeps the record stores de-identified. But the control plane is version-controlled git, and `people.yaml` carries both `display_name` and `github_login` for every person. Purging a value from a tracked file is a commit: the prior value remains in history, and the GitHub login remains besides — in generated CODEOWNERS files, in commit authorship, and in every pull-request approval the evidence chain of Section 32 cites. **Git history is not rewritten to satisfy an erasure request**, because rewriting it would destroy the evidence chain and breach the append-only invariant this system is built on.

The specification therefore does not claim an erasure it cannot perform. What it commits to is bounded and deliverable:

* **Purged or pseudonymised on request**, where applicable law grants erasure: the current registry entry's `display_name`, self-reports, non-load-bearing telemetry, and the deletable classes named above. The person record itself is retained inactive with its identifier never reused (Section 7.1).
* **Retained under the stated lawful basis**, and named as retained rather than quietly kept: person identifiers already committed to git history, including display names and GitHub logins in prior revisions; commit authorship; and the approvals, decisions and evidence-chain records those reference. The lawful basis is stated in the retention class declaration (Section 91.1), and a departing person is told this at exit rather than discovering it later.
* **Not offered at all**: history rewriting, and deletion of any record the evidence chain depends on.

An erasure request is handled by the Founder, recorded as a decision, and executed against the deletable classes only. Where a request reaches beyond them, the decision record states plainly which parts were performed, which were refused, and on what basis — the refusal is recorded, not avoided.

Two consequences follow and are binding. The **object-locked organisation export** (Section 45.3) is immutable by design, so data already exported cannot be purged from it; its declared retention period bounds how long that persists, and the retention period is declared in the control plane rather than left implicit. And **names are forbidden in record bodies at schema-validation time** — a record carrying a display name where a person ID belongs fails control-plane CI, because the de-identification of the record stores is the one part of this that genuinely does hold.

---

# Part X - Views and Operating Rhythm

The operating system carries state so that people do not have to. This part defines every surface on which that state is presented, the one view built for the Founder, and the daily and weekly rhythm in which humans and machines share the same clock.

## Section 92. Dashboard and View Architecture

### 92.1 The surface inventory

The system does not build a bespoke user interface. Every surface is an existing tool: Grafana fed by DevLake, Prometheus and Scorecard exporters; GitHub Projects boards; the GitHub pull request interface; YAML registries edited in any editor and validated by CI; Remote Control for approving long-running sessions from a phone; alerts via a GitHub Actions webhook into a messaging channel. Building an internal web application is an explicit non-goal: it would require a maintainer the team does not have, and it would become a second source of truth. The single deliberate accommodation is that the individual self-view is delivered as a generated per-person document rather than a dashboard, which is what removes the need for an enterprise dashboard licence or a bespoke web application.

One dashboard does not serve every audience. The complete set of presentation surfaces, each with its access layer under the two-layer architecture of Section 90 (Access Control Architecture):

| # | Surface | Audience | Layer | Medium |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | General engineering dashboard | Everyone | A | Grafana |
| 2 | Per-product operational panel | Product owners, Team Lead, Founder | A | Grafana |
| 3 | Eight operator views | Per view, below | A | Grafana |
| 4 | Team Lead engineering-health view | Team Lead | A | Grafana |
| 5 | Founder view — portfolio | Founder | A | Grafana |
| 6 | Founder view — people tab | Founder; a people_intelligence delegate only via a dated assignment | B | Grafana — a second, Founder-only instance on the operations VM, holding the separately-credentialed people datasource (D75) |
| 7 | Individual self-view | The person, about themselves only | B | Generated per-person document |
| 8 | Formal performance review pack | Founder | B | Generated document per review period |

Layer B-M is gated by the people-intelligence capability, which the Founder holds and which is not delegable (D109); Layer B-S, the individual self-view, is delivered to its subject and requires no capability at all (D110). Sensitive people data never enters the general engineering datasource, and the people datasource is never registered in the shared Grafana instance: the people-intelligence surface runs as a second, Founder-only Grafana instance on the operations VM, so instance separation — not folder permissions alone — is what keeps Layer B out of reach of shared-instance editors (D75).

### 92.2 Presentation discipline

Every surface obeys the same discipline: headline state first, then only what is outside threshold, then everything else on demand. Executive summary first, drill-down second. Not a wall of charts. A signal presented on a first screen must carry an action or a decision; a signal that carries neither is a drill-down.

Drill-downs, never top-level signals: AI subscription usage, raw PR counts, CI internals. Individual activity data is not a drill-down on any general surface at all — it exists only inside Layer B. General surfaces show team and product aggregates; no general dashboard offers a per-person raw-activity drill-down.

### 92.3 Dashboards as configuration

Dashboards are defined as JSON in git and provisioned automatically. This is what makes a dashboard schema change a versioned, rollback-able platform change under Section 61 (Platform Change, Canary and Rollback): a dashboard that misleads is rolled back exactly like a workflow that fails.

**Data age is a panel element, not a stated intention.** Section 64.2 classifies dashboards and health reports fail open, degrade visibly, show data age — and that behaviour is implemented here or nowhere, because Grafana renders the newest row of a stalled datasource with no visual difference from a live one. Every panel in the provisioned JSON declares a `max_source_age` and carries a source-age element computed from its datasource's newest row; past that age the panel renders its stale state instead of its value. Control-plane CI fails the dashboard JSON when a panel declares neither, on the same lane that already makes a dashboard change a versioned platform change. The acceptance test is executed with the health computation job stopped: the Founder view reports its own staleness rather than rendering last-known values as current. A stale dashboard presented as current turns the Monday-morning ritual into the mechanism by which staleness is confirmed as health.

### 92.4 The general engineering dashboard

Layer A only: product health across the four dimensions of Section 6 (Unified Terminology and Glossary) — Engineering, Reliability, Business, People/Capacity, each independently reported, never composited; reliability state; team-level operational health; capacity aggregate; team bandwidth; Ready queue state; QA backlog; architecture backlog; production state; active incidents.

### 92.5 The per-product operational panel

One panel per product showing: last deployment; deployment status; current artifact digest; production health; error rate; last incident; rollback count; UAT status; verification coverage; Scorecard score; restore freshness against the rolling 90-day window (or the tighter cadence its reliability_criticality demands); knowledge redundancy status; lifecycle status; launch status; platform compatibility state; active temporary assignments with expiry dates; shared-service dependencies; monthly cost against the declared infrastructure.monthly_budget_band (Section 50, Cloud Cost Observability).

### 92.6 The eight operator views

| View | Audience | Shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team Lead capacity | Team Lead, Founder | Plan queue, architecture queue, approval queue, blocked people, Ready coverage, routine reviews absorbed |
| Review network | Team Lead | Load per reviewer role, turnaround, rejection rate, familiarity, knowledge redundancy per product |
| Platform rollout | Team Lead | Products by platform compatibility state, canary status, transitional products with owners and deadlines |
| Drift | Team Lead | Declared versus actual state mismatches, by drift class (Section 53) |
| Orphan | Team Lead, Founder | Responsibilities with no owner |
| Dependency | Team Lead | Products by shared service, by external dependency, by provider |
| Background layer | QA, Team Lead | Queue depth, acceptance by task class, suspended classes |
| Platform operations queue | DevOps, Team Lead | Every scheduled control-plane obligation with its due date and holder: restore rotation, credential rotation windows, patch cadence per component, drill schedule, expiring assets, platform changes in flight. The calendar work of Part VI, forward-looking, in one place — memory is not a control (Section 49.1) |

The review-network view presents reviewer load as role-level and team-level distribution for matrix balancing; it is an operational allocation surface, not performance evidence, and its data is never carried into any evidence bundle except through the governed route of Section 81 (Role-Specific Evidence Models).

### 92.7 The Team Lead engineering-health view

Layer A. Operational engineering management.

Shows: product allocation; product demand; team-level capacity; team-level bandwidth; reviewer distribution; Ready queue state and preparation quality; verification bottleneck; architecture bottleneck; operational bottlenecks; team capability gaps that affect safe work assignment; the three-state `allocation_state` field per person (Available / Constrained / Unavailable, from Section 90 — no history, no percentage, no composition, no trend, no evidence); cross-review coverage; knowledge redundancy at product level; delegation opportunities; product-level succession readiness. The Team Lead's own KRA/KPI, workload and development feedback do not appear on this view: the Team Lead receives their own evidence through the generated self-view document like everyone else (Section 90.6).

Does not show: individual KRA/KPI performance or evidence; individual utilisation detail or history; individual performance trend dashboards; performance concern signals; promotion candidates; improvement plan or exit information; compensation; Founder management notes; individual comparative analysis; individual management-attention rankings.

Used for: planning; allocation; coaching; technical development; architecture staffing; hiring diagnosis; evidence preparation for Founder review. The design test: the Team Lead can answer "how should I allocate engineering work?" without being able to answer "who is being considered for promotion or exit?"

### 92.8 The individual self-view

A generated per-person document, produced from Layer B on the same cadence as the underlying evidence, delivered privately to the person it describes. It contains: their own role and responsibilities; their own active framework version; their own KRA/KPI; their own evidence; their own workload, capacity and assignments; their own capability matrix with confidence; their own trends; their own feedback; their own review history and next development priorities. No peer data, no rankings, no other person's signals. Transparency of one's own evidence and privacy of other people's management records are both required; delivering this as a document rather than a dashboard is what makes both enforceable without new infrastructure.

### 92.9 The formal performance review pack

Layer B, access-controlled, generated per review period under Section 89 (Evidence Bundles, Review Packs and Auditability). Labelled as evidence for review, never as a rating, and ending with the human-decision statement. It is an input to a Founder-owned conversation, not a verdict.

### 92.10 Entry points

| Actor | Enters through |
| --- | --- |
| Founder | Grafana. One view, Monday morning |
| Team Lead | The portfolio board — aggregated across all products, filterable by horizon, owner, reviewer, blocked state, lifecycle and compatibility |
| Developer | Their product board and their terminal or editor inside the product repository |
| QA | The verification backlog and CI results |
| Temporary specialist | The specific repositories in their scope. They see nothing else, and their access ends on its date without anyone remembering |

### 92.11 The notification contract

Every surface in this Part is one of two things, and nothing else may page a person.

**Push events** are delivered to the designated messaging channel — a configuration value, never a hard-coded destination. The push list is closed: a Gate 1 submission, pushed to its approver; a Gate 2 request and any reroute to the Backup Owner or Cross-Reviewer; a verification block or unblock; Blocking-class drift; delegation expiry and temporary-person expiry warnings; a launch sign-off request; a pending Founder decision; a support first-touch breach. Every push event exists in the Section 97 event taxonomy — an event absent from the taxonomy cannot page anyone. Within the push list, pending-decision prompts that carry no legal or notification clock coalesce into the morning digest rather than pushing individually; immediate push is reserved for prompts carrying a clock (Sections 43.1, 21.3) and for the rest of the closed push list (D79).

**Wait surfaces** are everything else: dashboards, boards and generated reports. They are consulted on the rhythm of Section 94 and send nothing unsolicited.

If something appears urgent enough to page a person and is not on the push list, the correct response is a governed addition to the push list and the event taxonomy, never an ad-hoc alert.

The scheduled digests named in this contract are wait-surface documents: where the background worker harness — Hermes Agent — produces one, it does so as a registered no-agent job under default-deny scheduling approvals (`approvals.cron_mode: deny`), and every digest links back to the surfaces it summarises (D72). Push events are different: they are delivered by the notification-routing subsystem — the Actions webhook into the designated messaging channel (Sections 92.1 and 99.2) — which is agentless and independent of the background layer. No Hermes instance is ever the only pager, and no push event depends on the background window or on any harness being up. The contract's guarantees are unchanged by this: the digest renderer is an implementation detail, and its replacement changes nothing for recipients. The push list stays closed, wait surfaces send nothing unsolicited, and the designated messaging channel remains a configuration value.

## Section 93. The Founder View

### 93.1 One surface

There is exactly one Founder surface. It answers one question — where should I spend my attention? — and it is not a large dashboard: the first screen shows fewer things than any operator view, and everything beyond the first screen is drill-down. The view has two parts: the portfolio view (Layer A) and the people tab (Layer B, behind the separate people-datasource credential).

### 93.2 The first screen: five portfolio dimensions

| Dimension | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| Product attention | Every product classified Healthy / Watch / Action Required, with the reason on the same line |
| Constraint | What currently limits throughput — review, verification, planning, architecture, engineering capacity, Founder-decision latency, or product priority |
| Reliability | Active incidents, production health, rollback trend, restore freshness |
| Capacity | Developer, verification, planning and machine-queue capacity |
| Business | Active customers, revenue importance, usage trend, support load, customer-impacting incidents |

A Scorecard score drop never sends the Founder to browse raw scores: it arrives either as a decision prompt (where a Founder decision is genuinely required) or as an owned line on the Reliability dimension, naming the product, the drop and the owner already acting on it.

Five standing lines share the first screen:

* The operating-system health line: Healthy / Degrading / Impaired from Section 52 (Operating System Health), with the top contributing signals named. This is a triage entry point, never a composite score.
* The founder-coordination trend: the target — under 30 minutes of founder coordination per day and zero status meetings — is measured on this view itself, as Coordination-category attention hours attributed to the Founder (Section 67, Human Attention Economics), and shown as a trend.
* The Founder total OS ritual hours line: the Founder's total hours across every ritual in the Section 57.2 ritual inventory, sourced from the attention ledger across all categories, shown beside the coordination-time trend so that coordination time is never mistaken for the whole of the Founder's operating-system load.
* The Founder-decision latency metric: median time from decision prompt or evidence bundle to Founder decision. The Founder is a diagnosable constraint like any other.
* The open-prompts line: the pending-decision register (`records/decisions/pending/`) renders as a single line listing every open decision prompt with its age. When a decision is recorded, its originating signal carries a badge — decided DEC-x, remedy in flight, review date — until the review date passes, so a decided signal never re-presents as a fresh alarm.

### 93.3 The eight decision questions

The portfolio view answers eight questions, in this order, with drill-down rather than density:

1. **Which products need attention?** Ranked list, at most five entries on the first screen.
2. **Why?** One sentence per product, naming the dimension: engineering, reliability, business, or people/capacity.
3. **What type of problem is it?** People, process, architecture, verification, business priority, or external.
4. **What is the current bottleneck?** The single diagnosed portfolio constraint, with its evidence.
5. **What decision is required from me?** Framed as a decision, with options, never as a status update. Often the correct answer is "none — the Team Lead has this", and the view must be willing to say so.
6. **What happens if I do nothing?** The projected consequence and its horizon.
7. **What happens if I add one person?** The scenario output for the most plausible addition, with its ramp assumption, invoked in one click from Section 72 (Forecasting and Scenario Planning).
8. **What happens if I deprioritise a product?** The attention released and where it would go — the same one-click scenario mechanism.

The view presents decision prompts, never work queues. It never assigns tasks, never lists PRs awaiting the Founder, and never surfaces anything whose correct owner is the Team Lead without saying so.

**The eight arrive in three phases, not one.** Questions 1–5 are answerable from the Section 93.2 dimensions and the Section 52 signal table, and are the Phase G3 exit target. Question 6 needs the capacity forecast job and arms at G5; questions 7 and 8 are one-click scenario outputs and arm at G6 (Section 98.5). A question not yet armed renders **unarmed — not yet instrumented**, naming the phase that arms it — never an empty panel, never a silently missing row. The view saying what it cannot yet answer is the same honesty the arming discipline of Section 52.2 requires of every signal.

### 93.4 The answerability requirement

The Founder must be able to answer four questions in under five minutes: which product needs my attention; why; what decision is required from me; and is this an engineering, product, people or business problem. If the view cannot support that in five minutes on a Monday morning, the view is defective regardless of how much data it contains.

### 93.5 Design constraints

* No metric appears without an action or a decision attached.
* The first screen fits on one page; everything else is drill-down.
* The coordination-time target is measured on this view and shown as a trend, not asserted.
* The view names its record stores: every number on it is traceable to a canonical store under Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions).

### 93.6 The people tab

Layer B. Founder-only, or a dated people_intelligence delegate. Framing: decision prompts, never raw telemetry. The people tab carries its own answerability bound, mirroring 93.4: the top people decision prompts render first, and the Founder must be able to answer which people decision is required, why, and with what confidence in under five minutes. A people tab that cannot support that is defective regardless of how much data it contains. Its content groups:

* **Team capacity**: total available; committed; reserve; utilisation composition; safe bandwidth; sustainable utilisation; capacity by role; capacity trend; forecast with horizon and confidence.
* **Team health**: overload; under-utilisation; review concentration; knowledge concentration; incident concentration; architecture concentration; capability gaps; Team Lead load; QA load; succession.
* **Individual people, per person, never as a ranking**: capacity; utilisation; workload; product allocation; role; framework version and KRA/KPI; evidence trend; contextual factors; capability maturity; confidence; management signals.
* **Staffing**: rebalance candidate; temporary specialist candidate; hire candidate with evidence pack; the non-hire remedy where one exists; forecast; ramp; expected effect.
* **People development**: recognition candidate; development candidate; promotion candidate; capability growth; succession readiness.
* **Formal management**: performance concern evidence; coaching history; improvement plan evidence; exit consideration evidence.

Every individual and formal-management signal visibly carries: "Decision support. Human decision required." Every Founder-facing signal carries: why; evidence; context; trend; confidence; available options; and a recommended next review date.

The people tab exists to let the Founder open one private view on Monday and answer twenty-two questions:

1. Is the team healthy?
2. Do we have enough capacity?
3. Who is overloaded?
4. Who is under-utilised, and why?
5. Where is bandwidth?
6. Where is work concentrated?
7. Where is knowledge concentrated?
8. Where is QA constrained?
9. Where is the Team Lead constrained?
10. Do we need to rebalance?
11. Do we need to delegate?
12. Do we need to coach?
13. Do we need to develop someone?
14. Do we have a promotion candidate?
15. Do we need a specialist?
16. Do we need to hire?
17. Is there a genuine performance concern?
18. What evidence supports that concern?
19. What systemic factors exist?
20. What is the confidence?
21. Should we change the product portfolio?
22. What decision is required from me?

Each answer carries why, evidence, context, trend, confidence, available options and a recommended next review date. Any answer that cannot be supported that way is reported as unsupported, not approximated. Question 21 is not answered from people data: portfolio change is answered by the Layer A economics view (Section 68.3), which the people tab references as a summary group rather than duplicating.

## Section 94. Daily and Weekly Operating Picture

### 94.1 The cast — roles, not people

| Actor | Type | Primary surface | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder | Human | Founder view, Scorecard | Strategy, portfolio priority, budget, hiring, lifecycle, people decisions |
| Team Lead | Human | Portfolio board, GSD | Sequencing, architecture, standards, Ready queue, escalation, platform changes, reviewer-matrix changes |
| Acting Team Lead | Human, dormant | Same when active | Continuity |
| Developers | Human | Product boards, GSD, AI subscription | Products owned and cross-reviewed; scheduled client demos on their products |
| Mobile Developer | Human | Same | Mobile products, heavier manual UAT, external release latency |
| QA | Human | Verification backlog, CI | Verification contracts, UAT, release readiness |
| DevOps | Human | Platform operations queue (Section 92.6) | The control plane's calendar work: fifth-tier credential rotation, patch cadences, drills, restore-test pairing, asset expiries, the runner and Hermes host estate |
| Support triager | Human, per-product declared triager (default: Primary Owner) | Per-product intake channels | First-line triage into the defect taxonomy (Section 22) |
| Temporary specialist | Human, scoped | Scoped repositories | Their declared capability only |
| CI | Machine | — | Tests, build, security, artifact, validation |
| Reconciliation | Machine | — | Drift detection, expiry revocation, orphan detection |
| Renovate | Machine | — | Dependency PRs |
| Scorecard | Machine | — | Risk score per product |
| DevLake → Grafana | Machine | — | Portfolio metrics |
| Background layer | Machine | — | Draft work, conditional on benchmark |

### 94.2 A single day, humans and machines on one clock

```
TIME     HUMANS                                MACHINES
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
00:00    ░ nobody working ░                    CI on pushed branches
                                               Renovate scanning
02:00                                          Scorecard full scan
                                               Security scans
                                               Reconciliation run
04:00                                          DevLake ingestion
                                               [Background layer drafts]
06:00                                          DevLake refresh complete
07:00                                          Background layer HARD STOP
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
09:30    ▓ EVERYONE IN ▓
         Lead   → portfolio triage, drift and orphan alerts
         QA     → overnight CI failures, draft review
         Devs   → cross-review queue (cheap, no AI)
         Triager→ overnight support intake triage
         Founder→ Monday only: Founder view
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10:30    █ HEAVY AI BLOCK — window fresh █
         Devs   → plan and execute phases
         QA     → verification contracts
         Lead   → Gate 1 approvals, architecture
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
13:00    ▒ lunch ▒
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
14:00    ░ WINDOW TIGHT — human work ░
         Devs   → review, specs, debugging, local UAT
         Devs   → CLIENT-FACING: scheduled demos, support
                  calls, UAT walkthroughs (demo record written)
         QA     → staging manual UAT
         Lead   → Horizon 3 planning, Ready queue refill
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
15:00    █ WINDOW RESET — second heavy block █
         Devs   → remaining execute tasks
         QA     → production verification
         Lead   → escalated / high-risk / platform review only
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
17:00    ▓ SHIP WINDOW ▓
         Reviewers → Gate 2 approvals
         Approvers → production approvals
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
18:30    ░ EVERYONE OUT — no evening obligation ░
                                               Machines continue
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

Working hours are the same core hours, applied per each person's declared working calendar, with one to two hours of personal flex; part-time schedules are configuration, not exceptions. Maximum overlap is deliberate — review latency is the constraint this protects. Staggered shifts were considered and rejected: they add review latency to buy coverage the business does not need.

Client-facing time is part of the day, not an interruption to it. Demos, customer UAT walkthroughs and support calls are scheduled preferentially into the window-tight block, generate demo records or support records (Section 97), and accrue Coordination-category attention hours against the product. A day plan that pretends client-facing time does not exist produces a capacity model that lies.

The two heavy-AI blocks assume roughly two subscription window cycles per working day. If observed behaviour differs, adjust after the first fortnight.

Monday is the exception the plan acknowledges: the Monday morning is structurally meeting-heavy (portfolio review, standup, and the afternoon Lead-and-QA session displaced from it), so Monday plan submissions target the 15:00 block. A developer who submits earlier does so expecting a same-day decision by 15:00 under the Gate 1 turnaround target (submitted before 13:00, decided the same working day) — either way, no Monday plan waits overnight undecided.

### 94.3 Developer daily activity

| Time | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 09:30 | Standup, 10 minutes, blockers only (94.8); check board; check cross-review queue | Today's item identified |
| 09:45 | Cross-review PRs on products I review | Gate 2 approvals |
| 10:15 | Read `STATE.md` on today's product | Context loaded |
| 10:30 | Discuss phase | `CONTEXT.md`, decisions |
| 11:00 | Plan phase | Plan submitted to Gate 1 |
| 11:30 | Work another item while awaiting approval | — |
| 12:00 | Execute phase | Code, draft PR |
| 14:00 | Window tight — human work; the after-midday support-intake pass (22.2); scheduled demos and client calls land here | Reviews, specs, debugging; intake triaged; demo record where a demo ran |
| 15:00 | Second execute block | Remaining tasks |
| 16:30 | Local UAT | `uat.md` steps confirmed |
| 17:00 | Mark PR ready; respond to review | PR ready |
| 18:00 | Update `STATE.md` | Handover-ready |
| 18:30 | Stop | — |

On Mondays the 11:00 plan submission shifts: developers target the 15:00 block for plan submission, or submit in the morning and expect a same-day decision by 15:00 per the Gate 1 turnaround target (94.2).
A developer who is Primary Owner of a product with an `ai_runtime_dependency` carries one further standing call on the day. Where the overnight AI-eval run raised SIG-42 (Section 38.3), its triage — fallback, re-pin, or accept-and-record — takes the 09:35 slot ahead of cross-review, because the same-day SLA starts at 09:30 while cross-review runs to a working-day target. It is one triage per product per night, timeboxed to a calibrated block (initial value 30 minutes) and logged as Incident-category attention (Section 67.2). A triage that plainly exceeds the block is an incident, not a slot: it is escalated as one rather than eaten by the day, so the displaced delivery is visible in the plan instead of surfacing later as a missed commitment.
**The morning block is a fixed budget, and it is fully allocated.** 09:30–10:30 holds the standup, the board and cross-review queue check, cross-review itself, `STATE.md` — and, for whoever holds the triager assignment, the overnight support-intake pass (22.2). It does not stretch into the heavy-AI block: that block is where the fresh subscription window is spent, and colonising it trades plan quality for review latency, which is the one trade this plan exists to prevent. Triage time is a per-product budget — calibrated configuration, initial value 5 minutes per product per pass — carried in the product's load model (Section 68), so the cost scales visibly as the portfolio grows. Where a triager's owned-product count makes the pass overrun the block, the Team Lead reassigns triager duty (22.3) rather than lengthening the morning. Repeated overrun is a calibration input, never a personal one: adjust after the first fortnight.

Nobody ever: approves their own PR; deploys to production without the correct approver; works on an onboarded product lacking a verification contract — pre-onboarding products operate under Section 96 recorded risks; uses a free cloud LLM tier; or sets an API key.

### 94.4 QA daily activity

| Time | Activity | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 09:30 | Triage overnight CI failures across all products | Triage list |
| 09:45 | Review background-layer draft PRs | Accept / correct / reject with task-class reason |
| 10:30 | Author verification contract for the next onboarding product | `verification/contract.yaml` |
| 11:30 | Define UAT steps for in-flight features | `verification/uat.md` |
| 14:00 | Manual UAT on staging; customer-facing UAT sessions where scheduled | Pass / fail recorded |
| 15:30 | Production verification after deploys | Smoke results confirmed |
| 16:30 | Coverage mapping for tomorrow's plans | Coverage confirmed per requirement |
| 17:30 | Release readiness sign-off | Green light or block |
| 18:30 | Stop | — |

QA does not review code line by line. QA decides what proves a feature works, before it is built.

```
OLD QA                        NEW QA
──────                        ──────
code written                  requirement written
    ↓                             ↓
QA tests it                   QA defines what proves it
    ↓                             ↓
bugs found late               plan REJECTED if unprovable
    ↓                             ↓
QA is the bottleneck          machine enforces the contract
```

### 94.5 Team Lead daily priority model

Times are illustrative; the priority order is not.

| Priority | Activity |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Portfolio and board triage, including drift and orphan alerts |
| 2 | Plan approvals (Gate 1), including change classification |
| 3 | Unblock people |
| 4 | Architecture and cross-product decisions |
| 5 | Horizon 3 planning |
| 6 | Refill Ready-to-Execute queues |
| 7 | Escalated, high-risk and platform review only |
| 8 | Standards and constitution maintenance |
| 9 | QA, onboarding and verification planning |
| 10 | End-of-day readiness check |

The end-of-day readiness check (priority 10) verifies four things before the Team Lead stops: tomorrow's Ready coverage per person — every developer has a Ready item waiting; no unactioned Blocking-class drift; no canary awaiting overdue verification; and no submitted plan older than its approval turnaround target. Anything failing the check is actioned before end of day or explicitly carried over with a recorded reason.
