**Only these interrupt the Team Lead:** architecture-class review requests, high-risk review, blocked people, cross-product decisions, incident escalation, Blocking-class drift alerts, blocking orphans. Routine PR notifications do not, and the Team Lead does not subscribe to them.

The Team Lead thinks across Today, This Week, Next 1–4 Weeks, Next 1–3 Months, and Portfolio-wide Future. The role is engineering operating manager for the portfolio, not senior developer.

### 94.6 Founder weekly rhythm

| When | Activity | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday 09:30 | Founder view — the five portfolio dimensions and the OS-health line | Which products need attention |
| Monday 09:45 | Scorecard drops, arriving as decision prompts or owned lines on the Reliability dimension — never as raw scores to browse | Risk remediation decision, or none — the named owner has it |
| Monday 10:00 | Constraint dimension | Which bottleneck, if any |
| Monday 10:15 | People tab (Layer B) — the twenty-two questions as needed | People decisions, or none |
| Monday 10:30 | 20 minutes with Team Lead | Unblock, reprioritise |
| Midweek, default Thursday | Standing decision window, thirty minutes — the default drain of the pending-decision register (D79) | Every open decision prompt actioned, deferred with a date, or explicitly declined |
| Monthly | Layer B operating session — bundle, self-view and pack generation run as a script under the Founder's own identity in a credentialed session; machine identities hold no people data | — |
| Daily | Nothing required | — |
| As needed | Business priority, budget, hiring, lifecycle, SEV-1 awareness, customer commitments, leave approvals | Strategic |

The midweek decision window means decision latency is measured against a known cadence rather than ambient responsiveness: a prompt raised on Tuesday has a guaranteed drain on Thursday, and the Founder-decision latency metric (Section 93.2) reads against that rhythm. As elsewhere in this Section, the day and duration are defaults — adjust after the first fortnight if observed behaviour differs (D79).

The Founder never reviews code, never approves routine PRs, never assigns tasks to individuals, and never dispatches incident responders.

### 94.7 Machine activity

| System | Trigger | Does | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CI | Every push | Tests, build, security, validation, parity | Runner-estate fixed cost (Section 49) |
| Artifact build | Merge to default branch | Immutable artifact, digest recorded, SBOM emitted | Free |
| Staging deploy | Artifact built | Deploy plus smoke | Free |
| Production deploy | Approval granted | Same digest, never rebuilt | Free |
| Smoke tests | Post-deploy | Health, version, critical flow, dependencies | Free |
| Reconciliation | Nightly and on registry change | Drift, expiry, orphan detection | Free |
| Renovate | Nightly | Dependency PRs | Free |
| Scorecard | Nightly | Risk score per product | Free |
| Security scans | Nightly | Static, container, secret and licence scanning | Free |
| AI-eval run | Nightly, every product with ai_runtime_dependency | Scheduled evaluation suite against the product's eval set; results written to records/eval/; a regression raises SIG-42 (Red, routed to the Primary Owner), coalesced to one triage per product per night with a named slot in the day (Sections 38.3, 94.3) | Metered AI usage within the product's declared budget band |
| Restore-rotation scheduler | Nightly | Advances the rolling restore rotation and opens the restore-verification task for the next product due | Free |
| Support email-ingest hook | On inbound support email | Writes the support intake record, starts the first-touch clock; intake anomalies raise SIG-41 (Amber, routed to the Team Lead) | Free |
| Digest generators | At leave approval, on return, and on their declared schedules | Handover, return, morning and role digests as wait-surface documents with links back to the boards; run as platform workflows (subsystems N, P), triggerable by the background worker via workflow_dispatch (D71) | Free |
| Restore test | Monthly, rotating subset | Restore verification, timestamp written | Free |
| Organisation export | Scheduled | Repositories plus issues, PR metadata and boards to independent storage. The audit log is **not** included on the Team plan — its API is Enterprise-only, a recorded accepted risk whose compensating cadence is the manual audit-log review of Section 45.3 | Free |
| Asset expiry check | Daily | 30-day expiry and vendor-deadline alerts | Free |
| Cost ingestion | Daily | Spend versus budget band per product | Free |
| DevLake | Continuous | Ingest to Grafana | Free |
| Background layer | 18:30–07:00, conditional | Draft PRs from whitelist, executed by the Hermes Agent background worker harness (D69) | Hardware only |
| PR-review engine | Pull request opened or updated | Advisory machine review via Hermes against the local inference endpoint; comments only — never approves, never blocks, never satisfies a gate | Hardware only |
| Founder ops console | Founder query or scheduled digest | Read-only conversational answers over Layer A operational data via Hermes, sender-allowlisted to Founder identities; no writes, no Layer B | Hardware only |

Free means no metered line item; VM-hosted jobs carry the fixed VM and storage cost tracked under the control-plane budget band (Section 103). Rows marked Free execute on the self-hosted runner estate or on free platform features; the runner estate's fixed cost is carried once in the Section 49 asset inventory, not repeated per row (D80).

Weekends: all of the above continues. The background layer gets 48 continuous hours — its highest-value window. Human weekend work is governed by Section 47 (Weekend and Out-of-Hours Exception Policy).

### 94.8 Cadence beyond the day

| Cadence | Who | Activity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Daily 09:30 | Team | 10-minute standup, blockers only |
| Monday 09:30 | Founder | Portfolio review on the Founder view |
| Monday 14:00 | Lead and QA | Week's onboarding and verification sequence — scheduled in the window-tight block so the Monday heavy-AI block is not colonised by meetings |
| Friday 15:00 | All | Deployment freeze begins |
| Friday 16:30 | Whoever the Section 98.5 self-report scope covers (D79) | Weekly banded attention self-report (Section 97.4) — five minutes, scheduled rather than assumed, and placed before the Ready-queue refill while the week is still in mind |
| Friday 17:00 | Lead | Ready queue refilled for Monday |
| Friday, throughout bootstrap | Founder | Weekly bootstrap log entry: gates stubbed and armed, bootstrap exceptions opened and closed, phase completion checks run and their results (Section 95.4) — two of the three fields pre-filled by the generator |
| Monthly | QA | Restore test on the rotating subset — one verification per product due that month, roughly three at eight products and seven to nine at twenty, each a QA-plus-credential-holder pairing. The load is a booked line in the QA Capacity Profile (Section 69.2) and in Remaining Safe Bandwidth (Section 70.3), never absorbed as slack; a stale `restore_tested` blocks CI, so a stalled rotation propagates into blocked merges |
| Monthly | Lead | Dependency, Scorecard, cost-band and asset expiry sweep |
| Monthly | Founder | Layer B operating session: bundle, self-view and review-pack generation run as a script under the Founder's own identity in a credentialed session |
| Monthly | Lead | Judgment-capture ritual, 15 minutes: the month's classification and routing judgment calls recorded so they feed Coordination attention and calibration |
| Quarterly | Founder and Lead | Operating-system review, consuming a generated review pack assembled by the health-report generator from the registries and ledgers — the Team Lead no longer hand-assembles it; the generator run is triggered, and its narrative sections drafted and flagged as drafts, by the Hermes Agent background worker harness through the existing generator workflow (D71), with all judgment content human-written — on a timeboxed agenda: weekend activations, TOIL, knowledge redundancy, lifecycle review, business-engineering tradeoffs, hiring signals, canary set review, transitional and pre-onboarding product review, automation-ledger review including the OS's own entry, and KPI calibration scoped to flagged signals only |
| Per review period | Founder | Performance review packs and Founder-owned reviews (Section 84) |
| Quarterly | Lead | Control-plane disaster recovery drill |
| Annually | Lead | Domain auto-renew verification |
| As needed | Founder | Founder ops console — a read-only conversational query surface over Layer A operational data (Hermes Agent, D69), sender-allowlisted to Founder identities. The Founder may ask it operational questions: event-log digests, product and queue state, drift and expiry summaries, background-layer output. It can never write records, decisions or board state; never reach Layer B; never grant, record or satisfy an approval. Every answer links back to the authoritative surface it summarises |

**Quarterly rituals are staggered, not stacked.** Several Founder-touching obligations share the quarterly cadence and nothing above stops them landing in one week. Each movable ritual therefore names the month of the quarter it occupies — **calibrated configuration**; initial values: operating-system review in month 1; escrow seal audit and its functional verification (Section 14.4) in month 2; control-plane disaster-recovery drill in month 3 — recalibrated by the ritual attention-hours budget line of Section 57.2 when measured hours diverge from budgeted. Review conversations stay at the period boundary, because a review held away from the period it reviews is a different ritual. A load that averages to an hour and a half a week and arrives as a twenty-hour week is not the same load, and the first ritual dropped is the one with the weakest forcing function — which is exactly why the ones with no signal behind them are the ones given their own month.

### 94.9 Automation writes state; humans write meaning

Manual status maintenance is the enemy of a no-status-meeting operating model.

| Machines write | Humans write |
| --- | --- |
| Deployed artifact digest | Decisions and rationale |
| Verification status | Judgment calls |
| Test and CI results | Exceptions and their justification |
| UAT result records | Product strategy |
| Restore test timestamps | Explanations |
| Reviewer matrix validation | Architecture direction |
| Ownership and Team drift flags | Incident narrative |
| Role and capability drift | Postmortem analysis |
| Permission drift | Lifecycle decisions |
| Knowledge redundancy status | Classification of ambiguous changes |
| Lifecycle-driven configuration state | Customer communication |
| Platform compatibility state | Business tradeoffs |
| Canary and rollout state | Requirement changes |
| Deployment health | Demo narrative and follow-ups |
| Incident state transitions | |
| Ready-queue miss records | |
| Orphan detection results | |
| Temporary assignment expiry | |
| Asset expiry warnings | |
| Cost-band breach flags | |

Humans write meaning. Machines write measurable state. Nobody is asked to hand-maintain a metric the system can derive.

# Part XI - Implementation

The operating system is built in phases, each independently valuable and independently abandonable, over an existing portfolio of live products, by a team that begins as one person. This part defines how the build starts honestly, how live products are brought under governance without fiction, where every record lives, what gets built in what order, and what the build surface actually is.

## Section 95. Bootstrap Mode and the Solo-Founder Build

### 95.1 The gate-independence problem

Nearly every safety invariant in this specification assumes at least three to four humans holding context on the repository in question. No self-approval, Gate 2 independence, cross-review, "the production approver is never the deploying actor", QA as a separate verification authority — where no second context-holding human exists, these are literally unsatisfiable: branch protection requiring another approver blocks the Founder's own merges, and there is no second human to hold the approving role. Pretending otherwise produces the most dangerous failure the access model warns about: a gate that appears to be working and is not.

Bootstrap Mode makes the shortfall explicit instead of silent — and it is scoped **per repository**, never per company. The shortfall exists only where no second context-holding human exists: the control-plane and operating-system tooling repositories during the solo build. Product repositories whose existing teams hold Write satisfy gate independence immediately, run fully armed from day one, and never enter bootstrap. While a repository has fewer context-holding humans than gate independence requires, each affected gate on that repository runs under a declared, expiring bootstrap exception recorded in the exception registry (Section 54, Exception Registry and Break-Glass) — the first dogfooding of the exception registry, before any product ever needs it.

### 95.2 Bootstrap exceptions

One exception per relaxed gate, in the standard exception schema, naming the repositories it covers:

```yaml
# exceptions.yaml — bootstrap entries
- id: EXC-BOOT-001
  type: bootstrap
  scope: gate-2-independent-review
  affected:
    repositories: [control-plane, os-tooling]
  policy: no-self-approval
  reason: no second context-holding human holds Write on these repositories during the solo build
  risk_accepted: unreviewed changes reach the default branches of the named repositories
  compensating_control: >-
    full CI verification contract on every push; append-only history, nothing
    rewritten; production deploys still require the explicit approval event
  compensating_control_record: CI run history on the named repositories
  compensating_control_cadence: per-push
  requester: founder
  authority: founder
  owner: founder
  start: 2026-09-01
  expiry: 2026-12-01         # expiry is mandatory; renewal is a recorded decision
  review_date: 2026-11-01
  renewals: 0
  deactivation_trigger: second context-holding engineer with Write onboarded to the named repositories
  closure: null              # trigger_satisfied when the trigger fires
```

Rules, binding:

* Every bootstrap exception names the gate it relaxes, the repositories it covers, the compensating controls, an owner, an expiry and a deactivation trigger. An exception without an expiry is rejected by CI like any other.
* Phase 1 (Section 98.2) ships a **minimal `exceptions.yaml` schema validator** in control-plane CI — expiry present, owner present, deactivation trigger present — so bootstrap exceptions have mechanical teeth from week one. The full exception-lifecycle validation of Phase G2 extends this validator; it never replaces the week-one check.
* A bootstrap exception never covers a repository whose existing team already satisfies the gate — the product repositories arrive with their teams and are armed immediately.
* Renewal is a recorded decision, and an exception re-opened for the same scope after closure counts as a renewal — there is no fresh-ID dodge.
* The gates are **configured but not yet binding** on covered repositories. The unarmed configuration is defined exactly: require-PR and direct-push blocking stay on; required approving reviews is set to 0; the workflow-identity gate is not yet enforcing. The armed configuration — required approving reviews at the specified count, the workflow-identity gate active on production deploys — is recorded beside the unarmed one, so arming a gate is a configuration flip, not a build project.
* During bootstrap the Founder holds the operational capabilities — plan-approval, code-review, production-approval, incident-response and verification judgments — explicitly recorded in `people.yaml` under the bootstrap exception, and sheds each as the corresponding role fills.
* Ownership-slot orphan checks (Cross-Reviewer, Backup Owner) run under the corresponding bootstrap exceptions until the headcount thresholds of the activation checklist are reached — the empty slots are declared, not silent.
* QA-judgment calls — benchmark usability and verification authority — are exercised by the Founder under the recorded verification-authority bootstrap exception until the QA role is filled.

### 95.3 What remains binding even in bootstrap

Bootstrap relaxes independence requirements only. The following hold from day one, because retrofitting them is impossible or ruinously expensive:

* **Digest immutability**: the artifact deployed is the artifact verified; CI rejects any production deploy whose digest differs from the staging-verified digest.
* **Verification contracts**: no product completes onboarding without one, and pre-onboarding products carry the Section 96 accepted-risk record instead; the solo builder does not exempt their own products.
* **Secrets tiers and the API-key-free environment**: `env | grep -i api_key` returns empty everywhere, from the first machine.
* **Append-only history and effective dating** on every registry and record — history cannot be retrofitted by definition.
* **The constitution and the untrusted-input rule** for all AI runtime use.
* **Safe defaults and fail-closed classification** in every provisioning template.
* **The explicit production-approval event**: even where the approver and the deployer are the same person, the approval is a distinct recorded event, so the evidence chain of Section 32 (Production Evidence Chain) stays answerable.* **The registry-change lane's staged apply and authority-delta gate** (Section 26.4): the one lane whose owner review is, in bootstrap, the Founder reviewing the Founder is the lane that most needs a mechanical check.

### 95.4 The activation checklist

Each gate arms as headcount allows. The checklist is executed for real — including the negative tests — at each threshold, not assumed:

| Headcount reached | Gates armed | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 humans with Write | No self-approval; Gate 2 independent review; most-recent-push approval | A self-approved PR fails branch protection; a Read-only approval does not satisfy it; a Write-holding cross-reviewer approval does |
| 3 humans | Production approver ≠ deploying actor; cross-review matrix with real routing | A deploy attempted by its approver is rejected; the review-routing table resolves to a person who is not the author |
| QA role filled | Independent verification authority; release readiness sign-off; UAT ownership | A release blocked by QA stays blocked; verification contracts reviewed and owned by QA |
| 4+ humans | Backup Owner coverage; knowledge-redundancy floor; responder rotation | Orphan detection reports zero blocking orphans; every product has a non-author reviewer and a backup |

Throughout bootstrap, a **weekly bootstrap log entry** in the control-plane repository records which gates are stubbed and which are armed, which bootstrap exceptions opened or closed that week, and which phase completion checks were run with their results. The Founder writes it; it takes minutes; and it is the evidence the activation checklist later cites — a closure decision references log entries, never memory. The entry is a fixed three-field template under `records/bootstrap-log/`, and the generator pre-fills two of the three from `exceptions.yaml` and the CI run history, so the Founder writes only the judgment lines — that is what keeps it to minutes rather than assuming it. It has a detector: control-plane CI raises **Blocking** drift when the newest entry is older than the calibrated staleness window, initial value 7 days, changed only by a recorded decision. And it has a slot in the rhythm — a Friday item in the Section 94.8 cadence. An evidence base that nothing makes happen is reconstructed from memory at exactly the moment the closure discipline exists to prevent that.

Rollout enablement is a sized deliverable, not a by-product: it is budgeted in attention hours in the operating system's standing ledger entry, on the same standard Section 62.3 applies to tool replacement. Phase 1 also produces a **one-page per-repository transition note** for the existing team, owned by the Founder: how to merge this week under the new branch protection, who reviews what, and what changes when the next gate arms. The note is the difference between a team that experiences governance arriving and a team that experiences its merges mysteriously breaking. The note names who to ask when a merge blocks, and that path is a named human — the Founder during bootstrap, the Team Lead once the role fills — with a same-day response commitment for the two weeks after branch protection lands on a repository. Where the note would have to state a review routing that does not yet exist, it says so and names the date Phase 3 populates the assignment registries, rather than publishing a routing nothing can resolve.

Closing a bootstrap exception is a recorded decision referencing the verification evidence. Any gate whose exception expires unclosed escalates to the Founder as a Red operating-system health signal; stubbed gates have a habit of staying stubbed, and the expiry date exists precisely to prevent that.

## Section 96. Brownfield Transition Governance

### 96.1 The problem

The portfolio's products are live and serving customers before the operating system exists. Onboarding runs at three to four weeks per product; for the full portfolio that is roughly two quarters during which some products are governed and some are not. "Cannot be onboarded" is meaningless for something already in production. Ungoverned interim operation and invisible half-adoption are both failure modes, and both get explicit machinery.

### 96.2 Pre-onboarding operating mode

Every product that exists but has not completed onboarding is placed in a governed pre-onboarding mode — a declared state, exactly analogous to transitional platform compatibility (Section 60), never an undeclared gap. The minimal ruleset that applies immediately, before any contract, pipeline or board exists:

| Requirement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Backups verified | A backup exists, and one restore has been performed and recorded — even if the full rotation cadence is not yet running. No Primary Owner exists before Phase 3, so the block's named `maintainer` and `escalation` pair confirm instead (96.3), and this recorded restore is the one the Phase 6 rotation entry cites rather than a second restore of the same product six weeks later |
| Access inventoried | Every credential, admin account and deploy path is listed; no unknown access remains |
| Alerting attached | At minimum an uptime check and an error-rate alert route to the standard alert channel |
| Accepted risks recorded | Every rule not yet met is written down as an accepted risk with an owner |
| Named deadline | A dated onboarding completion target; missing it is a Red signal, not a silent slip |
| Interim response authored | A required `interim_response:` stanza, written at intake: how to redeploy today, where the last known-good build lives, and which parts of the Section 42.3 response flow are waived under which accepted risk |

For an S5 product (production with no staging, Section 96.6) the restore target is a **throwaway environment** — never production — and the target is recorded in the block.

The pre-onboarding block is written in Phase 2 into a **minimal stub `product.yaml`** containing only product identity and the onboarding block; the full contract completes the stub at Phase 3 (Section 98.2). Pre-onboarding accepted risks are mirrored as entries in the exception registry (Section 54), so the single-answer property holds: one registry answers "what rules are currently relaxed, where, and until when".

```yaml
# product.yaml — Phase 2 stub: identity plus this block only; completed at Phase 3.
# The onboarding block is removed at onboarding completion.
onboarding:
  status: pre_onboarding        # pre_onboarding | onboarding | complete
  entered: 2026-09-08
  deadline: 2026-11-14
  owner: <team_lead>
  maintainer: <person>          # interim responder pair, per Section 96.3
  escalation: <role-holder>
  backups_verified: true
  access_inventoried: true
  alerting_attached: true
  accepted_risks:               # each mirrored as an exception-registry entry
    - no verification contract yet; releases are manual and recorded by hand
    - branch protection minimal; single approver
  interim_response:             # required at intake, per Section 96.2
    redeploy: <how a redeploy is executed today — command, actor, access needed>
    last_known_good: <where the last known-good build or artifact lives>
    response_flow_waivers:      # Section 42.3 steps waived, each under a named accepted risk
      - <waived step>: <accepted risk it is waived under>
    restore_target: <environment restores are tested against; a throwaway environment for S5>
```

### 96.3 Interim incident handling

A production incident on a pre-onboarding product is a real incident: it is recorded in the incident store (Section 97), uses the severity scale of Section 42 (Incident Management and Detection), and is triaged by the same people. What differs is honesty about capability — the incident record notes the product's pre-onboarding status, and no SLO or detection-latency metric is computed against a product that has not yet declared a support model. Responders for pre-onboarding products default to the pair recorded in the pre-onboarding block — `maintainer` (the person who responds) and `escalation` (the role-holder who is escalated to) — until the assignment registry covers the product.

Regression-test follow-ups generated by a pre-onboarding incident have no governed board to land on yet; they are routed into the product's intake gap assessment (Section 96.6) as scheduled onboarding steps, so the incident's lessons arrive with the product rather than evaporating.

### 96.4 Adoption-health signals

Reconciliation only watches configured products, so half-adoption — boards rotting, UAT skipped, a contract present but stale — must be made visible deliberately. The following feed the Section 52 (Operating System Health) signal table:

* Products in pre-onboarding mode past their named deadline (Red).
* Products onboarded on paper whose boards show no state transitions for a sustained period while commits continue (Amber — execution is bypassing the tracked surface).* Products whose boards look too good: cards created and closed within the same working day, cards whose first state transition postdates the first commit on the same item, and Done items followed by a fresh card on the same code path inside the reopen window (Amber — the curation direction of board gaming). Each threshold is calibrated configuration; initial values: same-day create-and-close above 20% of the window's cards, first-transition-after-first-commit above 20% of the window's cards, and a reopen window of ten working days. Recalibrated against observed distributions at the calibration review (Section 84.5). Board hygiene is scored as individual evidence on eight of nine people (Section 79.2), so abandonment cannot be the only direction watched — a curated board reads as adoption success on every other surface here.
* Products with a verification contract whose CI has not executed it on any push in the reporting window (Red — a paper contract).
* UAT steps defined but never recorded as executed for shipped changes (Amber).
* The portfolio adoption ratio: fully onboarded products as a fraction of all live products, trending to 100% by the last named deadline.

### 96.5 Pacing and sequencing

Realistic pace is three to four weeks per product for anything not already deploying through CI/CD; the first product takes longer, and subsequent products inherit the pattern and the scaffolding. Sequencing rule: highest `classification.reliability_criticality` first — the products where an ungoverned incident hurts most spend the least time in pre-onboarding mode. Within equal criticality, sequence by business.criticality, then by expected onboarding cost, cheapest first. The sequence and its deadlines are recorded as a decision and reviewed at the quarterly operating-system review.

### 96.6 Intake gap assessment — the standard starting-state taxonomy

Existing products arrive in every state of maturity, and no two arrive alike. Onboarding therefore begins with a recorded **intake gap assessment** per product, authored from the named template artifact in the control plane (`templates/intake-gap-assessment.md`) so every assessment covers the same ground: current state measured against the target standard, every gap becoming either a scheduled onboarding step or an accepted risk with an owner and the named deadline. The assessment is stored beside the pre-onboarding block and is the input to the Section 98 per-product phase plan. The background worker harness may produce a machine-drafted assessment from the template against the repository's observable state — draft-only, on local inference, permitted only where the product's S10 gate allows machine processing of its metadata and `ai_processing_permitted` is set; the recorded assessment is always written by the human assessor (D72). The maturity ladder of Section 65 (Operating Maturity Levels) is the measuring stick: intake places each product at its honest level (usually 0 or 1), and onboarding is the climb.

**The target standard — the operating interface every onboarded product meets:**

| Standard | Defined in |
| --- | --- |
| Repository in the company organisation, branch protection from template | Section 11 |
| Valid `product.yaml` with ownership, criticality, support model | Section 15 |
| The eight make commands and required files | Section 33.1 |
| The three HTTP endpoints (`/health`, `/version`, `/metrics`) | Section 41.2 |
| Three environments (local, staging, production) with parity checked | Section 33 |
| Verification contract (automated, UAT, smoke; AI eval where declared) | Section 31 |
| Immutable-artifact pipeline, same digest staging → production | Sections 32–34 |
| CI-only migrations, backward-compatible one cycle | Section 34.3 |
| Backups with one verified restore; then the rolling cadence | Section 44 |
| Boards as execution truth; work through the gates | Sections 23–29 |

The table states the standard for the default `service` profile; a product declaring a different `conformance_profile` (Section 15.7) meets the equivalent evidence its profile defines wherever the service interface does not apply.

**The universal floor — applies to every live product on day one, regardless of state.** It is the six §96.2 items verbatim — backups verified; access inventoried; alerting attached; accepted risks recorded; interim response authored; named deadline — plus the portfolio-wide Phase 1 actions: repository moved into the organisation; branch protection applied; secrets out of the repository and inventoried. Nothing on the floor waits for onboarding — and nothing on the floor is free. The floor is **nine items across every live product**, which at eight products is seventy-two tracked obligations: it is a checklist artifact with one row per item per product, each row carrying a named executor drawn from the product's existing team (Section 95.4) and a date, not a paragraph anyone can declare complete. It carries its own duration in the roadmap rather than riding inside Phase 1's week; costed honestly against the portfolio's starting states it is several weeks, and a floor declared done on paper is exactly the invisible half-adoption 96.4 exists to catch, occurring in the one week 96.4 cannot see, because the health report carrying its signals is a G1 deliverable. Sequencing follows the criticality order of 96.5 rather than all products at once, and a lower-criticality product still outstanding on a floor item carries a dated accepted risk for it, mirrored into the exception registry like any other. The floor's scope includes the operating system's own machine estate: the hosts running Hermes Agent instances — the background worker harness, the PR-review engine and the founder ops console — are estate machines and meet the same six items from the day they exist (D69); their `HERMES_HOME` directories are sensitive-at-rest and covered by the backup and access-inventory items like any other estate data.

**Starting-state taxonomy and the path from each.** States compose — a real product is usually in several at once; the assessment records all that apply:

| # | Starting state | Immediate action (pre-onboarding) | Onboarding path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | No CI and no CD — manual everything | Universal floor; releases recorded by hand as accepted risk | Full Phases 4–6: environments → verification → pipeline. The reusable workflow library means this is instantiation, not invention |
| S2 | CI only — tests run, deployment manual | Keep the existing CI; record manual deployment as accepted risk | Migrate CI onto the pinned reusable workflows; add artifact build with digest, environments, deploy workflows (Phase 6). Existing tests seed the verification contract. Phase 6 completion check includes: legacy deploy path disabled and its credentials revoked |
| S3 | CD only — auto-deploy with no meaningful tests | **The most dangerous state**: an unverified change reaches production automatically. Gate the existing CD immediately using one of the three named patterns of the **interim-CD gating pattern library** — (1) disable auto-deploy and name a manual deployer; (2) insert an approval webhook in front of the existing CD; (3) freeze CD entirely and deploy from artifact by hand — with the interim approver named in the onboarding block. Where none of the three can be applied at once, record continued operation as a Red accepted risk with the shortest deadline in the portfolio | Verification contract FIRST (Phase 5, out of normal order), then rebuild CD as the governed pipeline (Phase 6) |
| S4 | Local development only — nothing deployed, or deployed ad hoc | Universal floor; if something *is* serving users ad hoc, inventory how | Phase 4 creates staging and production as governed environments from the start — greenfield-like, often the cheapest onboarding |
| S5 | Local + production, no staging | Every change is currently verified in production or not at all — record as accepted risk; restore target is a throwaway environment, recorded in the block | Provision staging with parity (Phase 4); until parity passes, changes to this product are treated as high-risk (progressive delivery preferred). Phase 6 completion check includes: legacy deploy path disabled and its credentials revoked |
| S6 | A "UAT" environment only, or odd environment names | Map the existing environment to its true role — a UAT box that behaves like staging IS staging; rename in configuration, not in infrastructure | Fill the missing environments per Phase 4; parity check tells the truth about whether the mapped environment actually matches production |
| S7 | No tests at all | Accepted risk; no AI-assisted feature work on this product until a contract exists (the portfolio invariant) | Phase 5: AI drafts the automated suite during working hours, QA reviews, corrects and takes ownership; `uat.md` authored from how the product is actually exercised today |
| S8 | Not containerised / no reproducible build | Record build steps as they exist | Containerise during Phase 4 where practical; where genuinely impractical, the product must still produce an immutable, digest-identified artifact of some form — the digest invariant is not waivable, the packaging format is |
| S9 | Repository on a personal account or outside host | Move into the organisation immediately — this is universal-floor, week 1, for every product at once | — |
| S10 | Secrets committed in the repository or `.env` files | Treat as a live credential exposure. Rotation of every exposed credential is mandatory and sufficient; a minimal Section 43 incident record is always filed. Purging the secret from history is optional and happens only via an authorised, recorded history-rewrite exception — rotation, not rewriting, is the control. No AI-assisted session opens the repository until the S10 check passes — universal floor | Secret tiers applied at Phase 4 |
| S11 | No monitoring, no health endpoints | Universal-floor uptime check externally; endpoints come later | The three endpoints added during Phase 4 — deliberately trivial to implement in any stack |
| S12 | Mobile / store-delivered product | Nothing special pre-onboarding | Declare conformance_profile: client-app (Section 15.7); standard path otherwise — store submission is the deploy step, release latency declared, heavier UAT mix declared in the contract (Sections 16, 31.2) |
| S13 | Product with heavy tech debt / legacy stack nobody wants to touch | Assess honestly: is this product worth onboarding at full standard? | The lifecycle answer may be Maintenance (Section 18) — reduced obligations, but the universal floor and restore testing still apply. Not every product must reach Level 3+; an internal tool held at Level 2 deliberately is a valid, *recorded* outcome (Section 65) |
| S14 | Product already meeting most of the standard | Fast-track: intake assessment, contract authored, gaps closed | Days, not weeks — the assessment exists precisely so these products do not pay the full onboarding tax |
| S15 | Multi-product monorepo | Universal floor on the shared repository | Either split into per-product repositories, or declare a shared-repo product set: path-scoped branch protection and CI, and a per-product contract for each product in the repository. Product and Repository remain separate concepts either way |
| S16 | Customer-hosted / on-premises production | Universal floor on what the company controls; record what it does not | Declare `conformance_profile: customer-hosted` (Section 15.7): customer-attested deploy and restore records, or a recorded exemption with a compensating control |
| S17 | Library/SDK or batch pipeline — no serving interface | Universal floor | Declare `conformance_profile: library` or `batch` (Section 15.7) and meet its equivalent evidence: registry version plus consumer contract tests, or job success and data-freshness signals |
| S18 | Platform-rebuild deployment — the product deploys by git-push to a PaaS (Vercel/Netlify/Render class) that rebuilds per environment, so staging and production are separate platform builds and the byte-identical-digest invariant is structurally unsatisfiable there | Record the equivalent evidence as the product's immutable identity: the pinned commit SHA plus lockfile plus recorded build configuration (D78) | Replatforming to the container pipeline is the onboarding step wherever the product's `classification.reliability_criticality` demands the true digest chain; until then the recorded equivalent evidence is the identity the evidence chain cites |
| S19 | Customer data committed in the repository — production dumps, real call recordings, exported spreadsheets, support transcripts, or test fixtures built from live customer records | Treat as a live disclosure of customer data, not untidiness. Inventory what is present and where; notify under the product's `data.regulatory_notification_hours` where the classification requires it; remove the data from the working tree immediately. History is append-only, so purging it requires the authorised, recorded history-rewrite exception — there is no rotation-equivalent remedy here, which is exactly why this check is mandatory and not deferred. No AI-assisted session opens the repository until the S19 check passes — universal floor | Fixtures replaced with declared-provenance fixtures (Section 38.3); the `data:` block completed at Phase 4; any deletion obligation for the exposed records recorded in `records/deletion-requests/` (Section 97.2) |

Two intake notes travel with the taxonomy. A store account owned by a personal Google or Apple account is the mobile-store analogue of the personal-hosting state (S9): transfer to the company account is scheduled at intake, or its absence is a dated accepted risk. A production database shared between two products is declared at intake, and backup and restore ownership is assigned to a named product then — never left implicit between the two.

**The Phase-5 QA queue rule.** Onboarding at portfolio pace queues verification work on QA, and the queue needs a declared discipline rather than an implied one. Each product carries a **QA-takeover SLA** — initial calibrated value: two weeks from the AI-drafted suite landing to QA having reviewed, corrected and taken ownership — and a breached SLA is a QA-capacity signal at the weekly review, never a personal one. During Phases 4–5, **manual feature work on the product is permitted** under the recorded accepted risks of the pre-onboarding block; only AI-assisted feature work waits for the verification contract (the portfolio invariant). Onboarding does not freeze a live product's roadmap — it governs how the roadmap ships in the interim.

**Rules.** The gap assessment is honest or it is useless: a product claiming S14 that is actually S2 will be exposed by the Phase 4–6 completion checks, which are executed as written, never assumed. No product skips the universal floor. No product carries an undated accepted risk. And the nineteen-state taxonomy is configuration, not a closed list — a starting state not listed here is added to the table when first encountered, with its path, rather than handled silently.

## Section 97. Records, Events and Data Conventions

### 97.1 The convention

Canonical operational records are structured, append-only YAML records in the control-plane repository. GitHub Issues and Projects boards are the live workflow surface on which work happens — and that surface *generates* the records; nobody transcribes. Metrics derive from these stores, never from hand-maintained numbers, and every dashboard metric names the record store it derives from. A metric that cannot name its store does not ship.
**Time is written one way.** Every record and event timestamp is stored in UTC with its offset, so records written by any host, runner or human compare directly. Every rule expressed in business days, working hours or wall-clock time resolves against the declared working calendar and operating timezone held in the leave records (Section 6.4) — never against a runner's local time, which is how a Friday-freeze gate silently admits the deployments it exists to prevent. A metric derived over a business-day clock names the calendar version it resolved against, so a later calendar correction is re-derived from the preserved raw timestamps rather than argued about.

The write path is split by author and by repository. Workflow-written records and events land in the **records repository** through the **records-writer** machine credential — the fifth secrets tier of Section 40.1 — a GitHub App installation token whose fine-grained `contents: write` is scoped to that repository alone and reaches no registry at all (D89). Human edits to records travel the normal review lane, as pull requests under branch protection like any other change. No machine approval occurs anywhere on either path — the credential writes records; it approves nothing (D76, as amended by D89).

### 97.2 Canonical record stores

| Store | Path convention | Written by | Generates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Incident records | `records/incidents/` | Incident workflow, from the incident issue template | Detection latency, MTTR, severity trends, incident concentration |
| Postmortems | `records/postmortems/` | Human, from template; closure tracked | Learning-loop items, pattern candidates (Section 58) |
| UAT results | `records/uat/` | CI job on UAT completion, from `verification/uat.md` execution | UAT coverage and pass rates |
| Estimate-vs-actual | `records/estimates/` | Board automation at item close (**band and point value, elapsed, and elapsed net of recorded Blocked time**) | Forecast calibration (Section 72); Estimation Accuracy (Section 78) |
| Deployment records | `records/deployments/` | Deploy workflow | Evidence chain (Section 32), rollback trend, deployment frequency |
| Restore-test records | `records/restore-tests/` | The restore-test workflow, plus the human integrity confirmation through the RECORD-VERIFICATION-RESULT dispatch (Section 44.3) | `restore_tested` per product (Section 44.2), restore-test currency (SIG-17), failed-restore escalation |
| Decision records | `records/decisions/` | Human, at the moment of decision | Decision latency, decision quality (Section 63) |
| Pending decisions | `records/decisions/pending/` | The record-decision CLI when a decision prompt is opened; the record moves to `records/decisions/` when decided | Decision queue depth and age (Section 103.8) |
| Breach records | `records/breaches/` | Security-incident workflow, when an incident is classified as a breach | Breach count, notification-deadline compliance |
| Deletion requests | `records/deletion-requests/` | Deletion runbook via the RECORD-VERIFICATION-RESULT dispatch | Deletion SLA compliance against `data.deletion_sla_days` (Section 51.1; EC-98; AT-105) — the statutory deletion clock, distinct from the support first-response clock of 22.4 |
| Security reviews | `records/security-reviews/` | Security reviewer, from template | Finding count by severity, unfixed-finding age |
| AI evaluation runs | `records/eval/` | The scheduled eval runner and pin-change CI (Section 38) | Eval pass rates, regression detection (SIG-42) |
| Launch records | `records/launches/` | The launch-pack generator at launch-readiness sign-off | Launch readiness evidence, launch cadence |
| Demo records | `records/demos/` | Human, brief, after each client demo or UAT walkthrough | Demo cadence evidence, Coordination attention hours |
| Support records | `records/support/` | Support intake workflow (Section 22) | Response-target compliance, support load |
| Onboarding records | `records/onboarding/` | Onboarding workflow at phase completion; human for judgment steps | Onboarding time to first accepted PR, portfolio adoption ratio |
| Leave records | `records/leave/` | Founder or delegate on approval | Capacity profiles (Section 69) |
| Exception registry | `exceptions.yaml` | Humans with authority; expiry by reconciliation | Exception count, renewal rate (Section 54) |
| Policy register | `policies.yaml` | Policy lifecycle (Section 55) | Policy count and net growth |
| Pattern register | `patterns.yaml` | Pattern detector plus human confirmation (Section 58) | Recurrence detection |
| Event log | `events/` (append-only, one file per event) | Every workflow | Everything below |
**Write freshness is an instrument, because zero is the good value.** Every store above declares an expected maximum inter-write interval in `os-health.yaml`, computed from the git commit timestamps on the store's path so the check holds even when the health computation's other inputs are broken: a store past its interval is Amber, and Blocking for `events/`, `records/deployments/` and `records/uat/` (Section 53.1). Without it, a workflow whose record-write step fails silently renders every count-shaped derived metric as zero — no ready-queue misses, no anomalies, no regressions — which is indistinguishable from health, and the presentation discipline of Section 52.3 then gives that silence no screen space. For the same reason the deployment-record and event writes are **required, failing steps** of `deploy-production.yml` rather than trailing best-effort ones: a deploy whose record cannot be written is a deploy whose evidence chain does not close, and the eleven questions of Section 32 are unanswerable for it afterwards. Each control-plane machine credential carries its **expiry date**, not only its rotation cadence, in the operational asset inventory, so the 30-day expiry alert fires on it like any other asset (Section 49).

Two of the new stores carry binding structure. A **deletion-request record** carries four timestamps — `requested`, `verified`, `executed`, `confirmed` — plus the named executor; the deletion runbook is executed through CI, never ad hoc; the record includes the subprocessor propagation checklist (each subprocessor holding the customer's data, with its own deletion confirmation); and the backup carve-out policy statement — deleted data persists in backups until rotation expires them, and is never restored into live systems — is a written artifact customers can be given. A **security-review record** carries findings with severity and disposition; any finding left unfixed is linked into the Portfolio Debt Inventory (Section 56) with an owner and a date, so unfixed findings age visibly rather than silently.

**RECORD-VERIFICATION-RESULT** is the single pattern by which a human manual result reaches the machine: a `workflow_dispatch` with structured inputs — product, item, mechanism, pass or fail, evidence link — that writes the corresponding record and appends the event. Manual UAT and verification results (Section 31), restore-test confirmations (Section 44) and support-loop closures (Section 22) all reach their stores through this dispatch; nobody edits a record file by hand to report a result.

Support records carry a `detection_source` field whose values include `founder_direct` and `customer` alongside the intake channel, so that reports arriving through the Founder are recorded rather than absorbed. Change records and PRs carry an `agent_authored` flag, set at Gate 1 and at PR creation and defined in the Section 97.3 event taxonomy; every metric needing AI-origin data sources from that flag, never from inference after the fact.

Representative schemas — every record carries `record_schema_version`, `id`, `product`, `timestamp`, and never edits in place (corrections are follow-up records). An absent `record_schema_version` reads as version 1; the field is stated explicitly on every record written from Phase 1 onward, so a reader never has to infer a record's shape from its date. Record and event schemas are versioned contracts under Section 60.2 like any other:

```yaml
# records/incidents/2026-09-14-solvox-001.yaml   (example)
id: INC-2026-09-14-001
product: <product>
severity: SEV-2
detected: 2026-09-14T02:11:00Z
detection_source: alert          # alert | customer | internal | support_intake
responded: 2026-09-14T08:35:00Z
resolved: 2026-09-14T10:02:00Z
customer_impact: partial degradation, 3 customers
resolution: rollback to digest sha256:...
postmortem: records/postmortems/2026-09-16-solvox.yaml
pre_onboarding: false
```

```yaml
# records/deployments/…yaml
id: DEP-2026-09-12-014
product: <product>
digest: sha256:...
approved_by: <role-holder>       # never the deploying actor once armed
approval_event: <run url>
staging_verified: true
uat_record: records/uat/…
smoke_result: pass
rollback_of: null
```

```yaml
# records/decisions/…yaml
id: DEC-2026-09-10-003
decider: founder                 # actor LOGIN (GitHub username), not role name
prompt_received: 2026-09-08
decided: 2026-09-10
subject: second QA hire deferred; rebalance executed instead
options_considered: [hire, rebalance, reduce-verification-scope]
evidence: [link, link]
review_date: 2026-12-01
```

```yaml
# records/demos/…yaml
id: DEMO-2026-09-11-002
product: <product>
customer: <contact-list ref>
given_by: <person>
duration_minutes: 45
outcome: follow-up items filed as work items
```

### 97.3 The event log

An append-only event log carries the full event taxonomy. Every workflow that changes state appends an event — written as its own file, one file per event, never a concurrent append to a shared period file, so parallel workflow runs never contend for the same file; period views are derived by aggregation. Events land in the records repository through the records-writer write path of Section 97.1 (D76, as amended by D89). The log is the substrate for every derived metric and for reconstruction after any dashboard failure.

**The event envelope, binding.** Every event carries the same envelope, and an event missing any envelope field is rejected at write time:

```yaml
# events/2026-09-14/EVT-2026-09-14-000317.yaml   (example)
event_schema_version: 1          # stated on every event written; absent reads as 1
event_id: EVT-2026-09-14-000317
event_type: plan_approved        # from the closed enum; never free text
occurred_at: 2026-09-14T09:31:04Z
recorded_at: 2026-09-14T09:31:06Z
actor: lead-1                    # the registry identity that acted, human or machine
product: <product>
subject_ref: records/decisions/DEC-2026-09-14-002.yaml
payload:                         # per-type fields, declared with the type
  gate: 1
  agent_authored: false
```

**Event types are identifiers, not prose.** Every entry in the taxonomy below has exactly one stable `event_type` identifier — lower-case, underscore-separated, never renamed once shipped. The enum is declared in `platform.yaml` beside the supported contract versions, because it migrates exactly as a contract schema does (Section 60.2); control-plane CI rejects any event whose `event_type` is absent from it, and the enum ships populated in Phase 1 so no workflow ever writes an untyped event. A new event type is a governed addition to the enum and to this taxonomy — the same governed addition Section 92.11 requires before anything may page a person. Retiring an identifier marks it retired in the enum and never removes it, because the events that carry it are append-only and stay readable. Without this, two workflows written months apart emit `plan_approved`, `plan-approved` and `Gate 1 approval` for the same event and split every metric derived from it, silently.

The tracked events:

Work item created · moved to Ready · assigned · Ready-queue miss recorded · plan submitted · plan rejected with reason · plan approved (Gate 1) with `agent_authored` flag · change class assigned · impact scope assigned · reversibility class assigned · requirement changed materially · re-plan triggered · execute started · PR opened with `agent_authored` flag · review requested · Gate 2 approval with reviewer role · CI pass or fail per check · parity check result · artifact built with digest · staging deployed · staging smoke result · UAT executed with result · merge · production approval from-digest and to-digest · hotfix authorised · incident opened with severity · incident resolved · postmortem completed · regression test added for a production bug · security incident opened · credential rotated · restore test executed with result · secret or certificate expiry alert · asset owner reassigned · lifecycle transition · launch readiness signed off · reviewer matrix change · knowledge redundancy status change · person added · person role changed · person departed · orphan detected · orphan resolved · temporary assignment created and expired · acting team lead activated and deactivated · drift detected by severity · drift repaired · product created · product split · product merged · product transferred · shared service created · shared service breaking change
