### 97.4 Attention-hour derivation

Attention hours use the single eight-category taxonomy of Section 67 (Human Attention Economics) — Engineering, Review, Verification, Planning, Architecture, Incident, Operational, Coordination — plus an `unplanned` flag on any entry for work entering Horizon 1 without Horizon 2 preparation, and a `ritual` flag on any entry belonging to a ritual in the Section 57.2 inventory, set by the workflow or record that opens that ritual and never self-reported (Section 67.2). Derivation rules, per category, in order of preference machine trace first:

| Category | Derived from |
| --- | --- |
| Engineering | Authored commits and PR activity windows on owned products, including agent-directing sessions |
| Review | PR review sessions: review-requested to review-submitted activity windows, Gate 2 and cross-review |
| Verification | UAT record execution windows, verification-contract commits, CI failure triage sessions, release sign-off events |
| Planning | Gate 1 activity, planning-board transitions, Ready-queue refill sessions, Horizon 3 board work |
| Architecture | Architecture-class review activity, architecture decision records, cross-product design sessions |
| Incident | Incident-record participation windows, from response to resolution, plus postmortem authoring |
| Operational | Deployment approvals and executions, restore tests, asset and dependency sweeps, ops-VM maintenance |
| Coordination | Standups, handovers, demo records and client-facing sessions, status conversations, unplanned interrupts |

**From activity window to attention hour, binding.** A named interval — a review window, an incident window, a Gate 1 window — bounds the *search* for attention; it is never itself the duration. Within the interval, the person's attributed events cluster into **activity sessions**: consecutive events separated by no more than the **idle gap** belong to one session, and a wider gap ends it. A session's duration is the span from its first event to its last; a single-event session counts as one granularity unit. Elapsed wall-clock time between an interval's bounds is never an attention hour — a pull request left open overnight is one short session, not fourteen hours of Review.

* The **idle gap** is **calibrated configuration** with an initial value of 30 minutes.
* Attribution granularity is **calibrated configuration** with an initial value of 0.25 hours, rounded to nearest, never to zero.
* **Category precedence.** Section 67.1 requires each hour to carry exactly one category, so a session falling inside two windows resolves in this fixed order and the losing categories receive nothing: Incident, Verification, Review, Engineering, Architecture, Planning, Operational, Coordination. Incident outranks everything because an incident window is the one interval whose attention is not discretionary.
* **Product attribution.** A session whose events touch one product attributes to that product; a session touching several splits across them by event count; a session touching none attributes to the portfolio.
* **The daily reconciliation, binding.** Derived hours for a person on a day never exceed that person's scheduled availability for that day in the Capacity Profile (Section 69.2). Sessions are truncated in reverse precedence order until the reconciliation holds, and each truncation is recorded.
* A day whose derived hours exceed scheduled availability **before** truncation is an **instrument defect**, not a workload finding. It raises a drift finding against the ledger and never enters a Capacity Profile, a workload state (Section 83) or the Founder view.

**Declared limitations** — Section 84.6 requires every metric to declare them, and the attention hour declares them here. It is a **lower bound** on attention: thinking that leaves no event leaves no trace, so Architecture and Coordination are systematically under-counted. The parameters above are hypotheses until calibrated, and the calibration runs once at Phase G3 — at least two people band-report a single week in parallel with the derivation, and the divergence is recorded as the metric's stated error bar and re-recorded at each calibration review (Section 84.6).

Where no machine trace exists — chiefly Coordination and parts of Architecture — a weekly banded self-report applies: bands, not minutes; weekly, not daily; **one band per category, unattributed to any product**; at most 5 minutes per person per week. Per-product attribution is never asked of the person — the week's band is apportioned across that person's products in proportion to their machine-derived activity shares for the same week, and to the portfolio where no share exists. Asking someone to recall a week of interrupts, standups, handovers, demos and mentoring and split each across six or seven products breaches the five-minute cap on arithmetic before anyone tries it, and a cap breached is a collection design to be simplified, not a person to be chased. If collection costs more than that, the collection design is wrong and is simplified before the metric is adopted. Founder coordination time is simply Coordination-category hours attributed to the Founder. Any figure that includes self-reported hours carries a **self-reported** provenance label wherever it renders, and carries it permanently — the rule Section 103.14 applies to pre-Phase-1 baseline estimates applies to Coordination for as long as its sources leave no machine trace. Coordination is therefore never presented as a derived category beside genuinely derived ones without the label, and any forecast or capacity allowance that consumes it names it in its assumption list (Section 72.3). Attention hours are never individual performance evidence; general surfaces aggregate them at product and portfolio level only.

### 97.5 Ready-queue-miss recording

A Ready-queue miss is recorded automatically, never on trust. The detector: when a person picks up a work item that has not passed through Ready — a board transition from Backlog directly to Planned or In Progress, or an item started while the product's Ready queue is empty — the board automation appends a Ready-queue-miss event with who, which date, and which product, and opens a one-line cause prompt for the Team Lead (why the queue was empty). The Planned column is the normal assignment step (Ready → Planned → In Progress) and passing through it is never a miss. The Blocked flag marks committed in-flight work: clearing the flag and resuming the item is a resumption, not a fresh pickup, and is never counted as a miss. The miss count is a standing planning-health metric; the cause notes are the meaning humans add.

Section 29.4 states the condition and this section states the detector; they are one metric, and two clarifications keep them coextensive. **Completion with an empty Ready queue counts.** Where a person completes an item and the product's Ready queue holds no suitable item for them, the board automation appends the event on the completion transition — the idle case is the one the definition most cares about, and it produces no pickup for a pickup-shaped detector to see. **A bypass with a full Ready queue does not count.** A Backlog-to-Planned or Backlog-to-In-Progress transition made while suitable Ready items exist is recorded with reason `ready_bypass` as a board-hygiene finding for the Team Lead, and never enters the SIG-06 count. Either way the event carries the full Section 29.4 field set — who, which date, which product, why the queue was empty, whether the Team Lead was blocked, and whether product priority changed recently — the last three supplied by the cause prompt, never inferred.

### 97.6 Retention

Append-only permanence applies to state, decisions, approvals and canonical records — everything in Section 97.2 keeps its full history with effective dating. Raw activity telemetry — session timestamps, per-event activity traces used to derive attention hours — may be aggregated or discarded after its declared diagnostic window. Retention classes are declared in the control plane and owned by the Founder; people-layer retention additionally follows Section 91 (Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart).

## Section 98. Implementation Phases and Roadmap

### 98.1 Roadmap shape

One roadmap, three tiers. The Foundation tier (Phases 1–7) builds the delivery operating system and onboards the portfolio; the Governance tier (Phases G1–G8) instruments the operating system itself; the People tier (Phases P1–P8) builds capacity and management intelligence on top of governance data. Extensibility features must not delay the basic operating system. Throughout, the build runs under Bootstrap Mode (Section 95) until headcount arms the gates, and live products sit in pre-onboarding mode (Section 96) until their phase completes.

**The P0-before-P2 rule, binding:** no P2 or P3 capability may be started while a P0 capability is unbuilt. This is the primary defence against building the interesting parts first.

**Calendar-gating honesty:** the critical path of the upper tiers is elapsed operation time, not engineering effort. Pattern detection needs realistically two quarters of incident and exception history; capacity forecasting needs at least two quarters of attention data; framework evolution needs at least two full review periods of evidence. No amount of build acceleration compresses this, and no predictive layer is built before its data exists.

**The operating system prices itself:** the OS carries a standing automation-ledger entry (Section 57, Automation Value and AI Output Measurement); the quarterly review weighs OS ritual cost against delivered value; and the platform investment gate (Section 59) applies to the OS's own phases — each Governance and People phase passes the same gate any platform investment passes. If a phase cannot justify itself, it is not built.

**Declined is a state, not an absence.** A phase that fails its own gate is recorded as `declined` — a recorded decision carrying the gate answers, the dependent capabilities forgone and a review date — and `declined` is distinct from `unbuilt`. A declined P0 releases the P0-before-P2 lock: the decision was made, not deferred, and a lock that cannot be released turns one declined phase into a permanently frozen tier, which is how the rule gets silently dropped instead of applied. An unbuilt P0 holds the lock exactly as written. Every Section 103 measure whose only source was a declined phase is marked `unbaselined` (Section 103.14) and is deleted at the next quarterly review under Section 84.6 — the operating system does not carry measures it decided not to instrument. Re-opening a declined phase is a fresh decision at the review date, not a resumption.

### 98.2 Foundation Phases 1–7

Launch-critical — must exist before the first pilot product completes onboarding.

**Phase 1 — Foundation (Week 1; the Section 96.6 universal floor runs alongside it on its own declared duration and its own per-product checklist, never inside this week)**

* Consolidate all products into one company-owned GitHub organisation
* Create the control-plane repository; author `people.yaml`, `roles.yaml`, `platform.yaml`
* One AI subscription per person from the approved runtime list, held at least a quarter
* Verify `env | grep -i api_key` returns empty on every machine, including shell profiles and repository `.env` files
* One project board per product plus the aggregate portfolio board (or the single-Project fallback of Section 29)
* Organisation base permission Read; Teams grant Write per the permission model — **within Week 1 and before branch protection is armed**, from an interim assignment set that Phase 3 replaces with the registry-derived one. Arming a Code-Owner-and-approval gate while no Team grants Write leaves nobody whose approval counts, and Section 95.4 names the result exactly: a team that experiences its merges mysteriously breaking
* Branch protection on every repository with required review and approval of the most recent reviewable push. **The required-status-check list starts empty per repository** and is populated as each check comes into existence — CI checks at that product's Phase 4, the verification contract at Phase 5, the pipeline checks at Phase 6. A required check no workflow emits blocks every pull request indefinitely; a list that silently stays empty is a gate that reads armed and is not. Each phase's completion check names the contexts it adds
* Environment deployment branch and tag policies applied from the template on every environment (Section 33.4)
* Verify plan-tier dependencies: branch protection on private repositories, environment protection rules, Projects aggregation
* Record bootstrap exceptions for every gate that current headcount cannot satisfy (Section 95)
* Author the operating system's own standing ledger entry in `economics.yaml` — the seven investment-gate answers for Phases 1–7, the predicted saving and the dated scoring commitment (Sections 57.2, 59.2). Every later phase adds its answers before it is committed

Completion check: no direct human push to any default branch succeeds on the control-plane repository, where the reconciler credential's declared repair scope (Section 26.4) is the **only** machine write path admitted — the records-writer holds no credential on this repository at all, because the record stores live in their own repository (Section 40.1, D89) — and a reconciler write outside its declared scope is Blocking drift; an approval from a Read-only account does **not** satisfy branch protection while an approval from a Write-holding Cross-Reviewer does (executed for real once headcount permits, per the activation checklist); an approval from a machine account does **not** satisfy branch protection — CODEOWNERS is generated to contain human identities only, and the check is executed negatively; organisation-enforced 2FA is verified active, with hardware keys or passkeys for the Founder, organisation Owners and platform-admin holders; no API key present anywhere; the minimal `exceptions.yaml` schema validator (expiry, owner, deactivation trigger present) is active in control-plane CI and rejects a deliberately malformed exception; Teams granting Write exist before branch protection is armed, so that no window opens in which no approval can satisfy the gate; a workflow pushed to a non-default branch declaring `environment: production` obtains no environment secret, executed negatively; a second organisation Owner or an escrowed break-glass Owner credential exists with a named escrow custodian — the consolidation week is when total-loss exposure peaks; and the organisation export's first run is scheduled in Phase 2, or its absence is recorded as a dated accepted risk (D80).

**Phase 2 — Visibility (Week 2)**

* DevLake and Grafana on the operations VM, connected to the organisation
* Scorecard baseline scan across all products
* Renovate installed
* Remote Control enabled for anyone who wants it
* The remote-access decision of Section 51 recorded — which mechanism, if any, the team uses to reach staging infrastructure and the operations VM remotely. A deferral is permitted only as a `policy_waiver` entry in `exceptions.yaml` with a mandatory expiry, an owner and a deactivation trigger (Section 54.2), so it inherits invariant 77 and SIG-39 and cannot age quietly. A decision record has no clock, and stubbed gates have a habit of staying stubbed (Section 95.4)
* Pre-onboarding blocks written for every live product not yet in the pipeline, each into a minimal stub `product.yaml` — product identity plus the onboarding block only — completed at Phase 3 (Section 96.2); each accepted risk mirrored into the exception registry

Completion check: every product visible in Grafana with a Scorecard score; the control-plane surfaces on the operations VM are reachable only over the private path of Section 51.4, or that requirement is carried as a dated `policy_waiver` in `exceptions.yaml`; every live product either onboarding or in declared pre-onboarding mode with a deadline.

**Phase 3 — Registries and Standards (Week 3)**

* Assignment registries populated: Primary Owner, Cross-Reviewer, Backup Owner, responders per product
* GitHub Teams created, derived from the registries
* Constitution file written, including the untrusted-input rule and the unattended-agent rule
* `product.yaml` authored for every product at `contract_version: 1`, CI validation active — completing the Phase 2 pre-onboarding stubs into full contracts, and including both criticality fields, the support model, the commitments block and the budget band
* Repomix installed* Reconciliation v0 over the registries just populated — detect and block only: Teams versus registries, expiry revocation, protection drift, and orphan detection at blocking severity (Section 99.4 item 6). Auto-repair is not built here; the repair levels are early hardening (Section 98.3), because auto-repair is the riskiest code in the system
* Scaffolding v0 — `create-product` and `add-person`, generating repository, Teams, CODEOWNERS, branch protection and registry entries with zero hand-editing; a portfolio of eight products crosses the pays-for-itself threshold immediately (Section 99.4 item 3)
* Background layer benchmark run, executed through the Hermes Agent single-shot configuration — the go/park decision for the background layer is made here
* Hermes background worker cage stand-up — the one estate slot this phase builds, registered in `tools.yaml` before first use, with its own OS user and `HERMES_HOME` (D69). The benchmark above must pass **before** the background worker slot activates — committing to the harness does not pre-empt the benchmark, and a parked benchmark parks every local-inference slot, because all three model configurations depend on the same local inference endpoint existing. The PR-review engine and the founder ops console are **not** phase deliverables: each stands up only when its Section 39.5 activation trigger fires (the console only if free CI notifications prove insufficient; the review engine only with the local endpoint live), each registered in `tools.yaml` before first use. Personal-seat local-inference profiles are adopted per person as demand arises and are never a phase gate

Completion check: contracts validate; registries, contracts and Team membership agree, machine-verified.

**Phase 4 — Environments (Weeks 4–5, per product)**

* Local environment contract — the eight standard commands
* Staging provisioned with parity to production
* GitHub Environments with scoped secrets; the Section 27.2 workflow-identity gate on the production environment
* Parity check job active

Completion check: someone unfamiliar with the product runs `make setup && make dev && make test` successfully; `make parity` reports no divergence; every required file of Section 33.1 is present, `AGENTS.md` included; and the required-status-check contexts this phase adds are listed in the repository's branch protection and actually reported by a run.

**Phase 5 — Verification (Weeks 5–7, per product)**

* AI writes the automated test suite using subscriptions during working hours
* QA reviews, corrects and takes ownership
* `verification/uat.md` authored
* Smoke tests written
* CI runs the full contract on every push
* Where the product declares an AI runtime dependency, the evaluation suite lands under `verification/` here (Section 38)

Completion check: verification contract present and passing; QA signed off. QA review runs under the per-product QA-takeover SLA of Section 96.6 (initial: two weeks from the AI-drafted suite landing); a breached SLA is a QA-capacity signal, never a personal one.

**Phase 6 — Delivery Pipeline (Week 7, per product)**

* Immutable artifact build with digest recording and SBOM emission
* Staging deploy plus smoke
* Production approval gate with self-review prevention (or its recorded bootstrap exception)
* Rollback tested at least once, deliberately
* Backup configured; one restore test performed and recorded, entering the rolling 90-day rotation

Completion check: a deliberate rollback succeeded in staging; restore test recorded; the eleven-item evidence chain answerable for one real deployment; and the production-approval test verifies the workflow-identity gate — the approval actor is recorded, and the deploy fails closed when the approver equals the deploying actor — never tier-dependent environment required reviewers, which on private repositories are an Enterprise-only feature (D73).

**Phase 7 — GSD Activation (Week 8, per product)**

* GSD Core installed at a pinned tag, minimal profile
* Project initialised, `.planning/` created
* Constitution referenced in `CONTEXT.md`
* Model routing and profile configured, keys verified against the pinned release

Completion check: a first plan passes the plan-checker and is approved at Gate 1.

Realistic pace: 3–4 weeks per product for anything not already deploying through CI/CD, sequenced highest reliability_criticality first (Section 96.5). The first product takes longer; subsequent products inherit the pattern and the scaffolding. Across Phases 5–7 the QA-takeover SLA (Section 96.6) paces the verification queue product by product, and the interim rule of Section 96.6 applies throughout: manual feature work continues under the recorded accepted risks; only AI-assisted feature work waits for the contract.

### 98.3 Early hardening

Built while moving from 2–3 products to the full portfolio:

| Capability | Why it comes second |
| --- | --- |
| Reconciliation auto-repair (Level 3) and drift classification | Detect-and-block reconciliation, including orphan detection, ships in Phase 3 over the registries it watches; auto-repair waits until detection has run clean for weeks, and drift classification needs several products before drift is a real risk |
| Versioned contracts (`contract_version` enforcement) | Needs a reason to change a schema |
| Platform change process and canary set | Needs enough products for a canary to be meaningful |
| Change manifests | Needs cross-product changes to exist |
| Acting Team Lead designation | Should be in place before the first extended absence |
| Person lifecycle scaffolding | Needed before the first hire or departure |
| Operational asset inventory and vendor deadline watch | Needed before the first certificate expiry, roughly month 3 |
| Support intake and triage per product | Needed as soon as customers can report defects |
| Organisation export job | Needed before the first restore test of the export, within the first quarter |
| Product launch readiness gate | Needed before the first new product launches |
| The remaining provisioning operations — `change-role`, `remove-person`, template evolution | Scaffolding v0 (`create-product`, `add-person`) ships in Phase 3, because a portfolio of eight products crosses the pays-for-itself threshold immediately; the rest follow the first role change and the first departure |

### 98.4 Scale activation

Activated as the organisation grows, each on its trigger — never on the calendar:

| Capability | Activation point |
| --- | --- |
| Shared service registry and consumer contract tests | First genuine shared service |
| Dependency graph views | Roughly 10 products, or the first shared service |
| Product split and merge processes | First split or merge |
| Temporary specialist and contractor model | First contractor |
| Platform compatibility migration | First contract schema change |
| Data and privacy extension | First regulated-data customer requirement |
| Transfer or acquisition process | First transfer |
| Second review cluster | Roughly 12 people |
| Domain activation in topology | Per Section 66, when a second Team Lead exists |

### 98.5 Governance-tier phases G1–G8

Instrumentation over the running Foundation, not a platform build. Each phase is independently valuable, independently abandonable, and leaves the system coherent. Durations assume this work competes with product delivery for the same attention.

**Phase G1 — Operating-system observability (P0).** Deliverables: `os-health.yaml`; the health computation job; the Operating System Health Report in Grafana (Section 52); drift classification applied to existing reconciliation findings; reconciliation Levels 1–4 (Section 53); the control-plane versus data-plane dependency audit; immutable-history schema rules; verification and re-recording of the pre-Phase-1 baseline estimates for the Section 103 minimum measure set — the one-time banded self-estimates captured before Phase 1 (Section 103.14) are checked against early instrumented data and re-recorded, never mixed with ledger-derived figures. Dependencies: reconciliation, DevLake and Grafana operational. Exit: the Founder answers "is the operating system healthy?" from one screen; zero Blocking drift open; baselines verified and re-recorded. A measurement programme with no baseline can prove nothing.

**Phase G2 — Exception and policy governance (P0/P1).** Deliverables: `exceptions.yaml` with CI validation and automatic expiry via reconciliation (already dogfooded by bootstrap); break-glass standardisation and post-use review; `policies.yaml` populated from the existing rulebook; gradual enforcement stages (Section 55); safe defaults applied to provisioning templates; fail-closed control classification (Section 64). Exit: every existing exception has a record and an expiry; every policy has an owner and a review date; the exception-expiry and break-glass acceptance tests pass (Section 100).

**Phase G3 — Attention and portfolio economics (P1/P2).** Deliverables: the attention ledger with the Section 97.4 derivation rules; Founder and Team Lead coordination-time tracking; four-dimension product health reporting; attention ranking; the full Founder view (Section 93); criticality fields live in every contract. The self-report is staged: machine-derived attention activates for everyone at zero collection cost; the weekly banded self-report activates for the Founder and Team Lead only, and extends to the team when a named consumer — G5 forecasting or people-tier activation — goes live, recorded then as a scope decision (D79). Dependencies: G1–G2; DevLake field coverage confirmed. Exit: machine-derived attention data flows for every person; the Founder and Team Lead self-report costs under 5 minutes per person per week; the Founder view answers questions 1–5 of Section 93.3. Questions 6, 7 and 8 depend on forecasting and scenario deliverables that arrive at G5 and G6; until then they render **unarmed — not yet instrumented** under the Section 52.2 arming discipline, and G3 does not wait on them. A phase gated on a later phase's output is not independently abandonable, which is the property this tier is built on.

**Phase G4 — Failure-pattern learning and debt governance (P1).** Deliverables: `patterns.yaml` and the candidate detector; the incident learning loop with tracked generated work and closure conditions (Section 58); debt fields and the Portfolio Debt Inventory (Section 56); decision-quality measurement (Section 63). Dependencies: realistically two quarters of G1 data. Exit: the pattern acceptance test passes; no postmortem older than 30 days with unclosed items.

**Phase G5 — Load model and predictive capacity (P2).** Deliverables: PLU model version 1 and first calibration; the capacity forecast job; the verification demand forecast for QA; the bottleneck diagnosis chain including Founder-decision latency; forecast retrospective scoring. Dependencies: at least two quarters of G3 attention data. Exit: forecast accuracy scored and reported honestly; the Founder view answers question 6 of Section 93.3.

**Phase G6 — Scenario modelling and automation value (P2/P3).** Deliverables: the scenario calculator and primitives (Section 72); quarterly automated bus-factor scenarios; the automation ledger, automating the OS's own standing entry authored in Phase 1 (Section 57.2); background-layer output-value measurement. Dependencies: G5. Exit: the Founder obtains add-one-person and sunset-one-product projections without asking anyone to build a spreadsheet; the Founder view answers questions 7 and 8 of Section 93.3, completing the eight.

**Phase G7 — Organisational scaling readiness (P1 build, P3 activation).** Deliverables: `topology.yaml` with dormant domains and the escalation resolution rule; delegation assignment types, including founder-delegation types; domain-aware routing verified while dormant; the second Team Lead activation playbook. Exit: the topology acceptance test passes with domains both dormant and simulated active, with zero product contract edits.

**Phase G8 — Operating-system optimisation (P1/P2).** Deliverables: platform SLOs with error budgets; the platform change budget and churn detection (Section 59); the tool register and retirement path (Section 62); maturity-level assessment (Section 65); product-exit checklist automation; the first quarterly operating-system review executed end to end from the generated review pack — the review itself has run each quarter since the first, on whatever data existed (Section 57.2). Exit: the quarterly review produces at least one policy retirement, one automation verdict and one metric deletion. A review that only adds is a failed review.

### 98.6 People-tier phases P1–P8

The people tier must not delay or destabilise safe delivery operation. Each phase is independently useful and independently abandonable.

| Phase | Scope | Depends on | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | Team and people capacity instrumentation: Capacity Profile, utilisation composition from existing attention hours, remaining safe bandwidth, Team Capacity View (Sections 69–71) | G3 attention ledger | P1 |
| P2 | Registries and framework mapping: person, role, capability and assignment registries as configuration; Performance Framework Registry; the evidence mapping of Section 79 completed directly from the framework source, including all outstanding rows; instrumentation status classified per KPI; **the Layer B datasource separation of Section 90** — the second Founder-only Grafana instance, the separately-credentialed people datasource (D75), three-state field handling and the generated per-person self-view document, all of subsystem L | Framework v1 source (Section 78); subsystem L (Section 99.2) | P1 |
| P3 | Team health and workload: concentration signals, individual workload health, overload and under-utilisation detection with calibrated sustained thresholds | P1–P2 | P1 |
| P4 | Performance evidence bundles: per-person bundles, context adjustment, variance classification, confidence, Layer B access-controlled views | P2–P3, plus the Layer B datasource separation of Section 90 | P1 |
| P5 | Founder decision support: decision matrices, coaching and recognition signals, promotion readiness, override recording (Sections 85–86) | P4 | P2 |
| P6 | Staffing and scenario planning: staffing diagnosis, rebalance-before-hire evaluation, hiring evidence pack, people scenarios (Sections 72–73) | P1–P5 | P2 |
| P7 | Capability and succession: capability maturity with confidence, succession readiness, operational dependency risk (Sections 82, 87) | P3–P4 | P2 |
| P8 | Framework evolution: KPI calibration review, revision proposals, new framework versions with effective dates (Section 84) | At least two full review periods of P4 evidence | P3 |

Sequencing rules, binding:

* P2 is completed by reading the framework source directly, never by inferring content from summaries. Captured content is preserved verbatim and never downgraded on a failed re-read.
* P4 must not begin before the Layer B datasource separation is implemented and verified. It is a P2 deliverable, never an assumption; *verified* means AT-089, AT-091, AT-097 and AT-098 pass and invariant 109 holds. People evidence cannot be generated before it can be access-controlled at datasource level.
* No Layer B evidence bundle may be generated for any person whose framework mapping still carries an outstanding marker.
* P8 must not begin before there is enough real evidence to justify a change. Changing targets on thin evidence is worse than leaving them alone.

### 98.7 Team size and composition

Lean, and deliberately so.

* Foundation: the Founder solo under Bootstrap Mode, at high AI leverage for schema, validator and workflow codegen; per-product verification content is QA and human judgment once QA exists, and is the grind of the second quarter.
* G1–G2: one person, part-time — ideally the Team Lead or a senior developer holding the architecture capability — with the Founder reviewing outputs. Roughly 2–4 weeks of effort spread across a quarter.
* G3–G5: the same person plus QA input on verification demand definitions. Roughly 1–2 weeks per phase.
* G6–G8 and the People tier: one person, opportunistically, with the background machine layer drafting report jobs and queries under review.

No dedicated platform team, no dedicated data engineer, and no new headcount is justified by the governance or people tiers themselves. If either tier appears to require a hire, the scope is wrong.

## Section 99. Build Surface and Components

### 99.1 What is actually being built

The operating system is not an application. It is an operating model implemented as configuration and glue over commodity tools: GitHub as source of truth and enforcement plane; Grafana, DevLake and Prometheus as the presentation layer; YAML registries in a control-plane repository; scheduled jobs as the backend. What gets built is a schema-and-validator suite, a reconciliation engine, a provisioning and scaffolding CLI, a reusable CI/CD workflow library, a metrics and report computation layer, and dashboard provisioning — a GitOps operating-system distribution for one company, not a product for third parties.

### 99.2 The subsystem architecture

| # | Subsystem | What must exist | Cx | Depends on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Control-plane repository | Versioned YAML registries and contracts: people, roles, assignments, platform, topology, per-product contracts and verification contracts, the governance files (os-health, policies, exceptions, patterns, economics, platform-roadmap, tools), the people-layer entities, and the record stores of Section 97 | M | — |
| B | Schema validation and CI gate engine | Multi-version schema validators, referential integrity (assignments name existing non-departed people; dependencies name existing services), date rules (mandatory end dates for non-employees, restore-tested within window, expired assignments fail), the 24x7-without-rota and commitments-conflict blockers, exception-without-expiry rejection, unclassified-control rejection | M | A |
| C | Reconciliation engine | Scheduled diff of declared versus actual GitHub state; graded responses at Levels 1–5 (Detect / Warn / Auto-repair / Block / Escalate); automatic expiry revocation; orphan detection at blocking severity; auto-repair only toward stricter declared state | L | A, B, D |
| D | Provisioning and scaffolding | Create-product, add-person, change-role, remove-person operations: repo from template, Teams from registries, generated CODEOWNERS, branch protection, environments with scoped secrets, registration in every surface with zero hand-editing | L | A, B |
| E | Reusable workflow library | ci, build, deploy-staging, deploy-production, migrate, restore-test, org-export, background-queue — consumed by pinned tag; the digest invariant enforced in code; parity job; delta-gated security and licence scanning; SBOM emission; Friday-freeze time gate | L | A |
| F | Evidence chain store and query | The eleven-question answerability for any production artifact; `/version` digest-match monitoring (100%; any mismatch is a P0 investigation); append-only history with effective dating | M | E |
| G | Plan-checker and Gate 1 tooling | Automatic plan rejection (missing verify command, nonexistent symbols, unaddressed decisions, slopsquat check against live registries, schema change without rollback strategy); change-class, impact-scope and reversibility confirmation; computed requirement set at plan time | L if built in-house | — |
| H | Dashboards and views | Grafana provisioned from JSON in git: every surface of Section 92 | L | I, F, C |
| I | Metrics pipeline | DevLake nightly ingest; Prometheus scraping `/health`, `/version`, `/metrics`; Scorecard scheduled scan with drop detection; the event-log taxonomy; attention ledger; metric source discipline | L | A, E |
| J | Background machine layer (conditional) | Isolated machine running the Hermes Agent harness (pinned commit) in its caged background-worker configuration, single-shot local inference, whitelist queue, machine account with draft-PR-only authority, task-class statistics with auto-suspend, 07:00 hard stop — built only if the CPU benchmark passes | L + hardware | D, E |
| K | AI runtime contract enforcement | Approved-runtime and approved-extension lists as configuration; API-key-free checks at onboarding and quarterly; secret-stripping pre-flight; constitution referenced from every context file; model-regression benchmark process | M | A |
| L | Access-control architecture | Org base Read plus Teams-derived Write; branch and environment protection as the enforcement boundary; five secret tiers; fail-closed classification; the Layer B split — a second Founder-only Grafana instance carrying the separately-credentialed people datasource (D75), three-state field, generated self-view documents | M–L | A, D |
| M | Operations VM | DevLake, Grafana, reconciliation, health computation, Scorecard, Renovate, expiry checks, restore rotation, org export; disposable (rebuild under 4 hours from GitHub, tested quarterly); never in any product's runtime path; patched on the declared cadence of Section 62 | M | — |
| N | Work tracking conventions | Boards per product plus portfolio aggregate (or the single-Project fallback), horizon semantics, Ready-to-Execute definition, automatic Ready-queue-miss recording | M | — |

| R | Notification routing | Actions webhook to messaging channel; per-product alert channels; documented phone-escalation path; Founder and Team Lead out-of-hours channel; no paging apps for developers | S | — |

Complexity: S under a week, M one to three weeks, L three to eight weeks, XL multi-month — for one competent engineer with AI assistance, excluding per-product content work. Rough total: 10–14 engineer-months for the full surface at single-implementer pace, excluding per-product onboarding content and excluding the calendar time the upper tiers need for data accumulation.

**Dependency spine:** A (registries) → B (validation) → C (reconciliation) and D (provisioning); E (workflows) → F (evidence chain) → H/I (views and metrics); I is the feedstock for nearly all governance-tier and people-tier computation; P is hard-gated on L's datasource separation.

### 99.3 Spec'd versus design-open

Specified with implementable precision: every registry and contract schema (direct transcription to JSON Schema is possible); the state machines (product lifecycle, migration failure cases, incident and security flows, person lifecycles, policy enforcement stages, pilot–rollout–fleet, break-glass bounds, degraded modes); the directly executable tables (review routing, production approval routing, verified GitHub permission semantics, branch protection checklist, the eleven evidence questions, drift classes with response times, orphan types with severities, weekend quotas, the Section 52 signal table, the Section 90 permission matrix, the Section 79 evidence mapping); the acceptance tests of Section 100; and the invariants of Section 101, which function as a compliance checklist.

This specification also closes, by decision, several matters an implementer would otherwise have had to invent: where operational records live and how events are captured (Section 97); how attention hours are derived per category (Section 97.4); the Ready-queue-miss detector (Section 97.5); the Layer B mechanism without an enterprise licence or bespoke web application (Section 90 and Section 92.8); solo-build gate handling (Section 95); and brownfield interim governance (Section 96).

Design-open — the implementer must still invent, and each is logged as such at build time:

1. **The attention classifier and constraint diagnosis algorithm** — Healthy/Watch/Action Required with the reason on the same line, and "which constraint binds", are signals whose classification logic must be formalised from judgment.
2. **The `make parity` declaration format** — comparing local configuration schema against staging and production declarations presumes an environment-schema format to be defined once and reused.
3. **Plan-checker internals** — verify every assumed capability against the exact pinned GSD release before configuring it; budget building the checker in-house if verification fails.
4. **DevLake field coverage** — several metrics (routine reviews absorbed cross-checked against the routing table, reviewer familiarity, reviewer-spread measures) require bespoke computation beyond DevLake's models; confirm coverage before Phase G3.
5. **Machine sources for context checks** — most of the fifteen systemic context checks of Section 80 lack machine-detectable sources; the variance-classification engine is a context-assembly aid that proposes only the classes it can evidence, with the humans named in Section 80.2 classifying the rest, and the computable boundary is drawn by the builder.
6. **KPI instrumentation projects** — every evidence-mapping row marked "available after instrumentation" in Section 79 is its own mini-project (DoD compliance checks, escaped-defect avoidability, crash reporting, device matrix, the Voice AI evaluation harness — the last already mandatory under the verification contract where declared).
7. **Calibration methods** — PLU fit, forecast scoring, sustainable-utilisation bands, the Section 97.4 attention-session parameters and the Section 72.3 confidence table are deliberately left as quarterly refits against observed data, with no method prescribed.

### 99.4 The minimal honest V1

V1 is the Foundation launch-critical set for 2–3 pilot products, plus the near-free P0 governance design rules baked in from day one — roughly 30% of the build surface, delivering the Founder's actual Monday-morning value: declared state enforced, drift visible, orphans impossible to miss, every production artifact traceable.

1. Control-plane repository, schemas and CI validation — with effective dating and append-only discipline from the start, because retrofitting history is impossible by definition.
2. GitHub enforcement: one organisation, base Read, Teams-derived Write, branch protection with most-recent-push approval, environments — completion checks executed as written.
3. Scaffolding v0 (create-product, add-person): a portfolio of eight products crosses the pays-for-itself threshold immediately.
4. Delivery pipeline with the digest invariant, one tested rollback and one recorded restore test per product — the single highest-safety-per-effort item; it makes the evidence chain answerable.
5. Verification-contract skeleton with CI presence enforcement — the load-bearing invariant "no onboarded product without a verification contract" (pre-onboarding products follow the Section 96 pathway) cannot be deferred.
6. Reconciliation v0, detect and block only — Teams versus registries, expiry revocation, protection drift, orphan detection. Auto-repair is deferred until detection has run clean for weeks; auto-repair is the riskiest code in the system, and its stricter-only rule is enforced in code and tested.
7. Founder view v0 from GitHub API and reconciliation output plus Scorecard — DevLake is heavy and safely deferrable a few weeks in a solo build; review and cycle-time metrics need team activity to be meaningful anyway.
8. From the governance tier, only: the exception registry with mandatory expiry (bootstrap needs it on day one), safe defaults in provisioning templates, fail-closed classification written down, and the control-plane/data-plane invariant test.
9. From the people tier, nothing initially except schemas designed with effective dating; capacity views activate when real people are working in the system, and Layer B decision support waits for its gates — the datasource separation itself is a P2 deliverable (Section 98.6), deferred in sequence, never unscheduled.

Explicitly deferred: the background machine layer (its own benchmark gate decides), shared-service registry (first genuine shared service), split/merge/transfer processes, dependency-graph views, versioned-contract migration machinery, domains and topology activation, all predictive economics and forecasting, and all Layer B decision support.

### 99.5 Technology-shape decisions

* **Git host: GitHub, effectively fixed.** The access model is built on GitHub-specific verified semantics — approval counting requires Write, environments, CODEOWNERS, Teams, outside collaborators, audit log, Projects. Porting to another host rewrites the provisioning and access subsystems wholesale. **Plan-tier posture is settled (D73):** branch protection on private repositories requires the Team plan — non-negotiable, verified. Environment required reviewers are Enterprise-only and are not depended on: the Section 27.2 workflow-identity gate is the designed production-approval mechanism, with Enterprise as an optional recorded strengthening.
* **CI: GitHub Actions.** Reusable workflows consumed by pinned tag are the canary and rollback unit for platform changes; not portable without redesign, and not required to be.
* **Dashboards: Grafana + DevLake + Prometheus**, self-hosted on the operations VM, dashboards as provisioned JSON. Confirm DevLake's required database engine and version for the pinned release before install — it determines the compose file and the control-plane backup procedure.
* **Identity bridge:** `people.yaml` keys on the GitHub login; capability-derived Grafana access uses GitHub OAuth into Grafana plus a sync job from the registries. No separate IdP. This choice is made before Layer B is built.
* **Layer B mechanism:** a second, Founder-only Grafana instance carrying the separately-credentialed people datasource, never registered in the shared instance (D75); the individual self-view is a generated per-person document. No enterprise licence, no bespoke web application, and panel-hiding is explicitly insufficient — separation is at instance level and tested.
* **Boards:** the single org-level Project with a product field is the default; per-product Projects with aggregation are the upgrade if the aggregation capability verifies. The fallback is the more buildable option and loses nothing the operating model needs.
* **Records:** YAML records in the control-plane repository, generated from the live GitHub surface, per Section 97. Chosen once, before dashboards, because half the metrics load-bear on it.
* **Background layer:** local single-shot inference on a dedicated machine; the CPU benchmark (prompt-processing bound) is run before buying anything, and a failed benchmark parks the layer without shame.
* **Tool independence is a tested property:** removing any named third-party system — including any future externally-integrated work-management tool — changes nothing in the operating model; the acceptance tests of Section 100 include this test generalised to every named external tool.

### 99.6 Top build risks

| # | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Scope drift toward productisation — building installer, tenancy and upgrade machinery for third parties multiplies scope several-fold and contradicts the non-goal | Build the internal distribution for this company only; revisit only after it has run in anger |
| 2 | Evidence-plumbing gap — dashboards ship empty or drift into hand-maintenance if the record stores are not built early | Section 97 is built in Foundation, before any dashboard that reads from it |
| 3 | Bootstrap gates staying stubbed — relaxed gates have a habit of remaining relaxed | Expiring exceptions with deactivation triggers; unclosed expiry escalates Red (Section 95) |
| 4 | Plan-checker dependency volatility — Gate 1 load-bears on a third-party tool in a category with high mortality | Verify every capability against the pinned release immediately; budget the in-house build as the fallback; all planning artifacts remain plain markdown and YAML |
| 5 | GitHub tier or behaviour dependencies failing silently — an unavailable protection feature reproduces the silent-gate failure | Verify-before-Phase-1 checklist; fallbacks recorded as accepted risks, never assumed |
| 6 | Reconciliation auto-repair as the most dangerous code — a write-scope, org-admin automation whose bug loosens security or locks everyone out; the reconciler is the highest-privilege identity in the system | Detect-only first; repair classes enabled one at a time; stricter-only rule enforced in code and tested; the reconciler's own credential in the top secrets tier with its compromise treated as a security incident |
| 7 | Instrument-before-operate bureaucracy collapse — dozens of signals and thresholds built ahead of real rhythm become alert fatigue, and the Founder stops looking | P0-before-P2, data-before-forecasts, the presentation discipline, and the quarterly review's forced retirement of at least one metric |
| 8 | People-layer trust failure — Layer B leakage, perceived surveillance or a leaderboard-shaped view poisons adoption of the entire OS | Datasource-level separation tested, the self-view document, the no-surveillance invariants of Section 91, and the P4 gate that blocks evidence generation until access control exists |
| 9 | Data quality riding on human discipline — board hygiene, state files and UAT records are only as good as daily habits; predictive layers compute confidently on garbage | Machines write state wherever plumbing exists; roll out per product and prove one product's loop end to end before scaling instrumentation |
| 10 | The control plane becoming an unowned product — one VM carrying DevLake, Grafana and every job, maintained by nobody in particular | The ops VM has a named owner, an SLO, a declared patch cadence, a tool-register entry and a non-optional quarterly restore drill under four hours |

Secondary risks, logged: a cross-reviewer implemented with Read-only permission fails silently (the completion checks catch it); QA remains the most acute single-person dependency in the model — the standing risk and its mitigation ladder are governed where QA capacity is defined, and the people plan matters as much as the build plan; and the current-configuration snapshots (roster, KRA/KPI content) are configuration captured from their source, never inferred from this document, and go stale if not maintained as such.

## Section 100. Acceptance Tests

The operating system is complete only if every test in this section passes by configuration, onboarding and record-keeping alone — with no redesign of the architecture. Each test is verified at the implementation phase (Section 98, Implementation Phases and Roadmap) where the capability it exercises activates. If any test requires rewriting the architecture, the architecture is not sufficiently extensible and the defect is in this specification, not in the situation.

The catalogue contains **110 tests**, numbered AT-001 to AT-100 plus AT-101 to AT-103 (placed with the Platform domain), AT-104 to AT-107 (placed with the Governance domain) and AT-108 to AT-110 (placed with the Access domain), grouped into six domains: Extensibility, Lifecycle, Platform, Governance, People, and Access.

### 100.1 Extensibility

| ID | Test | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AT-001 | Add product 21 | Scaffolding operation plus onboarding phases. Every surface enumerates from the registry; health, economics and dashboards pick the product up automatically. No dashboard, workflow or script contains a product list |
| AT-002 | Add a person | People Registry entry, role assignment, capability grant, new-person lifecycle. Reconciliation grants access. Capacity profile, ramp curve and the Insufficient Evidence state initialise correctly. No workflow, architecture or dashboard change |
| AT-003 | Team Lead absent two weeks | Acting Team Lead is pre-designated, holds dormant capability and activates by configuration. Gate 1 and architecture escalation continue |
| AT-004 | Team Lead changes permanently | Role and assignment change only; no workflow redesign. A new Acting Team Lead is designated at once |
| AT-005 | A QA engineer becomes Team Lead | Role change with an effective date; capabilities and assignments recalculated; the new role's evidence model applies from the effective date; the performance period is segmented with no retroactive evaluation; no architecture change |
| AT-006 | Two new QA members join | QA role capacity scales automatically. No single-QA assumption exists anywhere in the system |
| AT-007 | A new role is introduced | Role profile plus performance-framework mapping added; no architecture change |
| AT-008 | A temporary specialist or contractor joins | Scoped, dated, capability-limited entry. No ownership, no production access. Employment type supported; capacity and expiry handled; reconciliation revokes on the end date without human action |
| AT-009 | A new technology stack is introduced | The product conforms to the operating interface for its declared conformance profile (Section 15.7) — for the default `service` profile, the eight commands, the three endpoints and the verification contract. The operating system does not change |
| AT-010 | One product has three repositories | Product and Repository are separate concepts. One contract, one owner set, one dashboard entry; branch protection and CI applied to all repositories |
| AT-011 | AI provider changes | The approved runtime list is configuration. GSD, verification, GitHub, CI, production, ownership and review routing are all unchanged |
| AT-012 | Team doubles in size | Capacity, allocation and health models scale without redesign |
| AT-013 | Product count doubles | The capacity model and staffing forecast scale through the product registry alone |
| AT-014 | The performance framework is replaced completely | The new framework version activates; capacity, health, the evidence pipeline, dashboards and decision support are all unaffected. No system rewrite |
| AT-015 | A KPI is removed | Historical periods are preserved with the old KPI; future periods use the new configuration |
| AT-016 | A second Team Lead and product domains are introduced | Only `topology.yaml` changes; zero product contracts, workflows or dashboards are edited. Escalation resolves through topology. The people layer is unchanged |

### 100.2 Lifecycle

| ID | Test | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AT-017 | A person leaves | Exit lifecycle runs. Reconciliation revokes access; orphan detection surfaces every unowned responsibility; blocking orphans cannot be dismissed unresolved. Succession activates, performance evidence is archived, history is retained. No architecture change |
| AT-018 | A temporary assignment expires | Reconciliation removes it without human action; access is revoked and capacity recalculated |
| AT-019 | A product splits | Split process runs. Two contracts emerge; the original resolves to a successor identity or to sunset — never ambiguous. Historical evidence is preserved under the original identity |
| AT-020 | Products merge | Merge process runs. Verification contracts are merged, never dropped. Both histories remain queryable under their original identities |
| AT-021 | A permanent ownership change is executed | The Team Lead executes it under the reviewer-matrix-change capability; it is recorded as a decision; a Founder-view notification is generated automatically. No Founder approval step exists or is required |
| AT-022 | Founder continuity activates | The founder is unreachable beyond the declared trigger period: the standing delegation activates; the second organisation Owner or escrowed break-glass owner credential is verified usable; the founder-only account inventory is current; Layer B contingency access functions. Verified by periodic drill, not assumed |

### 100.3 Platform

| ID | Test | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AT-023 | GSD version changes | Platform change process. The canary set verifies first. Products may run different pinned versions during rollout via `platform_compatibility` |
| AT-024 | A shared CI workflow breaks | Impact analysis before rollout; the canary catches it; platform rollback reverts the workflow tag. Consumption is by pinned tag, so unmigrated products are unaffected |
| AT-025 | A platform contract schema changes | Versioned contracts. Both versions supported simultaneously. Canary migrates first, the fleet migrates gradually, a deprecation deadline is published. No simultaneous fleet migration is ever required |
| AT-026 | A platform change progresses pilot → rollout → fleet | Per-stage verification at each step and a working, tested rollback |
| AT-027 | A new platform policy propagates | Introduced without hand-editing twenty product files; it flows from `policies.yaml` and the reusable workflows |
| AT-028 | GitHub unavailable for several hours | Degraded Engineering Mode. Products keep serving customers; local work continues on distributed git; state is reconciled on recovery, never assumed |
| AT-029 | The entire control plane is unreachable | All products continue serving customers, and a production rollback can still be executed via the documented manual path |
| AT-030 | A control-plane tool is disabled | Product workflows continue; `.planning/`, verification contracts and product contracts remain readable and usable without it |
| AT-031 | A named external tool is removed | Removing any registered **integration** — the work-management example included — changes nothing in the operating system. Boards, records and metrics continue from the operating system's own stores; the integration's declared exit condition executes cleanly. This holds for every named third-party integration. The test scope is integrations, not the declared platform substrate: the git host is exempt by the stated carve-out of Section 62.5, and its replacement is governed by the tool replacement playbook (62.3) and its loss by the organisation export (Section 45.3) |
| AT-032 | Self-observability | The operating system detects and reports a failure in its own reconciliation, health job or dashboard freshness |
| AT-033 | No auto-loosening | Reconciliation presented with a stricter-than-declared production control raises it for human review and does not relax it |
| AT-034 | Governance layerability | The delivery core (Parts I–VI) runs correctly with the removable governance artifacts removed — `os-health.yaml`, `policies.yaml`, `patterns.yaml`, `economics.yaml`, `platform-roadmap.yaml`, the scenario calculator, and the maturity-assessment and forecast jobs. The reconciliation engine and the exception registry are core-resident machinery and are never removed — the core depends on them from day one. Each implementation phase in Section 98 can be adopted in order with no change to the core |
| AT-035 | GitHub organisation export restores | The scheduled organisation export restores successfully to an independent environment, each data class through its own recorded mechanism per Section 45.3 — Projects boards via their GraphQL dump, never assumed present in a migration archive — and the restore test is recorded within the same rolling 90-day discipline as product backups (D80) |
| AT-101 | Three simultaneous SEV-1s | Three Primary Responders lead their incidents independently per Section 42.4; the escalation role coordinates responder collisions and shared-resource contention without personally repairing all three systems; the Founder is informed, not dispatching. If one person is Primary Responder on two incidents, one reassigns to its Backup Responder and the event is recorded as a capacity incident |
| AT-102 | The seeded reconciliation canary | Every reconciliation run must find the deliberately seeded canary drift. A run reporting zero findings — the canary included — is a **failed** run, raises SIG-13 (failed reconciliations), and triggers the gap procedure; a reconciler that finds nothing is assumed broken, never assumed clean |
| AT-103 | Production restore without hand-held credentials | Every product declaring a `recovery:` block carries `restore-production.yml`, generated from the template, and the workflow executes end to end with an exceptional-authorisation record and without any credential being handed to or typed by a human — access is granted through the workflow's scoped identity for the run, and the run, its authorisation and its result are recorded |

| ID | Test | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |

| AT-037 | A failed exception is visible | An exception that cannot be auto-revoked becomes Blocking drift on its expiry date and appears on the Founder view |
| AT-038 | A same-scope exception reopened counts as a renewal | Closing an exception and re-opening one for the same scope increments the renewal count; a fresh ID does not reset it |
| AT-039 | A bootstrap exception expires | A bootstrap-mode gate exception carries an expiry and an activation checklist. When the headcount trigger is met or the expiry passes, the gate arms or the exception surfaces as Blocking drift — it cannot lapse silently |
| AT-040 | Pattern to work | A third occurrence of the same failure class produces a pattern candidate and a tracked remediation item with a closure condition |

| AT-042 | A future bottleneck is projected | The Team Lead receives a projected constraint with a horizon at least 4 weeks before it materialises, and the projection is retrospectively scored |
| AT-043 | QA demand is forecast | QA can see projected verification demand for the next 6 weeks by product |
| AT-044 | An economic decision is evidenced | A lifecycle decision can be evidenced with actual attention-hour data rather than impression |
| AT-045 | Bureaucracy check | The quarterly review retires at least one policy, one metric or one automation, or explicitly records why nothing warranted retirement |
| AT-046 | Baseline integrity | Every operating-system success measure in Section 103 has a recorded pre-Phase-1 baseline, or is explicitly marked as unbaselined |
| AT-047 | SEV-1 detection latency is measured | Detection-to-response latency is recorded per incident. A business-hours product's SEV-1 "immediate" clock starts at detection; a product declaring an extended or 24x7 support model whose declared `coverage_window` is not fully covered by the accepted windows of active rota members fails contract validation |
| AT-048 | Support intake flows to the defect taxonomy | A customer report enters the per-product intake channel, is triaged into the Section 41 (Observability and the Defect Taxonomy) categories, and produces a support-to-engineering handoff record; first response is measured against the severity targets in Section 22 (Customer Support Operating Contract) |
| AT-049 | `ai_runtime_dependency` evaluation enforcement | A product declaring an `ai_runtime_dependency` block without an evaluation suite under `verification/` fails CI, and a pinned-model change cannot merge without the suite passing |

| AT-104 | A support email becomes a governed record | An inbound support email becomes a structured support-board record with the first-response clock anchored to the message's received timestamp (D80), and the record closes only when the customer loop is closed — a fix shipped with no reply to the customer does not close it |
| AT-105 | A deletion request executes inside its SLA | A customer deletion request is executed through the deletion runbook via CI, with completion evidence — the four timestamps, the named executor and the subprocessor propagation checklist — recorded in `records/deletion-requests/` inside the declared `deletion_sla_days` |
| AT-106 | Gate 1 notification and turnaround | A Gate 1 submission notifies its resolved approver as a push event; breaching the approval turnaround target auto-raises the item's Blocked flag routed to the escalation role — a capacity signal, never a personal one — and the author may re-request to an active plan_approval_delegate or the Acting Team Lead designate as a recorded routing event |
| AT-107 | A scheduled eval regression blocks pin adoption | A regression detected by the AI-eval scheduled runner creates the category-five incident (external model behaviour change), raises SIG-42, and blocks adoption of the new model pin until the evaluation suite passes or a recorded exception accepts the change |
