## Section 101. Non-Negotiable Invariants

These are the rules the operating system never trades away. Every one is enforced by the platform wherever the platform can enforce it; the remainder are enforced by written policy with a named owner and a review cadence. The catalogue contains **111 invariants**, numbered continuously and grouped by theme.

**Every invariant carries an enforcement classification, and the classification is checkable.** Each of the 111 is exactly one of: **mechanical**, naming the CI check, branch-protection rule, reconciliation row or AT- identifier that enforces it; **policy**, naming the `policies.yaml` entry that carries its owner, review date and enforcement mechanism (Section 55); or **review-held**, naming the standing review that reads it and the role that chairs that review. The classification lives beside the invariant in the control plane and is authored at Phase G2, alongside the policy register it resolves into. Control-plane CI fails when an invariant classified `mechanical` names no live check or AT- identifier, when one classified `policy` names no live `policies.yaml` entry, or when any invariant carries no classification at all. This needs no twenty-seventh control-plane artifact — `policies.yaml` already holds owners and review dates, so what is new is the mapping, not a register. Without it the second clause above is an intention: an invariant that is neither mechanically enforced nor entered as a policy has no owner, no cadence, and nothing detects the omission.

### 101.1 Verification and Quality

1. No product completes onboarding without a verification contract; a live product not yet onboarded operates only under the declared pre-onboarding pathway of Section 96, with its absence recorded as an accepted risk with a named deadline.
2. Every production bug becomes a permanent regression test.
3. An untested backup is treated as no backup.
4. Restore testing runs monthly on a rotating subset, and every product is successfully restore-tested within any rolling 90-day window. `classification.reliability_criticality` may tighten a product's cadence; it never loosens it. A `restore_tested` date older than the window fails CI.
5. Verification contracts are merged, never dropped, when products merge.
6. Verification depth is never traded for verification throughput.

### 101.2 Review and Authority

7. Every product has a Primary Owner, Cross-Reviewer, Backup Owner and Escalation path, recorded in the contract and matched by team membership.
8. Every normal change receives independent review from someone other than its author.
9. No self-approval, enforced mechanically by requiring approval of the most recent reviewable push.
10. The Team Lead is not the routine reviewer — *routine review* is defined once, in Section 23.2. Exceeding 2 routine reviews per week is an investigable signal.
11. Authority is evaluated against capability and assignment, never against role name alone.
12. Production approval is never self-approved and is a separate event from Gate 2 approval.
13. Reviewer-matrix and product-ownership changes — temporary and permanent — are executed by the Team Lead under the reviewer-matrix-change capability and recorded as decisions. Every permanent ownership change generates a Founder-view notification: visibility, not approval.

### 101.3 Planning

14. H1 is committed, H2 is prepared, H3 is candidate.
15. Ready-queue misses trend to zero; the queue does not routinely reach zero for anyone.
16. A material requirement change on committed work triggers re-planning through Gate 1 when the verification path changes, the impact scope widens, the reversibility class worsens, the change becomes architecture-class, or the estimated scope grows beyond the calibrated threshold (Section 29.5). A reclassification in the benign direction — a narrowing scope, an improving reversibility class — is updated in place.

### 101.4 Machine Authority

17. Machine authority is constrained; machine output volume is not artificially throttled.
18. The background machine layer cannot merge, approve, deploy, or reach production credentials or databases — enforced by permissions and, for workflow dispatch, by the actor gate on every privileged workflow (Section 37.3), not by policy.
19. Failed and rejected machine output is retained, because the failure signal is the input to task-class analysis.
20. External or repository-provided text is data, not authority.
21. Unattended personal-agent runs are permitted only on branches; their output is flagged as unattended and never merges without the full human gate sequence.

### 101.5 Delivery and Production

22. The production artifact is the same digest verified in staging. Never rebuilt.
23. Never rebuild an artifact to work around registry unavailability.
24. The production database is inaccessible from developer machines.
25. Production secrets are environment-scoped and never present locally.
26. A fully compromised workstation must not yield production access.
27. Rollback is preferred to hotfix, and requires no prior approval during a SEV-1.
28. Non-reversible changes require an explicit recovery strategy and never claim rollback capability.
29. SEV-1 restoration takes priority over quota, fairness and scheduling rules.
30. Out-of-hours work is exception-based, authorised in advance by the Founder or the Team Lead, quota-bound, compensated and recorded; where the Team Lead is the person working and the Founder is unavailable, the Acting Team Lead designate authorises, or the activation is self-recorded and countersigned on the Founder's return (Section 47.2). SEV-1 restoration needs no prior authorisation.
31. A 24x7 support commitment cannot be accepted without funded response capacity.

### 101.6 Founder and Role Boundaries

32. The founder does not manage daily task assignment.
33. The founder does not review routine code and does not dispatch incident responders.
34. Founder absence does not halt engineering; the founder-only decision list is short and strategic.
35. An Acting Team Lead is designated in advance and holds dormant capability, so activation is configuration rather than a competence question.
36. The Team Lead operates engineering and recommends; the Founder is the final authority for every formal people decision.
37. No automatic formal improvement plan, no automatic termination, no automatic promotion, no automatic compensation change, no automatic formal warning. Automation never makes personnel decisions.
38. Every people signal is decision support; the Founder decides.
39. Founder continuity provisions exist with the same rigour as Team Lead succession: a second organisation Owner or escrowed break-glass owner credential, a current inventory of founder-only accounts, a pre-designated successor arrangement, and a standing delegation trigger.

### 101.7 State and Truth

40. Humans write decisions and meaning; machines write measurable state.
41. GitHub remains the durable engineering source of truth.
42. GSD Core is replaceable workflow tooling, not the source of truth. All artifacts remain readable without it.
43. No second workflow overlay competes with GSD. The designated work-management system is the operating system's own execution-truth boards.
44. Declared state is reconciled against actual platform state, and silent drift is not permitted.
45. No artifact becomes a dumping ground; the source-of-truth hierarchy resolves every conflict.
46. Derived data is computed, never hand-maintained. Metrics derive from the canonical record stores of Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions), never from hand-maintained numbers.
47. History is append-only for state, decisions, approvals and records; records are not deleted and state changes are recorded, not overwritten. Raw activity telemetry may be aggregated or discarded after its declared diagnostic window; retention classes are declared in the control plane and owned by the Founder.
48. Source extraction failure never downgrades existing verified data; historical records are never silently overwritten.
49. Every operating-system metric has an owner and a defined response, or it is deleted.

### 101.8 Dynamic Model

50. People, roles, capabilities and assignments are separate concepts, and each is dynamic configuration.
51. People are never hard-coded into architecture logic. Current team membership is not architecture.
52. Product count is never hard-coded into architecture logic.
53. New products are configuration plus onboarding, never platform redesign.
54. New people, new roles and new frameworks are configuration plus onboarding, never workflow redesign or architecture change.
55. Ownership changes are declarative and take effect through reconciliation.
56. Role changes trigger capability, permission and assignment recalculation.
57. Departures trigger orphan detection, and blocking orphans cannot be dismissed unresolved.
58. Temporary assignments carry a mandatory end date and expire without human action.
59. No permanent single-person dependency exists without visible risk. Knowledge redundancy is measured, not assumed.
60. Knowledge rotation is mandatory; ownership rotation is conditional.
61. The performance framework is dynamic, versioned configuration; the framework in force is not architecture. Framework versions are explicit, and changes are not applied retroactively without a documented exception.

### 101.9 Products and Dependencies

62. A Product is the business unit; a Repository is the implementation unit. A product may have several repositories.
63. Shared services have named owners, declared consumers and versioned compatibility.
64. Cross-product dependencies are declared and discoverable.
65. Product split and merge preserve historical evidence.
66. Product transfer preserves operational and business continuity; secrets are rotated by the receiver, never transferred.
67. An inbound transferred or acquired product runs full onboarding; nothing is assumed to meet the verification requirement.
68. Product lifecycle is explicit, and operational burden follows lifecycle.
69. Product launch readiness is distinct from engineering onboarding.
70. Business health is a first-class portfolio signal, not a downstream report.

### 101.10 Platform

71. Platform changes are versioned, impact-analysed, canaried, verified and reversible.
72. Portfolio-wide changes never roll out to the fleet without passing a canary first.
73. Contract schemas are versioned, and simultaneous fleet migration is never required.
74. Transitional products carry a named migration owner and a deadline; transitional never becomes permanent.
75. The control plane observes products and is never in their runtime path. A GitHub, registry, provider or control-plane outage does not stop products already running.
76. Product runtime must not depend on control-plane availability.
77. Every exception has an expiry; an exception without one is invalid and fails CI. An exception re-opened for the same scope after closure counts as a renewal — a fresh ID does not reset the count.
78. A new policy may not begin at Enforce unless it is a critical security control.
79. New people, products and tools default to minimum privilege and draft state.
80. Every control is explicitly classified fail-closed or fail-open.
81. Auto-repair may only move the system toward the declared, stricter state.
82. Changes to this specification and its enforcing tooling follow the platform-change process of Part VII: versioned, canaried, reversible.

### 101.11 Cost and Tooling

83. Engineering tooling runs at fixed cost: free, self-hosted, or a flat per-person subscription. No free cloud LLM tiers, and no metered LLM APIs in engineering tooling. Metered inference inside a product's runtime is product COGS — permitted, budgeted under its `ai_runtime_dependency` block, and monitored.
84. API keys remain absent from developer environments.
85. GSD Core is pinned to a tagged release; third-party GitHub Actions are pinned to full commit SHAs; reusable workflows are consumed by pinned tag.
86. AI provider choice is replaceable, and an AI provider outage does not stop engineering.
87. Every architecture and security policy is enforced by the platform wherever the platform can enforce it.
88. Every product declares an `infrastructure.monthly_budget_band`; a cost anomaly is a Red health signal and a classifiable incident.
89. The operating system prices itself: it carries a standing automation-ledger entry, and its ritual cost is weighed against its value at the quarterly review.

### 101.12 People and Fairness

90. Attention hours, utilisation, Product Load Units and output volume are never individual performance evidence.
91. Role-specific outcome and quality evidence may inform a Founder-owned review, always with the mandatory context adjustment of Section 80 (Systemic Context Adjustment and Variance Classification).
92. No single metric determines any people decision.
93. Systemic causes must be checked before individual attribution.
94. Performance expectations are role-specific; there is no universal performance framework.
95. Team health is separate from individual performance.
96. No keystroke, screen, webcam or online-presence surveillance.
97. No AI token usage as performance.
98. No single-number productivity score, for a person or for a team. PLU is never an employee-ranking metric.
99. No employee ranking or leaderboard.
100. New joiners require an evidence window; before it elapses the answer is Insufficient Evidence, and insufficient evidence produces no negative signal.
101. Under-utilisation is diagnosed, and is never presented as underperformance.
102. Rebalance is considered before permanent hiring where practical; no hire is authorised without a diagnosed structural constraint. Time-to-merge is a symptom, not a hiring trigger.
103. All formal management decisions are auditable.
104. Confidence must accompany every people signal.
105. The operating system is an evidence engine, not an HR replacement; it optimises company outcomes and human attention, not metric volume.

### 101.13 Access and Privacy

106. Individual people-performance intelligence on the management surface (Layer B-M) is Founder-only, gated by the `people-intelligence` capability, and **not delegable**; the individual self-view (Layer B-S) carries one person's own evidence to that person and is outside this rule. At the application and datasource layers this is absolute. Host-level administrative access to the machine carrying the store is not a grant of it and never confers the capability: it is the single named, recorded accepted risk of Section 90.3, bounded by a stated compensating control and a dated review.
107. The Team Lead receives only the minimum operational people data required for engineering execution.
108. Employees see their own evidence and feedback, not peers' private data; peers never receive management-performance information about colleagues.
109. General engineering dashboards never expose sensitive performance data and carry no per-person raw-activity drill-downs; individual activity data lives only in Layer B. The underlying people datasource is separately credentialed, and sensitive people data never enters the general engineering datasource.
110. Conduct evidence is handled separately from performance bundles, and the conduct complaint path functions when the subject is the Team Lead or the Founder.
111. No customer data in repositories. Customer data lives in product databases, never in git — not in fixtures, not in support records, not in incident evidence; records reference customer data by identifier, never by copy. Three detectors enforce it: the fixture-provenance check (Section 38.3), the by-identifier construction of support records (22.2), and the S19 intake gate (Section 96.6). The verification authority owns the standing policy entry and its review cadence.

---

## Section 102. Edge Case Catalogue

Every case carries a crisp resolution that follows from the rules elsewhere in this specification; none requires new architecture. The catalogue contains **112 cases**, numbered EC-1 to EC-112 and grouped into eleven domains.

### 102.1 People

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-1 | New developer joins | People Registry entry, then the new-person lifecycle. Cross-review shadow, then cross-review active, then ownership. Write granted per repository as assignments are made. Ownership never on day one. Joining mid-performance-period initialises ramp tracking and the Insufficient Evidence state — no evaluation before the evidence window elapses |
| EC-2 | New QA joins | Same lifecycle. Shadows verification-contract authoring before owning one. Splits the verification backlog by product, not by activity type, so each holds end-to-end context |
| EC-3 | New Team Lead joins | Onboards as a senior developer first. Acting Team Lead designation transfers only after demonstrated portfolio understanding. Founder decides timing |
| EC-4 | Acting Team Lead required | Pre-designated person activates. Capabilities granted for the period with an end date. Gate 1 continues, architecture escalation continues, incidents continue |
| EC-5 | Founder unavailable (planned or short) | Engineering continues fully. Only the short founder-only list waits. Pre-delegation available for planned absence. Extended or permanent unavailability escalates to Section 14 (Founder Continuity and Absence) |
| EC-6 | Developer resigns | Exit lifecycle. Backup Owner assumes ownership. Orphan detection runs; blocking orphans resolved before the last working day where possible. Succession activates, performance evidence is archived, access is revoked, history is retained |
| EC-7 | QA resigns | Verification authority temporarily to the Team Lead for low-risk changes, recorded per change. Products with `manual_uat: required` cannot ship. This is the most acute single-person dependency in the model and drives the second QA hire per the standing-risk mitigation ladder |
| EC-8 | Team Lead resigns | Acting Team Lead provides immediate continuity. Founder decides permanent replacement. A new Acting Team Lead is designated at once — the succession slot is never left empty |
| EC-9 | Developer changes role | Role transition process. Registry edit plus reconciliation; no manual repository editing. The performance period is segmented at the effective date per Section 84 (Performance Periods, Framework Evolution and KPI Calibration); the new role's evidence model applies forward only |
| EC-10 | Contractor joins | Scoped, dated, capability-limited. No ownership, no production |
| EC-11 | Temporary specialist joins | Same, typically with one specific capability such as `security-review` |
| EC-12 | Person account compromised | Containment before investigation. Suspend, revoke, inspect, rotate, re-review their recent approvals. Security incident flow |
| EC-13 | Developer workstation compromised | Same containment. The trust boundary limits blast radius to source and branch pushes. Re-review changes authored from that machine |
| EC-14 | Temporary assignment expires | Reconciliation removes access automatically. If the work is unfinished, extend deliberately with a reason rather than letting it lapse silently |
| EC-15 | Conduct complaint about the Team Lead | The complaint path routes around the subject: directly to the Founder, and via the external or alternate route where the subject is the Founder. Suspension pending investigation reuses `access_status: suspended`. Conduct evidence is held separately from performance bundles; the operating system scopes itself to operational containment and record-keeping per Section 88 (Conduct Concern Protocol) |

### 102.2 Team Capacity

| ID | Case | Owner | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EC-16 | Primary Owner absent (short) | Team Lead | Cross-Reviewer takes review duty. No queue behind one person |
| EC-17 | Cross-Reviewer absent | Team Lead | Reassign for the duration, preferring prior exposure. Write granted for the period, removed after |
| EC-18 | Owner and Cross-Reviewer both absent | Escalation role | Escalation role reviews personally or assigns a third person with a briefing. Recorded as a knowledge-redundancy incident |
| EC-19 | Team Lead overloaded | Founder | Detected by capacity metrics before company-wide slowdown. Corrective actions in order: narrow architecture-class criteria; delegate standing decisions per Section 13; rebalance the reviewer matrix; reassign ownership; improve backlog preparation; remove unnecessary approvals; add planning capacity; then a second Team Lead per Section 66. "The Lead works harder" is not a corrective action |
| EC-20 | QA overloaded | Founder | Diagnose first. If verification *authoring* is the constraint, shift authoring to developers with QA reviewing; automate regression; rebalance verification. If UAT *execution* is the constraint, that is the hiring signal — triggered by measured verification demand, not product count |
| EC-21 | Developer overloaded | Team Lead | Rebalance the Ready queue; if persistent, produce a rebalance candidate with capability fit and onboarding cost, and if still persistent rebalance the ownership matrix |
| EC-22 | Multiple reviewers overloaded | Team Lead | Review bottleneck confirmed. Reduce PR size first; hire second |
| EC-23 | Team grows 7 → 9 | Founder | Add verification capacity and a senior who reviews as well as builds. Reviewer matrix expands; per-person cross-review load falls. No architectural change |
| EC-24 | Team grows 9 → 12 | Founder | Consider splitting the portfolio into two review clusters with the Team Lead coordinating across both, or adding a second Team Lead. Do not add a management layer |
| EC-25 | Entire team overloaded | Founder | Team or organisational cause. Reprioritise, defer, automate, then hire — in that order, from team capacity, forecast and demand evidence |
| EC-26 | Team under-utilised | Team Lead | Ready-queue diagnosis first, then portfolio priority review. A planning cause, never a set of individual signals |
| EC-27 | One person under-utilised | Team Lead | Diagnose the cause — allocation or blocking — then allocate or unblock. Never presented as underperformance |
| EC-28 | Review load concentrated in one person | Team Lead | Reviewer-matrix rebalance; widen eligible reviewers using the capability matrix |
| EC-29 | Incident load concentrated in one person | Team Lead | Responder rotation; backup activation |
| EC-30 | Architecture knowledge concentrated in one person | Team Lead, Founder | Deliberate routing, capability development, delegation — from architecture-change authorship and capability-matrix evidence |
| EC-31 | Ready queue empty | Team Lead | Planning-capacity review from Ready Queue Miss records. No individual signal |
| EC-32 | Ready queue full but low quality | Team Lead | Enforce the Ready-to-Execute definition; watch rework-after-start and re-planning rate |
| EC-33 | High output but poor quality | Team Lead | Coach on quality, review depth and definition of done; never reward volume |
| EC-34 | Low output but high-impact work | Team Lead | Present impact context; suppress volume comparison. A misleading metric, not a performance problem |
| EC-35 | One developer supporting many products | Team Lead | Consolidate allocation, reduce context switching — from active-product and switch-rate evidence |
| EC-36 | Major outage consumes team capacity | Team Lead | Recompute capacity; exclude the outage window from delivery expectations with a record |

### 102.3 Portfolio

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-37 | New product created | Scaffolding operation, then onboarding phases. Automatic discovery on all surfaces. No dashboard hand-editing |
| EC-38 | Product stack changes | The product conforms to the operating interface for its declared conformance profile (Section 15.7) — for the default `service` profile, the eight commands, the three endpoints, the verification contract. The central operating system does not change. Update `infrastructure:` in the contract and re-run parity |
| EC-39 | Product becomes multi-repository | Add repositories to the `code.repositories` list. One contract, one owner set, one dashboard entry. Branch protection and CI applied to all |
| EC-40 | Product splits | Product split process. Original resolves to a successor identity or to sunset. Historical evidence preserved |
| EC-41 | Products merge | Product merge process. Verification contracts merged, not dropped. Both histories remain queryable |
| EC-42 | Product transfers | Transfer process. Secrets rotated by the receiver, never transferred. Inbound products run full onboarding |
| EC-43 | Product temporarily needs more capacity | Temporary contributor assignment, dated, expires cleanly |
| EC-44 | Product temporarily loses its owner | Backup Owner assumes operationally. Team Lead coordinates. Not a permanent transfer |
| EC-45 | Product becomes strategically important | Founder raises `business.criticality`. Team Lead reassesses ownership, knowledge redundancy and support model; where `classification.reliability_criticality` also rises, the incident reserve, verification depth and backup readiness rise with it. A newly critical product with Red redundancy is an immediate remediation item |
| EC-46 | Product becomes commercially irrelevant | Lifecycle transition to maintenance or sunset. Frees CI, monitoring, Renovate, backups, Scorecard and attention |
| EC-47 | Product enters maintenance | Per the lifecycle table. Ready items archive to H3. Ownership continues. Capacity is reallocated and its debt reclassified per Section 56 (Technical Debt Governance) |
| EC-48 | Product pauses | Renovate off, monitoring and backups continue, ownership retained |
| EC-49 | Product resumes | Dependency catch-up first, then features. Re-verify platform compatibility |
| EC-50 | Product sunsets | Deployment halted. Customer migration as H1 with a named owner. Shared-service consumers migrated first |
| EC-51 | Product archived | Zero ongoing capacity. Removed from matrix, board and dependency graph. Final backup verified and retained |
| EC-52 | Founder changes priority | Founder states the business priority. Team Lead re-sequences H2 and H3, preserves H1 context, records the decision. In-flight work is not discarded; it is paused with state preserved |
| EC-53 | Portfolio reaches 20 products | See the staffing arithmetic in Section 103. A design target subject to measured capacity |
| EC-54 | Portfolio exceeds 20 | Requires more owners, or lifecycle demotion, or both. The architecture does not change. The Capacity and Business dimensions make the choice evidence-based |
| EC-55 | One product dominates capacity | Visible in the Capacity dimension. Founder decides whether it reflects genuine business value. If not, it is a scope problem, not a staffing problem |
| EC-56 | Product complexity changes | Primary Owner and Team Lead update the PLU inputs and workload context; expectations re-baseline forward only |

### 102.4 Dependencies

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-57 | Shared service changes | Automatically cross-product impact scope. Consumer contract tests run. Breaking changes require a major version and a migration window. Consumers migrate on their own schedule |
| EC-58 | Cross-product dependency breaks | Shared-service owner leads. Consuming-product responders handle customer-facing mitigation. Escalation role coordinates. Consumers do not each independently debug the service |
| EC-59 | External provider outage | Dependency health monitoring distinguishes this from a product fault. Dashboard groups by provider. No code change attempted. Founder handles customer communication if material |
| EC-60 | Customer-specific integration breaks | Classified as a customer integration defect, not a code defect. Fixed in configuration where possible. No code deployment for a single customer's configuration |
| EC-61 | Vendor announces an API sunset, store policy deadline or OAuth change | Enters the asset inventory as an external-deadline entry with a named owner and configurable alerts (30-day minimum, longer for large migrations). Recorded against the vendor-deprecation pattern class; migration work is planned through the normal horizons, not discovered at the deadline |

### 102.5 AI Build-Time

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-62 | AI provider outage | Switch to an approved fallback runtime. If none is available, manual engineering continues. No gate, deployment or verification depends on an AI provider |
| EC-63 | AI provider subscription changes | The runtime list is configuration. Update the approved list; people migrate. No workflow change |
| EC-64 | Model regression | Benchmark process on a representative task set before adoption. Newest is not assumed better. Nobody is forced to switch |
| EC-65 | Prompt injection attempted against an engineering agent | Constitutional rule; plan-checker symbol and package verification; Gate 2 human review; and the background layer's structural inability to merge, approve or deploy. Any successful injection reaching a PR is a security incident and gets a permanent regression test |
| EC-66 | Background layer output quality degrades for a task class | Acceptance falls below threshold; the class auto-suspends. Rejected PRs and reasons retained. Team Lead investigates prompt, model or task selection and may restore |
| EC-67 | Background layer generates 100+ PRs | Not a problem by design. Queue depth is a signal, not a fault. Review by task-class acceptance rate, prioritising historically high-acceptance classes. Do not throttle output. Use the queue to identify where reviewer capacity must grow |
| EC-68 | AI-generated change causes a production defect | Identical handling to any other production defect. Incident, rollback or flag disable, postmortem, permanent regression test. Additionally: which gate should have caught it, and why did it not? |
| EC-69 | Machine output rises while review capacity stays constant | Structural, not personal. Narrow background task classes by measured yield; never throttle output; never count volume for any person |
| EC-70 | Background model quality improves | Re-baseline task-class expectations. No individual credit for model improvement |
| EC-71 | Background model quality deteriorates | Task-class quality signal and whitelist review — from yield, rework and revert rate by class. Never an individual penalty |
| EC-72 | AI seat exhausted during an incident | No incident path depends on an AI runtime: detection, rollback and response are AI-free by construction. The responder continues manually; the exhaustion is recorded as seat-lifecycle evidence per Section 39 (AI Subscription and Seat Lifecycle), never as a response failure |

### 102.6 AI In-Product

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-73 | Provider deprecates or silently changes a production model | A behaviour change with no deployment — the fifth defect category, external model behaviour change. The `ai_runtime_dependency` evaluation suite re-runs to characterise the change; the declared provider fallback behaviour applies; migrating the pinned model is a normal change with a manifest, review and the evaluation suite as its verification |
| EC-74 | End-user prompt injection against a product AI feature | The product's declared prompt-injection surface and controls apply. Classified under the abuse classification of Section 43 (Security Incident Workflow); a successful injection becomes a permanent case in the product's evaluation suite |
| EC-75 | Runtime inference cost spike | Product COGS, not tooling. The declared cost ceiling and anomaly alert fire; classified as a cost incident per Section 50 (Cloud Cost Observability); containment may include rate limiting or the declared fallback, never an unbudgeted silent overrun |

### 102.7 Platform

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-76 | GitHub outage | Degraded Engineering Mode. Products keep serving. Merges, CI and deployment pause. Reconcile on recovery; do not assume |
| EC-77 | Artifact registry outage | Running production unaffected. New deployments pause. Never rebuild to work around it |
| EC-78 | Shared CI workflow breaks | Caught on canary before fleet rollout if the process was followed. If it reaches the fleet, platform rollback: stop, revert the workflow tag, validate canaries, fix, re-canary |
| EC-79 | Product contract schema changes | Versioned contract migration. Both versions supported. Canary first. Fleet migrates gradually. Deprecation deadline published |
| EC-80 | Verification schema changes | Same process |
| EC-81 | GSD version upgrade | Platform change. Canary set verifies. Products may run different pinned versions during rollout |
| EC-82 | Dashboard schema changes | Platform change. Dashboards are JSON in git and version-controlled; rollback is reverting the provisioned definition |
| EC-83 | Operating system upgrade | Platform version increments. Changelog, compatibility statement, migration process, rollout and rollback all required |
| EC-84 | Platform rollout fails during canary | Stop immediately. Do not proceed to fleet. Roll back the canaries. Record in the manifest. Fix and re-canary |
| EC-85 | Platform rollback needed after fleet rollout | Stop rollout, revert the workflow or schema version, restore the prior state, validate canaries, resume only after correction. The operating system must be at least as recoverable as the products it manages |
| EC-86 | GitHub organisation suspended, compromised or lost | Loss, not outage — Degraded Engineering Mode does not cover it. Compromise is a security incident with containment first. Recovery runs from the scheduled organisation export (repositories, issues, PR metadata and boards — never the audit log, which the Team plan cannot export, Section 45.3) held in independent storage and restore-tested on the 90-day discipline; the DR failure-scenario table carries the org-compromise and org-suspension rows |
| EC-87 | A named external integration is removed | The integration's registered exit condition executes. Nothing in the operating system changes: execution truth, boards, records and metrics live in the OS's own stores. This holds for the work-management integration and for every other named third-party integration, and is verified by AT-031. The declared platform substrate — the git host — is outside this case by the Section 62.5 carve-out; its replacement is a project under 62.3, not a property under AT-031 |

### 102.8 Infrastructure

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-88 | DNS outage | Distinguished from an application defect. Named domain owner. Wait and communicate. If resolution points somewhere unexpected, it is a security incident, not an outage |
| EC-89 | Certificate failure | Asset inventory alerts at 30 days. If it expired anyway, renew and investigate why the alert produced no action |
| EC-90 | Secret rotation failure | Documented rotation procedure per product. If rotation requires deployment, that is a design weakness recorded as H3 work |
| EC-91 | Database restore failure | Immediate escalation. A live reliability risk, not a scheduling problem. The product's recovery capability is unproven until a restore succeeds |
| EC-92 | Operations VM failure | Control-plane outage. Products keep running. Rebuild from GitHub. Target under 4 hours. Tested quarterly |
| EC-93 | Product infrastructure provider outage | Per the declared `provider_outage_behaviour`. Dashboard groups by provider. Founder handles customer communication |
| EC-94 | Cloud cost spike | Spend leaves the `infrastructure.monthly_budget_band`: Red health signal, named owner, cost-incident classification. Diagnose leaked credential, runaway autoscale or egress first; a compromised key is simultaneously a security incident |
| EC-95 | DDoS or abuse event | The abuse classification of Section 43 applies. The product's declared controls — rate limits, provider-level DDoS posture, abuse-report intake — are the first line; response ownership follows the incident model, and customer communication follows Section 22 |

### 102.9 Business

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-96 | Major customer escalation | Founder handles the relationship. Team Lead translates commitments into sequencing. Commitments requiring out-of-hours capacity require funded capacity first. The reallocation is recorded as context for all affected people's performance periods |
| EC-97 | New 24x7 support contract proposed | Cannot be accepted without a funded rota. A commercial decision with a staffing cost, surfaced before signature — alongside the commitments-block conflict checks of Section 21 (Customer Commitments and SLA Registry) |
| EC-98 | Customer requests data deletion | `data.deletion_supported` and `deletion_sla_days` declare capability. If unsupported, it becomes engineering work before the commitment can be honoured |
| EC-99 | New data residency requirement | Declared in `data.residency`. A conflict with the declared provider region is a blocking conflict, surfaced before contract signature |
| EC-100 | Revenue concentrates in one product | Founder decides whether ownership and redundancy adequately protect it. A high-revenue product with Red knowledge redundancy is a serious business risk, not merely an engineering observation |
| EC-101 | Product usage declines to near zero | Lifecycle review. A technically healthy product with no customers is not an engineering failure; it is a portfolio decision |
| EC-102 | High-revenue product becomes technically fragile | Risk escalation. Reliability remediation plan with a named owner. Check knowledge redundancy simultaneously |
| EC-103 | Low-revenue product consumes large engineering capacity | Sunset or maintenance candidate. The Capacity and Business dimensions together make this visible without anyone having to argue it |

### 102.10 Support and Customers

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-104 | Support load increases on one product | Visible in the Business dimension. Often a quality or usability problem rather than a support-staffing problem. Investigate the product before hiring support |
| EC-105 | Support-load surge | The per-product intake channel and triager role absorb it; triage into the defect taxonomy separates defects, incidents and requests; first-response targets by severity hold or are consciously breached with a record. A sustained surge is a quality signal on the product first, a staffing signal second |

### 102.11 Governance

| ID | Case | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EC-106 | Founder incapacity or death | The founder-continuity provisions of Section 14 activate: the standing delegation trigger fires after the declared unreachable period; the second organisation Owner or escrowed break-glass credential restores administrative control; the founder-only account inventory (billing, registrar, banking, app stores, AI vendor admin) directs the successor; the pre-designated successor and legal arrangement carry the decisions the delegation cannot. Engineering continues throughout — the founder-only list is short by design |
| EC-107 | A second founder, board or investor arrives | The dormant resolution rule of Section 66 (Organisational Topology, Domains and Governance Evolution) activates: founder-class capability scope is split and recorded when it happens, exactly as domains split Team Lead scope. No structure is built before it is needed |
| EC-108 | Incident on a not-yet-onboarded brownfield product | The product's pre-onboarding operating mode names its minimal ruleset, accepted risks and responders; the incident is handled under that record, honestly short of the full evidence chain. The gap between what happened and what the onboarded process would have provided feeds the postmortem and accelerates the onboarding-deadline review per Section 96 (Brownfield Transition Governance) |
| EC-109 | A silently-vacuous reconciliation run | A reconciliation run completes "clean" while actually checking nothing — a broken query, an empty product enumeration. The seeded canary drift exposes it: a run that fails to report the canary is a failed run (AT-102), raises SIG-13, and the gap procedure runs to establish what the vacuous window may have missed. Silence is never taken as health |
| EC-110 | Client-app crash spike mid-staged-rollout | The staged store rollout is halted at its current percentage immediately; the declared kill-switch or feature flag disables the offending path for users already updated; an expedited review classifies the defect and the fix or rollback ships through the store's expedited path; stranded users — those on the crashing version who cannot roll back a store install — get the declared mitigation (server-side flag, forced-upgrade prompt or degraded fallback). The incident record notes rollout percentage at halt |
| EC-111 | A temporary specialist expires with open gate-relevant work | The fourteenth orphan type (High): a temporary person's end date arrives while a review, verification judgment or approval they hold is still open. Orphan detection warns the assignment's sponsor at T-minus-7 days; at expiry the open work reassigns explicitly — extend the assignment deliberately with a reason, or route the work to the Backup Owner or Cross-Reviewer as a recorded event. Access still expires on the date; the work never lapses silently with it |
| EC-112 | The Acting Team Lead authors a plan during the Team Lead's leave | The Acting Team Lead holds Gate 1 approval and cannot self-approve their own plan. Resolution: a reciprocal delegate — a pre-designated second approver (typically the most senior developer) holding leave-scoped Gate 1 authority for exactly this case — approves it; where none is designated, a leave-scoped exception records the self-approval with the risk accepted and an expiry at the Team Lead's return. Either path is recorded; neither is silent |

## Section 103. Success Metrics and Baselines

Every metric here declares the eight attributes of Section 84.6 — definition; source; time window; baseline; expected interpretation; known limitations; owner; and defined action on breach. There is no shorter list: a metric carrying five of the eight is not calibrated, and two lists of required attributes would be two rules. The tables below render the columns an operator reads; the full declaration for each measure lives beside it in `os-health.yaml`, the one register for metric metadata in this system (Section 52.6). **Trends matter more than absolute thresholds**; where a fixed target is given, treat it as a review trigger rather than a law. An empty or not-yet-baselined record store renders as **unbaselined**, never as a miss — the Section 52 arming discipline applied to metrics: a metric with no data yet is unarmed, and an unarmed metric cannot fail (D77). Every metric derives from the canonical record stores and event log of Section 97 (Records, Events and Data Conventions) — never from hand-maintained numbers. None of these metrics is individual performance evidence; general surfaces aggregate at product and portfolio level per Section 91 (Retention, No-Surveillance, Fairness and Anti-Goodhart).

### 103.1 Level 1 — Engineering

| Metric | Source (record store) | Cadence | Target | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PR cycle time per product, median and 90th percentile | DevLake | Daily | Stable or falling | The 90th percentile matters more; a rising tail with a flat median means some PRs are stuck |
| CI pass rate | GitHub Actions | Daily | Above 90% | Below this, CI instability is masking real signal |
| Plan rejection rate and reason distribution | Plan-checker records | Weekly | Watch the reason mix, not the rate. Zero rejections means the gates are not working | Rising "no verify command" indicates weak preparation; rising "symbol does not exist" indicates model or context problems |
| Verification coverage per product | Verification contract | Per merge | 100% of requirements mapped, and every contract's seeded-defect case failing | Coverage counts mappings, not discriminating power. A contract whose seeded-defect case passes is an instrument-health failure, not evidence (Section 31.2) |
| Ready-queue misses | Board automation records | Weekly | Trending to zero | A Team Lead capacity signal, never an individual signal |
| Cross-review turnaround, median and 90th percentile | DevLake | Daily | Median under 1 working day | The tail identifies which reviewer is saturated |

### 103.2 Level 2 — Delivery

| Metric | Source (record store) | Cadence | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment frequency per product | Deployment records | Weekly | Rising |
| Lead time, merge to production | DevLake | Weekly | Falling |
| Deployment failure rate | Deployment records | Weekly | Under 15% |
| Rollback rate | Deployment records | Weekly | Under 10% of deployments |
| Merged-but-not-deployed count | Merge versus deployment records | Daily | Near zero |
| Production digest matches approved digest | `/version` versus approval record | Per deployment | 100%. Any mismatch is a P0 investigation |

### 103.3 Level 3 — Reliability

| Metric | Source (record store) | Cadence | Target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Availability per product | Prometheus | Continuous | Per `classification.reliability_criticality` |
| Error rate per product | Prometheus | Continuous | Below declared threshold |
| MTTR | Incident records | Monthly | Falling |
| Incident frequency by severity | Incident records | Monthly | Falling |
| Detection-to-response latency | Incident records | Monthly (recorded per incident) | Falling; interpreted against each product's declared `support_model` detection expectation — a business-hours product is measured from detection, an extended or 24x7 product from occurrence |
| Restore freshness | Product contracts | Daily | Every product within the rolling 90-day window; tighter where `classification.reliability_criticality` demands it |
| Failed restore tests | Restore-test workflow records | Per test | Zero. Any failure is immediate escalation |
| Undeclared weekend activations per quarter | Out-of-hours state-changing events in the event log (Section 97.3) and DevLake activity, measured against each person's declared working calendar, **minus** the activations recorded in the exception registry — the residual is the metric | Quarterly | Zero. Reported at team level and never named, per Section 91.7. A declared, authorised SEV-1 activation is never penalised and does not count against this target; a non-zero residual is a coverage and policy signal to the Founder, never a finding about a person |
| Drift incidents by severity | Reconciliation records | Weekly | Blocking drift: zero |
| Blocking orphans outstanding | Orphan detection | Daily | Zero |

Weekend-metric interpretation note: watch for the **freeze-adjacent severity-inflation pattern** — an incident classified SEV-1 shortly before or during the Friday freeze acquires authorisation-free out-of-hours work as a side effect. A cluster of freeze-adjacent SEV-1s is reviewed against the severity definitions at the postmortem, and a confirmed inflation enters the pattern register; the review targets the classification, never the responder.

### 103.4 Level 4 — Business

| Metric | Source (record store) | Cadence | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Active customers per product | Business systems | Monthly | Justifies engineering allocation |
| Revenue importance per product | Business systems | Quarterly | Prioritisation input |
| Product usage trend | Product analytics | Monthly | Lifecycle decisions |
| Support load per product | Support records | Monthly | Quality signal, often mistaken for a staffing signal |
| Support first-response time by severity | Support-board events via the Section 99.2 email-ingest hook (event log; the clock anchors to the message's received timestamp, never the ingest event — a polling ingest must not flatter the metric (D80)) | Weekly | Within the targets declared in Section 22 (Customer Support Operating Contract) |
| Infrastructure cost versus `monthly_budget_band` per product | Billing exports | Monthly, with continuous anomaly alerts | Within band. An unexplained excursion is a Red health signal and a classifiable cost incident |
| Customer-impacting incidents | Incident records | Monthly | The metric that matters most to customers |

Without Level 4, it is possible to build an excellent engineering machine serving products nobody uses.

### 103.5 Platform Health

| Metric | Target | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Products on current contract version | Rising toward 100% | Migration progress |
| Products `transitional` | Falling; none past deadline | A transitional product past its deadline is Action Required |
| Products `unsupported` | Zero | Deployment is already blocked |
| Platform changes canaried before fleet | 100% | Any exception is a process failure |
| Platform rollbacks per quarter | Low, but not zero | Zero may mean canaries are too conservative |
| Reconciliation clean-run rate | Rising | — |
| Temporary assignments past expiry | Zero | Reconciliation should make this structurally impossible |

### 103.6 Business and Engineering Tradeoffs

Engineering throughput is never optimised independently of business value.

| Situation | Reading | Decision owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High revenue, low engineering efficiency | Investment decision. Possibly justified, possibly a rewrite candidate, possibly under-owned | Founder, informed by Team Lead |
| Low revenue, high engineering effort | Sunset or maintenance candidate | Founder |
| High customer growth, high verification load | Hiring signal — verification capacity, not developers | Founder, on QA capacity evidence |
| Technically healthy, commercially weak | Not an engineering failure. Lifecycle decision | Founder |
| Commercially strong, technically fragile | Risk escalation. Reliability remediation plan; check knowledge redundancy | Founder and Team Lead jointly |
| All health dimensions green | Candidate to reduce attention-hours allocation, not to keep polishing | Team Lead |

### 103.7 Team Lead Capacity Thresholds

These exist so the founder can tell when the operating model needs adjusting, not when the Team Lead should work harder.

| Metric | Threshold | Source (record store) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plans waiting for approval | Under 3 at any time | Board |
| Average plan approval time | Under 4 working hours | Board |
| Architecture decisions outstanding | Under 5 | `.planning/` and board |
| Production approvals waiting | Under 2 | Environment approval queue |
| Cross-product decisions waiting | Under 3 | Board |
| Blocked people | Zero | Board |
| Ready coverage | Above 90% | Board |
| Team Lead review queue | Under 3 | Review requests |
| Routine reviews absorbed by Team Lead (the Section 23.2 definition) | Under 2 per week | Review records cross-checked against the routing table |
| Platform changes in flight | Under 2 concurrent | Change manifests |
| Blocking orphans outstanding | Zero | Orphan detection |

That routine-review threshold is the safeguard. Without a hard number, "the Team Lead is not the routine reviewer" degrades into a preference within a quarter. Exceeding it is investigable, not punishable — it usually means architecture-class criteria are too broad or a reviewer is absent.

The Team Lead capacity view exists to tell the founder when the operating model itself needs adjustment. Corrective actions, in order of preference: narrow architecture-class criteria; delegate standing decisions; rebalance the reviewer matrix; improve backlog preparation; reduce unnecessary approval points; reassign product ownership; add a planning or engineering peer.

### 103.8 Founder Capacity

The Founder is a diagnosable constraint, measured with the same honesty as everyone else — as a system property, never as a performance score.

| Metric | Source (record store) | Cadence | Target | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder decision latency | Decision records: median time from decision prompt or evidence-bundle readiness to recorded Founder decision | Weekly | Stable or falling | A rising median is a Founder-decision-latency bottleneck (Section 103.11), remedied by founder-delegation assignments, sharper evidence bundles and batched decision sessions — not by anyone waiting harder |
| Founder decision queue depth and age | Decision records | Weekly | No item older than the declared review cadence without a recorded reason | Ageing items indicate the founder-only list has silently grown |

### 103.9 Review Network Quality

| Metric | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Review load per person | Detects an unbalanced matrix before it becomes a bottleneck |
| Review turnaround per reviewer | Identifies saturation |
| Review rejection rate | Very low may mean rubber-stamping; very high may mean weak plans |
| Rework rate after review | Quality of review, not quantity |
| Post-merge defects attributable to review failure | The honest measure of review effectiveness |
| Reviewer product familiarity | Derived from recent contribution and review dates |

If a Cross-Reviewer does not understand a change: they say so. They do not rubber-stamp. The Team Lead pairs them with the owner for that one review, then reassesses whether the matrix assignment is right. A second mandatory reviewer is not added — the goal is accountability and expertise, not reviewer count. This behaviour is correct and must never be penalised.

### 103.10 Knowledge Redundancy

Per product, tracked automatically: Primary Owner; Cross-Reviewer; backup readiness; date of last meaningful contribution by the secondary engineer; date of last meaningful review by the secondary engineer.

| Status | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| Green | Secondary engineer has both contributed and reviewed within the defined window |
| Amber | Some exposure, incomplete redundancy |
| Red | Only one person has meaningful recent knowledge |

A Red product triggers remediation — pair the secondary engineer on the next change, or reassign cross-review. It does not automatically trigger forced ownership reassignment. **Knowledge rotation is mandatory. Ownership rotation is conditional.** Ownership may change when concentration is high, the backup has become capable, the product needs different expertise, workload needs rebalancing, or strategy changes. An effective owner is not moved off a product merely because a period of time has passed.

### 103.11 The Seven-Way Bottleneck Taxonomy

Time-to-merge is a symptom, not a hiring trigger. Diagnose the cause first. The remedy ladders below are summaries; the authoritative remedy ladders, including the full rebalance-before-hire sequence, are Section 73.2 (Workforce Staffing Diagnosis and Rebalancing), and where this table and Section 73.2 differ, Section 73.2 wins.

| Bottleneck | Signal | Response (summary — full ladder in Section 73.2) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Review | Cross-review turnaround rising; reviewers at capacity; load unbalanced | Reduce PR size; rebalance the matrix; delegate; then add reviewer capacity |
| Verification | UAT queue growing; QA at capacity; contracts late | Verification automation and background-drafted suites; shift authoring to developers with QA reviewing; then hire QA |
| Planning | Ready-queue misses rising; Lead capacity metrics red | Narrow architecture-class criteria; delegate standing decisions; protect Lead planning time; then a second Team Lead |
| Architecture | Decisions outstanding; people blocked on direction | Batch architecture sessions; record standing decisions to prevent repeat questions |
| Engineering capacity | All other metrics healthy, throughput still short of demand | Rebalance and defer first; then hire a developer |
| Product priority | Work reprioritised repeatedly mid-flight; H1 churn high | A founder and Team Lead conversation, not a hire |
| Founder-decision latency | Decision queue ageing; median Founder decision latency rising; evidence bundles waiting | Pre-delegate standing decisions through founder-delegation assignments; sharpen evidence bundles; batch decision sessions — never a hire |

A second verification hire is expected to become relevant around product 12–14, but hiring is triggered by measured verification demand rather than product count. The same principle applies to every future hire.

### 103.12 Portfolio Capacity — the Honest Arithmetic

The target is approximately 20 products. The arithmetic must be stated rather than assumed. With four owners — three general developers plus one mobile developer:

| Portfolio size | Products owned each | Cross-reviewed each | Working knowledge each | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | ~3 | ~3 | 6 | Comfortable |
| 12 | ~3–4 | ~3–4 | 7–8 | Sustainable |
| 16 | ~4 | ~4 | 8 | At capacity; watch review turnaround |
| 20 | ~5 | ~5 | 10 | At or beyond the practical ceiling for four owners |

Lifecycle status changes the arithmetic materially. A product in `maintenance` or `paused` carries a fraction of the ownership load of an `active` one — no feature work, no Ready items, no plan approvals. A portfolio of 20 products where 6 are in maintenance and 2 are sunsetting carries roughly the load of 13 active products, which four owners can hold. The mobile developer typically owns fewer products, because mobile carries a heavier manual UAT burden and a release path with external review latency.

20 products is a design target, not a guaranteed ceiling. Actual sustainable capacity is determined by measured review, verification, planning and engineering constraints — not by this number. The system is built to tell you which constraint binds first. Reaching 20 *active* products with four owners is unlikely without either a fifth owner or lifecycle demotion of lower-value products, and the Capacity and Business dimensions exist to make that choice evidence-based rather than aspirational.

**None of these numbers appear in the architecture.** They are planning assumptions. The registries enumerate whatever exists.

### 103.13 Operating System Success Criteria

The goal is not more automation. The goal is less human coordination per unit of verified output.

| Measure | Source (record store) | Direction | Baseline | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder coordination time per week | Attention ledger — Coordination-category hours attributed to the Founder; part machine-derived, part weekly banded self-report | Down; target under 30 minutes per day | Banded estimate before Phase 1; verified at G1 | The primary goal of the whole system — measured where a trace exists, honestly banded where none does, and labelled with its provenance wherever it renders (Section 97.4) |
| Team Lead coordination hours per week | Attention ledger | Down, or flat while the portfolio grows | Banded estimate before Phase 1; verified at G1 | Flat under growth is a success, not a plateau |
| Engineering hours per product per month | Attention ledger | Down, median across portfolio | Banded estimate before Phase 1; verified at G1 | The business goal the attention ledger exists to measure — read only alongside the derived-versus-self-reported control of Section 91.7, because a rising agent-directed share narrows the observable window on its own |
| Review hours per product per month | DevLake | Flat or down under growth | — | Rising sharply indicates matrix imbalance |
| QA verification hours per product per month | Attention ledger | Down per product as contracts mature | — | Rising total with falling per-product is healthy growth |
| Status requests received | Event log — Coordination-category status-request events, weekly | Toward zero | — | The cleanest proxy for whether the system carries state; derived, never hand-counted |
| Ready-queue misses | Planning board records | Toward zero | — | A hard requirement, unchanged |
| Incident response time and rollback median | Incident records | Down | — | Rollback median under 10 minutes is a strong target |
| Founder decision latency | Decision records | Down | — | See Section 103.8 |
| Platform migration cost per fleet change | Change manifests | Down | — | Rising cost means the fleet is diverging |
| Onboarding time to first accepted PR | Onboarding records | Down | — | Best single indicator of context-switch cost |
| Offboarding time to zero orphans | Registries | Down; target under 5 working days | — | Directly serves the orphan-risk goal |
| Ownership transfer time to first verified change | Registries plus DevLake | Down | — | Tests whether knowledge is genuinely distributed |
| Verified output per human attention hour | Computed | Up over four-quarter trend | — | Portfolio-level only; never per person |
| Active policy count and net growth | Policy register | Flat or down after Phase 2 | — | Growth without retirement is bureaucracy accruing |
| Open exception count and renewal rate | Exception registry | Flat; renewals toward zero | — | Rising renewals mean policies need changing. A same-scope reopen counts as a renewal |
| Founder total OS ritual hours | Attention ledger, monthly — entries carrying the `ritual` flag (Section 67.2) | Flat or down, and below the declared Founder operating-load ceiling | Ceiling recorded before Phase 1 (Section 103.14) | Owner: Team Lead, not the Founder, because a party does not own the instrument that measures it. Breach is SIG-43, with a drift class and a response ladder; the quarterly review weighs the trend, it is not the detector |
| Aggregate tooling and control-plane spend | Billing exports and subscription records, monthly | Within the declared `control_plane_budget_band` (Section 50.1) | — | Owner: Founder. The control plane carries its own budget band, exactly as products do; an excursion is SIG-35 and is reviewed at the business review |
| Automation ledger net value | `economics.yaml` | Positive and rising | — | Proof the operating system pays for itself — the OS's own standing ledger entry included |

**Metric ownership and response, wholesale.** Sections 103.1 and 103.2 are owned by the Team Lead, Section 103.3 by QA and the Team Lead, Section 103.4 by the Founder, Sections 103.5, 103.7, 103.9 and 103.10 by the Team Lead, and Sections 103.8 and 103.13 by the Founder — unless a row states otherwise. Section 103.6 names its own decision owner per row; Sections 103.11 and 103.12 are diagnostic taxonomies, not metric tables. Where a table states no action on breach, the defined response is that the owner raises the adverse trend at the quarterly operating-system review and a **recorded decision** follows — continue, revise the measure, or act. Together these two grants satisfy Section 84.6 for every measure in this section: none is ownerless, none is response-less, and the missing-attribute limb of the delete rule never fires here. A measure may still be retired at that review for being useless — that is the review working — but never for lacking an attribute this grant supplies. Deleting the instrument that measures whether the operating system is worth operating is the most expensive way to satisfy a hygiene rule. A measure whose only source is a phase recorded as `declined` (Section 98.1) is marked `unbaselined` and deleted at the next quarterly review under Section 84.6.

### 103.14 Baselines Before Phase 1

**Baselines are captured before Phase 1 of Section 98 begins.** A measurement programme with no baseline can prove nothing. Pre-Phase-1 baselines are **one-time banded self-estimates** — bands, not minutes — labelled as estimates in the record and never mixed with ledger-derived data; the G1 deliverable is to verify and re-record them against early instrumented data, not to capture them again (Section 98.5). The minimum baseline set is: Founder coordination time per week, Team Lead coordination hours per week, engineering hours per product per month, developer disruption hours per month — Section 59.3's freeze condition cannot evaluate without it, and rollout is when it most needs to — and the Founder operating-load ceiling that SIG-43 breaches against (Section 52.2). Every other Section 103.13 measure carries either a recorded baseline estimate or an explicit "unbaselined" marker — verified by AT-046. A repeatedly overridden threshold anywhere in this section is a suspect threshold and enters the calibration review of Section 84.

## Section 104. Narrative and North Star

### 104.1 Monday Morning

It is Monday morning. The portfolio is around twenty products; the team is around ten people. The founder opens one screen.

Eighteen products are green. One is amber, one is red — and each dimension speaks for itself, because there is no composite score to hide behind.

The red product is Product 12. The attention panel shows why in a single line: production error rate elevated since Friday's deploy, and its restore-test date is 84 days old. The amber product is flagged for a different reason — it is `transitional` on the contract schema, its migration deadline is three weeks away, and the named migration owner is on leave. The constraint dimension shows verification capacity, not review capacity, as this week's limiting factor across the portfolio.

The founder does not open a terminal. They do not ask anyone what happened. The team lead already knows about the error rate: the alert fired Friday at 16:20, before the deployment freeze, and the primary owner rolled back to the previous artifact digest within eleven minutes. No approval was needed for the rollback; that is the rule. Rollback was possible because the migration in that release was backward-compatible, which the plan-checker had required before approving the plan. The error rate has been flat since. What remains is the root cause, and it is second in this week's Ready queue. The restore test is scheduled for Wednesday as part of this month's rotating subset. The transitional migration reassigns in two minutes — a registry edit, and reconciliation grants the new owner what they need overnight.

Further down the same screen, one product is engineering green, reliability green, business red — declining customers, rising support burden, and 180 attention hours last quarter for a revenue line that no longer justifies them. The system does not recommend sunsetting it; it presents the arithmetic and notes that two customers hold contracts running to March. Another product is reliability red for the third time this quarter, and the failure-pattern detector has already linked all three incidents to the same external payment dependency and opened a pattern record with an architecture remediation queued in H2. A third product needs nothing from the founder at all; the team lead has it, and the view says so explicitly.

Below the portfolio, one line: the operating system itself is Degrading, and the line names its top contributing signals. QA verification demand is projected to exceed capacity in five weeks, because three products reach launch readiness in the same window. The forecast has been right seven of the last nine times, and the view shows that record. Two options are presented: move one launch by three weeks, or bring forward the QA hire that has been in H3 since spring. The scenario output for the hire, ramp included, is one click away.

The founder opens one more view — the private one, behind its own credential. The team is healthy; one developer's workload has been trending high for four weeks, not yet sustained, cause already classified as allocation; a rebalance candidate is drafted with capability fit and onboarding cost attached. One promotion candidate shows sustained next-level indicators with the evidence, the context and the confidence. Nothing requires a decision today. The founder spends eleven minutes in total, and no one is asked for status.

Meanwhile a developer opens their board. They own three products and cross-review three others. Their morning starts with two cross-reviews: one from a colleague on a product they own, and one that the owner of a different product authored themselves — so it routes here rather than to the team lead. Neither takes long. The tests prove the code works; the reviewer is judging whether the approach was right. One of the two touches an authentication path. They flag it as possibly architecture-class rather than approving it. The team lead confirms the classification in eight minutes and joins the review. That is what the team lead's time is for — the morning goes to the payment-dependency architecture rather than Gate 1 queue triage, because plan approval for the internal-tools domain was delegated in April and has not needed to come back.

By 10:30 the developer is in a fresh subscription window and starts the plan phase on their next Ready item. The requirement was prepared last Thursday: acceptance criteria written, verification path identified, impact scope proposed, one architecture question already resolved. They do not have to ask what to work on, and do not have to work out how the feature should be verified. That thinking happened before the item reached Ready.

Overnight, the background layer produced nineteen draft test files across four products, and the reconciliation job found one drift: a repository whose branch protection had lost its required status check, probably during a settings change last week. That is Blocking drift, so deployment on that repository is already blocked and the alert is at the top of the team lead's queue. QA reviews eleven of the drafts, accepts eight, and rejects three with a note that the task class handling async database fixtures is producing weak output. The acceptance rate for that class drops below threshold and it suspends automatically. The rejected pull requests stay open with their reasons attached, because that is the data the team lead will use on Thursday to decide whether to fix the prompt or retire the class.

Nobody wrote a status report. Nobody attended a status meeting. The system carried the state.

### 104.2 The Final Quality Bar

The operating system is complete only when the Founder can open one private view on Monday morning and answer all of the following:

1. Is the team healthy?
2. Do we have enough capacity?
3. Who is overloaded?
4. Who is under-utilised, and why?
5. Where is bandwidth?
6. Where is work concentrated?
7. Where is knowledge concentrated?
8. Where is QA constrained?
9. Where is the Team Lead constrained?
10. Do we need to rebalance?
11. Do we need to delegate?
12. Do we need to coach?
13. Do we need to develop someone?
14. Do we have a promotion candidate?
15. Do we need a specialist?
16. Do we need to hire?
17. Is there a genuine performance concern?
18. What evidence supports that concern?
19. What systemic factors exist?
20. What is the confidence?
21. Should we change the product portfolio?
22. What decision is required from me?

**The answerability requirement:** each answer must carry its why, its evidence, its context, its trend, its confidence, the available options and a recommended next review date. If any of the twenty-two cannot be supported that way, the operating system is incomplete — regardless of how much of it has been built.

The same bar applies domain by domain. Capacity: team, role and individual capacity measurable; safe bandwidth measurable; utilisation composed rather than single-valued; sustainable utilisation configurable and calibrated; a forecast with confidence; overload detectable only on multi-signal evidence; under-utilisation diagnosable before interpretation. Team health: review, workload, incident, architecture and knowledge concentration; QA health; Team Lead health; capability gaps; succession; operational dependency risk — with no composite score. Performance: role-specific, anchored to the framework version in force, contextual, trend-based, multi-period, confidence-aware; no single metric, no raw-activity ranking. People decisions: Founder final authority on every formal decision; Team Lead operational and recommendation authority preserved; system signal only; no automatic improvement plan, termination, promotion, compensation change or formal warning. Privacy: Founder full access; Team Lead operational minimum with the three-state field; each employee's own view complete; peers no private people data; the people datasource separately credentialed; general engineering dashboards free of Layer B data. Framework: every person and role mapped or explicitly marked; exact source wording preserved; versioned; non-retroactive; missing instrumentation stated honestly; captured data never downgraded on a failed re-read; future replacement supported without system change. Extensibility: people, roles, capabilities, assignments, products and frameworks all changeable as configuration; history immutable; architecture stable.

### 104.3 North Star

A small technical team operates a large and changing software portfolio with low coordination overhead, high verified output, strong production safety, distributed product knowledge, predictable cost, evidence-driven hiring, minimal founder intervention and continuous machine assistance — and the operating system becomes more capable over time without becoming more bureaucratic.

The delivery core builds that machine. The governance layer makes the company better at running it: able to see its own health, budget its own change, expire its own exceptions, retire its own policies, learn from its own failures, and prove — in attention hours rather than assertion — that it is worth what it costs. The people layer keeps the humans inside it visible, fairly treated and honestly measured.

The company changes. People join and leave. Roles appear and disappear. Products multiply. The performance framework is rewritten. Technology changes. Leadership structure evolves. The operating system is not redesigned for any of it: only configuration, assignments, capability profiles, framework versions, product state and effective dates change.

And the operating system answers, without a status meeting:

- **Products** — which product needs attention, why, and whether the issue is engineering, reliability, business or people and capacity.
- **Team** — how much capacity exists, how much bandwidth remains, whether utilisation is sustainable, who is overloaded, who is under-utilised, and where work and knowledge are concentrated.
- **People** — whether a person is succeeding in their role, what evidence supports that, what context explains the result, what capability they are developing, whether they need support, and whether they are ready for more responsibility.
- **Management** — whether to rebalance, coach, recognise, promote, change a role, hire, engage a specialist, or begin a formal process.
- **Business** — whether people are allocated to the right products, whether human attention is going to the right places, which products deserve more engineering capacity, and which should enter maintenance or sunset.

The system never says "fire this person". It says "persistent performance concern requiring Founder review", and shows the evidence, the context and the confidence. The system never says "promote this person". It says "promotion candidate based on these sustained next-level indicators". The system never says "hire another QA because there are twenty products". It says "verification demand exceeds sustainable QA capacity for the calibrated sustained window, after these alternatives were evaluated".

The founder's job is to decide what the company builds next. Nothing in this specification answers that question, and no amount of operational instrumentation substitutes for it. The system's job is to make the cost, the capacity and the risk of every option honest — and to carry everything else.

This appendix is the permanent record of the decisions applied when the prior research documents (v3.3, v3.4, v3.5) and the engineering KRA/KPI workbook were consolidated into this Master Specification. It exists so that no resolution was made silently. Each decision is normative; the sections that implement it are the authoritative text.

| ID | Decision | Implemented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Internal operating system for the founder's own company; not productised for third parties | §1, §2 |
| D2 | The prior documents' freeze/continuity/amendment ceremony was generation scaffolding and is removed; this is one specification, changed through its own platform-change process | §1, Part VII |
| D3 | `escalation: team_lead` resolves through `topology.yaml` — to the domain lead where domains are active, otherwise to the single portfolio Team Lead | §10, §66 |
| D4 | Two criticality fields: `business.criticality` (business importance) and `classification.reliability_criticality` (operational stringency). Every rule names which field it reads | §6, §15, throughout |
| D5 | Restore testing: 90-day rolling window is the floor for every product; reliability criticality may tighten the cadence, never loosen it | §44 |
| D6 | Attention hours, utilisation, PLU and output volume are never individual performance evidence; role-specific outcome and quality evidence may inform a Founder-owned review with mandatory context adjustment. General dashboards aggregate; per-person views exist only in Layer B | §67, §80, §90, §101 |
| D7 | Four independent health dimensions per product (Engineering, Reliability, Business, People/Capacity); composite scores prohibited everywhere | §6, §52, §93 |
| D8 | One unified OS health-signal table with a single ID space; near-duplicate signals merged; the count stated honestly | §52 |
| D9 | New capability `people-intelligence` gates Layer B; Founder-held. **The delegation mechanism is removed by D109**: the capability is not delegable, and continuity runs through the Section 14.4 sealed contingency credential | §9, §10, §90, amended by D109 |

The following decisions were added when Hermes Agent was adopted at full strength as the estate's committed agent harness — the source verified at its pinned commit, every deployment slot named, and every use that would cross a constitutional wall explicitly rejected:

Each instance is separate: its own OS user, its own HERMES_HOME (classified sensitive-at-rest), its own cage configuration. Local inference only, via the custom provider against the estate's own endpoint; no vendor API keys anywhere; the model-selection benchmark gates activation. The load-bearing walls are enforced outside Hermes — host-level egress allowlist, GitHub-side draft-PR-only, systemd wall-clock stop, ESTOP sentinel — with the cage configuration contract as the second fence. Installation is a pinned-checkout install; the self-update path is never run; the pin moves only through the dependency-update workflow | §30, §35, §36, §37, §39, §49, §57, §62, §94, §96, §98, §99, §100 |
