The following decisions were added by the pre-implementation self-consistency audit — a line-by-line cross-check of the completed specification against itself, run before the implementation plan was authored. Each records a defect found in the specification's own examples or thresholds, and the correction applied:

| ID | Decision | Implemented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D81 | Every capability is defined before it is granted. `escalation`, `mobile-release` and `exceptional-approval` appeared in `roles.yaml` defaults with no row in the Section 9 capability table — grants with no defined authority, which the safe-defaults rule requires to resolve as denial. All three now carry table rows, and control-plane CI rejects any capability appearing in a role default, a person grant or an assignment type without one | §9, §9.1, §64.1 |
| D82 | The reference `product.yaml` and the Section 21.1 commitments example no longer ship a false `conflict_check: passed`. A 99.5% monthly SLA on a business-hours product with next-business-morning detection and a 240-minute RTO fails the uptime-feasibility row of 21.4; the template now records `waived-with-decision` and states why, becoming a worked example of the waiver path rather than a fixture that contradicts the check. Contractual `response_targets` are stated as measured **from detection**, never from occurrence, consistent with 42.2 | §15.1, §21.1, §21.4, §42.2 |
| D83 | One sustained window, everywhere. The flagship hiring case in 73.4 and the closing narrative in 104.3 stated "nine consecutive weeks" while every other passage and D15 fix every sustained threshold at the calibrated window (initial value six consecutive weeks). Both now reference the calibrated sustained window, so the staffing-diagnosis detector has one source | §73.4, §104.3, §6.5, D15 |
| D84 | The drift budget's two middle classes are budgeted on deliberately different bases, and the difference is now stated rather than contradicted. Amber scales per product (16 at eight products, 40 at twenty) because it is routine remediation debt; Red is deliberately held flat at 3 portfolio-wide because it measures material unremediated risk the team can hold in attention at once — a property of the team, not of the portfolio. Red binding harder as the portfolio grows is the intended pressure | §53.4 |
| D85 | Out-of-hours escalation thresholds are set below the quotas they guard. The prior trigger fired at exactly the company quota, where no further activation was authorisable anyway, so it gated nothing. The company trigger is now two-thirds of quota; product-level counting is explicitly per product regardless of who worked the activations; reaching a personal quota is a coverage signal to the Team Lead and never a finding about a person; and Founder overrides consume quota for threshold purposes | §47.3, §47.7 |
| D86 | The declared substrate exemption is stated rather than assumed. Tool independence governs *integrations*; the git host is the enforcement plane itself — branch protection is the gate, Actions is the pipeline, the workflow-identity check is the production-approval mechanism of record — so the universal quantifier in the non-goal, in 62.5 and in AT-031 never covered it. Exactly one system holds the exemption, its replacement runs the 62.3 playbook as a project, and its loss is carried by the 45.3 organisation export. Adding a second declared substrate is a platform change | §2.3, §45.3, §62.3, §62.5, AT-031, EC-87, inv. 41 |

The following decisions were added by the pre-implementation readiness audit — five adversarial audits (buildability, human load, internal correctness, failure modes, adoption and economics) run over the specification before the implementation plan was authored, in which every finding was independently refuted or confirmed. Two thirds of what was raised was already addressed somewhere in this document and was refuted on that basis; what follows is what survived. The version is unchanged: no invariant was reversed, no acceptance test was invalidated, and no architectural decision was undone. These decisions close gaps in the document rather than changing what it specifies.

| ID | Decision | Implemented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D87 | Privileged-workflow isolation. The runner-group rule of D80 closes the fork attack, which is not the attack this estate has: the machine account holds Write, a branch push executes CI, and a long-lived runner carries whatever that job left behind into the next privileged job. The privileged workflows are a closed set — `deploy-production.yml`, `migrate.yml`, the rollback workflow, the production-restore workflow — and run on hosted runners by default, since D80's fixed-cost reasoning covers CI volume rather than the privileged tail. The declared exception, where a production plane requires a fixed egress address, is an `--ephemeral` self-hosted runner in a `privileged` group that never accepts a branch-push job. Each privileged workflow asserts its own runner tier and fails closed; three Blocking drift rows detect the rest | §39.5, §49.1, §53.1 |
| D88 | The erasure commitment is made true rather than aspirational. Purging a `display_name` from a tracked file is a commit — the prior value stays in history, the GitHub login remains besides, and git history is not rewritten because rewriting it would destroy the evidence chain. §91.8 now states three classes: what is purged on request, what is retained under a stated lawful basis and named as retained, and what is not offered at all. A departing person is told this at exit. Two consequences are stated rather than left implicit: the object-locked export cannot be purged, so its retention period is declared; and names in record bodies fail schema validation, because the de-identification of the record stores is the part that genuinely holds | §91.8, §91.1, §45.3, §97.2 |
| D89 | The record stores live in their own repository. A ruleset bypass actor bypasses the rule wherever the rule applies; GitHub does not scope bypass by path, so D76's records-writer was in fact an unscoped write credential on the repository holding every file from which authority is resolved, and the Blocking-drift rule meant to catch misuse could not fire. Records and events move to a separate repository with no protection rules, written by a GitHub App token scoped to that repository alone. The control-plane repository's protection is correspondingly stated without exception: no machine identity is a bypass actor on it. The same reasoning applies to the Renovate bypass, which is split across two rulesets so that the compensating check does not sit inside the ruleset it compensates for | §40.1, §97.1, §97.3, §33.2, §98.2, supersedes D76 in part |
| D90 | Every capability is defined before it is granted, swept to completion. D81 closed this for three capabilities; `devops` remained, named as the executing authority for eleven mandated actions with no row in the capability table — including the rotation of the two highest-privilege machine credentials in the system. The capability is defined, the roles the current roster requires exist in the registry, and the CI rule added under D81 now has nothing left to reject | §8, §9, §9.1, §19.1, §40.1, §49.2, §71.2 |
| D91 | Deployment branch and tag policies are the control that makes environment-scoped secrets true. Branch protection governs what merges; a deployment branch policy governs what may reach an environment's secrets, and a repository with the first and not the second holds production credentials behind nothing. Every environment carries one from the template at creation, restricting `staging` and `production` to the default branch and protected release tags. This is available on the Team plan and is not the Enterprise feature §11.4 excludes | §11.3, §33.2, §33.4, §53.1 |
| D92 | Blocking-class drift blocks a repository through a named mechanism. "Fails CI" was claimed for conditions that go bad without a push — a lapsed restore test, a departed owner, an expired assignment — but a required status check that last ran green stays green, so the detection existed and the blocking did not. The reconciler holds a check-run-write scope and posts a named required check on every affected repository, failing while a Blocking finding is open against that product | §53.2, §40.1, §44.2, §15.4 |
| D93 | Declared state is canaried like enforcement code. Invariant 72 protects the fleet from a bad workflow and left declared state uncovered, while registry edits are Gate-1 exempt, reconciliation runs on registry change, and bootstrap leaves the control-plane repository without independent review. A registry change applies to the canary product set first and holds the fleet for one cycle. The reconciler's own write scope is narrowed to generated `derived/**` files the registries reference, so a machine write to a registry becomes detectable Blocking drift rather than an in-scope write | §26.4, §40.1, §53.1, §61.1, §61.5 |
| D94 | Detection does not depend on the machine it is supposed to be independent of. §45.2's claim that responders work from sources independent of the operations VM was false: Prometheus, Grafana alerting and health computation all run on it, so its loss removes machine detection for every product simultaneously and removes the instrument that would report that. An external dead-man's-switch outside the VM, outside GitHub and outside the product providers pages the phone-escalation path directly | §45.2, §46, §51.5, §42.2 |
| D95 | The workstation trust boundary is stated for the control plane, not only for production. Ops-VM root is accepted as a Layer B confidentiality concession and silently confers the machine-credential store; §51.5's enumeration of what the VM does not hold omitted the tier it houses; and the compromised-workstation blast radius stated in five places is incomplete for the one holder with VM admin. A second boundary is declared — a fully compromised engineering workstation must not yield the control-plane machine-credential store — with the credential held so that VM-root does not passively read it, and the Layer B store separated from the shared host | §40.1, §40.3, §43.4, §51.4, §51.5, §90.3 |
| D96 | Reconciler-credential detection is behavioural rather than temporal. "Use outside its scheduled window" is near-vacuous for a credential that legitimately fires hourly, nightly and on every registry merge, and is silent entirely for read-side abuse. Per-run caps on objects mutated, an expected-source assertion, a run-count ceiling and a signed run record replace it; a run without a matching scheduled trigger is Blocking. The reconciler publishes per-run API-call counts so read-side anomalies are visible without the audit log | §40.1, §51.2, §53.1 |
| D97 | Verification contracts are tested for discriminating power, not only for presence. Five separate checks stopped at presence and greenness, so a contract asserting nothing satisfied all of them and shipped green through Gate 2, the evidence chain and Maturity Level 2. The seeded-canary philosophy this document already applies to reconciliation is applied here: each contract declares a seeded-defect case it must fail, and a run that passes the seeded defect is a failed run | §31.1, §31.2, §52.2, §65, §96.4 |
| D98 | Instruments do not read from the register of their own compliance. The undeclared-weekend-activation metric was sourced from the exception registry, which by definition contains only declared activations, so it could only ever read zero — and it measures the system's most visible promise to the team. An out-of-hours detector reads the event-log timestamps that already exist | §47.3, §91.7, §103.3, §97.3 |
| D99 | The Foundation roadmap states whether its week labels are configuration elapsed or build elapsed. §98.2 stamped absolute weeks on phases whose deliverables §99.2 prices three to ten times higher, and §98.1's calendar-gating honesty paragraph scoped itself to the upper tiers. The phases split into a Build track dated by subsystem with its complexity band, and an Onboarding track whose per-product phases are relative to the subsystems they consume. Pre-onboarding deadlines are set from the Onboarding track, not from the labels | §98.1, §98.2, §98.3, §99.2, §99.4, §96.2 |
| D100 | Phase exit criteria name only what that phase can deliver. G3's exit required Founder-view questions answerable only by G5 and G6, while G5's dependency is two quarters of G3 data — a cycle that no amount of effort breaks. Exit criteria are scoped to their own deliverables, and the questions a phase cannot yet answer render as unarmed under the D77 arming discipline rather than as failures | §98.5, §93.3, §52.2, §72.5 |
| D101 | Week one arms gates in an order that can be satisfied. Branch protection requiring a Write-holding Code Owner approval was scheduled before any Team granted Write, and required status checks before any workflow emitted them. Teams are derived and granted first, from an interim assignment set that Phase 3 replaces, and the bootstrap arming pattern of §95.2 — configured but not yet binding, with the armed configuration recorded beside it — is reused rather than a second approach invented | §98.2, §11.1, §11.3, §95.2, §95.4 |
| D102 | The derivation functions the measurement layer rests on are specified rather than assumed. Attention-hour duration had named sources and no duration rule, and §99.3 listed the matter closed; reserve was both subtracted from capacity and counted inside the utilisation denominator, with "reserve exhausted" undefined while gating two workload states; three overlapping workload vocabularies had no mapping to the three-state field the Team Lead actually allocates from; and overload emitted at two different thresholds. Each is defined once, with the calibrated-configuration convention and a stated initial value | §67.3, §69.1, §69.2, §70.1, §70.3, §83.2, §83.3, §90.5, §97.4, §99.3 |
| D103 | Records, events and the states they describe carry schemas. The event log is the substrate for every derived metric and was excluded from the versioned-contract mechanism, with no envelope, no closed event-type enum and no version field — unevolvable by construction in an append-only store. An event envelope and a record schema version are declared, and both stores join the §60.2 versioned-contract mechanism. Alongside them: `access_status: suspended` gains the exit transition it never had, the product lifecycle table is closed, and the exception closure enum covers every exception type | §7.1, §18.2, §43.3, §54.1, §60.2, §88.3, §97.2, §97.3 |
| D104 | The operating system can see its own cost. No signal among the forty-two watched whether the system was worth running, and the one metric that could see total Founder load carried no signal ID, no threshold and no response — reviewed by the party it measures, inside the ritual whose cost was its largest line. Four signals are added (SIG-43 to SIG-46) covering Founder operating load, operating-system net value, change-budget breach and audit-log review staleness, each owned by a party other than the one it measures where §52.5's calibration rule requires it. The standing ledger entry moves to Phase 1 as a hand-authored stub, so the investment gate can gate the phases it is supposed to gate | §52.2, §52.4, §52.5, §57.2, §59.2, §93.2, §98.2 |
| D105 | Enforcement claims name an owner and a cadence. §101 promised every invariant is enforced by the platform where it can be and by written policy with a named owner and a review cadence otherwise, and no artifact held either. The catalogue carries the ownership and cadence it promised; invariant 111 gains a detector; and the three invariants claiming enforcement "by network and credential architecture" are marked as policy-enforced until the infrastructure specification that would make them architectural exists | §101, §111, §40.2, §52.6 |

The following decisions were added by the post-audit review, which examined the amended specification against nine proposed changes. Two were rejected on the evidence — one asked to renumber the concept ladder from seven to eight, which would blur the deliberate distinction that platform version sits outside the person-to-product chain rather than on it; the other reported a duplicate acceptance test that does not exist. The remaining seven are below.

| ID | Decision | Implemented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D106 | No role default carries a dangerous capability. Section 7.1 and Section 64.1 both state that a new person enters with no `production-approval` and no dangerous capabilities and that capabilities are never inherited silently from a role default, and invariant 79 makes minimum privilege binding — while `roles.yaml` granted `production-approval` by default to five roles, contradicting all three. The dangerous set is named and is explicit-grant-only: `production-approval`, `platform-change-approval`, `platform-admin`, `security-review`, `migration-review`, `exceptional-approval`, `lifecycle-decision`, `people-intelligence`. Control-plane CI rejects a role default containing any of them. Role defaults now carry only what describes the shape of the job | §7.1, §8, §64.1, §101 #79 |
| D107 | Append-only is enforced on the records repository rather than asserted. D89 removed the protection rules that previously made record history durable, which was necessary for the credential to append without review and left immutability — invariant 47, Section 63.1 — resting on nothing. Rewriting is blocked and appending is not: a ruleset with no bypass actor blocks force push and deletion while permitting fast-forward commits; commits are signed by the writing identity and an unsigned or foreign-signed commit is Blocking drift; and the reconciler anchors the records head SHA into the protected control-plane repository each run, so a head that does not descend from the last anchor is proof of rewriting at Level 5. The object-locked export is the slow anchor; the per-run SHA is the fast one | §40.1, §53.2, §63.1, §97.1, §101 #47 |
| D108 | The founder-decision delegate cannot carry a formal people decision. Section 74.5 reserves every formal people decision to the Founder and invariants 36 and 38 make that binding, while `founder_decision_delegate` carried an unbounded "named decision scope" that would have validated a delegation of promotion, exit or compensation. The delegable scope now excludes all of them by name, and a delegation naming one fails schema validation | §10.1, §10.3, §14.2, §74.5, §101 #36, #38 |
| D109 | Layer B access is not delegable. The routine `people_intelligence_delegate` is removed. At the scale this operating system is built for it had no holder: the Team Lead is barred from that data by Sections 90.2 and 90.5, and the design test of 90.5 — that the Team Lead can allocate engineering work without being able to answer who is being considered for promotion or exit — depends on that bar. A standing delegate widened the most sensitive boundary in the system for no operational gain. Continuity under Founder incapacity runs through the sealed contingency credential already held in the Section 14.4 escrow, as a recorded break-glass event. Absence pauses Layer B generation; it does not delegate it | §6.11, §9.1, §10.1, §10.3, §14.2, §14.4, §74.5, §90.4, §92.1, AT-090, §101 #106, amends D9 |
| D110 | Layer B names its two surfaces separately. One store fed two things with different audiences and different access rules: the Founder-only management surface holding every person's evidence, and the encrypted per-person self-view holding one person's own. Bundling them made invariant 106 either false or silently excepted, since every employee reads their own. **Layer B-M** is the management surface, capability-gated and not delegable. **Layer B-S** is the self-view, delivered to its subject, requiring no capability. Unqualified "Layer B" means Layer B-M | §6.11, §90.1, §90.6, §92.1, §92.8, §101 #106 |
| D111 | The declared working calendar exists. Capacity (69.1), the Capacity Profile (69.2) and the day plan (94.2) all read "the person's declared working calendar", and no section defined it and no control-plane file held it — the same defect class as an attention-hour source with no duration rule. A `work_arrangement` block on the person record declares timezone as an IANA identifier, per-weekday schedule, FTE, arrangement and public-holiday set. Leave and schedule are separate declarations and neither substitutes for the other, because a system holding only leave prices a part-time week and an absent week identically. FTE is a capacity multiplier and never a status; arrangement is scheduling context and never people evidence, with the no-surveillance rules of 91.2 applying in full | §7.3, §7.2, §52.6, §69.1, §69.2, §69.3, §94.2, §91.2 |
| D112 | The coverage validator has an input. D87 gave each product a declared coverage window and named rota members; the check resolving them had nothing on the person side to resolve against. Each member's `accepted_coverage_window` (Section 7.3) is matched against the product's declared window, and the check fails closed where a member has no work arrangement, no accepted window, or an accepted window not covering the segment assigned to them — which is the failure mode the 24x7 blocker exists to prevent | §7.3, §15.6, §47.9, §52.6, completes D87 |

The following decision was added when the implementation planning pass read this document mechanically and found damage the amendment pass had introduced into it.

| ID | Decision | Implemented in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D113 | Table integrity is verified by row, not by line. The amendment pass of D87–D112 applied several hundred edits, and thirteen of them appended a new table row to the end of the preceding row instead of onto its own line, joining two rows with `\|\|`. Every count check run afterwards counted *lines* beginning with a row marker, so a merged row was invisible to the very check meant to catch it — and two subsequent repairs, made in good faith against those counts, inserted duplicate rows for `AT-110` and `S19` that already existed inside a merge. The damage is repaired: thirteen joins split, the duplicate `AT-110` and `S19` rows removed, and a duplicated `SIG-43` — two different signals independently given the same identifier — resolved by renumbering the unclosed-learning-loop signal to **SIG-47** and giving it the priority tier it never had. Counts corrected to their true values: forty-seven signals, thirty control-plane artifacts. The rule this establishes is binding on every future amendment: a count is verified against parsed rows, a duplicate-identifier check runs over every identifier space, and no line in a table may contain more than one row | §52.2, §52.4, §52.6, §96.6, §100.6, D44 |
